507.title: dak-postprocessing
507.content: Skill dak-postprocessing: What the DAK post-processing phase produces after the IG Publisher runs — the JSON/JSON-LD surface, the DAK API hub, and the metadata-to-Liquid bridge — and how an IG repository’s own site gets the same sidecars from the cached AST (ig-site:sidecars). Read before changing a post-processing step, and before assuming the Publisher produced something it did not. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: dak-postprocessing · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Layer: smart-base, DAK kind, except the two Library strippers, which are fhir-harness — see §”One step is not WHO’s”. Everything WHO’s build (.github/workflows/ghbuild.yml) runs between publisher.jar finishing and deployment, gated by do_dak and by the contentTypes.dak section of the root index.config.json (see dak-preprocessing, which also says where the scripts come from). Each step runs inside the Publisher’s Docker container (docker exec -w /work ig-run python3 …), against output/.

508.title: The steps, and what each accomplishes
508.content: | # | script | what it produces | . | 1 | strip_library_binaries.py | removes base64 content.data from Library resources | . | 2 | strip_library_content.py | replaces inline CQL/ELM with a URL reference | . | 3 | generate_logical_model_schemas.py | a JSON Schema per logical model | . | 4 | generate_valueset_schemas.py | a JSON Schema per ValueSet, plus the enumeration-response schemas | . | 5 | generate_jsonld_vocabularies.py | JSON-LD vocabularies from the ValueSet expansions | . | 6 | generate_dak_api_hub.py | dak-api.html — the hub page, and the .openapi.json / .displays.json sidecars | . | 7 | update_translated_image_refs.py | rewrites image references inside translated HTML pages | . | 8 | generate_smart_liquid.py + inject_smart_liquid.py | IG metadata → Liquid variables, and the include injected into every markdown page | . Steps 3 and 4 share one workflow step. Steps 1–5 belong to fhir-harness, not to this overlay: they only transform what the Publisher emitted and add no constraint or profile. They stay in this table because ghbuild.yml still runs them in this phase. check:fhir-harness-exclusions reads the script names from this table and dak-preprocessing’s and refuses them in fhir-harness, except these five. Steps 6–8 are the WHO surface.

509.title: Step 8 is the seam
509.content: generate_smart_liquid.py reads the Publisher’s output/. It scans it for {ResourceType}-{id}.json and, for each, emits Liquid assignments named . smart__<ResourceType>__<id_normalized>__<category>__<key> . with categories url__canonical, url__page, url__json, text__display, link__html, and elements__<key> for scalars (name, title, description, status, version, …). Ids are normalised by replacing every non-alphanumeric character with _. This already turns IG Publisher metadata into variables Jekyll processes, aimed at the Publisher’s own Jekyll. Moving to just-the-docs re-points this bridge rather than building a new one. It is one build behind . The script writes input/pagecontent/smart.liquid.md, which the Publisher only processes on the next build, and also writes output/smart.liquid.html directly so the page exists in this one. A surface that needs two builds to converge cannot drive an incremental staging loop; under just-the-docs the variables are computed and consumed in one pass.

510.title: One step is not WHO’s
510.content: Steps 1 and 2 strip base64 binaries and inline CQL/ELM out of Library resources. Nothing in either is DAK-shaped: any FHIR IG that embeds CQL (any IG using hl7.fhir.uv.cql) produces oversized Library resources. By the smart-stack-layering test — would a non-WHO FHIR IG need this? — they belong in fhir-harness. The deploy phase’s “Delete files >100MB before deployment” step is the same concern one layer down.

511.title: Steps 3–6 are the DAK API
511.content: The schema, vocabulary and hub steps produce the surface the artefact index binds (ig-artifact-ingestion): .schema.json, .displays.json and .openapi.json per artefact, .jsonld vocabularies, and the enumeration schemas (ValueSets.schema.json, LogicalModels.schema.json). No IG publishes an artefact-index instance: an enumeration schema is a schema of a response, whose example happens to hold the list. On an IG repository’s own site: ig-site:sidecars . An IG repository whose index.config.json names smart-base as its site’s landing declares no steps of its own. The site route (cat-harness-tools stage-local.ts) runs the landing layer’s ig-site:sidecars, which is ig-site-sidecars.ts: . | It runs fhir-harness’s ig-api-gen.ts, the generic port of steps 3–6’s generators, over the cached AST. This layer passes only the label and its data types’ JSON-LD prefix. | The per-artefact sidecars, including <stem>.openapi.json, go to $SITE_WORK/ig-api/sidecars/. The enumeration schemas and the Swagger UI page openapi/index.html go to $SITE_WORK/ig-api/site/, which fhir-harness serves at the site root without replacing a path the site already holds. | $SITE_WORK/ig-api/ig-api.json says {"label": "DAK API"} when the IG declares a DAK (index.config.json contentTypes.dak, or a legacy dak.json; scripts/ig-dak-metadata.ts). Otherwise fhir-harness’s default label, “IG API”, stands. | . fhir-harness binds and serves the sidecars (ig-repo-site.ts, fhir-harness ig-build-pipeline §”The IG repository’s site route”) and never learns the DAK name. ig-index:build runs the same step when it builds an IG’s artefact index. The hub page is fhir-harness’s: ig-api-hub.ts draws it from the artefact index’s bound sidecars, with one loader, on the docs site, an IG site and an IG repository’s own site. This layer names only what WHO calls it: ig-api.json gives the label and the marker an IG’s own dak-api.md holds (<!-- DAK_API_CONTENT -->), and fhir-harness puts the hub at that page.

512.title: Step 5 depends on expansion, which depends on a terminology server
512.content: generate_jsonld_vocabularies.py reads ValueSet expansions, which exist only if the Publisher expanded them, which depends on tx, the optional terminology server input. With a dead or restricted tx the step produces fewer vocabularies, warns and fails nothing. A thin vocabulary output is not evidence of a thin ValueSet: check the expansion first.

513.title: Step 7 renders nothing and is not translation
513.content: update_translated_image_refs.py rewrites <img> references inside translated HTML that has already been built. Where the locale layer is part of rendering there is no built HTML to patch, and the step has nothing to do.

514.title: What the QA reports say, and where they go
514.content: Every script here uses the same QAReporter as the pre-processing scripts and emits a phase report: successes, warnings, errors, files_processed, files_expected, files_missing, and a summary with counts and a completion timestamp. qa.json from the Publisher run is uploaded as a workflow artifact. The qa-report graph typology (cat-harness-tools schemas/sdlc/qa-report.ts) takes the shape these scripts emit. Its schema enforces three rules: a summary may not disagree with the details it counts; files_missing must be a subset of files_expected, so an empty result stays distinguishable from a not-found; and running is never a pass — qaReportVerdict returns unknown for a script that died before finishing, not ok.

515.title: Binary artefacts on deploy and on release
515.content: The generic rule and the measuring Tool are ig-binary-artefacts and ig-binary-audit. What the WHO workflows do: . | ghbuild.yml deploys output/ with its binaries. The only binary step is “Delete files >100MB before deployment”, and no Publisher binary is that large. Each branch build deploys to branches/<branch>/, so each preview carries another full copy, full-ig.zip included. | On a GitHub release, release.yml hands off to smart-html. It runs only if publication-request.json exists, then calls WorldHealthOrganization/smart-html/.github/workflows/release.yml (pinned by commit). That runs smart-html’s scripts/ig_publisher.py, which builds and publishes into the smart-html webroot, leaves ig-build-zips/ out of the sitepreview copy, moves only files over 100 MB plus a copy of output/package.tgz into release-assets/, and uploads that to the release tagged GITHUB_REF_NAME. So a release gets package.tgz and, in practice, nothing else; every other binary goes to the webroot. | create_package_release.py is called by no workflow. It would cut a release and move the 19 named binaries out of output/. | downloads.md lists 19 release assets that no release carries, and leaves out full-ig.zip, the largest. fix_release_links.py correctly rewrites its WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base release links to the building repository; the list itself is what is wrong. | . These workflows belong to the WHO repositories and are not changed here.

516.title: Where the counterparts are
516.content: dak-preprocessing — the steps before the Publisher, most of which only populate sushi-config.yaml’s pages: and menu:. ig-publication — the Publisher run and the authority to release. ig-artifact-ingestion — the artefact index that binds what steps 3–6 produce.

518.title: dak-preprocessing
518.content: Skill dak-preprocessing: What each DAK pre-processing step does before the IG Publisher runs, which steps exist only to feed the Publisher’s page index, and how the phase runs as the overlay on fhir-harness’s AST cache refresh (dak-pre-export.sh). Also which files in a DAK repository are authored and which are generated, and the SEMVER rule for DAK and IG versions. Read before changing, assuming or moving a pre-processing step. Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: dak-preprocessing · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Layer: smart-base, DAK kind (smart-stack-layering), with two steps that are not pre-processing at all — see §”Two of these are authoring, not pre-processing”. DAK Preprocessing is everything WHO’s build (.github/workflows/ghbuild.yml) runs between checkout and publisher.jar, gated by the do_dak input and by the contentTypes.dak section of the root index.config.json. Every script reads and writes that section through input/scripts/dak_index.py. An IG that still carries a legacy dak.json keeps building: dak_index.py --adopt-legacy reads it into the index for that build only, with a warning. Nothing is committed back. ghbuild.yml runs the copy in the IG’s own input/scripts/ when there is one, and otherwise downloads the script from litlfred/smart-base at a commit pinned in the workflow (SCRIPTS_BASE_COMMIT). Step names and script names are the stable handles; re-read the workflow before relying on a detail.

519.title: The steps, and what each one accomplishes
519.content: | # | script | what it actually does | . | 1 | generate_dak_from_sushi.py | writes contentTypes.dak into index.config.json from sushi-config.yaml plus branch/repo context — only when smart.who.int.base is a dependency and the section is absent | . | 2 | update_sushi_config.py | registers pages and menu entries in sushi-config.yaml, and writes placeholder markdown — see below | . | 3 | generate_dak_from_sushi.py, again | re-runs step 1 “with current branch context” | . | 4 | dmn_questionnaire_generator.py | emits FHIR Questionnaire resources from the DMN decision tables | . | 5 | transform_dmn.py + dmn2html.xslt + dmn.css | renders each DMN file to HTML for inclusion in a page | . | 6 | inject_translations.py | substitutes translated strings into the diagram sources before they are rendered | . Steps 1 and 2 share the workflow step “Prepare DAK environment”; steps 3–6 each have a step of their own.

520.title: What “get it into the IG index” meant — step 2, precisely
520.content: update_sushi_config.py does four things: . | Scans for resources — fsh-generated/resources/ (SUSHI’s output) and input/resources/ (static JSON), collecting every ValueSet and every logical-model StructureDefinition. | Writes a placeholder markdown page per resource into input/pagecontent/, as ValueSet-<id>.md and the logical-model equivalent, each carrying a <!-- DAK_API_PLACEHOLDER: … --> marker. A file that already exists with real content is left alone; the marker is how the script tells its own placeholder from an author’s page. | Registers dak-api.md in sushi-config.yaml’s pages: map, creating the pages: key if the IG has none. | Registers Indices → DAK API → dak-api.html in the menu: map, creating menu: and the Indices subsection if absent. | . So the “index” is sushi-config.yaml’s pages: and menu: maps: the IG Publisher’s Jekyll renders a page only if the file exists in input/pagecontent/ and pages: names it. Step 2 supplies both halves. Under the just-the-docs pipeline navigation is derived from sushi-config.yaml directly and the pages are folio pages, so this step has no job there. See ig-render-jekyll for what replaces it.

521.title: Two of these are authoring, not pre-processing
521.content: Steps 4 and 5 — dmn_questionnaire_generator.py and transform_dmn.py — mint artefacts rather than prepare a renderer: . | the questionnaire generator emits FHIR resources, which the Publisher validates, indexes and publishes like any other. Without it the IG is missing Questionnaires, not a page. | the DMN transform produces the only human-readable rendering of a decision table the IG has. | . They depend on nothing the Publisher does. They are content generation and belong upstream of the Publisher, as authoring steps of the DAK document kind. transform_dmn.py outputs HTML, which the JSON-only render contract does not take. Whether it gains a structured output or its HTML is treated as an embedded asset is still open.

522.title: Step 6 is conditional on who renders
522.content: inject_translations.py rewrites diagram sources before rendering because the Publisher offers no later hook. When pages render through just-the-docs, this platform’s locale layer does that for pages. Diagram sources are still rasterised outside Jekyll, so the step is still needed for them: do not remove it on the page argument alone.

523.title: Steps 1 and 3 — one fact, computed twice
523.content: generate_dak_from_sushi.py runs twice in ghbuild.yml; the second run (“Regenerate DAK configuration with current context”) recomputes the same section after the branch has been resolved. The DAK section is this platform’s own declaration, so compute it once, in the right order. Do not reproduce the double run when lifting this step.

524.title: What a QA report already exists for
524.content: Every one of these scripts instantiates a QAReporter and writes a phase report — successes, warnings, errors, files_processed, files_expected, files_missing, plus a summary with counts and a completion timestamp. The qa-report graph typology (qa-report/v1, holds: "state", cat-harness-tools schemas/sdlc/qa-report.ts) takes exactly that shape, upstream’s snake_case field names included, so no translation step sits between WHO’s producer and this platform’s consumer.

525.title: In the AST lifecycle: the overlay on fhir-harness’s refresh
525.content: smart-base’s IG is published from the AST on its cache branch (cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>), like every smart-* IG. The one writer of that branch is fhir-harness’s reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml (skill ig-build-pipeline, §”The AST cache lifecycle”). The plain AST exporter does not run this phase, so smart-base supplies it as an overlay; fhir-harness never names it. | The command is smart-base/scripts/dak-pre-export.sh (bun run cat smart-base:dak-pre-export). It runs steps 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, in that order, from this checkout’s own input/scripts/. It does not repeat step 3. Steps 4–6 run only when the IG declares contentTypes.dak. Any failure fails the run. | The caller is smart-base’s .github/workflows/ig-ast-refresh.yml: fhir-harness’s template plus pre-export: bash smart-base/scripts/dak-pre-export.sh. It runs by hand, and on every push to main that changes sushi-config.yaml, ig.ini or input/**. | What the cache records. This phase rewrites the IG’s inputs (sushi-config.yaml’s pages:/menu:, placeholder pages under input/pagecontent/). fhir-harness takes the clean commit’s input digest before the command runs, puts the inputs back after the export, and records the AST against the clean commit; the prepared tree’s digest goes under the manifest’s preExport. So the cache verifies on any clean checkout, and a merge that changes no input does not make it stale. | The counterpart after the export is fhir-harness’s ig-api-gen.ts, the generic port of the post-processing schema and vocabulary generators, run over the AST by ig-site:sidecars (dak-postprocessing). | . ghbuild.yml keeps its own copy of these steps for downstream repositories; it does not write smart-base’s cache.

526.title: Source of truth versus generated artefacts in a DAK repository
526.content: This extends the base IG rule in ig-build-pipeline §”Source of truth versus compiled, cached and rendered output”. Two rules: . | Across knowledge layers, authority flows L1 → L2 → L3 → compiled AST / rendered site (smart-guideline-end-to-end §”The order is a rule: L1, then L2, then L3”). L1 narrative guidelines and referenced tables (library/<bib>/l1-extraction/) ground the L2 DAK components (business processes, decision-support logic, core data dictionary, L2 form wireframes, personas, scenarios, indicators, functional/non-functional requirements); those ground the L3 FHIR artefacts (input/fsh/, input/cql/). Never patch an L3 artefact or a rendered page to contradict its L2 source, or an L2 table to contradict L1 without an L1 citation. | Within the repository, hand-edit only the authored inputs — never files written by DAK pre-processing, row generators, SUSHI, the AST refresh or DAK post-processing. dak-pre-export.sh and the QA suite (qa-checkers-dak.ts isGeneratedArtefact) both draw this line: | . | Authoritative source (edit here) | Generated, cached or rendered output (never hand-edit; 527.title: Version numbering: DAK SEMVER and how an IG’s version relates to its DAK’s
527.content: index.config.json contentTypes.dak.version (schemas/dak.ts DakDeclarationSchema, mirroring input/fsh/models/DAK.fsh) and sushi-config.yaml version both use exact MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: . | Increment | Bumps the DAK (contentTypes.dak.version) | Bumps the L3 IG (sushi-config.yaml version) | . | major (X+1.0.0) | Breaking L2 change in any of the nine DAK component types (DAK.fsh): removing or incompatibly redefining a core data element (dataElement), business process (businessProcess), decision-support table (decisionSupportLogic) or clinical rule, indicator (indicator) numerator/denominator, persona (healthInterventions), scenario (userScenario), L2 form wireframe (form), or functional/non-functional requirement (requirement); or rebasing onto a new L1 WHO guideline edition that invalidates prior L2 logic or data elements | Breaking L3 conformance change per ig-build-pipeline §”Version numbering: SEMVER for a FHIR IG” (removing/renaming a canonical resource, tightening cardinality or bindings, incompatible CQL/operation signature change, fhirVersion change, or breaking dependency major bump), or any major bump in the DAK it encodes | . | minor (X.Y+1.0) | Backward-compatible L2 addition: a new persona, scenario, BPMN workflow, DMN decision table or rule row, optional data dictionary element, L2 form wireframe, indicator or requirement; or extending an L2 value set without invalidating existing rows | Backward-compatible L3 addition (new profile, logical model, extension, ValueSet, CodeSystem, Library, PlanDefinition, Measure, Questionnaire, optional element/slice, or narrative page), or any minor bump in the DAK it encodes | . | patch (X.Y.Z+1) | Backward-compatible L2 editorial or bug fix: typos, descriptions, labels, translations or diagram layout; correcting a DMN cell or data dictionary description to match the existing L1 source without changing data-element semantics or workflow structure | Backward-compatible L3 fix (narrative prose in input/pagecontent/**, translations, example fixes, CQL/FML bug fixes preserving declared inputs/outputs and clinical intent, or rendering fixes), or any patch bump in the DAK it encodes | . How an IG’s version relates to its DAK’s: . | DAK and L3 IG in one repository (contentTypes.dak + contentTypes.ig) — lockstep. index.config.json contentTypes.dak.version, sushi-config.yaml version (and publication-request.json version on a release) carry the same MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH and matching status (draft | active | retired). Both move to the higher of the two increments: L2 minor with L3 patch is minor; an L3 major with L2 unchanged is major. | Update both files in the same commit. Step 1 seeds contentTypes.dak from sushi-config.yaml only when it is absent (if read_dak_section(repo_root) is not None: return), so editing version or status in sushi-config.yaml alone leaves contentTypes.dak stale. | . | Standalone L2 DAK and downstream L3 IG (l3-fhir-authoring). When the DAK (contentTypes: { dak }) and the IG (contentTypes: { ig }) live in separate repositories, each has its own MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH series; a major or minor bump in the DAK requires at least the same bump in the IG release that adopts it. | Adapted / country DAKs and IGs (l2-dependency-choice, l3-dependency-choice). The adaptation pins the upstream WHO DAK and IG in sushi-config.yaml dependencies: (and index.config.json dependencies) at an exact released version (bun run cat check:published-refs); its own contentTypes.dak.version and sushi-config.yaml version follow its own release series. | .

530.title: Data modelling — the entities, before the fields
530.content: Skill data-modelling: Build a data model: identify the entities a body of work is actually about, the relations between them, and the cardinalities — then declare it where the tools can read it. Process-agnostic technique; the CRDM phase that invokes it is crdm-data-model. Named by: CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, SWOT situation analysis, Questionnaire wireframe review, Guideline Updates, DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . One question, and everything else follows from it: . What are the things, and what is true of each of them exactly once? . A model is wrong in a way no schema check can catch when a fact that belongs to one thing is written on another. Typical shapes: a fact about a capability (what substitutes for it) copied onto every skill that uses it; a fact a BPMN diagram already states executably (which role takes over) repeated on a skill; a field naming performers in a vocabulary that resolves against nothing. Each is a field on the wrong entity, or a second copy of a fact that already has a home. Modelling first catches them, and costs far less than unwinding them later.

531.title: The procedure
531.content: 1. Name the entities, as nouns a domain expert already uses . Not the tables you expect to build. If the people who do this work say “attestation”, the entity is Attestation, even when it will be stored beside something else. A name you invented is a name nobody will look up. Stop when two candidate entities have the same identifier. They are one entity with two names, and carrying both is how a codebase ends up with a Role registry and an actor-id vocabulary that do not resolve against each other. 2. For each entity, say what identifies it . An entity with no identifier is an attribute of something else — that is the test, and it is decisive. If you cannot say what makes two of these the same one, you have found a field rather than a thing. 3. Put each fact on the entity it is about . For every fact, ask whose property is this? The question that settles the hard cases: . If this entity disappeared, would the fact still be true of anything? . What substitutes for X survives the disappearance of every skill that uses X, so it belongs to X. What this skill does when X is missing does not — it is the skill’s. 4. State cardinality in both directions, and mean it . “One attestation per report” and “one report per attestation” are different claims, and a model that states only the first cannot tell you whether a re-signature is an update or a second row. Write both. Where the answer is “many”, say what ORDERS them or admits there is no order. 5. Say which facts are derived, and never store those . A derived fact stored is a cache, and an unvalidated cache is worse than no cache. If a value can be computed from the model, computing it is the declaration — the role a process falls back to, for example, is recoverable from the diagram that executes it. 6. Declare it where a tool can read it . A model in prose is a proposal. A model in the declaration is a model. In this repository that means a graph typology in <name>.json, a Zod schema under the declared schemas directory, and a node kind that kg-export knows — placement is the skill that decides which. And ship a reader in the same change, because a field that is only documentation goes inert. A field with no consumer is not a model, it is a comment with punctuation. 7. Model VARIATION as inheritance, and earn a new kind with BEHAVIOUR . Two things are nearly the same. Do they get one type with a discriminator, two types, or one type and an override? . A new KIND is earned by a BEHAVIOUR difference — a consumer has to DO something different. Everything else is an OVERRIDE on an inherited default. So the default posture is inherit everything, override anything. A variant declares what it CHANGES; every unstated field comes from its parent. A variant that states no new behaviour is not a new kind, however different it looks. The test is on the consumer, not the values. Ask: does any reader of this model take a different code path? Different colours, sizes, labels or thresholds are the same behaviour with different inputs — one kind. Different FIELDS, different units, or a field whose meaning changes — the reader must branch, and that is a kind. Worked example: Theme . Theme dresses three surfaces: sticky notes, a website, a print publication. | variant | kind? | why | . | iris-web vs the default web theme | no | different hex values, same fields. Nothing branches. An override. | . | publication vs sticky | yes | a sticky theme’s geometry is {minWidth, padding, fontScale} across laptop \| mobile \| card; the WHO style guide states A4 \| A5 \| A5 landscape with trim size and margin, and no column width anywhere in 66 sections. minWidth means “before the grid reflows” — a fixed page does not reflow. A renderer MUST branch. | . Reusing {minWidth, padding, fontScale} for print, reading minWidth as trim width, would typecheck and mean nothing. A shape that typechecks is not a shape that models. And the palette stays SHARED across all three kinds, which is the other half of the rule: three kinds each with their own palette vocabulary would be three spellings of “accent colour”, free to disagree about what an accent is. What inheritance costs, and what it must not hide . A required field stays required after resolution, never before. “All three layouts, or invalid” is a property of the RESOLVED variant; a declaration that states one and inherits two is complete. Checking requiredness on the declaration instead is how inheritance turns into optionality by accident. And an inherited value is still a fact somebody must be able to trace. A variant that overrides a value cites why, the same as any other asserted fact — otherwise the model records what the value is and loses where it came from, which is the failure the uses[] rule exists to prevent elsewhere. 8. Point from the dependent at the general node . A relation between two entities is written on ONE of them. Write it on the entity that DEPENDS, pointing at the one it depends on. A general, reused node never holds a field naming the things that use it. The test is the step-3 question applied to the relation: if every user of this node disappeared, would the node still be complete? A skill with no task implementing it is still a skill; a task with no skill is not a task. So the pointer lives on the task. | relation | written on | never on | why | . | a task implements a skill | the BPMN task (<bootstrap.processes:skill ref>) | the skill | a skill is reused by many tasks in many processes; listing them makes every new process an edit to the skill | . | a voice speaks for a role | the voice (activeIn.roles) | the role (voice) | a role is what an actor does in a lane; how it sounds is a separate, swappable thing | . | a lane names a role | the lane (partitionElementRef) | the role (lanes) | the role names diagrams it cannot know about | . | a user story is for a role | the story (role, in scenarios/stories.json) | the role (useCases) | stories are added by whoever writes them, not by editing the role | . | a Tool satisfies a skill | the Tool (satisfies) | the skill (scripts, validators, mcpServices) | several Tools may satisfy one skill, and a script is added without editing the skill | . | a skill or capability discharges a requirement statement | the skill’s front matter or the capability (satisfies: req:<id>#<key>) | the statement (satisfiedBy) | a requirement is written once; what discharges it arrives later | . | a skill says how to read a graph typology | the skill’s front matter (graph-typologies:) | the kind (skill) | a kind is registered once; skills that read it come and go | . | a skill takes and produces a contract | the skill’s front matter (input:, output: — a path into the layer or an https IRI) | a directory named after the skill | the skill can then say its contract is elsewhere, and a contract no skill names is visible as unclaimed | . | a test checks a skill’s contract | the test run (skill, with its cases checked against the skill’s input:/output:) | the skill | tests come and go; the contract does not | . Prose counts. A skill body that says “the only step of initialize-harness” knows its caller just as surely as a field does, and goes stale the same way. Say what the skill does, not who calls it; the caller’s own declaration says the rest. The general node owns its CONTRACT. What a skill takes and returns is a fact about the skill, so it is declared there: an input and an output schema reference, each either a KG schema or a pinned external schema. Tasks, Tools and tests point at the skill and are checked against that contract. That is how a general node stays complete without naming its users. Declare which nodes are general, and let the audit hold the line. Which nodes are general is a modelling decision, so it is written down: the schema declaration’s doc comment carries @general. The general nodes are Role, Skill, Requirement statement, Graph typology, Capability, Actor and Process. kg:audit’s arrow-direction criterion then reports two things: a @general schema whose @ref names a declaration that is not general, and a BPMN <folio:…> element pointing from a process at anything but a skill, role, decision table, convention or precondition. It cannot see a bare string field with no @ref (step 9 is how those become visible) or prose, so a clean run is a claim about declared pointers only. Prose may name a dependent; data may not. The rule governs references, the things a tool follows. A general node’s prose can still name a dependent to explain itself. For example, a process’s documentation may say “feature-staging.yml publishes the branch” so the reader knows why a step exists; deleting such an explanation loses the reason a step exists. If the relation matters to a tool, it must also exist as data held by the dependent, like a workflow’s # bpmn: line. The prose then explains that data and does not replace it. What prose cannot do is notice a rename, so kg:audit’s advisory prose-names-resolve criterion lists a named path whose directory exists and whose file does not. A bare name that nothing in the repository carries is left undetermined, because it could be a run’s output, a folio’s file or an example. 9. Make every cross-node reference a typed KG reference . A reference is a claim that another node exists. A bare string makes that claim in a vocabulary nothing resolves: a typo, a rename or a deleted node reads exactly like a valid name. So a field that names another node holds a KG reference: the target’s kind and id, resolvable in the knowledge graph, and projected by kg-export as an @id link, never a literal. The IRI that link carries is <doc dir>/<kind>/<id>, never ….jsonld#<kind>/<id> — minted by the exporter, not by the model; kg-export §”Subject IRIs — a path, not a #fragment” owns that rule. Use the helpers that already exist rather than inventing one: . | helper | shape | for | . | KgRefSchema (schemas/kg/carried-note.ts) | {kind, id, note?} | any KG node | . | TaskRefSchema (schemas/kg/carried-note.ts) | {process, task} | a BPMN task: the pair, never a bare task id | . | VoiceRefSchema (schemas/content/voices.ts) | {instance?, voiceId} | a voice, possibly in another layer | . | SkillNameSchema (schemas/tools/tool-types.ts) | kebab id | a skill id, where a whole ref is not needed | . | module#Export, instance:module#Export (parseValidatorRef) | string with a checked grammar | a schema | . A reference that crosses into another layer says which layer. And a reference is resolved by a check, not trusted: the audit that reads the field fails on one that points at nothing. Free text stays free text only when it is not a claim about another node: a description, a note, a persona. Free text that names things the graph cannot point at is a reference that should be a node.

532.title: What falsifies a model
532.content: Write these down as you go and check them at the end. A model nobody tried to break is a diagram. | test | what it catches | . | name two layers that differ only in a field you called an identifier | the identifier is not one | . | find a fact you would have to update in two places | it is on the wrong entity, or duplicated | . | find a relation whose cardinality changes under a plausible future | the model states today’s data, not the domain | . | count the facts nothing reads | the part you modelled for its own sake | . | find two kinds whose consumers take the SAME code path | one of them is an override wearing a discriminator | . | find a required field a variant can never state | requiredness is being checked before resolution, not after | . | delete every user of a general node; is it still complete? | a field on the general node names its users (step 8) | . | rename a node; does anything still read as valid? | a reference is a bare string, not a KG reference (step 9) | .

533.title: What this skill is NOT
533.content: Not a storage design. Tables, files, indices and formats come after, and a model that assumed one of them has usually smuggled a storage constraint in as a domain fact. Not domain content. folio-assistant is the platform. A model of clinical recommendations, FHIR profiles or any one folio’s vocabulary belongs in that folio — this skill is the procedure, and the procedure carries no subject matter. See the platform-boundary rule in placement.

535.title: The comparison goes BEFORE the question, not inside the options
535.content: Skill decision-comparison: Lay a decision out as a comparison before you ask it — what each option does, its pro, its con, what it changes downstream, and how reversible it is — in the prose that precedes the question, never inside the option labels. Required whenever a choice is handed to a person. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . interaction-modality §4.1 fixes the order — context → options → recommendation → question — and requires each option to carry what it costs. This says what “the comparison” has to contain, and where it has to live. Not to be merged with decision-audit. That records why a decision was made, after the fact, and governs overruling a QA finding. This is about what a person is shown before they decide; a skill that tried to be both would be read at the wrong moment.

536.title: Why not in the option descriptions
536.content: A selection tool gives each option a short label and a short description. The trade-offs do not go there: . | A reader sees one option at a time, and a comparison is reading the rows against each other. | There is no room. Every trade-off gets compressed to its headline, and the second-order consequences are the first thing cut. | It cannot be re-read. The preamble stays in the transcript; a focused option label does not. | .

537.title: What a comparison contains
537.content: Per option, five things: . |   |   | . | What it does | the mechanism, in one line | . | Pro | what it buys, stated as a benefit rather than an absence of harm | . | Con | what it costs to do | . | Downstream impact | what it changes for everything else, afterwards | . | Reversibility | how expensive it is to undo once taken | . Then, once, for the set: the recommendation with its reasoning, and the default that applies if nobody answers. Cost and downstream impact are different . Cost is what the change takes: files touched, tests to rewrite, hours. Downstream impact is what the world looks like afterwards: what becomes easy, what becomes hard, what a future contributor now has to know, which other decisions are now foreclosed or forced. A cheap change with a large downstream impact reads best when only cost is shown. Say both, separately. Reversibility . opening-brief triggers on irreversibility and surprise rather than size, and the same measure applies here. Two options with identical cost and impact are not equivalent if one can be undone in an afternoon and the other is load-bearing within a week. State it per option.

538.title: Where it lives
538.content: In the prose that precedes the question. A table is usually right — the columns above are a table’s columns, and a table is the one layout that shows rows against each other. The options in the selection tool are then LABELS for choices already explained. A label names the option and, at most, restates its headline. A reader who has read the preamble should be able to choose from the labels alone; a reader who has not should find nothing new hiding in them. If the labels are where the information is, the comparison was never made.

539.title: When this does not apply
539.content: A small, reversible choice does not earn a table: the reader would pay attention for something that did not need it. The trigger is the same as opening-brief’s: would getting this wrong be expensive or surprising? If no, recommend and proceed. One-option “decisions” are not decisions. If the honest comparison has one viable row, do not manufacture alternatives to fill a table. Say what you are doing, say why the obvious alternative loses, and proceed.

540.title: Done properly, it also answers the count rule
540.content: interaction-modality §4.1 requires that with several decisions open you ask one in full and give a count for the rest. A full comparison is what “in full” means. The rest get a number, never a row from a table they cannot see.

542.title: Decision methodology selector
542.content: Skill decision-methodology-selector: Given a decision context, select the applicable methodology from the methodology graph. Reads the graph’s applies-when declarations, matches them against the context, and returns the ranked applicable methods with rationale. Extends methodology-adoption’s four-question protocol with quantitative method-selection criteria from the MCDM literature. Named by: CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, SWOT situation analysis, Questionnaire wireframe review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Guideline Updates, DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring, Phase 1: Planning, IRIS CDN initial load . Input: a decision context — what is being decided, how many alternatives, how many criteria, available data, time constraints, stakeholder count, reversibility, uncertainty level. Output: a ranked list of applicable methodologies, each with: . | the methodology name and its graph-node id | why it fits this context (matched applies-when) | why it does NOT fit the alternatives (matched not-for) | complexity rating | data requirements | .

543.title: Relationship to methodology-adoption
543.content: methodology-adoption carries the protocol — four questions asked in order, the first yes decides. This skill carries the implementation: given that the protocol routes the decision to a category (computable, evidence-grading, decision-record, decision-analysis), which specific methodology in the graph serves that category best for this context? . methodology-adoption names the lane; this skill names the runner.

544.title: Decision context schema
544.content: A decision context has these dimensions. Not all are required — an agent provides what it knows and the selector grades against what is declared. | dimension | type | when it matters | . | questionType | "computable" \| "evidence-grading" \| "decision-record" \| "decision-analysis" | Always — from methodology-adoption §”Choosing which applies” | . | alternativeCount | number | MCDM methods scale differently | . | criteriaCount | number | AHP pairwise comparisons grow as n² | . | criteriaWeightsKnown | boolean | Some methods derive weights, others require them | . | dataType | "quantitative" \| "qualitative" \| "mixed" | Aggregation methods need numbers | . | stakeholderCount | number | Group methods (Delphi, ANP) vs solo | . | timeConstraint | "minutes" \| "hours" \| "days" \| "weeks" | Eliminates complex methods | . | reversibility | "reversible" \| "costly" \| "irreversible" | Higher stakes → more rigorous method | . | uncertainty | "low" \| "moderate" \| "high" \| "deep" | Bayesian methods for deep uncertainty | . | sequential | boolean | True when decisions recur or adapt over time | .

545.title: Method families and when to use them
545.content: 1. MCDM aggregation methods . When: multiple alternatives scored against multiple criteria, quantitative data available, goal is a ranking. Source: Wang & Rangaiah, “Multi-Criteria Decision-Making: Aggregation-Type Methods” (arXiv:2509.06388). | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | SAW (Simple Additive Weighting) | First pass, well-understood criteria, all benefit-type after normalisation | Criteria on incomparable scales without good normalisation | Low | . | MEW (Multiplicative Exponent Weighting) | Criteria with exponential importance differences | Any criterion value is zero (product collapses) | Low | . | AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process) | Weights unknown, need stakeholder consensus on priorities | >9 criteria (pairwise comparisons explode: n(n-1)/2) | Medium | . | ANP (Analytic Network Process) | Criteria have interdependencies (feedback loops) | Simple independent criteria (overkill) | High | . | COPRAS | Benefit and cost criteria naturally separated | All criteria same direction | Medium | . | MOORA | Quick ranking with ratio normalisation | Need for weight derivation (requires pre-set weights) | Low | . | FUCA | Alternatives close in score, need tie-breaking | Very few alternatives (<3) | Medium | . | WASPAS | Combines SAW + MEW for robustness check | When SAW and MEW agree (no added value) | Medium | . 2. Probabilistic / sequential decision methods . When: decisions recur, data arrives over time, exploration-exploitation trade-off matters, experiments are costly. Source: Kristiadi, “Introduction to the Analysis of Probabilistic Decision-Making Algorithms” (arXiv:2508.21620). | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | Multi-armed bandits (UCB, Thompson sampling) | Repeated choice among options with unknown payoffs | One-shot decisions | Medium | . | Bayesian optimisation | Expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions, few evaluations | Cheap evaluations (just try them all) | High | . | Tree search (MCTS) | Sequential decisions with branching outcomes | No natural tree structure | High | . | Contextual bandits | Payoff depends on observable context | Context is not available or not meaningful | Medium | . The source backs bandits and Bayesian optimisation only: the ingested version has no tree-search chapter and does not mention contextual bandits, so those two rows are UNSOURCED. 3. Social / behavioral decision methods . When: multiple stakeholders, group consensus needed, behavioral biases must be accounted for. Source: Ravichandran, “Algorithmic Approaches to Sequential Decision-Making and Social Epistemology” (arXiv:2607.20636) — for grit-aware evaluation only. Delphi and nominal group technique come from the group-consensus literature and are UNSOURCED here. | method | best for | avoid when | complexity | . | Delphi method | Expert consensus without groupthink | Time pressure (<1 day) | Medium | . | Nominal group technique | Structured brainstorming → voting | >15 participants | Low | . | Grit-aware evaluation | Decisions requiring sustained investment | Reversible/low-stakes | Medium | . 4. Classical decision methods — UNSOURCED . When: well-understood problem structure, textbook applicability. No source in this repository. Nothing in library/ covers cost-benefit analysis, decision trees, game theory or expected utility, and no methodology node renders any of them. 547.title: Selection algorithm
547.content: function selectMethodology(context: DecisionContext): MethodologyRecommendation[] { // Step 1: Route via methodology-adoption protocol const lane = routeByQuestionType(context); // Step 2: Load methodology graph nodes const nodes = readMethodologyGraph(); // Step 3: Classify each node against the context const classified = nodes.map(n => ({ ...n, matchTier: classifyFit(n, context), // primary | secondary | excluded rationale: explainFit(n, context) })); // Step 4: Return primary matches first, then secondary. Excluded are named // but NOT recommended — per methodology-adoption, refusals are stated. return classified.sort((a, b) => tierOrder(a.matchTier) - tierOrder(b.matchTier) ); } .

Each recommendation names the paper or standard the method comes from. | Report no-match. If no methodology fits, that is the output — §”If none fits, that is a finding, not a licence.” | The graph is the catalogue. Do not recommend methods not in the methodology graph. If a paper describes a method worth adopting, the output is a recommendation to ingest it via §methodology-adoption, not to use it directly. | .

550.title: Deep document research
550.content: Skill deep-document-research: Answer a question from a corpus this folio already holds, iteratively, and stop on a stated condition. The four roles, the two stopping conditions and why both are load-bearing, the granularity choice, and the three things this repository must NOT adopt along with the method. Named by: Deep document research . Renders methodologies/doc-researcher.md — Dong et al., arXiv:2510.21603v1 — as something an agent here can run. Read the methodology node for what the paper claims and what it measured; this is the part you act on. It assumes a corpus, and does not build one. library-ingestion acquires and files; ingest-* derives structure; the L1 completeness gate says whether an entry is fit to use. This begins after all three.

551.title: The loop, and the only two ways out
551.content: plan → [ search → refine → evaluate ] → report ↑ | └── σ < τ and t < T_max . Stop when σ ≥ τ, or when t = T_max. Both, always. | Threshold alone never terminates on a question the corpus cannot answer, and a corpus that cannot answer a question is the normal case rather than the exception. | Cap alone stops an answerable question early, and the answer it returns looks exactly like a complete one. | . A loop with only one of them is not this method. Say which one you stopped on. An answer that hit T_max is an answer with known gaps; one that reached σ ≥ τ is not. A report that does not distinguish them hands the reader a confidence nobody established.

552.title: The four roles are four QUESTIONS, not four programs
552.content: |   | asks | . | plan | which documents could possibly bear on this, at what granularity, and what are the sub-questions? | . | search | what does the corpus return for this sub-question at that granularity? | . | refine | of what came back, what is actually relevant and not a duplicate? | . | report | what does the accumulated evidence say, and where can a reader check each claim? | . One actor may perform all four. The deep-researcher role is one swimlane because a role is an accountability, not a step: somebody stands behind the synthesis. Do not read the paper’s four agents as four roles.

553.title: Choose the granularity per question, and say you chose
553.content: The method’s substance is that a corpus parsed at several granularities lets a LATER step pick. A broad question is answered from summaries; a specific one from chunks. Picking once, in the pipeline, answers every future question the same way — which is the condition this method exists to escape. This checkout is not there yet. l1-blocks.ts produces blocks and sections exist; there is no summary level and no per-query choice. Until there is, say which granularity you searched rather than implying the corpus offered one.

554.title: Three things NOT to adopt with it
554.content: . | Machine descriptions as fact. The paper converts figures to text with a VLM and uses the output. Here an agent’s description is a draft and only a person confirms it (apply-image-verdicts.ts, cat-harness-tools schemas/content/narrative.ts): “an uncited narrative is indistinguishable from a transcription of the source.” Search over drafts if you must — and never report a draft as what the figure shows. | A sufficiency function you invented. The paper gives σ a symbol and a threshold and never says how it is computed. If you need one, propose it and have it adjudicated; do not bury a judgement in a number. | The paper’s numbers. 50.6% and “3.4× baselines” were measured on the authors’ own benchmark over their own 304 documents. They say nothing about this corpus. | .

555.title: Say what you did not find
555.content: The one failure this method makes easy: an iterative search that ends quietly looks identical to one that succeeded. Report the sub-questions that returned nothing, and whether that means not in the corpus or not found by this search. Those are different, and only the first is a fact about the folio.

564.title: Deletion requires explicit confirmation
564.content: Skill deletion-requires-confirmation: An agent never removes a durable artefact on its own initiative. Report what would go, with sizes and ages, and wait for the user to say so. Covers what counts as durable, the non-destructive move for each kind, and the rule that a workflow whose shape deletes something counts as a deletion nobody decided. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, A harness’s default rendering, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . One rule: . An agent does not remove a durable artefact on its own initiative. It reports what it would remove — with sizes, ages and what each one is — and waits for the user to say so. The rule is about the gap between an agent decided this was no longer needed and a person decided it: the second is cheap to obtain, and the first is never recoverable from the outside. A waiver is not an exception to it. The owner may grant the deletion gate in advance — for a session, a process run, or a named artefact class — and that grant is the person deciding. The agent never supplies the decision itself. A waiver carries the grantor, their verbatim words, one gate class, a scope and an expiry; one missing field means there is no waiver (confirmation-waiver). A deletion waiver is never blanket — a grant over build artefacts is not a grant over content — and it never reaches a work item: never delete a work item is a prohibition, and scrapped, with reasons, is always available.

565.title: Why removing something is not the inverse of creating it
565.content: A deletion destroys the evidence that it happened. A wrong file is visible and gets fixed; a removed one looks exactly like “there was never anything here”. The person who pays is not the person who acted. A sibling session, a reviewer following a link, the next agent — none can tell a deliberate removal from an accident. A scrapped work item records that something was considered and rejected; a deleted one leaves a sibling unable to tell abandonment from accident. The same holds for a staging preview, a witness or a library source. Asking is nearly free and reverting often is not. Confirming costs one line in a report and one word back; a wrong deletion costs whatever it took to produce the thing, and may never be discovered. This skill is the general rule; the work item rule in todo-manager is one instance of it.

566.title: What counts as durable
566.content: The test is not “is it committed” and not “is it large”. It is: . Could somebody other than me want this later, and would they be able to tell it was removed on purpose? . If the answer to the first is yes and to the second is no, it is durable. Durable — confirm before removing: . | artefact | why | the non-destructive move | . | a work item (beans/defs/*.md) | records that something was considered; ids are referenced from commits, issues and other work items | set status: scrapped with the reasons; beans archive MOVES resolved ones | . | a todo (todos/items/*.md) | it is a person’s outstanding work, not an agent’s | ask the person; an agent may neither close nor remove one | . | a staging preview (branches/<slug>/ on the publish branch) | it is the artefact a human assesses a rendered change from — unless the PR merged, when the main site now shows the same thing | merged → removed automatically; the merge IS the confirmation. Otherwise: while the PR is open, the staging:cleanup label applied by a person; once closed unmerged, a feature-staging.yml dispatch with cleanup_slug + a matching cleanup_confirm, since the label cannot reach a closed PR | . | a published page on the site | a URL somebody has linked or bookmarked | say what would 404 and let the owner decide; a redirect is often the answer | . | a QA verdict or witness | the previous answer is what separates “this broke today” from “this has been broken since it was written” | regenerate it in place; never remove it to make a sweep clean. Its record is the commit-keyed entry on the qa-reports branch; an entry there is removed only by qa:prune’s declared retention, never by hand | . | a QA attestation (test/attestations/**) | a judgement — agent, human or baseline pair — that no regeneration can reproduce | never removed to clear a finding; a stale one is re-judged, and the new judgement replaces it through its writer | . | library / uploads content | every knowledge-graph reference to a source resolves through library/; a file in uploads/ reads as absent to every consumer while still on disk | move it forward through the pipeline, or ask | . | a workflow instance (beans/workflows/*.json) | it is where a running process got to; a sibling session is reading it | complete or discard the instance through the engine, which records the fact | . | a branch, tag or ref somebody else pushed | it is the only copy of work that is not on main | leave it; say it looks finished with | . Not durable — rewrite or remove freely: . | scratch files in a scratchpad or temp directory, and anything you created this session that nothing else has seen; | build output: _site/, _kg/, dist/, node_modules/, test-results/; | a generated artefact being rewritten in place by its own generator. The distinction is in place: writing a fresh kg-qa sidecar over the old one is regeneration; removing a sidecar whose subject you could not load is a deletion, and a false pass besides. | . Three cases sit on the line and all resolve the same way — ask: a file you believe to be an orphan, a directory you believe to be empty, and a file whose only reference you have just removed, because in each the belief is exactly what would be wrong if you are wrong. Establish which layer owns a node before you propose removing it. In a multi-layer layout a file that looks orphaned here may be declared from somewhere else (placement).

567.title: What to do instead
567.content: Report, do not act. The report is the deliverable: . | Name every artefact. Assert by naming, never by counting — “4 previews are orphaned” is a statistic; “branches/<slug> (36.8 MB, last deployed 11 days ago, its PR merged) matches no open pull request” is something a person can answer. | Give the size and the age. | Say what is lost if it goes, in terms of what would differ — a 404 on a link, a reviewer unable to compare, a sibling unable to tell abandonment from accident. | Recommend one option and mark it as your recommendation, then say what happens if they say nothing — the frame interaction-modality §4.1 requires of every handed-over decision. | . Prefer the move that keeps the record: scrapped over deleted, archive over remove, redirect over 404, regenerate over unlink, a label over a workflow step. When the user does say so, do exactly that and no more. A confirmation to remove one thing is not a confirmation to remove the class it belongs to. If the scope is ambiguous, ask again. A standing confirmation for a class is the owner’s to give — never an inference. The worked case is the staging preview cap: the owner’s standing confirmation covers removing the oldest previews beyond a total size budget (3 GB), so the stage job removes them without asking per preview. A class confirmation covers the class as the owner last stated it; changing the rule is theirs. It does not waive the record: each rotation names the artefact, its age and its size — in the commit message, the job log and a removed render-log entry — and retires its staging-preview.json into branches/_retired/ rather than deleting it. It covers rotation over the cap and nothing else on the branch. See staging-review §”The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off”.

568.title: A workflow whose shape deletes something
568.content: A deletion nobody decided is still a deletion that requires confirmation. A publish step that clones the publish branch, removes everything on it and copies the new build in (a full replace with no kept files) deletes every artefact other workflows put there — for example every open PR’s staging preview — with no step anyone wrote with that intent, silently, and against any explicit retention rule elsewhere. Since there is nobody to ask at push time, the workflow must not be shaped that way: restore what it does not own (e.g. branches/) into the publish directory before the push. A removal policy needs a removal that can actually be confirmed. If the only sanctioned remedy cannot reach the artefacts a report names (a label on a PR that is already closed), the person is left with unsanctioned options. Give the confirmation somewhere to go — e.g. a dispatch whose confirmation input repeats the slug, and which re-evaluates liveness at removal time rather than trusting the report. A report that names live work invites a deletion. “No open pull request” is not “abandoned”; check recent activity before naming a candidate.

569.title: Name the instrument that produced the list
569.content: A candidate list must say where it came from. If a committed check computed it, quote the check’s finding and name the check. If you built the list by hand, say so, so the person can see they are being asked to act on a derivation rather than on a measurement. A hand-derived list SHORTER than the instrument’s is a harmless miss. One that is LONGER extracts a permission the instrument never justified — for example a slug rule re-implemented inline that names live previews of open PRs as orphans. So do not re-derive what a committed check already computes (goal-review rule 2, stated there for the reviewing side).

570.title: Applying it to your own code
570.content: Does anything you are writing remove something as a side effect of doing something else? A full-replace publish, a --prune, a cleanup step, a cache eviction, a git rm that globs. If so, name what it removes, in the code, and make sure a person chose it. If it is a sweep, does it act or does it report? A checker that finds accumulation reports it: every finding’s action names something a person does, as in bun run cat health, whose workflow opens an issue and removes nothing.

571.title: Checklist
571.content: . | Is the thing durable by the test above? If unsure, it is. | Is there a non-destructive move — scrap, archive, redirect, regenerate, label? Prefer it, and say you preferred it. | Have you named each artefact, with its size and age and what is lost? | Does the list say which instrument produced it — or, if you built it by hand, does it say that? | Have you given a recommendation, and said what happens on silence? | Did the user confirm this removal, rather than a similar one? | Does any code you wrote remove something as a side effect? Say so in the code, and check a person chose it. | .

573.doc: DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan
573.title: DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan
573.content: Process_DIIG · advisory · 11 step(s) . The nine-chapter sequence of the WHO/ITU Digital Implementation Investment Guide, as the Guide numbers it. Each chapter’s output is the next chapter’s input, and the two exclusive gateways are the Guide’s OWN progress checks (4.5 and 8.5) rather than gates added here. Adopted whole per methodology-adoption, and rendered from the ingested sections at who-iris/library/9789240010567-eng/. Chapter 1 is the Guide’s introduction — scope, key terms and when the Guide applies — so it is the start event’s documentation rather than an activity: nothing is performed there. ADVISORY, not strict. This is a per-methodology process and DIIG is somebody else’s method: the engine can report where a programme has got to, but what counts as an adequate answer to “have we identified the bottlenecks” belongs to the programme and its stakeholders, not to this repository. The four unrelaxable steps of the base editorial gate are untouched by it. WHAT THIS DIAGRAM DOES NOT DO. DIIG Table 3.3.1 scores bottlenecks on three 1-3 criteria and sums them into a ranking. The three criteria are adopted; the arithmetic is refused, per methodology-adoption — three ordinal judgements on incommensurable scales, summed with equal weight, produce a number whose precision is invented. So A_PrioritizeBottlenecks records each criterion’s answer and its reason and orders by argument. There is no computed score anywhere in this process, and a DMN-backed gateway would be the wrong shape for exactly that reason. i i i i i i i i i i i

576.doc: DIIG — from a health system bottleneck to a costed implementation plan
576.title: Steps
576.content: Every one of the 11 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Form the team and establish goalsA_FormTeam | Programme manager | methodology-adoption | DIIG Chapter 2. Determine roles and responsibilities; develop a common understanding of the health programme’s needs and goals; understand programme operations across levels of the health system. | . | Map the current state and confirm bottlenecksA_MapCurrentState | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | DIIG Chapter 3.1. Determine the health programme processes to target, map their workflows, identify and confirm bottlenecks. Then 3.2, a root cause analysis.This is where DIIG builds on CRDM, and it says so: “This process builds on the Public Health Informatics Institute’s Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM)”. Its three areas of concentration are business process analysis, business process redesign and requirements definition — two of which name diagrams this platform already executes. They are parallel tracks, not a composite: pick one per decision and name it. | . | Prioritize, and map to health system challengesA_PrioritizeBottlenecks | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | DIIG Chapters 3.3 and 3.4. Prioritize the bottlenecks, then map the programme-specific ones onto the generic health system challenges.THE ARITHMETIC IS REFUSED HERE. DIIG Table 3.3.1 asks three questions, each scored 1-3 — how much impact does this bottleneck have on the process, what is the likelihood of overcoming it, is it important to a wide range of stakeholders — and sums them into a Score and a Prioritized Ranking. The three criteria are adopted whole; the total is not. Record each criterion’s answer AND its reason, and order by argument. A ranked list reads as evidence in a way three stated judgements do not, and the weights were invented. | . | Determine appropriate digital health interventionsA_DetermineInterventions | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | DIIG Chapter 4. Select interventions for the prioritized challenges, assess whether the enabling environment can support them, identify functional requirements and user stories, map the future-state workflow, and check whether existing applications already meet the requirements.The interventions CONSIDERED AND NOT CHOSEN are part of the output, with why — methodology-adoption’s fourth refusal. A deleted alternative leaves the next reader unable to tell a decision from an oversight.Selection is from the Classification, and the who-digital-health voice governs the naming: an intervention is a capability, not the software that delivers it. | . | Plan the implementationA_PlanImplementation | Programme manager | methodology-adoption | DIIG Chapter 5. Infrastructure; legislation, policy and compliance, including data management, privacy and security, and the regulation of new technologies; leadership and governance, including external partnerships; workforce and training; services and applications. | . | Link to the enterprise architectureA_LinkEnterpriseArchitecture | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | DIIG Chapter 6. Assess the digital health enterprise architecture, identify the common and enabling components and shared services that make up the digital health platform, and link the investment to both. | . | Develop a budgetA_DevelopBudget | Programme manager | methodology-adoption | DIIG Chapter 7. Phases of implementation, cost drivers, and the budget matrix. This is the chapter that turns the preceding six into a COSTED implementation plan, which is the artefact the whole Guide exists to produce and the one a funder reads. | . | Monitor, and use data effectivelyA_MonitorAndUseData | Programme manager | methodology-adoption | DIIG Chapter 8. Establish a logic model, plan the monitoring and evaluation, establish a culture of data use, and manage adaptively — using the data to optimize the interventions rather than only to report on them.The full treatment of this chapter is a separate publication in this library, 9789241511766-eng, Monitoring and Evaluating Digital Health Interventions. It is a parallel track, not a sub-step: do not blend the two. | . | Make the value proposition and set next stepsA_ValueProposition | Programme manager | methodology-adoption | DIIG Chapter 9. The case made to whoever pays, and what follows. Scaling up is a different method and a different publication — 9789241509510-eng, The MAPS Toolkit — which begins where this implementation ends. | . | Open the beanCall_BeanOpen | Programme manager | calls Process_BeanOpenbean-coordination | Process_BeanOpen: check before you create, find out whose the bean is, and claim it — or leave it alone when it is someone else’s. The one place a claim is drawn (bean m8gz, owner 2026-10-24); the gateway after this reads which end it reached. | . | Close the beanCall_BeanClose | Programme manager | calls Process_BeanClosetodo-manager | Process_BeanClose: end the bean in a state that says why — complete and archive it, scrap it with its reasons and archive it, or record the blocker and hand it back.
