725.title: fhir-validation
725.content: Named by: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline . Skill id: fhir-validation · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Named by l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn (Validate against profiles, Build pipeline — SUSHI · validator · IG Publisher lane) and ig-incremental-build.bpmn (Validate the cone (fhir_validate), Publisher + validator services (JVM) lane). Validate an IG’s FHIR artefacts against the profiles and packages they claim to conform to. Sourcing. Conformance is defined by the FHIR specification and by the packages an IG depends on; the validator is HL7’s. This skill states how it is invoked in this harness and what each outcome is allowed to mean.

726.title: Inputs and outputs
726.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/fhir-validation/: . | in — igRoot (required), validationLevel, targetProfiles | out — overallStatus (required), sushiResult, publisherResult, conformanceResults | . SUSHI compiling is not conformance. FSH can compile to JSON that the validator then rejects, so a green sushiResult with an unrun publisherResult is not a pass.

727.title: The binaries
727.content: The package declares these capabilities (providesCapabilities in package-manifest.json); each is defined, with its detection command, in scenarios/capabilities/: . sushi --version # sushi-compiler (requires node-runtime) java -jar "${FHIR_VALIDATOR_JAR}" -version # fhir-validator (requires java-runtime) java -jar "${IG_PUBLISHER_JAR}" --version # ig-publisher (requires java-runtime) . fhir-validator is the standalone validator, distinct from ig-publisher, which builds a whole IG. An authoring loop runs the validator on single resources between builds; a release is cut from the publisher.

728.title: When a package host refuses you
728.content: SUSHI and the Publisher resolve the IG’s dependencies: from packages.fhir.org. Where that host is refused, the failure looks like a broken IG and is not one. Ask for the remedy: . bun run cat tools:remedy packages.fhir.org # → fhir-cache-seed-npm, with its command . Every network-dependent Tool declares remedies per host it reaches (check:tools enforces it), and fhir-harness/scripts/ig-cache.sh doctor prints the same answer for each host it finds unreachable. For packages.fhir.org it is fhir-cache-seed-npm --sushi-config sushi-config.yaml, and for versions npm does not carry, --mirror from a repository that fhir-package-mirror filled on a machine that reaches the host. Pin that repository with --mirror-commit <full 40-character SHA>: git cannot fetch an abbreviated SHA from a remote, and the seeder refuses one. A cloud session can fill the mirror without a person’s device, through a GitHub Actions runner: push a claude/mirror-* branch that edits packages.txt in the mirror repository, wait for its mirror.yml run, merge, re-seed. SUSHI also adds packages that sushi-config.yaml does not list, such as hl7.fhir.uv.tools.r4#latest. A #latest needs the registry to name a version, so offline it fails with errors that look like the IG’s own (for example logical-target … does not exist), even with the package in the cache. Serve the mirror as a registry on localhost, answering GET /<name> with dist-tags.latest and GET /<name>/<version> with the tarball, and run FPL_REGISTRY=http://127.0.0.1:<port> sushi build .. Check which version latest resolves to: it is the mirror’s highest, which is only right when the mirror holds the current release. Do not report “SUSHI cannot run here” before running tools:remedy. A refusal that tools:remedy answers with none is “could not determine” in the sense of the next section: say so, with the reason it gave.

729.title: A capability that is absent did not pass
729.content: If a probe fails, overallStatus is not a pass with an empty findings list. It is “could not determine”, and it is reported as such: a clean run over a validator that never started looks exactly like a clean IG.

730.title: Validating a cone
730.content: ig-incremental-build.bpmn validates a restricted cone — the artefacts a change touches — rather than the whole IG, and reports the cone it chose. That is a latency optimisation for the authoring loop. It does not gate a release: the full publisher build in l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn does. Do not let a green cone stand in for a green IG: a profile the change did not touch can still be broken by it.

731.title: After validation
731.content: Quality gates on the aggregate are quality-control; publishing is ig-publication. A validator’s verdict is an input to the QC reviewer’s decision, not the decision.

733.content: Skill folio-getting-started: The content-folio half of the harness’s getting-started skill: binds processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn and decisions/folio-intent.dmn, interprets describeRepository() content-type markers (folio, harness, dak, sushi), and routes new-content and specialised IG/DAK creation requests. 734.title: 1. Repository membership vs. isFolio
734.content: describeRepository() (schemas/content/content-type.ts) returns every marker a repository carries — folio, harness, dak, sushi — with the facts each states and any disagreement between them. describeRepositoryClosure() (schemas/kg/harness-config.ts) extends that through the dependency tree, attributing each membership to the layer that carried it. | folio and harness are distinct memberships. The declaration (<name>.json) says this is a layer; a config that declares contentType (<name>.config.json or inline in index.config.json) says this authors folio content. isFolio in folio-intent.dmn tests membership of folio specifically. | Multiple markers do not perturb the five branches. A folio that is also a DAK or carries a sushi-config.yaml takes the same branch in folio-intent.dmn as one that is not: use describeRepository() to inspect what the repository is, and isFolio to drive Gateway_Intent. | .

Scaffolding anything on new-content is a defect. | Specialised IG or guideline creation: when the user asks to create a domain Implementation Guide or guideline in a harness that specialises this layer, hand over to that layer’s creation skill discovered via skill_list. 738.title: When to use folio-init
738.content: Reach for folio-init when triage in getting-started or repo-conversion has settled that a new folio structure should be created: . | new-repo — a brand-new repository is being stood up to author a paper, document or DAK folio. | add-folio — an existing repository wants a new folio added alongside its existing directories (overlay), without overwriting its tracked files. | . Do not run folio-init when: . | The repository already has a <name>.json declaration and only needs a lower harness layer brought in at a pinned SHA — that is materialise, served by remote-mount (bun run cat mount:remote). | The user is converting existing prose in place (convert in repo-conversion.bpmn) — that uses ingestion, not a blank scaffold. | . Because folio-init runs before the target repository has a content type, the Tool is registered among the generic harness tools rather than inside a content-type adapter.

739.title: Write capability requirement and read-only degradation
739.content: folio-init is a writing verb: it creates directories, writes manifests and agent stubs, and (when git is available) prints the command that seeds the cat/<instance>/beans and cat/<instance>/todos orphan state branches. Before invoking folio-init to write, check that at least one write capability is present (scenarios/capabilities/): . | git-push — local filesystem write plus git remote push capability for the target repository and its state branches. | github-api — GitHub API token (gh / REST / GraphQL) able to create or populate the target repository and refs. | github-connector — MCP GitHub connector able to push the scaffolded files into the target repository. | . When no write capability is available (a read-only container or an unauthenticated session), folio-init degrades cleanly via --dry-run (dry_run: true on the MCP tool): it computes and returns the complete Markdown report of every directory, manifest, builder shim and config file it would write, without touching the filesystem or git refs. Never attempt a partial write when write capability is absent, and never report a failed capability probe as a completed scaffold.

740.title: What folio-init writes
740.content: Given title and one or more authors (plus optional content_type, slug, dir, link, assistant_path, force, dry_run), folio-init lays down: . | The folio directories and initial manifests — folio/ (or content/), uploads/, library/, the root <slug>.json layer declaration and <slug>.config.json, and the root index.config.json that instantiates it (index-config). | The builder shim (content/schema/builders) — block manifests in the folio import ../schema/builders rather than importing the platform path directly. Writing the path to the harness once in the shim means re-linking a folio (submodule ↔ sibling ↔ remote mount) is a two-file edit rather than a sweep across every block manifest. | The link back to the platform (--link) — links the harness via sibling (--assistant-path ../folio-assistant) or submodule, and writes .mcp.json and the .claude/ session-start hook (bun run cat state:mount) pointing at that link. | The agent instructions — AGENTS.md and the one-line CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md stubs pointing to it. | The work-plan state branches — declares beans and todos on the cat/<slug>/beans and cat/<slug>/todos branches and prints the seed command; once it has been run, bun run cat state:mount mounts a working store on the first session start (directory-conventions §”Where a NEW layer’s state lives”). | .

741.title: What to check afterwards
741.content: . | bun run cat check:declaration-resolution — every directory and asset the new <slug>.json declares resolves on disk. | bun run cat index:render:check — the generated AGENTS.md matches the new index.config.json and layer declaration. | bun run cat state:status — the beans and todos stores are mounted and writable. | .

743.title: Folio repository conversion — markers, orphaned evidence, and intake handoff
743.content: Skill folio-repo-conversion: The content-folio half of the harness’s repo-conversion skill: outside-content evidence and refutation candidate scanning, content-type marker declarations, and dispatching library and content buckets to document-intake and folio authoring. Named by: Getting started . The harness skill repo-conversion governs the read-only repository scan (scan-repo-content.ts), the three selection questions (Q1–Q3), marker selection (--markers), merging existing AGENTS.md / README.md / .gitignore, and provisioning gh-pages. When converting an existing project into a content folio, apply these rules alongside it.

744.title: 1. Preserving outside-content evidence and refutations
744.content: In repositories with formal, scientific, or analytical content, crucial evidence and counterexamples often live outside the primary content tree (content/ or folio/). Carrying only the content tree drops the evidence that some claims are false. scan-repo-content.ts classifies outside-content artifacts into read-only candidate classes with their linkStatus: . | classification | description | examples | . | math_proof | Formal proof or theorem outside content tree | docs/audits/*.lean, math/*.lean, Coq .v, Isabelle .thy | . | computation_script | Numerical or symbolic calculation / verification script | docs/audits/*.py, computations/*.py, .sage, .ipynb, .jl | . | macro_definition | TeX macros, custom commands, environments, or math tables | macros.tex, tables/*.tex, preamble.tex, defs.tex | . | audit_refutation | Audit refutation or counterexample falsifying a claim | docs/audits/*is-false*.lean, audits/counterexample.py | . | derivation_note | Informal derivation note or scratchpad | docs/notes/derivation*.md, derivations/*.md, scratchpad.md | . | linked: referenced by at least one block or manifest in the content tree (linkedBy). | unlinked: orphaned evidence not linked by any content block — present these candidates to the author before importing so refutations and computations are linked or ingested rather than left behind. | .

745.title: 2. Dispatching the converted buckets
745.content: Once the author has answered Q1–Q3 and chosen the declared markers in index.config.json or <name>.json: . | library bucket: hand the selected reference documents to document-intake and l1-document-ingestion (processes/library/l1-document-ingestion.bpmn). | content bucket: hand the author’s own chapters and prose to document-authoring and document-structure (or the active content type’s adapter skills). | .

753.title: /getting-started — what did they actually ask for?
753.content: Skill getting-started: Triage what a person means when they ask to create a folio, and route them. Five requests share one sentence — a folio in a new repo, folio-assistant overlaid on an existing repo, a second folio in a layer that already has one, a content object they called a folio, or something the filesystem cannot tell apart. Reads the repository facts, runs them through the folio-intent decision table, asks a selectable question for what facts cannot settle, scaffolds, and reports the published URL. Use whenever a user asks to create, start, set up, or initialise a folio, a paper, a DAK, an IG, or “folio-assistant” itself. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, KG to public portal, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Getting started, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan, SMART Guideline end to end . Process: the content core’s processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn. Decision table: the content core’s decisions/folio-intent.dmn.

754.title: The landing page is the layer’s own description
754.content: A folio’s home page opens with its description inside its backdrop, both declared in the repository’s declaration. Nothing about any particular layer is written into the template, so a downstream folio does not inherit the platform’s grumpy cat. Where the markdown node is: description in <name>.json. It is markdown and it is rendered as-is. There is no separate landing page to keep in step with it, because a description in two places will disagree with itself. How the picture is declared: an image with role: "landing" and a layout (laptop, mobile, card), plus a textRegion giving, as fractions of the image, where words may safely be drawn. textRegion is authored, not computed. It states where the composition is quiet, which is a judgement: find it by rendering candidate boxes over the image and looking at them, not by deriving a number from the aspect ratio. Run bun run cat docs:harness after editing, and --check in CI. Three states: . | declared | rendered | . | backdrop with region | description drawn inside it | . | backdrop, no region | picture shown, words placed below it | . | no backdrop | words alone | . An undeclared region means do not overlay, never anywhere is fine, because text positioned by guesswork lands on the picture. A folio with no art is ordinary. A viewport with no variant falls back to the widest available, and the fallback is reported — that crop’s region is wrong for a narrow screen, so a consumer can decline to overlay rather than place text somewhere nobody chose. Reader-facing walkthrough: docs/start/getting-started.md §8. A new layer’s beans/ and todos/ are not written into its checkout. By default folio_init declares them on their own branches, cat/<instance>/beans and cat/<instance>/todos, and prints a one-time seed command. Say so when you hand the scaffold over: until the seed has been run and mounted, an empty beans list means not mounted, not no work. The rule, the branch naming and the override live in directory-conventions §”Where a NEW layer’s state lives”.

755.title: 0. Why this skill exists
755.content: folio_init scaffolds a folio, and it does it well. What it cannot do is know whether scaffolding is the right move, because the sentence that reaches it — “create a folio”, “set me up with folio-assistant”, “I want to start a paper” — is spoken by at least five different people: . | they mean | what they have | the wrong move costs them | . | new-repo | nothing yet, or an empty directory | — (this is the safe default, and the only one an agent may assume) | . | overlay | a repository with their own work in it | a folio scaffolded on top of a project the agent never looked at | . | add-folio | a folio-assistant layer already | a second repository they did not want, and a split corpus | . | new-content | a folio, and they wanted a document in it | an entire empty folio, and the chapter they asked for still not written | . | ask | any of the above, undeclared | — | . Four of these five states look identical from the user’s sentence, and three of them look identical from the filesystem, so the triage always runs.

756.title: 1. Read the facts — mechanical, read-only, before anything is written
756.content: Three facts, and nothing else. Gather them by looking, not by asking: . # isFolio — does an instantiated config here declare a contentType? # The root <name>.config.json files, and index.config.json, whose instances # may carry contentType inline (index-config skill). grep -lq '"contentType"' ./*.config.json 2>/dev/null && echo isFolio=true || echo isFolio=false # repoHasContent — does the tree hold somebody's project, as opposed to being bare? # Ignore VCS bookkeeping and editor droppings; count anything else. git ls-files | grep -vE '^\.(git|github|vscode|idea)/' | head -1 . statedIntent is the third, and it is a fact about the conversation: one of new-repo, overlay, add-folio, new-content, or unstated. It is unstated until the user has actually said which — never inferred from tone, from the repo, or from what would be convenient. A user who says “I want to add a chapter” has stated new-content; a user who says “create a folio” has stated nothing, because that sentence is what the five requests have in common. isFolio is ONE MEMBERSHIP of a set, and the set is what a repository is. describeRepository() (schemas/content/content-type.ts) returns every marker a repository carries — folio, harness, dak, sushi — with the facts each states and any disagreement between them. describeRepositoryClosure() (schemas/kg/harness-config.ts) extends that through the dependency tree, attributing each membership to the layer that carried it. folio and harness are different types. The declaration says this is a layer; a config that declares contentType says this authors folio content. That config is a root <name>.config.json, or its entry in index.config.json, where inline fields overlay the imported file (index-config). Listing a layer in the index makes it instantiated, not a folio. cat-harness/ carries the first and not the second — it is a harness and is not a folio. isFolio is exactly membership of folio: the DMN documents the input as a config in the working directory that declares a contentType, not its mere presence. So a repository being several things at once does not perturb the five branches. They key on folio-ness alone, and a folio that is also a DAK takes the same branch as one that is not — it is still already a folio, still has content, and the user has still either stated an intent or not. Use describeRepository when you want to know what a repository is; this probe when you want to know which branch to take. isFolio is about the working directory, not about the user. Somebody who has used folio-assistant before, in another repo, is still in an isFolio=false directory. Their experience is not a fact this table reads — it changes how much you explain, not which branch you take.

757.title: 2. Let the table decide
757.content: Feed the three facts to workflow_complete on Gateway_Intent, or read folio-intent.dmn directly. Do not supply an outcome: the gateway is computed, and workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied answer there on purpose. The table returns one of five branches. Two of its seven rules return ask, and that is a result, not a failure to produce one: . | already a folio, intent unstated → ask. add-folio, new-repo and new-content are all consistent with what is on disk. | not a folio but has content, intent unstated → ask. overlay and new-repo are both consistent, and overlaying somebody’s repository on a guess is not recoverable by a git checkout. | not a folio, nothing here → new-repo. The one state that answers itself. | .

758.title: 3. Ask — as options, never as prose
758.content: When the branch is ask, put the question as a short list of selectable options. Not a paragraph, not an open “what would you like to do?”, and not a question whose answer has to be typed out. Load interaction-modality first; it decides the form the question takes, and for some users free text is not an available input at all. The list, phrased in the user’s terms rather than the branch names: . | Start a new folio in a new repository — nothing here gets touched. | Add folio-assistant to this repository — keeps what is here; I’ll look through it first and show you what I find before importing anything. | Add another folio to this repository (offer only when isFolio=true). | Add something to the folio that’s already here (only when isFolio=true) — a chapter, a document, a DAK component. | Tell me more — for the user who wants to describe it in their own words. | . Then ask what they want to get started on, offering the top-level content types this platform knows about, because “a folio” is not something anybody actually wants: . | content type | what it is | profile | . | paper | a scientific paper or book, with formal claims backed by Lean and typeset through LaTeX | paper | . | document | structured prose — policy guidance, a standard, a report. No Lean, no required TeX | document | . | WHO SMART DAK | a Digital Adaptation Kit (L2): personas, business processes, data elements, decision tables | dak | . | WHO SMART IG | a FHIR Implementation Guide (L3) built from an L2 DAK | dak | . Record the answer as statedIntent and evaluate the table again. The user’s answer is a fact like any other — it feeds the gateway, so the loop in the diagram runs back to Task_ReadFacts rather than jumping straight to a branch. When a remote repository is involved, ask which mode — and never infer it from push access. A remote git repository is assumed read-only (read-from). Having push access to a remote is never permission to modify it, and instantiating on a remote repository writes nothing there without the user’s explicit permission for that repository. Ask which mode they want, with materialize-or-reference as its own question: . | Keep it here (read-from) — build and render from the remote KG in this repository (stage-ig-sites into /<instance>/), and ask whether to materialize its assets locally or reference it in place (materialize-remote / materialize-on-demand). | Put a harness on the remote repository (written-to) — instantiate the harness in that remote repository itself and build in its own CI (stage-ig-sites --only <instance> --source .), only after explicit permission for that repository. | .

759.title: 4. Route
759.content: | branch | do | . | new-repo | Ask for the name. Create or use the empty directory, then folio_init. | . | overlay | Hand off to repo-conversion — scan first, import second, and never in the other order. The scan’s markers are offered as picks (§2a, Task_ChooseHarnessed): the harness declares only what the person chose — declare, don’t slurp. | . | add-folio | folio_init against a new top-level slug in the existing layer. Do not re-link the platform; it is already linked. | . | new-content | Stop. This process ends here. Hand off to the active content type’s authoring skill. Scaffolding anything on this branch is the bug. | . An empty repository gets main before any feature branch. GitHub makes the first branch pushed to an empty repository its default, so run init-folio (it seeds main first) or push main yourself before pushing anything else. A specialised content type is routed by its own creation skill. When the answer to step 3’s second question names a domain content type shipped by a higher harness layer, hand over to that layer’s creation skill (discover it via skill_list). It reads the same facts and adds the in-repository staged sub-KG option — staging inside the current repository first so nothing outside the repository changes until the owner confirms. Where folio_init does not handle that content type directly, the new-repository route scaffolds with --instance. A second folio can leave later. What add-folio creates, and any staged sub-KG, may later move to a repository of its own. That is sub-kg-lifecycle: stage it in place, then create the repository and delete the in-repo copy, each only on the owner’s confirmation.

760.title: 5. After scaffolding — seed the plan, then publish
760.content: . | Seed the work plan. One work item per top-level thing the author named in step 3. Run the exact-title existence check in todo-manager.md §”Check before you create” first — beans create is not idempotent. | Provision gh-pages — before Pages is switched on. This is Task_ProvisionGhPages in the process, and it carries the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn (the gh-pages Tool’s subprocess — render-kg-to-cdn): a gh-pages branch must exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision: it checks git ls-remote --heads origin gh-pages and, only if the branch is absent, pushes an orphan gh-pages holding a placeholder index.html and .nojekyll. It is idempotent and never forces a push; without --provision the script creates no remote branch, it only reports unprovisioned with the exact command. Then switch Pages on with Source: “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — not “GitHub Actions”, when the publish workflow pushes gh-pages (the script prints the source it expects). Every publishing route reaches this step: new-repo, add-folio, and the overlay route through repo-conversion — including an overlay or new repo that remote-mounts its dependencies, which never reaches this section by itself. | Start the Pages build and report the URL. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --wait. It checks the branch first, derives the site address, says whether a publish workflow exists and which Pages source it needs, and probes until the site answers. | Say which of the four states you got, and never blur them: . | unprovisioned — there is no gh-pages branch (exit 3). Go back to step 2; nothing later can succeed until it exists. | live — hand over the link, and say what is on it. | not-yet — a measured 404. Give the address, say the first build has not landed there yet, and say roughly how long it takes. | unknown — no URL could be derived, or the probe failed. Say that. “Should be live shortly” is a claim you do not have evidence for. | . | Tell them the corpus is by reference, and how to change that. A fresh harness holds references, not the remote content itself, which can be hundreds of gigabytes. When they need part of a remote subgraph locally, that is an ask made later, as the need appears. Name the skill (materialize-on-demand) and the one command that shows what is already held (bun run cat cache:index), so they learn the option exists here rather than by finding a schema. Do not materialize anything now. | .

761.title: 6. Anti-patterns
761.content: . | Scaffolding on ask. The table returned a question; answering it yourself with the convenient branch defeats the table. | Treating “I’ve used this before” as add-folio. Experience is not a filesystem fact and not an intent. | Asking in prose. “Could you tell me a bit about what you’re hoping to build?” is a wall for a user who types with difficulty, and it produces a worse answer than the numbered list. | Announcing a Pages URL you have not probed. See step 5. | Going straight to folio_init because the request seemed obvious. Every one of the five requests seems obvious to the person making it. | Switching Pages on before gh-pages exists, or choosing “GitHub Actions” as the source for a workflow that pushes gh-pages. Step 2 first; the source is “Deploy from a branch”. | .

On the overlay path it declares in index.config.json exactly the markers picked at Task_ChooseHarnessed, and none it was not given. Refuses rather than overwrites when a folio is already present. | . | Seed the work planTask_SeedPlan | Onboarding agent (system) | todo-manager | The first beans: what the author said they want to get started on, one bean per top-level content object they named. | . | Provision gh-pagesTask_ProvisionGhPages | Publish — GitHub Pages | getting-started | Before Pages is switched on, make sure the gh-pages branch exists — the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn, first half. git ls-remote --heads origin gh-pages; if absent, bun run cat-harness/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision pushes an orphan gh-pages holding a placeholder index.html and .nojekyll (idempotent; never forced; the script creates no remote branch without the flag). Then Settings → Pages → “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — not “GitHub Actions” when the publish workflow pushes gh-pages. 769.title: GitHub Pages’ contract
769.content: Skill github-pages: The contract GitHub Pages keeps as the host of a rendered Knowledge Graph: serve the gh-pages branch at the publication root URL, exactly as committed, and answer 404 for what is not there. A mechanical Actor plays this Role; this is what it must do, and what it is tested against. Named by: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages . A host plays a Role, and this is the Role’s contract: what it must do, and what it is tested against. It decides nothing. pages-status is the test: it asks the publication root URL and each document address, and reports pushed, not-pushed or could-not-determine. It sits in the GitHub Pages lane of render-kg-to-github-pages. The Site Publisher, following render-kg-to-github-pages, is the other side of each step.

770.title: Responsibilities
770.content: . | Serve the gh-pages branch at /, once Pages is on with that source. | Serve what is committed. After a deployment commit, the publication root URL, its README.html and every document address answer with the committed files. | Answer 404 for what is not there, so a missing page is a failure a check can see, not an empty success. | .

771.title: Not its responsibility
771.content: Choosing the root URL or the Subgraphs, staging, or deciding whether a push landed. Those happen in the Site Publisher’s lane.

772.title: github-pages (skill)
772.content: The skill github-pages as its source file bootstrap-tools/skills/github-pages.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

773.title: Glossary terms
773.content: Skill glossary-terms: Add terms to a layer’s glossary: local SKOS terms (folio-glossary/v1) with a definition, a code and links to external SKOS concepts, and references to whole external schemes. Rendered on the glossary/ page; gated by check:glossary. Authored terms go to gettext (.pot) for translation; a paper’s glossary is one more scheme. Named by: Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Classify and code content . A glossary can reference external SKOS schemes, and that is the preferred way.

774.title: Where terms go
774.content: Core declares the glossary directory in folio-assistant-core.json. Its graph typology is perInstance, so every folio built on core has a glossary/. Each *.glossary.json is one SKOS concept scheme, $schema: "folio-glossary/v1" (folio-assistant-core/schemas/glossary.ts).

775.title: Reference first, define second
775.content: | you have | write | . | a term somebody else already defines in SKOS (ISCO-08, an EU authority table, a W3C vocabulary) | a local term with exactMatch (or closeMatch, broadMatch, narrowMatch) to the external concept IRI. Do not copy its definition. | . | a list of external terms this folio uses | members: the external concept IRIs, emitted as a skos:Collection | . | a whole external scheme | a remoteGraphs entry in the declaration with graphTypologies: ["glossary"]: known about, not held | . | a term only this folio defines | a local term with prefLabel, definition, and notation for its code | .

776.title: Three states, never two
776.content: . | authored: a person wrote or approved the definition. It must have one. | candidate: extracted from a source and not yet curated. It may have no definition, and the page marks it. | could-not-extract: the source names a term the extractor could not read. It carries a reason a person can act on. | . A candidate is never presented as a definition. An extractor writes candidates; only a person moves one to authored. A paper’s definition block counts as that person: its author wrote the definition and marked it (see “A paper’s glossary” below).

777.title: How a term is linked: the workflow
777.content: Terms are linked across the glossary, the narrative and the knowledge graph with a few shared joins, not a framework. One join key: the SKOS term (its id, or its IRI from another layer). Everything else points at it, and nothing copies it. | thing | how it names the term | . | the defining site | the term’s source: its glossary row (an L1 section line, or the document’s glossary table block). One node-kind structure for every term. | . | a narrative block that explains the term at length | the block’s defines: [<term id>] (and :defterm[...]{#id} inline). Provenance, not a second definition. | . | other uses in prose | nothing to write: matched at build time (term-passages.ts) and linked by --link-terms | . | an acronym | notation on the term, never a second list. The acronyms table is drawn from it (glossary:table). | . | an organization | focus (W3C ORG), shared ones in smart-ra organizations.glossary.json | . | an ArchiMate element | the element’s skosConcept property (glossary-archimate.ts) | . | a BPMN lane or task, DMN decision, skill, Tool | the generated candidate schemes (glossary-extract.ts); exactMatch when one is the same concept | . | a FHIR code | exactMatch / closeMatch to the CodeSystem concept; the code stays a CodeSystem | . | an external glossary | exactMatch to its IRI, members, or a whole scheme in remoteGraphs | . Where terms come from. | Ingesting a source (L1, DTH, DAK): bun run cat glossary:from-source reads its glossary and abbreviations sections into verbatim candidate terms with source: <file>#L<line> (l1-document-ingestion). No per-handbook script. | Authoring in the narrative (dth-hrh): the glossary file is edited, and the chapter is drawn from it (glossary:table, or the folio’s own build). A block that explains a term lists it in defines. | External: reference, don’t copy (below). | . What a reader gets. Every authored-scheme term has a page (glossary:page, glossary/instance/<instance>/<scheme>/<term>/). It shows the definition and acronym, Defined in (its glossary row), broader, narrower (computed), related terms, matches, ArchiMate elements, and In the narrative: the blocks that explain it, then those that use it. A Capitalized label in prose links to that page when the document build passes --link-terms, which dth-init sets for every DTH. Warnings, never failures. bun run cat glossary:links reports a source that is missing from a mounted layer, and a defines id that no scheme holds. With --all it also lists terms the narrative never uses. The acronym report is glossary:acronyms.

778.title: Conventions
778.content: Every folio follows these; none re-decides them. The layer namespace. A term’s IRI is <instance namespace>glossary/<scheme id>/<term id>. The layer namespace is built from the layer’s declaration (iriBase, version, and the stub of a sub-layer) by instanceNs in folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-page.ts; schemeIri and termIri are in folio-assistant-core/schemas/glossary.ts. For example: . | layer | namespace | . | folio-assistant-core | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/ | . | ihris (its own site) | https://litlfred.github.io/ihris/ihris/ns/ | . The namespace is never the asset’s path: moving the asset must not move the term. A term is minted by the layer that owns its source. A scheme and its terms live in the namespace of the layer whose root holds the SOURCE ASSET, not of the layer whose glossary/ directory holds the file: . | In a folio with sub-layers, that is the sub-layer (instanceNs(<sub-stub>), under the folio’s own publication root). It is never the root layer, even when the glossary/ directory is declared at the root. In ihris, a term drawn from ihris-manage is minted in ihris-manage’s namespace, not ihris’s. | A code list extended by several packages belongs to the layer that DEFINES it. Say so with the scheme’s own source (a repository path in that layer). Each term’s source still points at the package that contributed it. | A scheme whose terms are sourced in several layers and that names no defining source is refused, never guessed: split it, one scheme per layer. folio-assistant-core/glossary/ holds two platform schemes for that reason, core’s and cat-harness’s. | No two layers share a namespace, and a scheme IRI is unique across every layer. | . check:glossary enforces all of this (schemeOwner and collect in glossary-page.ts, and the checks in glossary.test.ts); glossary-extract.ts mints extracted terms by the same rule. When a check fails, fix the generator or split the authored scheme. Never edit the output. One ConceptScheme per code list. This follows schemas/code-list.ts (codeListToSkos): “a code is addressable and two lists may share a code without sharing a concept”. The same code in two lists gives two concepts. A relation between them is a SKOS match, never a merge. The basis of a match is recorded, never assumed. A match comes from a mapping the repository verified, such as a FHIR ConceptMap whose equivalence implies one: . | equal/equivalent gives exactMatch; | wider/subsumes gives broadMatch; | narrower/specializes gives narrowMatch; | nothing else gives a match. | . Any other basis needs the owner’s explicit acceptance. One example is a ValueSet that binds a local code list to the external code system itself, so that the local code is the external code. Once accepted: . | the scheme’s description names the basis and the ruling; | the builder lists the accepted systems explicitly; | QA recomputes the matches from the same source. | . ihris’s ISCO-08 lists to ESCO are the worked example. An IRI built from a publisher’s pattern but never dereferenced says so.

779.title: Then
779.content: bun run cat glossary:page writes the index, docs/glossary/index.md (the authored terms with A–Z and a filter box, the counts, the sources, schema.org DefinedTermSet JSON-LD, and a link to every asset type’s page), one page per asset type at docs/glossary/<type>/index.md (skills, tools, bpmn-activities, dmn-decisions, schema-fields: that type’s extracted terms, with A–Z and a filter box), and one SKOS JSON-LD file per scheme under docs/assets/glossary/. Each term is on exactly one page. bun run check:glossary is the gate: it fails on a document that does not validate, on a stale page, and on a page over its size budget (64 KB for the index, 1 MB for an asset type’s page). A page over budget is split further, never given a bigger budget. The harness’s swimlane-role terms (swimlane-glossary, the swimlane-glossary skill) are one more source the page links to, not copies of.

780.title: Extracted terms
780.content: glossary:page also extracts a candidate term from every knowledge-graph asset that carries a title and a description (folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-extract.ts): skills, Tool nodes, BPMN tasks and call activities, DMN decisions, and schema fields with a doc comment. One scheme per asset type per layer (kg-skills, kg-tools, kg-bpmn-activities, kg-dmn-decisions, kg-schema-fields), written to generated/<instance>/<type>.glossary.json inside core’s glossary/. | They are generated. Never edit them: fix the asset, then re-run. | The kg- scheme prefix is reserved for them. An authored scheme that takes it fails check:glossary. | A definition is the asset’s own text, verbatim. An asset with no description gives a candidate with no definition. | To promote one, author a term in a glossary of your own with a definition you have checked, status: authored, and the same source. | BPMN lanes and roles are not extracted: the swimlane ledger carries them. | Extracted terms are on their asset type’s page, never on the index, and each carries the “candidate, extracted” badge. Only authored terms go into the schema.org DefinedTermSet, which is on the index. | .

781.title: Ordered glossaries — logical order, not A–Z
781.content: Some glossaries (bootstrap’s, for one) are read top to bottom: each term is defined only by terms above it, and never by itself. Do not sort them A–Z. | ordered: true on a glossary says its terms array IS the order. Each term’s requires lists the local ids its definition uses; the schema refuses one that is later, itself, or not in the glossary. checkDeclaredOrder (schemas/dependency-order.ts) is the same check for any authored order. | In SKOS the order is a skos:OrderedCollection (memberList as an RDF list), each use is dcterms:requires, and isDefinedBy — the schema or standard that defines the term — is rdfs:isDefinedBy. | On the page an ordered scheme is its own numbered section at the top of the index, with its “Uses” links, and is not repeated under the A–Z bar. | A schema whose $defs carry uses IS an ordered glossary, read by termsOfSchema in glossary-page.ts: the definitions stay in one place, the schema, and the glossary cannot drift from it. They are authored, not candidate: a person wrote and approved them in the schema’s source, and the collector only reads them out. | The uses list is authored, not inferred. A text matcher over the definitions is a guard that the list and the prose agree (graph.test.ts); a word can appear without being used as a term. | .

782.title: Translation: authored terms only
782.content: bun run cat glossary:pot writes one gettext template per scheme that has an authored term, to translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.pot under cat-harness’s declared translation-sources directory, beside the BPMN templates in processes/, through the same pipeline (formatPot, the same timestamp-blind comparison); the translation status page counts them. bun run cat glossary:pot:check is the gate. | Only authored terms are extracted: prefLabel, each altLabel, and the definition, in the source language (en when given per language). A candidate reaches a template once a person promotes it. | The term’s IRI is the translator comment, never a msgid. It stays the same in every language; only labels and definitions are translated. | translations/<locale>/glossary.po is a different file (terminology hints for translation-block-qa). Do not confuse it with the glossary/ directory. | . Translations and the per-locale pages . A translation is a .po beside its template: translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po. bun run glossary:page reads every such file (readGlossaryTranslations, through glossary-pot.ts’s potPath) and produces two things: . | a page per locale, docs/<locale>/glossary/index.md, listing every authored term with its translated label, alternative labels and definition. An entry with no translation shows the source text marked (untranslated) — never silently English, never dropped — and the page states how many terms are fully translated; | language-tagged SKOS: the published <instance>--<scheme>.skos.jsonld carries skos:prefLabel and skos:definition once per language (@language), the source as en. | . check:glossary covers both, stale and orphan alike. A translation is UNOFFICIAL until a person signs it off. Every glossary .po says so in its header and records Last-Translator: folio-assistant agent (drafted, unofficial) when an agent drafted it; every locale page carries translation_status: unverified. Keep code, identifiers and standard names (BPMN, SKOS, ODRL, PROV-O, JSON, IRI, $schema, needs) as written, and give each capitalised defined term ONE rendering per locale across every scheme. Subject areas and fixed translations . Owner, 2026-11-07 (glossary review, “scoped fixed terms”). Three fields and one rule, in schemas/glossary.ts: . | field | where | meaning | . | subject | scheme, optionally a term | the subject area the translations bind in (dcterms:subject), a local id: harness-vocabulary, digital-health-trust, who-health-guidance. A term’s overrides its scheme’s; with neither, the term binds only within its own scheme. | . | translationStatus | term | per locale, official or unofficial; a locale not listed is unofficial. It records sign-off, never the translation. | . | (none) | the scheme’s .po | the translation itself. | . A fixed translation is derived, never flagged: an authored term whose scheme catalogue holds a non-empty, non-fuzzy msgstr for its prefLabel (isFixedTranslation). There is no #, fixed flag and no label in the JSON, so the .po stays the one place a translation lives. Precedence applies within a subject area. Across the layers a layer needs, the more authoritative (lower) layer fixes a term’s translation for its subject area, and a higher layer only adds. A match in a different subject area — the harness’s policy (策略) in a health guide’s sentence (政策) — is a sense check note for a person, never a violation. translation:glossary:check reads these fields. Use scopeNote for the prose a reader needs; it is never compared.

783.title: Source glossary first
783.content: When a folio is written from a source document (a WHO handbook, say), its terms come from that source’s own glossary before anyone writes one. | Latest edition. Use the most recent edition in the library. If it lacks something an older edition has, use the older one and say so on the term. | Verbatim, as candidates. Extract every glossary entry as a folio-glossary/v1 term, status candidate, the definition copied word for word with its page. Keep the source’s spelling as an altLabel when the prefLabel is normalised. | Read the PDF when the ingest missed it. A glossary the library entry does not hold (a missed section, a missing indicator sheet) is read from the PDF, and the scheme says so. | Structure the source gives is kept. Modules, indicators and the like become concepts too, linked (broader, related) to the glossary terms they cite. | Record what the source never defines. A term the source uses but does not define is a candidate with no definition and a scopeNote saying so, not a definition we write. | Place the scheme with the source. It lives beside the document’s library entry (for WHO publications, in the WHO publications IG), so every folio that cites the source shares one scheme. | Use the source’s words downstream. Blocks, diagrams and ArchiMate names use the source’s terms and link to their concepts, not a paraphrase. | . A conflict between the source’s definition and another scheme’s is raised as an issue on the repository that owns the other scheme, quoting both. Neither is chosen by the agent.

784.title: Deprecating a term: a change set, decided later
784.content: Replacing one term with another (for example “Core Data Element” replacing “MDS-HRH”) is proposed, not applied. The agent records a change set with the old term, the new term, the reason, and every place the old term appears. It changes no text and no glossary entry. An agent review, started later by an editor, decides it. Once decided: . | the old term stays in the scheme, so old links still resolve, with a scopeNote saying it is deprecated and why, and related to the new term (folio-glossary/v1 has no deprecated status yet; adding one is a schema change, not part of this rule); | the folio’s own prose moves to the new term; | quoted source text is never changed: a quote keeps the term it was published with. | .

785.title: A paper’s glossary
785.content: The paper builder (folio-assistant-core/scripts/build-glossary.ts, skill glossary-build) also writes the paper’s terms as one folio-glossary/v1 scheme, paper-<paper directory>, into the glossary directory the paper’s OWN layer declares. The page picks it up through collect() like any other scheme, so the IRIs are in that layer’s namespace (a sub-layer’s for a paper in a sub-layer, never the root’s). | the owning block | its :defterm paragraph | status | . | kind: "definition" | found | authored: the author wrote the definition | . | any other kind | found | candidate: extracted from a theorem, remark, … | . | any | not found | could-not-extract, with the reason | . The definition is the :defterm paragraph, verbatim, with directives replaced by their labels. The slug is the term’s notation. Never edit the scheme: edit the paper and re-run the builder. A layer that declares no glossary directory gets a notice and no scheme; add { "id": "glossary", "path": "glossary/", "dependents": "reproduce", "graphTypologies": ["glossary"] }.

786.title: Organizations and acronyms
786.content: An organization (WHO, HL7, ISO, GS1, a national regulator) is a glossary term like any other, plus a focus: SKOS’s foaf:focus link from the concept to the organization, which is typed with W3C ORG. The concept keeps the words: prefLabel is the full name, notation is the acronym, and altLabel holds other spellings. The organization keeps the facts about the organization. { "id": "who", "prefLabel": "World Health Organization", "notation": "WHO", "definition": "…quoted from its source…", "status": "candidate", "focus": { "type": "FormalOrganization", "homepage": "https://www.who.int/", "subOrganizationOf": ["un"] } } . | type is a W3C ORG class: Organization, FormalOrganization, OrganizationalUnit or OrganizationalCollaboration. | subOrganizationOf names a local term that has a focus, or an organization’s IRI. sameAs links the same organization in another register, such as ROR or Wikidata. Give an identifier only when you have checked it; never guess one. | Without iri, the organization’s IRI is <term IRI>/_focus. | . One home per organization. An organization that several handbooks use (WHO, HL7, ISO, GS1, UNICEF, USAID) is defined once, in the shared reference architecture’s organizations scheme. A handbook lists it under members and does not copy it. An organization only one handbook names, such as a country’s regulator, stays in that handbook’s glossary. An acronym is scoped to its meaning. Use the document’s own expansion, and check it in context. In the WHO product catalogue handbook, “FDA” is the Rwanda Food and Drugs Authority, not the US Food and Drug Administration. When the document’s acronym would mislead a reader, record it as a candidate and raise it in the document’s review log. Do not fix the quoted text yourself. Finding the acronyms that are missing. The QA criterion acronym-in-glossary warns, block by block, about an acronym that no glossary the folio can see holds as a notation, prefLabel or altLabel. It warns and never fails. For the whole folio, with counts and the expansion the document gives (its abbreviations table, or “Long Name (ACR)”), run: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-acronyms.ts --folio folio . Each row is a candidate for a person to decide on. Words set in capitals (RESOURCES in a figure), plural forms (GTINs) and the folio’s own ids (PC-R-05) are left out.

787.title: Architecture elements: the model drawn from the graph
787.content: A reference architecture’s elements live in the knowledge graph, and the ArchiMate model is drawn from it, with the relationships on each glossary term. A term that names an element is a glossary term like any other, plus a focus that is the element: its ArchiMate type, and its relationships to other terms’ elements. { "id": "client-registry", "prefLabel": "Client Registry", "definition": "…quoted from the document…", "status": "candidate", "focus": { "archimate": "ApplicationComponent", "relationships": [ { "type": "Realization", "target": "client-identification" }, { "type": "Access", "target": "client-record", "accessType": "read" } ] } } . | archimate is the element type, as ArchiMate’s exchange format names it. | relationships[].type is one of ArchiMate 3.2’s eleven. target is a local term whose focus is an element, or an element’s IRI. accessType is only for Access. | In JSON-LD the element is <term IRI>/_focus, typed archimate:<Type>, and each relationship is a predicate such as archimate:serving. | . The Tool archimate-from-glossary (bun run cat archimate:from-glossary --instance <dir> --model <id> [--write] [--prune] [--check]) makes the model agree. It matches each element by its skosConcept property, never by name. It names and documents the element from the term, creates any element the model lacks (on no view: place it in Archi, or with archimate-detangle), and adds the relationships the terms list. A type that disagrees is reported, and a person decides. A relationship between linked elements that no term lists is removed only with --prune. Archi keeps the layout: no box moves. Its report counts the elements that still point at no term. An authored ArchiMate model is never a source of the glossary. Never write a term, label, definition, focus or relationship into a glossary from a model someone authored in Archi. The words come from the source documents; the model only depicts them. The one exception is a model that was ingested: received from elsewhere and held as a source under the layer’s library/. Such a model can seed the glossary once with --seed --from library/<entry>/<file>.archimate (--write to write). Every term an element of it already points at, and that has no focus yet, takes the element’s type and its relationships to the other linked elements. From then on, the glossary is the source. The Tool refuses --seed on any model outside library/. The read-only “depicted by” links on a term’s page (glossary-archimate) read the model’s skosConcept on each build and write nothing into the glossary, so they are allowed.

788.title: Not here
788.content: A clinical code system is FHIR CodeSystem/ValueSet, not a glossary: convergence stops at SKOS. A glossary term may exactMatch a clinical concept; it does not become one.

789.title: glossary-terms (skill)
789.content: The skill glossary-terms as its source file folio-assistant-core/skills/library/cataloguing/glossary-terms.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

790.title: Graph detanglement — the practice, not the migration
790.content: Skill graph-detanglement: Drive a tangled graph toward a clean partition, so a sub-graph can be split off when it grows too large or when a business reason separates it. The staged practice — declare in place, detangle, isolate, extract — and the seventeen moves for measurement, ordering, judgement and enforcement. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: graph-detanglement · Package: graph-management . A repository grows until part of it wants to leave. Sometimes the reason is size, sometimes it is semantic — “split only where consumers or cadences differ” (docs/concepts/architecture/migration-plan.md). Either way the move is the same and the mistake is the same: treating the split as a migration to be executed rather than a practice to be run. This skill is the practice. Its subject is any graph with directed edges whose nodes are being partitioned: TypeScript modules into repositories, blocks into chapters, skills into packages.

791.title: The one rule, at four scales
791.content: At block scale — pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts, the detangler-no-dependency-cycle criterion: . “a cycle is reorder-invariant — when two blocks each uses: the other, or a longer loop closes, NO chapter ordering removes the forward edge. A cycle signals a genuine structural tangle: prune one dependency edge, merge the mutually-defining blocks, or factor the shared content into a third block both depend on.” . At repository scale — scripts/repo-partition.ts, the gate’s own failure message: . “A repo may not import one that depends on it. Either the CLASSIFICATION is wrong — check the target’s layer before the importer’s — or the import is.” . At knowledge-graph scale — kg-detangle.ts (bun run cat kg:detangle), over the layer stack each <instance>.json declares in needs. The repository and knowledge-graph scales share ONE verdict function, schemas/kg/layer-direction.ts. An edge is wrong-direction exactly when its target layer is not among what the source layer declares it may reach — ALLOWED for repos, needs plus itself for layers — and no reasoned permit names it. A layer with no needs is undetermined, reported in its own column, never read as clean. The function stops at direction: whether an allowed edge is a restatement or essential is the adjudicator’s call, so those edges stay unclassified with the verdict as their basis. The direction count is the one detangle number that is GRADED, and it is graded in a gate of its own — bun run cat kg:detangle:direction, blocking in CI. Everything else this tool measures stays pinned: kg:detangle:check fails on a stale or orphaned sidecar and never on a number, because the carve is an adjudication a person makes and grading it would be the tool overruling the adjudicator. A module’s bucket is taste. An edge whose target layer is not among what the source layer’s <instance>.json says it may reach is a contradiction between two declarations, which no adjudication makes consistent, so it is the one thing here a machine may refuse. Two flags, two scripts, two CI steps, so a red run says which question broke. Two things that gate reports and refuses to grade, both because grading them would be grading a could-not-determine: . | undetermined edges — an endpoint’s layer declares no needs. Failing on these would be the gate deciding a layering nobody declared. | the denominator — the count is over the edges that resolve. Dangling refs are excluded before any edge is classified, so a 0 is “0 among the edges that resolve”. The gate prints the excluded count and its breakdown, so a pass cannot hide an edge that failed to resolve. | . It is not check:partition’s second opinion. That tool’s root is one layer, so it partitions a future layout by path rule among that layer’s own modules; this checks the present layout against declared needs across layers. Either can be green while the other is red, and Phase I.1 of the migration plan needs both. At term scale — a glossary declared ordered (logically tight, non self-referential). Each term’s requires must point UP, and checkDeclaredOrder in schemas/kg/dependency-order.ts names every forward, self and missing use. It is the block-scale rule with terms for blocks: a forward requires is a forward edge, and two terms defined by each other are a cycle no ordering removes, so the moves are the same three — drop the use, merge the two terms, or factor the shared idea into a term above both. The rule and its form on the page are in glossary-terms §”Ordered glossaries”. Same rule, four scales, two vocabularies. Prune, merge, or factor into a third are the only three moves, and “the classification is wrong” is the fourth possibility the block- and term-scale versions do not have because a block’s chapter is not in doubt the way a module’s layer is. Everything below is machinery for finding out which of the four you are looking at.

792.title: The four stages, and each is a gate
792.content: Nothing moves until the stage before it measures zero. The stages are not advice about sequencing; each is a state the graph is in. 1. Declare in place . The sub-graph is declared where it already sits. Still inside the repository, still connected, nothing moved. The declaration gains a directory entry with its graphs[] kinds; a sub-graph that owns its own layout gains a nested declaration (beans/beans.json, todos/todos.json) whose paths resolve against its own directory, so the whole graph relocates by moving one folder. Declaring is cheap and extracting is expensive. The methodology graph typology is defined by exactly this property: “extractable (somebody else’s work, adopted, so it lifts out with its declaration when the field moves on)”. 2. Detangle . Drive cross-edges toward zero. This is the long stage and the rest of this skill is about it. 3. Isolate . The sub-graph carries its own declaration, its own namespace, its own published artefact. bootstrap/ is the demonstrated case: its own declaration, its own bootstrap: namespace — the prefix IS the stub, see kg-export §”A prefix is the stub” — its own graph document. 4. Extract . Only once edges are zero and the declaration stands alone. A directory move rather than a file-by-file sift. The five-point gate is in docs/concepts/architecture/migration-plan.md Phase II and is not restated here. For a Knowledge Graph leaving as its own repositories — a content repository and a tools repository — the rest of the method, from splitting the tools out to the cutover, is kg-separation and its process kg-separation.bpmn.

793.title: The seventeen moves
793.content: Measurement . 1. Read the unassigned column before the edge count. A low edge count over an unclassified corpus is the same false comfort as a green check over an empty one: “these are not cross-edges — they are edges this tool declined to judge. Do not read them as clean.” The same false comfort at a different join is covered-is-not-reachable: a skill showing as covered is not evidence that its code is reachable. Read that skill before concluding a corpus is covered. 2. The count rises when the measurement improves, and that is correct. Folding previously-unjudged edges in raises the wrong-direction count. A detangling count that only ever falls is not being measured honestly. 3. Quote both numbers, not only the one that improved. An edge can move rather than vanish. 4. An assignment is verified by re-running, never by being locally reasonable. The obvious move, even the one the tool’s own message asks for, can raise the count. Ordering . 5. Move the shared target first, then the importers. Classifying leaves before their shared schema targets adds edges; moving the targets first does not. 6. A schema moves with its script, or you mint the edge you meant to retire. 7. Declaration and readers first, files second. Update the declaration and every consumer while the files are still where they are, verify green, and only then git mv. The reverse order makes every gate red at once with no way to tell which failure is which. 8. Some fixes are two steps and only work in one order. Reclassifying handlers alone can make the composition root cross the line to mount them; a step that is edge-neutral by itself (resolving routes by variable specifier) can be what makes the reclassification a net win. Judgement . 9. Read what a module is FOR, never what directory it sits in. Layer is not by directory, and a name says what something is for while an argument list says what it does. 10. The triage question, in either of two equivalent forms. “Does it act on the PLATFORM or on CONTENT?” and “does it need a folio to have anything to do?” A sharper cut: needed to RUN a process is tooling; DESCRIBES one is core. And for the renderable side: if it renders, it is not the harness’s. 11. Check the TARGET’s layer before the importer’s. The gate’s failure text says so. 12. A keyword classifier gives false signals on filenames, and will keep reclaiming. fsh in fsh-guts.ts matches the FHIR-Shorthand keyword; content in content-type.ts sends marker machinery to core. Every keyword assignment is provisional against a read of the module, and removing a misclassification needs an exact entry rather than deleting the old one, because a rule that classifies by name will keep reclaiming it. 13. Inverting a dependency does not remove the edge if the new holder sits in the same layer. 14. The fix is not an exemption, it is the right owner. An exemption is what you write when ownership is genuinely ambiguous, and then it carries its reason inline. Enforcement . 15. A check is an error only once its count is zero, and enforce per axis. Turning a red gate on teaches the next agent to append || true (see the ruff comment in code-quality-gates.yml). 16. Watch the new gate FAIL before trusting it. Re-introduce the defect deliberately and see exit 1. A gate that cannot fail is indistinguishable from one that passed. 17. Merge main before trusting a local green; CI builds the merge ref. A gate that passes locally and fails in CI can be a newer, stricter gate on the merge commit, not flakiness.

794.title: Declare a falsifier, and mean it
794.content: State in advance the result that would show the classification wrong (for example, “if classifying these RAISES the cross-edge count, the classification is wrong rather than the tool”). When it fires, read the new edges rather than arguing them away, and change the plan. A falsifier that never fires is decoration.

795.title: Measurements that are not measurements
795.content: . | A measurement you know to be inconclusive is not a measurement. If an earlier rule (an exact list consulted first) means your change never applied, say the experiment was inconclusive. | An edge that several passes called intractable is an edge nobody read. Open the file before deferring it. | A grep that under-reports reads exactly like a clean result. A pattern like from "\.\./*skills/ cannot match ../../skills/, and an export {} block can hide consumers that tsc finds. | Enumerate dispatch points before proposing a mechanism. It is how you find the ones already built, and as an audit it survives a bad hit rate where a choice between guesses does not. | .

796.title: What the metric will not tell you
796.content: From the editorial side, measured on a real corpus: . “an unconstrained search cleared 66 of 236 forward references — and a narrative review of its 53 moves found 18 of them made the paper worse. Reducing the metric and improving the reading are different objectives, and they diverge often enough that the difference is not a rounding error.” . “Expect the reviewed yield to be roughly a third of what the raw metric promises, and prefer it.” . So: a guard is not an objective. Pinned nodes, atomic families and container boundaries constrain the search, and split and merge are never auto-dischargeable — they rename things and ripple through every reference.

799.title: A sub-graph wants to leave
799.content: Process_GraphDetanglement · strict · 8 step(s) . Part of a repository wants to leave, for size or a semantic reason: four gated stages measure it out of the graph before anything moves, and an administrator authorises the extraction. THE FOUR STAGES ARE GATES, NOT ADVICE: nothing moves until the stage before it measures zero, and they are drawn because a rule in prose is one an agent under pressure talks itself past. Each gate here is a DECISION TABLE: workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome at a cat-harness.processes:decision gateway, so the branch is computed from the counts a tool already produced rather than asserted. THE SHARPEST GATE IS Detangled?, AND IT IS SHARP BECAUSE OF ITS RULE ORDER. unassignedEdges &gt; 0 returns unknown BEFORE the cross-edge rule is reached, so a zero cross-edge count over an unjudged corpus cannot be read as a pass: unassigned edges are edges the tool declined to judge, not clean ones. A person can skip that rule; a table cannot. EVERY GATE HAS A THIRD STATE AND NONE OF THEM RENDERS IT AS CLEAN. Declared in place? answers unknown on a declaration that did not parse rather than “not yet”, because one says the work has not started and the other says nobody can tell. Detangled? answers unknown on an incomplete measurement. Both route to End_Unknown, which is a REFUSAL to advance — the process stops rather than proceeding on a guess. DECLARING IS CHEAP AND EXTRACTING IS EXPENSIVE, WHICH IS THE POINT. Stage 1 moves nothing: the sub-graph is declared where it already sits, still inside the repository, still connected. STAGE 2 IS A LOOP, AND THE LOOP IS LOAD-BEARING. Prune, merge, factor, or reclassify returns to Measure rather than to the gate, because an assignment is verified by RE-RUNNING and never by being locally reasonable. The four moves are the only four: the first three are the block-scale rule, and “the classification is wrong” is the fourth the repository scale adds because a module’s layer is in doubt the way a block’s chapter is not. ISOLATION IS NOT ZERO EDGES. A sub-graph with no inbound edges can still carry no declaration, no namespace and no published artefact, and lifting that directory produces a repository that cannot say what it is. bootstrap/ is the demonstrated case and the shape to match. THE EXTRACTION IS A PERSON’S DECISION, AND THE LANE SAYS SO. Authorise the extraction sits in the Administrator lane because an extraction moves durable artefacts out of a repository, and deletion-requires-confirmation is not a courtesy the agent may waive: the agent reports what would move, and waits. The administrator lane is the one whose activities change the substrate every other diagram’s lanes bind to, which is exactly what a repository cut does. i i i i i i i i
