805.title: Graph rendering: one set of rules for every drawn graph
805.content: Skill graph-rendering: Draw any graph in a harness (schemas, processes, a folio’s block graph and any formal relation its content type adds, a detangle partition) so the picture is derived, checkable and readable. Ten rules, which engine to lay a graph out with and why, and how each graph typology here applies them. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . Skill id: graph-rendering · Package: graph-management . One set of rules applies to every drawn graph, so that each drawing does not follow conventions of its own. This skill is the general part. It says what any drawing of a graph owes its reader. The per-graph skills say how one generator meets it: uml-overview for schemas, bpmn-authoring for processes, and content-graph for a folio’s blocks. A drawing is how a person READS a graph. graph-detanglement is how the graph is RESTRUCTURED, and it needs the drawing: a partition you cannot see is a partition you argue about from numbers alone.

806.title: The ten rules
806.content: The failure each rule prevents is stated beside it. | Draw from a declared graph, never by hand. Every node and edge in the picture is read from a source: a schema, a declaration, a BPMN file, a uses[] list, a dependency cache. A wrong picture is fixed at its source. A hand-edited diagram is overwritten on the next run, and a check fails while it is stale. | Groups are declared sub-graphs. A box around nodes is a named sub-graph (a directories[] entry, a chapter, a package), never a grouping the renderer invented. | No empty box without a reason. A node drawn with nothing in it reads as a rendering fault. A node with no fields to show carries one line saying why. A node whose shape could not be determined is drawn dashed, as a finding, never as a quiet empty shape. | Edge kinds are drawn distinctly and never merged. A graph has more than one kind of edge (edge-kinds-and-blast-radius). Editorial uses[] and a content type’s formal edges, enforced and prose-only references, and a field-carried link versus one declared elsewhere (the UML’s dashed bootstrap.processes:skill edge) each get their own line style and a legend. Merging two kinds into one line destroys the signal every metric on that graph is computed from. | Pick the layout engine by what the graph is, and write down why. See §”Layout engines” below. The choice is a claim with a measurement behind it, not a taste. | Offer two orientations from one source. A tall graph on a wide screen and a wide graph on a phone are both unreadable. Derive the second view from the first (landscapeOf in scripts/plantuml-render.ts) rather than keeping two sources that can drift apart. | Declare colour once. Colour a node by its family (for the UML: schema, scenario, process, state, test) in one stylesheet, and have every renderer read that stylesheet (uml-palette.ts). A second palette is a second answer free to disagree with the first. | Stamp the output with its source’s hash. A rendering whose staleness check needs the renderer is a check CI cannot run: Java, a browser, or a font set that measures text a pixel differently. Write the sha256 of the exact source text into the output and compare stamps. The UML and block-graph SVGs do this through scripts/plantuml-render.ts, which every PlantUML generator shares, with its pinned jar and one JVM for all diagrams. | Show it in a zoomable figure. On the site, use the bpmn-figure markup so docs-ui.js adds zoom, reset and full-width controls, and the export ones: download the SVG, download a 2× PNG, or copy it (as an image where the browser allows, else as SVG text, and it says which). A pages template missing layout: default renders with no site script and so no controls, and nothing reports it. There is ONE viewer, and every diagram on a folio or IG page gets it. It is mountFigure in docs-ui.js; mountFigures decides what is a figure. Do not write a second one for a new kind of page. Extend what mountFigures and inlineDiagrams recognise instead. It takes each way a page embeds a drawing: . | embedded as | taken by | where it appears | . | .bpmn-figure markup | always | the process pages | . | an inline <svg> | always (an icon-sized one, or one inside a link or nav, is not a figure) | Mermaid, an IG’s {% include x.svg %} (PlantUML) | . | <img src="x.svg"> | always; inlined first | UML overviews, workflow figures | . | <object data="x.svg"> | always; inlined first, and its fallback text becomes the name | the IG Publisher’s convention for a pre-rendered diagram | . | a raster <img> | only on a page that opts in with data-fa-figure-images, and only when the column has shrunk it | an IG’s .drawio.png architecture drawings | . The raster row is an opt-in because a raster image on the platform’s own pages is as often a card face or a photo. A site build that knows its images are drawings stamps the attribute on the page. The IG site build does this on every IG page, and its own skill (ig-site-links) says where. This skill names no layer, because the viewer belongs to the platform. At 100% a plain figure is shown at its own width, capped at the column. It is not stretched to fill the column. A figure that is wider than its column scrolls inside its card and never runs past the page’s edge. The viewer is keyboard-operable, because the profile is low-dexterity. Drag-to-pan is an accelerator, never the only way to pan (board-windows §”The floor”). The figure takes focus (Tab from its toolbar). While it has focus, the arrow keys pan it, + and - zoom, and 0 resets. An arrow key is taken only when the figure can scroll in that direction. Otherwise the page scrolls as usual. The tools layer’s test/ig-diagram-viewer.e2e.ts checks all of this on a fixture page. | Put the measurement on the drawing. When a graph is being partitioned, show each group’s detangle numbers (size, cohesion, links in and out) beside the group, so the picture and the metric are read together. The UML overview pages do this through detangleResultsDir (schemas/kg/detangle-sidecar.ts), the same function the detangler writes through. A number shown without its picture invites arguing about the number. | .

807.title: Layout engines
807.content: Measured on the UML overview. Re-measure before relying on it for a different graph. | engine | use it for | what it gets wrong | . | stored layout (BPMN DI) | a graph whose author placed the nodes | nothing to choose: never re-lay a graph that carries its own layout | . | ELK (!pragma layout elk in PlantUML) | the compact, portrait default; it routes edges around boxes | it lays everything top to bottom and ignores left to right direction and arrow hints (output byte-identical). Unconnected groups end up in one wide row. | . | ELK + hidden links | a grid of unconnected groups (an overview) | nothing, if the column count suits the orientation: ceil(√(n/2)) for portrait, ceil(√(2n)) for landscape | . | Graphviz dot, left to right, polyline edges | the landscape view of a connected graph | it can route a long edge across a box, which is why ELK stays the portrait default. Use nodesep 70, ranksep 160. | . | Graphviz with orthogonal edges | avoid | it places edge labels away from their edges and runs lines through boxes. | . | Mermaid (dagre) | a secondary view where CSS classes on nodes matter | the same model came out three times taller than ELK’s | . | Graphviz dot in the browser (WASM, unflatten then dot) | the interactive view a reader rearranges by dragging nodes (kg-subgraph-layout) | like ELK it sets unconnected clusters, and unconnected nodes in one cluster, on one rank: fold both into grids with invisible, marked anchors | .

808.title: Applying it
808.content: | graph | source | groups | edge kinds | renderer today | owes | . | schemas | graph-typology registry, Zod schemas | <instance>/<sub-graph> | composition; field-carried vs declared elsewhere | gen-uml-overview.ts (PlantUML, Mermaid and the DOT of the Interactive view), gen-object-model-uml.ts | meets all ten | . | processes | .bpmn files | pools and lanes | sequence, message, call | render-bpmn.ts (stored layout) | rule 6 (orientation) does not apply: the author placed it | . | folio blocks and any formal relation the content type adds | buildContentGraph in pipeline/content-graph.ts; status from the content type’s status source | chapters | editorial (uses[], interprets), solid, vs formal (the content type’s own edges), dashed purple | gen-content-graph-uml.ts (Tool content-graph-uml), run from a folio | meets rules 1 to 8. Rule 9 waits on a folio page to show it; rule 10 on detangle scanning a folio | . | detangle partition | the sidecars under detangleResultsDir | detangle groups | enforced / recorded / prose | numbers only; the UML pages show them (rule 10) | a drawing of the cross-group edges themselves | . A folio is content, and content lives in a folio repository, not here. Apply the rules there through the platform’s generator, and ask the owner before a PR in a content repository the owner has said to ask about. The editorial and formal relations are one drawing, not two. buildContentGraph holds both over the same blocks, so gen-content-graph-uml.ts draws them together and keeps them apart by line style. Status fills come from the same stylesheet as the family colours (--fa-uml-status-* in uml.css). A human review outranks an agentic one, which outranks a machine-derived status. For a paper folio, where the formal relation is Lean’s, the science layer’s lean-formal-graph (skill_fetch lean-formal-graph) says what that edge and status source are, and which older drawings this one supersedes. Never populate uses[] from a formal graph to make a drawing look connected. The editorial relation is authored; see AGENTS.md and uses-editorial-review. Rule 4 is how the drawing keeps them apart.

811.title: Guideline Updates
811.content: Process_GuidelineUpdates · strict · 8 step(s) . Taking up a new version of a guideline, or a changed lower layer, is a re-pin and a review at once. The steward maps the affected layers and re-pins them in dependency order. For each re-pin, the adaptation team compares the old version, the new version and its own adaptations. A change that touches no adaptation or policy merges on the technical path. One that does goes to the adaptation committee, which decides for each adaptation whether to keep, revise or retire it. Revisions are ordinary content changes (Process_ContentChangeReview), and the re-pin merges with them. The loop runs until every layer is current. i i i i i i i i

822.title: Hand back to the discussion
822.content: Skill hand-back-to-discussion: A sibling agent, spawned during or working beside a live agent-human discussion, hands every card, question, decision, result, blocker or piece of context back to the discussion agent that is talking with the person, and never leaves it only in its own thread. The discussion agent asks the person (ask-the-person), marks every copy answered, and routes the answer back. A review sheet or issue in play is an extra channel. Use whenever an agent that is not the one talking with the person has something the person must see. Named by: Ask the person, Hand back to the discussion . The procedure behind Process_HandBackToDiscussion. It joins two rules that already bind: ask-the-person (how a question is put) and the relay paragraph of interaction-modality §4.1 (a relayed question says where the answer goes). This skill is the missing step between them: who puts the question, and how the answer gets back.

823.title: Why
823.content: A card posted only in a sibling’s own thread is not seen by the person, who is talking with the discussion agent elsewhere; the decision stalls, or reaches the person only by reconstruction. A feedback channel in play (a review sheet, an issue) is used as well.

824.title: The two roles
824.content: | role | who | does | . | Discussion agent (session-coordinator) | the agent the person is talking with right now: a project coordinator, the parent of a subagent, the session that spawned a swarm | shows the hand-back to the person, asks with ask-the-person, marks every copy answered, routes the answer back | . | Sibling (sibling-session) | any agent the discussion agent spawned, or one working beside it on the same goal: a project thread, a subagent, a workflow agent, a cloud session | composes the hand-back once, with the analysis it alone has, and acts on the answer | . You are a sibling when your brief names a discussion agent, or when you were started by another agent while a person was talking with it. A sibling that is not sure hands back anyway: one extra copy costs a line, and a missed card costs a stalled decision.

825.title: The brief names the discussion (spawning agent)
825.content: An agent that spawns a sibling during a live discussion puts the discussion link in the brief (definitions.discussion of the input schema): who the discussion agent is, how to reach it, the standing card rules, and any feedback channel in play (a review sheet’s id and tab, an issue). See process-state §”A coordinator that briefs a thread”. A sibling has nothing else that tells it.

826.title: Input and output
826.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In (the hand-back): from (title, link, process), to (the discussion link), kind (decision, question, context, result, blocker), a one-sentence summary, ask (the ask-the-person input, unchanged, for a decision or question), context (for the others), links, channels (always discussion, plus any of own-thread, project-chat, review-sheet, github-issue, github-pr), answerRoute, blocking, and supersedes when it replaces an earlier one. | Out (the record): shown (every copy, discussion first), state (open, answered, withdrawn, superseded, informed), the ask-the-person output, chosen, quote, answeredIn, marked (the strike-through edit per copy) and deliveredBack (proof the answer reached the sibling, with citesPerson). | .

827.title: Steps — sibling
827.content: . | Compose once. A question is the full ask-the-person input: what will differ, context, every option lettered with a one-line trade-off, the recommendation and why, what happens with no answer. The discussion agent must be able to show it without opening your thread. Context, a result or a blocker gets the same test. | Show it where you are. Post it in your own thread too (chat text, then the card), so the tappable card sits beside the work. Your own thread is never the only copy. | Mirror it to the feedback channel in play. When a review sheet governs the work, write the “Decision needed” block into the row’s agent column and set Agentic status to Needs you (the document layer’s review-sheet-script skill, §”A question to people goes in the sheet”). An issue or PR in play gets a comment. These are extra copies, never instead of the discussion. | Hand back to the discussion agent with the host’s route: . | host | route | . | Claude projects thread | message_coordinator (or message_thread to the discussion thread), the hand-back as plain prose in the schema’s order: summary, question, lettered options with trade-offs, recommendation, if silent, link to your thread | . | subagent (Agent tool, workflow agent) | your final report: the hand-back as a fenced json block that validates against the input schema, then a one-line summary. You cannot reach the person; the parent asks | . | sibling session | SendMessage to the discussion session | . | none of these | a comment on the issue or PR the discussion is about, and say so in your own thread | . | Keep working on the recommended option where it can be undone; stop where it cannot (blocking: true). | Act on the answer when it comes back. Only an answer that carries the person’s own words (a cited message, a card tap, a Blue-column cell) is their approval. A paraphrase from another agent is not. | .

828.title: Steps — discussion agent
828.content: . | Show it in the discussion, saying it comes from the sibling (title and link) and that you will pass the answer on. A question goes through Process_AskThePerson unchanged: the chat text in full first, then the card with the same letters. Never “see the card in thread X”. | Context, a result or a blocker that needs no answer: post it, state informed, done. | Take the answer from any copy. A tap on your card, a tap on the sibling’s card, or a Blue-column answer in the sheet all count. Take the first, and treat a later disagreeing answer as a new question. | Route it back on answerRoute, attaching the person’s own message by id where the host allows (citesPerson: true). | Mark every copy answered. A chat copy keeps its text: strike the question through and add [Edit: <letter> chosen by <who>, <time>]. A card you posted is closed with the chosen option. A sheet’s “Decision needed” block is replaced by the decision and who made it, and Agentic status moves on. A withdrawn or superseded hand-back is marked the same way with the reason. | A rule-level answer goes into the governing skill in the same turn (symbiotic-interaction §2). | .

829.title: Anti-patterns
829.content: . | A card only in the sibling’s thread. | A hand-back that says “see my thread”. A pointer is not the question. | The discussion agent rewriting the options. The sibling did the analysis; reword for the person if needed, but keep the letters and the recommendation, and say so if you change one. | The sheet as the only copy. People on the committee see the sheet; the owner in the discussion may not be looking at it. | An answer that never reaches the sibling. The person answered once; the sibling must not ask again. | .

843.title: Harness projections: CI writes them, the owner consents to every hand edit
843.content: Skill harness-projections: Who may write under .claude/, and when. The generated projections of the knowledge graph (.claude/commands/*.md from skill:commands, the assembled agent memory under .claude/agents/ and .claude/agent-memory/) are written by CI, which commits them to the PR branch, and never by an agent. A hand-edited .claude/ file (settings.json, its hooks, a hand-written command or agent definition) changes only with the owner’s explicit consent to that change: the agent shows the exact diff and the reason, asks first, and records the consent. Read before staging any path under .claude/. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review, Each IG, composed into a host docs site and rendered with just-the-docs, Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Review and publish a folio, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release .claude/ is what the Claude Code harness reads before any skill is loaded: the slash commands a person can type, the memory injected into a subagent, and the hooks and permissions every session runs under. An edit there changes how every later session behaves, including sessions that never see the commit.claude/ is one instance of a general rule. Every coding-agent Tool has config files, and some of them are projections of the graph: CI writes the projections, and a person consents to each hand edit.claude/ is named here because it is the agent-host directory the generators write. Which files a Tool reads, and which of them are generated, belongs to that Tool’s adapter. Securing what the agent may do at all is agent-permissions.

844.title: Two kinds of file, two writers
844.content: | kind | examples | source of truth | who writes the .claude/ file | . | projection (generated) | .claude/commands/<name>.md carrying a generated: key (skill:commands); the marked region of .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md (agent-memory); .claude/agents/* where the memory assembler writes them; .claude/skills/ synced from packages | the skill’s front matter, the memory nodes under memory/, the package | CI only. A workflow step runs the generator and commits the result to the PR branch. | . | hand-edited | .claude/settings.json and its hooks, a hand-written command (no generated: key), an agent definition’s hand-written body, a memory file’s ## Session log | the file itself | an agent, only with the owner’s consent to that exact change | . The rule for a projection: edit the source, not the projection. To change a slash command, change the skill’s user_invocable or description. To change what a subagent remembers, add or edit a node under memory/ (agent-memory). Push the source change and let CI write the projection. You may run a generator locally in its --check form, or into a scratch tree, to see what it would write. Do not stage or commit anything it writes under .claude/. This applies inside skill-registration too. skill:register runs skill:commands, which writes .claude/commands/ in a composed checkout. Commit what it writes everywhere else, and leave .claude/ to CI. Why CI and not the agent. A projection is correct only if it was generated from the tree that lands. An agent’s local run reflects the tree it had, and a hand-merged projection drifts from its source; the CI step runs on the PR head, so the projection on the branch is the one the merge will carry, from one writer.

845.title: Hand-edited files: consent per change
845.content: Before you write a hand-edited .claude/ file: . | Show the exact diff. Paste the unified diff itself, not a description of it. | Give the reason: what breaks or is missing without the change, and what the change does to every later session (a hook that runs on every tool call; a permission that stops a prompt). | Ask, and wait. The order is context, diff, recommendation, question (interaction-modality §4.1). “Go ahead” discharges this question, for this diff only. | Record the consent in the commit that makes the change, and as a comment on the PR: . claude-config-consent: by: <owner's login> on: <ISO-8601 date-time> file: .claude/settings.json diff: <sha256 of the diff shown> evidence: "<the owner's words, verbatim>" (<session link or comment permalink>) . | . A standing waiver does not reach this. Consent is per change, so there is no gate class for it in confirmation-waiver’s table, and a waiver that claims one is not a waiver. A broad instruction such as “fix the hooks” or “make the session start work” authorises the investigation. It does not authorise the edit. Bring the diff back. When a hook or setting gets in your way, report it; do not edit it. This is the same rule as prepare-merge §Guardrails (“fix the tool” rather than delete the branch), with one extra step: here, fixing the tool is itself a change that needs consent.

846.title: Where it sits in the process
846.content: merge-to-main.bpmn runs Task_RegenProjections in its build-pipeline lane before it reads any evidence. CI regenerates the projections on the head and commits them to the PR branch, and the evidence is then read on that new head. A PR whose projections are stale therefore cannot reach the merge gate looking green (merge-to-main).

847.title: What this does not do yet
847.content: . | The CI step is declared here, not built. In the platform repository, merge-main.yml runs regen (which includes skill:commands and agent-memory) and pushes to the PR branch, but only for PRs labelled merge-main when main moves. code-quality-gates.yml runs skill:commands:check and agent-memory:check and fails, but commits nothing. A step that regenerates the projections on every PR head and commits them is a workflow change in the repositories that carry .github/. That change is not made here. | No check refuses an agent-authored commit under .claude/. Telling a CI-written commit from an agent’s needs a committer convention (the bot identity the workflow pushes as), and a gate that reads it. | skill:register still writes .claude/commands/. Restricting it to --check for that one step would be a change to skill-register.ts. | .

848.title: harness-projections (skill)
848.content: The skill harness-projections as its source file cat-harness/skills/conduct/conduct-core/harness-projections.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

849.title: A tile is the harness’s, not the node’s
849.content: Skill harness-tiles: A tile is a function of the harness watching a directory, not of nodes. Where the tile set comes from, what a tile opens, and the two gaps it reports rather than hides. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . A tile is a function of a harness watching a directory, not of nodes. If a harness declares visualisers, each one gets a tile; a tile defaults to the theme, and a harness can declare one or more visualisations, each with a title. The tile set is not a new registry — it is the visualiser obligation made reachable. A harness declares its visualisers in its <instance>.json visualisers (HarnessVisualiserSchema), and kg:audit reports which directories owe one. A graph that owes a visualiser owes a tile, so the audit needs no second list free to disagree with it.

850.title: Where a tile goes — the declared route, and nothing else
850.content: Each visualiser is ONE declaration in the harness that owns it: . "visualisers": [ { "id": "library", "renderedBy": "library-viewer", "coversKinds": ["library"], "subgraphs": "instance" }, { "id": "todos", "renderedBy": "state-viewer", "covers": ["todos"], "alias": "todos" }, { "id": "fsh-guts", "renderedBy": "staging-graph-viewer", "covers": ["fsh-guts"], "publish": "staging-only", "writer": ["scripts/gen-fsh-guts-viz.ts"] } ] . | id is the URL segment; renderedBy names a Tool node (the implementation may live anywhere); covers names this harness’s own directory ids, coversKinds graph typologies, over every declared directory of them in the checkout. A harness never names another layer’s directory — that would be a lower layer naming a higher one. | The URL is computed, never chosen. visualiserRoute in schemas/kg/visualiser-route.ts is the ONE function every generator and reader uses: <harness>/<id>/ for the full KG, <harness>/<id>/<sub-graph>/ for one sub-graph (subgraphs: "instance" — one per covered layer — or "directory", nested under subgraphUnder[kind] where the visualiser declares one), and an asset path below either. Every page is written to that route under the site’s docs layer, so the file and the URL cannot disagree. A tile opens the sub-graph view when it exists, else the full one. | A page claims nothing. A page carries only rendered-by: <Tool>, as provenance; it carries no renders: or <meta name="renders">. A directory’s coverage.visualiser is filled IN MEMORY by withViewers from the declarations, never from disk. | Collisions are declaration errors. bun run cat check:visualiser-routes refuses two declarations resolving to one route (or one inside another’s subtree), a page drawn by a Tool outside every route that Tool is declared to render, a page under a route that names a different Tool, a visualiser covering a kind its Tool does not renders, and any renders: or coverage.visualiser on disk. | The short URL is an opt-in alias. alias: "todos" makes <base>/todos/ a redirect to <base>/cat-harness/todos/, composed by compose-docs.ts for every page under the route. An alias that names another alias, a harness, or anything the site already carries at its top level is refused by the gate before a build and by the composer during one. A tile always links the canonical route. | publish: "staging-only": compose-docs withholds the route (and its alias) from a canonical deploy. | .

851.title: Instantiated is a different fact from declared
851.content: Only the harnesses instantiated in the folio get tiles, not every dependency. Which layers are instantiated here is answered by the root index.config.json (instances[]), or without an index by each root <name>.config.json. That rule is index-config’s; the tiles only consume it, because the navbar cannot be derived from the declarations alone and a directory listing is not the question a reader is asking. Dependencies keep a group of their own rather than disappearing, so a reader looking for one is not answered with silence. A harness a KG subscription chose is instantiated by the same file, with no local declaration: its declaration is the substrate snapshot kg:subscribe cached at the pin. bun run cat kg:instantiate <subscription> <harness> writes the config and the harness’s state directories (and, under an index, the harness’s instances[] entry), and refuses a harness that was not chosen, not declared at the pin, or whose needs nothing here holds. The tile is drawn from the snapshot (scripts/subscribed-harnesses.ts): it links nowhere, because nothing of it is published here, and a snapshot that cannot be read is a finding on the tile rather than an empty one.

852.title: Which harness / is — the landing is index-config’s rule
852.content: The site’s landing page is one of the instantiated harnesses. It is never the layer the generator happens to live in, and never the repository’s name. Which one it is — site.landing in the root index.config.json (an layer name or "hub"), or the per-config site.landing flag without an index — is index-config’s rule. resolveLandingInstance in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts reads both, and check:landing-instance is the gate. When the landing is the neutral hub, / is the harness listing (harness_details.html, these tiles) and the todo panel — the landing sticky panel, not a second board.

853.title: “Harness” carries TWO senses, and only one of them is this rule
853.content: | sense | what it means | how you tell | . | 1 — instantiated here | this checkout runs it | an entry in the root index.config.json instances[] — or, in a folio with no index, a root <name>.config.json (index-config). Read the file, not a number quoted here | . | 2 — a layer others instantiate | a base a downstream repo stands up | nothing in this checkout. It is a statement about the layer’s role in the stack | . The rules on this page are about sense 1. Sense 2 is correct usage too: a layer can be declared, not instantiated, and declare no visualiser — so it owes no tile — while being exactly what a downstream repository instantiates. No count is given for either sense, because a count in prose is a claim nothing checks; ask the filesystem. Do not write a checker for this. A predicate on the word cannot separate its two senses, so it is an adjudication, not a check (adjudication). When the word is load-bearing, say which sense — “instantiated here” or “a layer downstream repos instantiate”.

854.title: A tile opens the LAYER, not a kind handler’s view of it
854.content: A viewer page is a RENDERING with its own IRI, separate from the asset it shows; see kg-viewer §”The asset and its rendering are two resources with two IRIs”. scripts/mount-instance-docs.ts carries the two routes: . | route | handler | what it is | . | /<kind>/<instance>/ | the kind’s, cat-harness’s | the default rendering any layer declaring that kind gets | . | /<instance>/ | the layer itself | its own themed root | . The tile’s target is the layer’s own themed root when it has one, and a handler’s viewer only when it does not. The viewers stay reachable, listed beneath. A layer has that root when it has its own site directory, read from its own declaration — never by probing the BUILT site, where a layer whose pages are generated at build time has none until its generator runs.

855.title: Order is the declared dependency stack, reversed
855.content: Bottom to top, computed from the declared needs, never written out as names: a name list is a rule true only for the layers somebody remembered. The spine’s head keeps the top and its floor keeps the bottom. A layer whose layer nobody declared is undetermined — placed below the head, alphabetically, carrying a finding that says its place is not derived. Absent is not []: one is nobody having said, the other is a layer asserting it sits on nothing. A broken graph does not blank the navbar. flattenDependencies returns an empty order on a cycle, which is right for a pipeline and wrong for a sidebar, where showing nothing hides every layer over one typo. The problems are reported and the list falls back to alphabetical.

856.title: Two gaps, reported rather than hidden
856.content: Both are the third state, and they are DIFFERENT findings: . | declared and not rendered — a graph the layer declares with no published page. Not linked (a dead link reads as “this site is broken”), and reported. | rendered and not declared — a page published under a kind the layer does not declare. Also not linked, because the declaration decides what a tile may claim to show — and reported, because staying silent would hide a working viewer behind a rule, and the remedy is one line in a declaration. | .

857.title: An inert row SAYS why, and “no viewer” is four answers
857.content: A declared graph with no published viewer appears in the navbar as a row that does not open. Drawing it grey is not saying it: . | A title on a non-focusable element is a label for a pointer and for nothing else — no keyboard path, and not reliably announced. | Dimming alone is state carried by contrast, and can pass the contrast ratio while saying nothing. | . The reason is content: real text in the row. It is in the accessibility tree, survives a stylesheet that does not load, and cannot disagree with a second signal. Do not use aria-disabled — nothing is a control, and marking a <span> disabled announces a widget that does not exist. “No viewer” is four states, told apart by inertNote (harness-tiles.ts): . | state | the row says | is it a gap? | . | declared publish: "staging-only" | staging only | no — withheld on purpose | . | layer declares renderExemption.of: ["visualiser"] | no viewer by design | no | . | a viewer exists off the conventional path | viewer not published | yes, and a different one | . | nothing declares a viewer | no viewer yet | yes | . One wording for all four would label an intended state a gap, which is as wrong as hiding a real gap. Neither navbar picks the words. They render what the generator gave them, which keeps them one navbar rather than two that agree by maintenance. A kind the generator said nothing about renders with no claim about why.

858.title: A tile, or an avatar? WHO DECLARED IT
858.content: A tile is what the HARNESS declares. An avatar is what the FOLIO holds. | the thing | renders as | because | . | a declared visualiser (the harness’s visualisers) — over a directory or sub-graph | tile, functional | the harness declares it; §”A tile is the harness’s” above | . | a set of schema instances — todos | tile, content | the harness declares the set; the instances are the folio’s | . | a note, a document, a materialised asset in the folio’s reproduce directories (library/, uploads/) | avatar | the folio holds it; it is the reader’s, not the harness’s | . A TILE IS ONE OF TWO KINDS, and they bind to different things . |   | functional tile | content tile | . | subject | a directory or sub-graph | a set of schema instances | . | bound to | a SKILL | a SCHEMA | . | resolved when opened | a tool that implements the skill | the instances | . | what empty means | a gap to report — a skill nothing implements is unreachable | a real state — “nothing outstanding” is not “broken” | . A functional tile names the SKILL, never the tool. schemas/tools/tool-types.ts makes tools that satisfy one skill interchangeable, so a tile bound to a tool breaks the moment another tool is chosen. Likewise VisualiserDeclarationSchema takes “one path, or several visualisations”: a sub-graph may be rendered more than one way. Empty is asymmetric. A content tile opening on zero instances is CORRECT and must not be hidden — an empty board and a person with nothing outstanding are opposite facts. A functional tile whose skill has no tool is a gap to report. THEME IS NOT A THIRD KIND. A theme is a palette and its art; a tile takes the avatar’s declared hue. Theme is how either one looks, never an alternative to being a tile. Size does not decide it . A whole materialised knowledge graph (such as cat-bootstrap or cat-harness) on the glass renders as an avatar. So these two tempting rules are wrong: . | “Many behind it → tile, one → avatar” — a materialised graph is many things and is an avatar. | “Opens a viewer over a set → tile” — opening that avatar opens a viewer over a set, and it is still an avatar. | . Declaration ownership decides: a materialised asset is in the reader’s folio however big it is. The same subject can be both. todos is a content tile in the strip and an individual todo is an avatar on the glass: the tile is bound to the SCHEMA and the avatar is one INSTANCE of it. What is checkable here, and what is not . Tile-vs-avatar is not. Nothing classifies a folio item; the rule governs authoring, and the renderer reads the graph an item came from, so a gate would be a declared property whose check cannot answer its own claim. “A functional tile names the skill, never the tool” IS: a declared visualisation naming a tool id where a skill name belongs is decidable against knownSkills() and the Tool graph. No such tile exists yet, so nothing is gated today.

859.title: The navbar icon row is DECLARED, and three states is not two
859.content: navbarIcons on the layer declaration. A closed set — close, todos, beans, processes, kg, fsh-guts, qr, launcher — because a free string lets a layer name an icon nothing draws. Seven is the cap and it is refused, never truncated: silently dropping an eighth entry would overrule the layer’s decision. fsh-guts is a control, like launcher: a button that opens the discarded-items list and carries its live count, not a link. It is also the way back the discard confirmation names, so that dialog says “the fish in the icon row” only when this icon is on the page, and points at Page settings otherwise (board-windows §”Send to fsh-guts asks first”). | declared | means | . | absent | inherit — walk needs, site owner as the floor | . | [] | show none | . | a list | this layer’s own answer | . Absent and [] must not collapse. The guard is !== undefined, never a truthiness test: a truthiness test turns “nobody has said” into “nothing to show”, and makes a layer that has not declared the field indistinguishable from one that wants a bare navbar. The distinction is kept at every layer: resolveNavbarIcons returns undefined for undetermined, harness-tiles.ts omits the field rather than writing [], sync-docs-harness.ts emits null, and the client draws no row and says so once. The walk is needs, not a second traversal. Nearest declaration wins, breadth-first toward the foundation — the direction resolveSkillDirs already composes. A new walk would be a second answer to “what is this layer built on”, free to disagree with the first. Destinations are looked up, never written down. They come from the layer’s own declared visualisations plus siteLinks, so an icon whose graph this layer does not publish gets no href and renders as a non-link. close and launcher carry no href on purpose: they drive controls on the page, and an href would make them look like navigation.

860.title: The theme avatar: the assignment is theme-mediated
860.content: The navbar’s mark is the layer’s theme card art, clipped — not its icon. The chain: . layer → its sticky contribution → the sticky’s theme → the theme’s imageRole → the layer’s images carrying that role → the card layout → its avatarRegion . resolveThemeBackdrop is the join and returns the DeclaredImage, so the crop comes with it. An indirection is not an absence: look through the theme before concluding no assignment exists. Take the card layout, not laptop or mobile. KgImageSchema refuses a non-square avatarRegion in pixels, and only the square crop can satisfy that: equal fractions on a landscape image give a box wider than tall, and the clip scales width and height separately. A card with no declared crop is a finding, not an avatar: the whole composition squeezed into a small frame is unreadable. Report it and fall back to the mark.

861.title: Where a tile lives, and what it must not eat
861.content: Tiles render in the navbar and on the glass: one declaration, per-surface visibility, never two registries. The sticky board carries NO tiles. | Removing a surface loses nothing only if the others still carry it. Every tile this repository declares names navbar and glass, so each stays reachable. A tile that named ONLY a surface that is not mounted would vanish silently — report it, do not re-route it on the author’s behalf. | board stays a legal value in TILE_SURFACES, and nothing mounts it, so existing declarations that name it stay valid (the “every field but ref is optional” rule in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts). A declaration saying ["board"] alone is valid and renders no tile; the graph-tiles e2e asserts both halves. | . They are collapsible, with the count on the summary so a collapsed list still says how much is behind it — a fixed-height sidebar of tiles must not push the page nav off the top. Theming comes from the avatar’s declared hue: one hue, both schemes derived, so no tile can be legible in one mode and invisible in the other. A per-instance palette would be a second colour vocabulary beside theme.ts.

862.title: On a folio’s own site, a tile describes the FOLIO
862.content: A page’s tiles describe the layer whose site the page is on. A folio’s own Pages site (an IG repository’s folio-site.yml, a document folio’s folio-staging.yml) wears the platform’s chrome, and the platform’s _data/harness.json comes with it: tiles, counts, icon row, rail scopes and title, every path root-relative to the platform’s site. Unscoped, the folio’s badges show the platform’s counts and its links 404. cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/foreign-site-scope.ts applies the rule to the data, once, for both passes (compose-docs --shell --instance, and rail-standalone-pages --foreign-site): . | the link points at | on a folio’s site it | count | . | the folio’s own root (/<instance>/…) | resolves inside the folio’s baseurl | kept | . | a page the folio’s declaration publishes at its site’s root (/beans/), when the folio IS the checkout’s root (rootOwnPages) | stays root-relative, on the folio’s own site | kept | . | another layer’s state graph (work items, todos, QA, health, uploads …) | is not linked; the icon says why in words | none | . | a platform content, context or derived graph (skills, processes, tools, schemas, docs …) | is re-based, absolute, onto DOCS_SITE_BASE, with its qualifier shown | none | . | a kind nothing classifies | is treated as state | none | . The state row is unlinked rather than shown at zero or re-based. Per schemas/ui/tile-count.ts, absent is a third state, never 0: a folio that declares no beans graph has said nothing about work items. Showing 0 would be a claim, and showing the platform’s number answers the folio’s question with somebody else’s. The icon keeps its place and its accessible name says, for example, *“ declares no beans graph"* (§"An inert row SAYS why"). Ownership is decided by where the link points, never by a kind of the same name. A folio that declares a qa directory does not borrow the platform’s QA tile and its count; borrowing it because the word matched would put the platform’s number back on the folio’s page. A count beside a borrowed link is dropped too: the link is accurate, but the number would still sit on the folio’s page next to the folio’s own. The qualifier is shown instead, so the tile reads as the platform’s. The host’s count projections are not chrome. compose-docs --shell leaves out every assets/**.json that declares a headline tile count, as it does _includes/generated/. A badge whose file 404s renders as ABSENT, with no number. A figure that is not a tile follows the same rule: . | figure | it came from | on a folio’s site it | count | . | the translation sweep badge | _data/translation-qa.json, the platform’s | the shell leaves the file out; the badge stays, inert, reading “QA: not published”, and says why: *“ publishes no translation QA sweep on this site"* | none, and not “not run”, which would be a claim about the folio | . | the navbar’s locale swap | _data/translations.json, the platform’s index of its own pages | the shell leaves the file out; the index reads as null, “could not determine”, and the navbar stays as built | n/a | . | the fsh-guts fish | a button whose count is fetched from this site’s /fsh-guts.json | the button is drawn only when the folio links its OWN fsh-guts; otherwise the fish is the row’s re-based link, named *“the platform’s: declares no fsh-guts graph"*, or an inert icon with the note | none, never ”?”: ? means the read failed | . A folio that publishes its own sweep or fsh-guts document gets its own figure back with no further change: foreignSite.absent (written by scopeHarnessData) only supplies the words for when the site carries nothing. The two _data/ files are named in HOST_DATA_PROJECTIONS, since neither declares what it describes. foreign-site-scope.test.ts fails on a shell that carries a _data/ file nobody has classified as chrome or projection. A folio that IS the root of its own site (for example one whose site is generated rather than a Jekyll tree) needs four more things: . | Its declared pages are its own. Its visualisers under its own site directory publish at the site root, by the same ownsSite || isRepoRoot rule siteDirMount gives its icon (harness-tiles.ts), and the scope keeps them (ForeignScope.ownPages). | The icon row’s own paths and counts resolve on the folio’s site. After scoping, every root-relative href left in the row is the folio’s, and so is the count.json its badge fetches. rail-standalone-pages --foreign-site writes the row’s data-fa-root as the page’s own site root (rowRoot), while its script and style still load from the platform (assetRoot). | Its mark loads from its own site (ownsCheckout). | An image mark can sit on the rail itself. The rail draws the layer’s tone square behind every avatar; a declared image with ground: "none" (KgImageSchema) is drawn with no tone. | . The pinned rail reserves its width. Hover and focus open the bar over the page, as a peek; pinning keeps it open, so .main moves over (docs-ui.css). The gate is foreign-site-scope.test.ts. It runs both foreign-site passes over a folio and asserts (a) no tile carries another layer’s count or links its state graph, (b) no href is left root-relative unless it is the folio’s own path, (c) the platform’s translation sweep and index are not shipped and the rendered head_custom.html hands the badge its words, and (d) the fish fetches no count from a site that has no fsh-guts. The client halves are in translation-badges.e2e.ts and navbar-row.e2e.ts. A check of a page’s chrome has to run on a site that is not the platform’s, because on the platform’s own site the platform’s tiles are right by construction.

863.title: The glass strip — pinned first, and “+N more” counts the rest
863.content: No tile may be silently off-screen: a reader cannot tell a tile scrolled out of view from a tile that does not exist. | The pinned set is DECLARED, never written into a surface. glassStrip on the layer’s declaration lists the pins in order: { "chrome": … } for the glass’s own controls (todos, filter, settings) and { "kind": … } for a graph typology. It is inherited along needs like navbarIcons, so absent inherits and [] pins nothing. sync-docs-harness.ts resolves each kind to ONE tile (resolveGlassStrip): the directory named for the kind, else the first glass tile that holds it. A kind several harnesses publish gets one slot, and the others wait in More, where their qualifiers tell them apart. A pinned kind that no tile holds is reported in glassStrip.unmatched and never skipped silently. | Fit, not scroll. The strip shows as many pins as fit at the current width, in declared order, and refits whenever its box changes. It never scrolls sideways (scrollWidth <= clientWidth is asserted at 1280×800 and 390×844). | The last tile says “+N more”, and N is exact. N counts every tile not on screen: pins with no room at this width, plus everything the reader keeps in More. Shown + N is always the total. The tile is a button named “N more tiles”; it opens More and moves focus into it. Pins that did not fit come first in More, marked as pinned. | The reader may still arrange. A strip the reader has arranged, by dragging or with the Strip and More buttons, overrides the declared default in that browser. The fit and the count apply to their arrangement too. | It starts HIDDEN. With no stored choice, the folio opens with the strip slid away. Only its tab shows, reading “Show tiles (N)”. The tab is the one control both ways (board-windows) and carries aria-expanded. The reader’s choice is remembered in this browser as 1 or 0, and storage that cannot be read counts as no choice: hidden. | . glass-strip-fit.e2e.ts holds the four fit assertions and glass-strip-default-hidden.e2e.ts the default.

864.title: summary and alsoWritten — what a reader sees, kept apart from why it was named
864.content: A harness section on the landing page shows the declaration’s summary, a one-line gloss, and lists alsoWritten, the other spellings of the name. A description made to carry them shows the reader a naming rationale or spellings that render as one line. Authoring notes belong in description or a _comment. The reader-facing line goes in summary, and alternative spellings go in alsoWritten as a list, never inline. A harness’s sticky shows the same text as the landing page. A sticky contribution declares bodyFrom: "summary", and the card’s words are readerText in schemas/content/sticky-contribution.ts: the summary (else the description), then the alsoWritten spellings after “Also written:”. That is the rule docs/_includes/harness_details.html applies, read from the same two declaration fields, so there is no copy of the text to keep in step. bodyFrom: "description" still parses, because the pinned bootstrap/bootstrap.json declares it. bun run cat landing:sticky:check fails when a card built from its declaration does not open with that text. A bodyAppend may follow the reader’s text, and a card with a literal body is not compared.

865.title: harness-tiles (skill)
865.content: The skill harness-tiles as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/harness-tiles.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

866.title: Asking a person, in one reusable way
866.content: Skill human-agent-discussion: Ask a person (or a sibling agent) for what no file holds. First determine where you are — the context, the Role you act as and theirs, the Process and task (or that you are idle) — and ask about whichever you cannot determine before anything else. Then context, the options, a recommendation and what happens with no answer, then ONE question. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Human–agent discussion, Initialize a harness . You are the agent that needs something only a person can supply: a choice, a judgement, or a step only they have the rights to perform. Every diagram in bootstrap that needs one calls processes/human-agent-discussion.bpmn as a call activity rather than drawing its own asking.

867.title: Before you ask: determine where you are
867.content: The diagram’s first three tasks come before any question, and each is declared as a precondition of the first one (bootstrap.processes:precondition … before="A_GiveContext"): . | determine | what you must be able to say | why it comes first | . | the context (A_DetermineContext) | what is already known, each fact with where it came from; which declaration governs it (the layer’s <name>.json, the diagram you are in, the Skill its task names); and whether the question has already been decided — earlier in the conversation, or in a declaration that quotes the person’s ruling | a settled question asked again reopens a decision and spends the person’s attention twice. Cite what you read, not what you remember | . | the Roles (A_DetermineRoles) | which Role you are acting as — the lane of the task that called this discussion — and which Role the person you ask holds | an Actor performs a task in a Process as a Role; nothing is a Role by nature. Who holds the decision decides whom you may ask: only the Requestor chooses a harness | . | the Process and task (A_DetermineProcess) | the Process, the lane and the task the question belongs to — “Process: Initialize a harness, at Determine the harness and repositories, as the Bootstrapping Agent” — or that you are in none: you are idle, classifying a request to find the Process it belongs to | a reader who does not know which Process you are in assumes the last one’s rules still hold | . Say all three in the message, as the first part of the context. A caller that already determined them hands them in; you check them rather than re-derive them. You are out of process — the Process is undetermined — when you cannot name it, when two candidates fit, when the step you believed was next is not the one the diagram enables, or when the work in hand is not what you said you would do. Do not infer your way back in. What cannot be determined is asked first . When any of the three cannot be determined, that becomes the first question of this same discussion (A_AskUndeterminedFirst), and the caller’s question waits, counted. Ask about the outermost first — the Process, then the Role, then the context — since the outer answer usually settles the inner. It goes through the same order as every question below, and it allows no default: a Process or a Role assumed rather than confirmed is an authority nobody gave you. Its answer is recorded, the three are determined again, and only then is the caller’s question put. If it is declined or met with silence, record what is still open and stop: a step completed in the wrong Process records an authority that was never given. I am in Initialize a harness, at Determine the harness and repositories, acting as the Bootstrapping Agent. I cannot tell whether you are the person who wants this repository set up, or relaying for someone: the request came from another agent’s message. If you are, I will ask you which harness next; if not, I will stop and record that the Requestor is unknown, since only the Requestor chooses. Are you the person who wants it set up? (One more question after this one.) .

868.title: The order is the rule
868.content: . | Context. Where you are (the three determinations above), what is being decided, what depends on it, and what you already know, each fact with where it came from. In the message itself: a link is where somebody goes for more, never where the terms are defined. | Options. Every option still open after you narrowed from context, each with what it costs and what it makes hard to undo. An option you could have ruled out yourself wastes the reader’s attention. | Recommendation. The option you would take, marked, and why. | What happens with no answer. Said before the question, so silence has a meaning both sides agreed to before it happened: the default, when the caller allows one, or “the question stays open and the work stops”. | One question, answerable by picking. With several decisions open, ask one in full and give a count for the rest. | . The test before you send it: can the reader answer without opening anything? If not, the question is not ready.

869.title: What can come back, and where each ends
869.content: | what came back | what you do | end | . | an answer that settles it | record it, and who gave it (a person or an agent) | Answered — or, when it answered a question about where you are, determine again and put the caller’s question | . | an answer that does not settle it (a kind instead of an option; two options) | follow up once, narrower, naming what is still open | back to the answer | . | a refusal | record what was asked and what is still open | Still open | . | nothing | apply the default only if the caller allows one, and say so; otherwise record what is still open | Default applied or Still open | . A default is the caller’s to allow, never yours. A caller allows one only when the decision is reversible and its own instructions name the default. It is recorded as assumed, with the default named, never as the person’s answer, and the next message tells them it was applied so they can reverse it. Which harness a repository becomes allows none: a wrong answer does not fail, it succeeds at being the wrong thing (confirm-harness).

870.title: The record
870.content: In the form the caller asks for. For bootstrap’s harness question that is a document conforming to discussion.output.schema.json (discussion). For a step only the person can perform (complete-initialization), it is the step with the person’s word beside it. A person saying “done” is recorded as their word, and the next check decides whether it holds.

871.title: Symmetric in its participants
871.content: The answering lane is a person or a sibling agent that already holds the answer. The record says which, because the two are evidence of different weight. Neither is refused, and they are not conflated.

879.title: Human Translation Workflow
879.content: Process_HumanTranslation · advisory · 16 step(s) . The human half of translation: a coordinator assigns a locale to a qualified translator, the translator works in their own tool, a subject-matter expert judges accuracy, and only then is the result official. You are in this process when a person is doing the translating. translation-workflow is the machine half — extraction, injection, staleness — and it hands off to this one at exactly the point a judgement is needed. The two are separate because completeness is mechanical and accuracy is not: the coordinator’s gate asks whether enough strings are filled, the reviewer’s asks whether they are right, and no amount of the first substitutes for the second. What makes a translation OFFICIAL is the reviewer’s sign-off, never the file being complete. i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i

885.title: ig-artifact-ingestion
885.content: Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: ig-artifact-ingestion · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Covers fhir-harness’s fhir-artifact-index graph typology (schema fhir-harness/schemas/fhir-artifact-index.ts). The artefact index of a FHIR Implementation Guide is a knowledge graph keyed by the IG’s own canonical URLs, linking each artefact to its JSON, JSON Schema and JSON-LD representations. No IG publishes such an index itself, so it is always assembled, and it records what each part was built from. This skill says how an index is assembled in this harness; it does not judge whether an IG’s content is correct (that is fhir-validation’s job).

886.title: Which IGs carry the IG API overlay
886.content: Every IG gets an index; the JSON Schema and JSON-LD links come only from an IG API (WHO calls it the DAK API): the per-artefact sidecars and the enumeration schemas (ValueSets.schema.json, LogicalModels.schema.json) that dak-postprocessing steps 3–6 produce. The index’s sidecarApi says which: . | present — sidecars were found and bound to artefacts; | absent — the source was read and held none; | unknown — nobody looked. unknown is not a kind of absent: only absent is a reason to stop. | . An IG with no IG API is a thin index, not an error.

887.title: Where the index is built: at publish, from the AST
887.content: An IG layer does not commit its fhir-artifact-index/. fhir-harness’s ig-index:build (fhir-harness/scripts/build-ig-indexes.ts) writes it at publish: . | document | schema | built from | . | index.json | folio-fhir-artifact-index/v2 | the IG’s cached AST, by ast-to-artifact-index.ts; its manifest says authority: "cache" | . | menu.json | folio-ig-menu/v1 | the IG’s own sushi-config.yaml menu:, at the commit the checkout’s lock pins (buildMenu) | . | releases.json | ig-releases/v1 | the repository’s GitHub releases, as pointers to their assets; a failed read writes no file, because no list is not an empty list | . | package.tgz | — | the AST’s resources, as package/<Type>-<id>.json, with a package/package.json from sushi-config.yaml | . | sidecars/ | — | the IG API sidecars a layer above writes (ig-site:sidecars), bound to the artefacts | . | contexts/ | — | each .jsonld under input/images/ whose only key is @context | . ig-identity.json (folio-ig-identity/v1: id, canonical, version, status, read from sushi-config.yaml) sits beside them when present. An IG with no identity file has no status this pipeline can state and draws no watermark; that is not “published”. Each document has a different source, so each carries its own provenance. Folding two together would give one file two answers to “where did this come from”. The menu is the IG’s own ordering of itself . sushi-config.yaml’s menu: is a nested map, and order is the file’s order. Never sort it: that would re-navigate somebody else’s IG. Read it from the source config, never from a screenshot: a picture carries no hrefs, and a closed dropdown looks like an empty one. The chrome comes from a chain, and only part of it is the IG’s own . An IG declares its appearance in no file it owns: it comes from the fhir.template chain its ig.ini names, for example . local-template → who.template.root 0.5.0 → fhir.base.template 1.0.0 . So the chrome (folio-ig-chrome/v2) is keyed by the chain’s top template and lives once, in smart-base’s themes/chrome.json, worn by every IG on that chain. It carries layers base-first, and every token records which package won it and what it overrode, which is how to answer whose value is this? For example who.css styles no #publish-box, so the yellow box is HL7’s: the token comes out from: "fhir.base.template" with overrides: []. An overlay is not a merge. --toc-box-border is 1px solid navy in HL7 and navy in WHO — each right in its own layer, but together they make HL7’s rule resolve to border: navy, which is invalid. Every layer parses on its own, so a naive merge ships a broken rule silently. Upstream defects are recorded, never corrected . The chrome mirrors its sources, defects included, and records whose each defect is: . | shape — one token name carrying different kinds of value across layers, as above. | malformed — a value that is not valid CSS on its own terms, such as --breadcrumb-text-color: ##555555 (a doubled # in HL7’s project.css). | . A carried defect shows up in generated pages looking exactly like an ingest bug, which is why the record names its owner. The detector matches one narrow pattern: a false positive would accuse someone else’s stylesheet of a fault it does not have. ingest:ig-chrome:check compares the committed chrome with the template chain. CI cannot fetch the template repositories, so with no source it exits 2 (could not determine), never 0, and it is registered as a report, not a gate. Run it by hand after cloning the IG and its templates.

888.title: What the AST does not carry
888.content: . | Category. The Publisher assigns editorial categories when it writes artifacts.html, after the AST is taken. The index uses the Publisher’s default grouping by resource type and names every artefact where a published grouping differs (--keep-published-grouping keeps the grouping of a committed index still on disk). | Where it is published. A canonical URL is an identity, not an address. The published base is the committed copy’s source.of when that names a published site, else the layer declaration’s iriBase, else none, and the run says which. Never derive either the published base or canonicalBase from the other. | . AST-built artefacts are materialized with purpose compiled, and carry the gates of folio-assistant-core/schemas/materialization.ts. sourceLoss and copyright stay unknown until someone establishes them; a permitted there would claim “no restrictions known” without having looked.

889.title: What is never invented
889.content: . | canonical is optional. Examples and instance resources have no canonical URL and are most of a large IG. Minting one produces an identifier that resolves to nothing while looking authoritative. | category absent never means “Other”. The IG’s own artefact page has a literal Other section; a second one would make the word mean two things. | A lossy field is left absent, not repaired. An absent field is a fact; a repaired one is a guess. | .

890.title: When the source is a published site
890.content: The schema also accepts an index read from a published IG (source.kind gh-pages, output or url), with provenance naming the published file each part came from. These are different evidence: output/ is a local build, gh-pages is what the world can see; never label one as the other. A published IG offers four partial views, none sufficient alone: . | file | holds | misses | . | canonicals.json | canonical URL, version, name | every artefact without a canonical | . | package.tgz → package/.index.json | every artefact’s type and id | titles, categories, canonicals | . | artifacts.html | the editorial category and human title (per-row title is ResourceType/id) | anything machine-readable | . | package.manifest.json | package id, version, FHIR version, build date | — | . Traps: . | Read the source, not the page about it. dak-api.html links the enumeration schemas under schemas/, but they sit at the published root. | openapi/openapi.json is not the IG API. On the WHO SMART Trust IG it is the DDCC Gateway API, subject matter that lives there. Key the overlay off each artefact’s own stem (<ResourceType>-<id>.openapi.json), never a directory scan. | .index.json is lossy (Organization entries can carry a truncated "type": "["). canonicals.json is the spine for anything canonical; a field seen only in .index.json stays absent. | .

891.title: Running it
891.content: bun run cat ig-index:build -- [--only <instance>] [--work <dir>] [--plan] . --plan prints what would be built and touches nothing. Exit 0: every IG found was built; 1: one or more failed (each named); 2: usage. An IG layer is found, with no declaration of its own, when it needs fhir-harness (directly or through a layer above), declares a repository, and that repository carries an AST branch family. A layer missing any of the three is skipped, and the run says which and why. To add an IG, give it those three; never commit or hand-edit the index it produces.

893.doc: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch
893.title: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch
893.content: Process_IgAstCache · advisory · 5 step(s) . How an IG repository’s own site is published, and how the AST it is built from is kept current (skill ig-build-pipeline §”The AST cache lifecycle”). THE RULE. An IG site is built from the IG Publisher AST read from the IG repository’s cache branch cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>, never from Publisher HTML. The publish refuses an AST that is not valid for the commit it publishes (ig-cache.sh restore then verify). A later commit that changes no IG input (sushi-config.yaml, ig.ini, input/) does not make the AST stale. THE REFRESH. The cache is written by ONE thing: fhir-harness’s reusable workflow .github/workflows/ig-ast-refresh.yml, which an IG repository’s Site publish calls as its first job (ast; template templates/ig-repo-site/site-publish.yml). It runs the Publisher through the AST exporter on a GitHub runner (Java, 10 GB heap, tx.fhir.org). It seeds the branch only from a commit on the default branch whose inputs equal the tip’s. A valid AST is a cache, not a release: every page drawn from it carries the provisional mark (ig-ast-delta). i i i i i

899.doc: Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?
899.title: Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?
899.content: Process_IgAstDeltaReview · advisory · 4 step(s) . The review step of an incremental FHIR IG build, as its own subprocess: list and inspect the differences between the incremental IG AST and what a full build would have produced, then accept them or raise a finding. WHERE IT SITS. In ig-incremental-build.bpmn it belongs between Task_Merge and Task_Qa: after the restored and rebuilt records are merged, before the QC gates read the aggregate. That diagram does not call it yet; ig-ast-delta §”Where this sits in a process” states the placement. WHAT IT GUARDS. An incremental build rebuilds only the cone of a change, computed on the BASE edges. If the cone rules miss a coupling, a resource that should have changed does not, and nothing downstream can tell: the merged AST looks exactly like a correct one. So a person reads the delta, and a difference nobody can explain is treated as a missed coupling. WHAT IT DOES NOT CLAIM. A clean review says the delta is explained, not that the IG is correct. The AST stays a cache: every rendered page carries the provisional mark, and a release is still cut from a full build (ig-publisher-reduction P4). i i i i
