965.title: ig-render-jekyll
965.content: Skill ig-render-jekyll: Rendering a FHIR IG’s content through the just-the-docs pipeline instead of mounting the IG Publisher’s finished HTML — the JSON-only representation contract, navigation derived from sushi-config.yaml, and the LHS rail. Read before adding a representation, a menu entry, or a page kind. Named by: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, Each IG, composed into a host docs site and rendered with just-the-docs . Skill id: ig-render-jekyll · Package: fhir-ig-base · Layer: fhir-harness . Render an IG’s pages as folio pages — markdown with front matter, through Jekyll and just-the-docs — from the Publisher’s structured output, never its finished HTML. Publisher HTML has no front matter, so the navbar, language bar, QA badges and translation surface cannot reach it; a folio page gets them all. Whether an IG repository gets this rendering is asked when it is adopted (default yes); see ig-build-pipeline §”Who starts a build”.

966.title: The three contracts
966.content: 1. JSON only . The Publisher emits JSON, XML and Turtle; only JSON is taken, wrapped in JSON-LD / JSON Schema. RDF, where needed, is projected from the JSON-LD. A representation that arrives and is not taken is recorded as a refusal. Not linked either. The site does not link a resource’s .xml or .ttl copy: JSON-LD nodes carry only JSON encodings, and the site.data artefact variables only url.json. The refusal record still counts what each IG published in those forms. 2. Navigation is derived, never authored . sushi-config.yaml already carries both maps the site needs: . | pages: — an ordered map of source file to title. That is the page order. | menu: — the grouping, including nested subsections. | . Derive the navigation from them. Do not hand-author a nav file or write entries back into sushi-config.yaml. When the config names a page that does not exist, that is a finding, not a reason to create a placeholder. 3. LHS rail, and the theme is captured rather than replaced . Navigation goes in the left-hand rail, not the FHIR IG’s top bar. The rest of the IG theme — CSS, typography, resource-page furniture — is captured into the theme layer rather than discarded. Nav position is a layout setting; nav contents are derived per build.

967.title: What the render reads in the IG repository
967.content: Only what the repository declares. Every reader on this path (build-ig-site, ig-site-data, ingest-ig-menu, ingest-ig-chrome, ig-repo-site) goes through scripts/ig-read-scope.ts, which honours contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json; anything outside it is not rendered. A repository with no section is read whole, with a warning. See ig-build-pipeline §”What this layer reads”.

968.title: Where the variables come from
968.content: artifactVariables (build-ig-site.ts) writes the per-artefact Liquid variables from the artefact index to _data/, read by the same Jekyll run: site.data.fhir.artifacts.<ResourceType>__<id> with url (canonical, page, json), text, link.html and elements.<key>, plus artifact_categories, artifacts_listed and artifact_lists. An element key the index does not hold is reported as not sourced, never written empty. The families and keys follow WHO’s generate_smart_liquid.py, a build script outside this layer, without its smart__ prefix: that prefix is WHO’s, and this layer does not know about WHO.

969.title: What parity means, and what it does not
969.content: Parity is a checklist of asset types and page kinds. A page kind the Publisher emits no data for cannot be rendered.

970.title: Thin pages, the default (--full-pages to opt out)
970.content: Every IG page is a thin HTML shell that loads its content from the JSON-LD graph, unless a build passes --full-pages. The shell is cat-harness-tools’ thinPageHtml. Artefact pages (gen-ig-pages.ts) . | Page address: artifact/<Type>-<id>.html, self-canonical. | The asset is a JSON-LD node, artifact/<Type>-<id>.jsonld with a .json twin, written by ig-artifact-jsonld.ts from the index (kind ig-artifact-jsonld; QA ig-artifact-jsonld.ts check over the built site). It uses the FHIR RDF class, dcterms, schema.org and PROV, and mints nothing. The page names the node as alternate. | One shared renderer. assets/ig-artifact.js fetches the node, then the resource’s local copy, draws the description, facts, identity table and elements, concepts or includes, and hands the narrative and JSON to ast-resource.js. The page carries only its title, key and a <noscript> link to the node and resource. | The rail is linked: folio-navbar: linked, and the rail pass (rail-standalone-pages.ts) links its style and scripts rather than inlining them. | The tab views are thin pages too, written beside the page wherever the site serves the artefact’s JSON: a compiled copy (--compiled-data) or, failing that, the Publisher’s own <Type>-<id>.json carried as data (--publisher-data <dir>, from the docs root). An IG repository’s site (ig-site:compose) passes only --compiled-data .: the AST’s copy, served once at the root as <Type>-<id>.json. Each view keeps the Publisher’s file name: . | -definitions: the snapshot’s element table, differential marked; | -mappings: each mapping declaration with the elements mapped to it; | the JSON view (.profile.json for a StructureDefinition, else .json), drawn by ast-resource.js; | -examples, for every StructureDefinition: the instances claiming it in meta.profile, or a note that there are none. | . Each uses the same shell (thinArtifactView) and renderer; the artefact’s page links them in a tab bar, and the narrative’s links to them are relinked. The change history, testing, XML and Turtle views are neither rendered nor published. The IG API view pages stay full pages. | Nothing under comparison-v*/ is published. ig-site:publisher-pages serves the AST’s data and reads no Publisher output. | In an IG site the docs root is the site root, so --compiled-data . points each resource at ../<Type>-<id>.json from artifact/. No ast-data/ mirror is published. | . The artefact list and the table of contents (build-ig-site.ts) . | One index node, artifact/index.jsonld (family folio-ig-artifact-index-jsonld/v1, same kind), lists every artefact once, in the Publisher’s order, each entry naming its node and carrying only what a list row shows; check holds it to the artefact index and each node. | artifacts.html is a thin shell over that node: a jump list of categories, a filter, then every category open (nothing collapsed), anchored #artifacts-<slug>. | What a list draws: . | The IG’s own ImplementationGuide is “This guide”, drawn first (#artifacts-this-guide), never as a “Not categorised” row; the toc lists it first too. | A category that mixes resource types is sub-headed by type (#artifacts-<category>-<type>; the Publisher’s “Other”: Basic, Questionnaire, DocumentReference…), and the jump list counts each type. | A table draws only the columns its rows fill. An instance (an artefact with no canonical URL) has no description, so the index copies what the resource states: its meta.profile (dcterms:conformsTo, drawn as the last path segment, linked when it is in the same IG) and its code (dcterms:subject). A definition’s core profile (shareablevalueset) is not shown. | . | toc.html is a thin shell. The IG’s own pages (sushi-config.yaml pages:, landing page first) stay in its HTML; the artefacts under each category are drawn from the index node. | Both are written by stageIgSite when StageOptions.artifacts.index is given, which stage-ig-sites.ts does unless --full-pages. Staging thin a site whose artefact pages were generated with --full-pages (no index node) is refused. | . The narrative pages (composeIgSite) . | The IG’s prose stays in the HTML, rendered by Jekyll; composed into a host site, the page wears thinIgLayout (_layouts/ig-thin-<instance>.html) instead of the host’s layout, so none of the host’s chrome (harness bar, SVG sprite, sidebar nav, inline scripts) is written into it. | Everything around the prose is linked: assets/ig-artifact.css, assets/ig-topbar.css, assets/ig-source-links.js and the rail (folio-navbar: linked). The IG’s top bar, edit links, footer and TOC declaration stay. | The thin page has no host search box or QA badges; it has its own search box and language picker block (below). | . The footer stays in view . Every IG page ends with the Publisher’s footer (ig-footer.liquid on the Jekyll pages, ig-artifact.js on the thin pages, one igSiteFooter object for both): publisher and copyright year, package#version, FHIR version, the build day, and Links: Table of Contents | QA Report | Version History | License, each value read from the IG’s package, sushi-config.yaml or AST and left out when none holds it. Unlike the Publisher’s, it stays at the bottom of the window (owner, 2026-11-06): it is the body’s last box, after <main> on every IG page, position: sticky (ig-artifact.css), so it spans the width beside the rail, the page scrolls under it and nothing is left behind it at the end of the page. The body is a column at least the window’s height with <main> taking the free space, so on a page shorter than the window the footer lands at the window’s bottom too. In print both are off: the footer is static, once, at the end. “QA Report” is qa.html, the harness’s QA report (ig-qa-page.ts): the FHIR QA the build holds (the Publisher’s qa.json carried with the AST, the AST’s record and validity) and the knowledge graph’s (cat-harness-tools kg-qa-report.ts). Search and the language picker . The folio rail replaces the theme’s side menu (#site-nav is dropped; IG_DROPPED in stage-local-ig.ts), and the IG’s top bar carries a search box over the IG’s pages and artefacts (ig-search.ts): . | ig-repo-site.ts compose writes the index, assets/ig-search.json (each IG page’s title and full text; each artefact’s title, id, name, key, canonical and description), and the client, assets/ig-search.js. The index is fetched on the box’s first focus, never on page load. | The box (form.ig-search, input #search-input) is in the composed pages’ .ig-topbar and the thin pages’ header.iga-top. It is not .search, so docs-ui leaves it in the top bar. A build that does not write the files (gen-ig-pages without --search, StageOptions.search unset) writes no box. | Any other built page lacking a box (for example an IG API hub page or openapi/index.html) gets one: publisher-pages puts a bar at the top of its body (header.ig-search-top: the IG’s name, the box, the picker’s slot; stampSearchBox, withSearchBar). The pass skips assets/ and runs only when the site serves a search index. | The language picker sits beside the box, in the empty <span data-fa-slot="locale"> that follows it, which docs-ui fills. A site with no IG bar keeps the picker in docs-ui’s band. | docs-ui draws the picker from a page’s fa-translation-meta block, which publisher-pages writes (cat-harness-tools lib/translation-meta.ts) into every built page lacking one, from the IG checkout’s translation declaration; set-html-lang.ts reads it afterwards. | . The root parity guard (cat-harness-tools site-parity.ts) refuses to publish a build lacking the search box or language block over a root that had them. The opt-out . gen-ig-pages.ts --full-pages and stage-ig-sites.ts --full-pages build full pages (composeIgSite(…, { fullPages: true })). Pass both or neither. --thin is a no-op; --thin --full-pages is refused.

971.title: What this does not replace
971.content: Which AST the pages are drawn from. An IG repository’s site is drawn from the AST on its cache branch, cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>, which a Publisher run on a runner refreshes; the publish refuses an AST not valid for the commit. See ig-build-pipeline §”The AST cache lifecycle”. The Publisher still runs: validation, dependency resolution and terminology expansion are its job and are not reproducible from cached output.

973.title: index.config.json: what this checkout instantiates
973.content: Skill index-config: index.config.json at an instantiation root says which harnesses the checkout instantiates, where each one comes from (local, or a remote mount pinned to a SHA), each layer’s config INLINE in its entry (a legacy <name>.config.json is only imported until --inline retires it), and which harness / is. Covers instantiated against declared, landing resolution and its error case, index.lock.json and its legacy fallback, the reserved index stem, the generated .gitignore block and its gate, and index-config:migrate (with --inline) for separated repositories. Named by: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Remote-mount a dependency . The schema is folio-index-config/v1 in cat-harness/schemas/kg/index-config.ts. The index is the ONE config. Each layer’s config is written inline in its instances[] entry. A <name>.config.json is a legacy file: imported only as a migration step, then retired with index-config:migrate --inline --write. Never create one — not to make a tool find a recipe, not for a new layer. If a reader only finds config in the file, that reader is the bug; fix it to read the index entry first. index.config.json holds three facts about how a checkout is instantiated: which harnesses are instantiated, which one is / (a checkout has one <base>/index.html), and where each one comes from, so each is stated once rather than spread across every root config. When it exists at the root it is authoritative. When it is absent, readers fall back to the root *.config.json files, their site.landing flags, and remoteMounts on the root declaration. { "$schema": "folio-index-config/v1", "instances": [ { "name": "folio-assistant", "source": { "local": { "at": "." } } }, { "name": "cat-harness" }, { "name": "my-ig", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "owner/my-ig", "ref": "<40-char sha>", "overrides": { "my-ig": { "whole": true } }, "trust": { "consent": { "...": "..." } } } } }, { "name": "my-guide", "contentType": "document", "site": { "build": { "sourceSteps": ["site:document"] } } } ], "site": { "landing": "cat-harness" } } .

974.title: Instantiated is a different fact from declared
974.content: A declaration (<name>.json) says what a layer declares. It travels with the harness into every checkout that uses the harness. An index.config.json entry says the layer is instantiated in this checkout. Without an index, a <name>.config.json at the root says the same thing. Tiles, the landing and the hub listing are all drawn from the instantiated set, which instantiatedHarnessNames(root) returns. Never derive that set from declarations or from a directory listing. The dependencies of an instantiated harness are not instantiated just because a mount’s closure brought them in. They keep a group of their own rather than disappearing. A harness that a KG subscription chose is instantiated the same way: kg:instantiate adds its entry, with its config inline, when the checkout has an index (and only without one writes a root <name>.config.json).

975.title: Inline, over a legacy import while one remains
975.content: Each entry’s effective config is built like this: . | Start from a legacy imported file, while one remains. That is import when it is given, else <name>.config.json, and only if the file exists. The target state is that no such file exists. | Overlay every other key of the entry (everything except name, import, source and _comment) as an inline HarnessConfig field. Objects merge key by key, and arrays and scalars are replaced. Inline fields win. | . effectiveInstanceConfig(root, name) computes it. readHarnessConfig(dir) returns it for any layer that an index lists, walking outward from the layer root and stopping at the first directory that holds either the index or the layer’s own config. A layer the index does not list is read from its own config file. Readers that are handed a root and a name (the site recipe in build-instance-site.ts) use readInstanceConfig in cat-harness-tools/scripts/instance-config.ts, which reads the same way and REPORTS every legacy file it reads. Retiring the files is index-config:migrate --inline --write: each imported file is folded into its entry by exactly the overlay above, so no effective config changes, and the file is deleted. index-config:inline:check fails while one remains.

976.title: Local or remote
976.content: . | source absent: local, at <name>/. | source.local.at: local, at that path. Use . for the layer declared at the root. | source.remote: a remote mount. It is a remoteMounts entry minus harness, which is the entry’s name. It reuses RemoteMountSchema instead of restating it, so it has ref (not pin), overrides.<name>.whole and .path, note, trust.consent and track, and every field added to RemoteMountSchema arrives with no edit here. | . There is one read path and one write path for remote mounts: . | Read: readDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot) returns the index’s remote entries when an index exists, else the declaration’s remoteMounts. If both carry mounts it throws and names both files. It never picks one. | Write: writeDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot, mounts) always writes index.config.json, seeding the index from the checkout first if there is none. It refuses while the declaration still carries remoteMounts. Nothing writes remoteMounts on a declaration. | .

977.title: Which harness / is
977.content: resolveLandingInstance(root) is the only reader. It applies these rules in order: . | condition | / is | . | the index is unreadable | invalid: the gate fails. There is no fallback to the flags, because the index was written to override them | . | the index’s site.landing names a layer it lists | that layer (by: "index") | . | the index’s site.landing is "hub" | the neutral hub: the harness listing and the todo panel | . | the index’s site.landing names a layer it does not list | invalid: the gate fails, and it is never a silent fallback | . | no site.landing (or no index), one layer | that layer (sole) | . | no site.landing, several layers, exactly one config flags site.landing: true | the flagged one | . | several flagged | the hub | . | none flagged | ambiguous: check:landing-instance fails, because the answer is never guessed | . | nothing instantiated | none: a state of its own, not a default | . gen-landing-data.ts and sync-docs-harness.ts ask this resolver. They do not use their own location. check:landing-instance also checks that the index and the root *.config.json files agree: . | A root config that the index does not import fails the check: without the index it would instantiate a harness, with it it does not, and nothing picks between them silently. | An import that names a missing file also fails the check. | An entry with no config file at all is the target state, and passes. | A legacy file an entry still imports is reported every time. It passes while it is a pending migration (every key it holds is either not inline or inline with the same value). It fails when the entry overrides one of its keys with a different value: the file’s value is then dead text that a reader of the file alone takes for the config. | .

978.title: A harnessed repository runs its checks on its own pull requests
978.content: Instantiating a harness in a repository includes turning its checks on there, through one reusable workflow the harness owns, never a copy per repository, so a layer is judged on its own pull requests and not only when an index re-pins it. Switching off a repository’s builds must not switch off its gates. The workflow is the tools layer’s .github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml. A repository calls it from a workflow of about fifteen lines that runs on pull_request: . jobs: checks: uses: <owner>/<tools-layer>/.github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml@main with: mode: layer # or `index`: the repository is its own index instance: <instance> # layer mode: its directory in the folio-assistant index path-in-repo: <instance> # where the instance sits in the repository ('.' at the root) . | layer mode is for a repository that an index mounts, such as cat-harness or the DAK layer. The workflow checks out folio-assistant and puts the PR in place of the locked mount. | index mode is for a repository that is its own index: an IG repository over the DAK layer, smart-ra, or a folio. Its own index.lock.json is replayed. | The gates are the harness’s graph checks over the repository’s own layer, plus every check:* / *:check script of that layer and its whole dependency harness (its transitive needs). Each is named <owning-instance>:<script>. | A PR fails only on what it newly breaks. Each gate and test runs on main and on the PR. Anything already red on main is listed, never hidden, and never counted against the PR. | . A layer PR that declares a new directory is red on two index gates it cannot clear. The index README lists every declared directory, so the PR leaves index:render:check and readme:sync:root:check stale, and only the index re-pin that takes the PR regenerates the README. Read those two as expected when they are the only new failures, and run them green in the index re-pin instead. Disabling a repository’s automatic builds is not disabling its checks. When an IG repository’s automatic gh-pages or IG Publisher triggers are switched off (the onboarding question in the FHIR IG layer’s ig-build-pipeline), the harness caller stays on.

979.title: The exemptions of the index’s own workflows
979.content: .github/workflows/ belongs to the index, so the steps CI runs there that the local gate set does not are exempted HERE, under gateExemptions.steps, each with a kind and a reason (GateExemptionsSchema, the same shape an layer declaration carries). They land in the same change as the workflow step, never ahead of it in a layer: an exemption for a step CI does not yet run matches nothing, and gates-workflows.test.ts refuses a stale exemption as it refuses an unclassified step. "gateExemptions": { "steps": [ { "match": "bun run cat state:push -- --id health", "kind": "ci-only", "reason": "…" } ] } . A layer still exempts its OWN scripts and steps in its own declaration.

980.title: index.lock.json, and the legacy name
980.content: The lock records what the declared mounts resolved to. It is generated by mount:remote and kept as a separate file. The legacy name is <root-instance>.mount-lock.json. The rules for each reader and writer: . | Writers write index.lock.json. mount:remote first renames a legacy lock onto the new name, so the old file is moved, never dropped. | Readers take index.lock.json first, then fall back to the legacy *.mount-lock.json, so downstream folios and old branches still replay. The readers are: . | mount-from-lock.ts | mountedInstanceRoots | mountedUnder in git-corpus.ts | mount:remote:check | . | Both files present is an error that names both. Two locks are never merged. | . mount-from-lock.ts imports only node:*, so it restates the rule inline and its test holds it to lockFilesIn. A re-pin ends with one commit per layer, and moves pins only forward (owner ruling, 2026-11-06, card “Pin target”, A). Every layer the change needs is pinned in the same re-pin, and the re-pin PR holds the pins and nothing else: a change that needs the new pins stacks on it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). The one exception is a change mutually dependent with the re-pin, where neither passes alone. It may share the PR, and the body says why. The rules are in remote-mount §”Re-pinning”.

981.title: The reserved index stem
981.content: index.config.json ends in .config.json, so a scan that treats “each root *.config.json is a harness” would find a harness called index. The index stem is therefore reserved across the board: . | rootConfigStems skips every index.* file. It is the one root scan; every other reader calls it or instantiatedHarnessNames. | findDeclarationFile skips every index.* file too. | The index schema refuses a layer named index, and hub, because that is the landing keyword. | . Do not add another copy of the scan: a new copy is how the reserved name leaks back in.

982.title: The generated .gitignore block
982.content: # BEGIN index mounts (generated from index.config.json — do not edit) /my-ig/ # END index mounts . The block holds one /<path>/ line per remote layer in the index, where the path is overrides.<name>.path, else <name>/. After those it lists every further layer root the lock records, because a mount’s closure can land layers that the index never names. Three things write the block: . | mount:remote | writeDeclaredMounts | index-config:migrate --write | . check:index-ignores fails when the block is missing or disagrees with the index. When an index exists, mount:remote does not append to .git/info/exclude: a local exclude rule is invisible to every other clone, so a path the committed block does not cover is reported as not ignored. Without an index, it still appends there.

983.title: Converting a checkout: index-config:migrate
983.content: bun run cat index-config:migrate # print the index it would write, and its findings bun run cat index-config:migrate --write # write it; move remoteMounts; write the block; rename the lock bun run cat index-config:migrate --check # exit 1 when --write would change anything (a gate here) bun run cat index-config:migrate --inline --write # also fold each <name>.config.json into its entry, and delete it bun run cat index-config:inline:check # exit 1 while any imported <name>.config.json remains bun run cat index-config:migrate --root <clone> # a separated repository's standalone checkout . The converter reads only the files under --root, so it runs on a standalone clone of any separated repository. | Which root configs it imports: a root <name>.config.json is imported only when name is a layer the checkout declares (at the root or one level down) or mounts. Anything else becomes an unmatched-config finding and is not imported. A repository cut from a fork, for example, can carry the fork’s own <fork>.config.json; importing it would instantiate a harness the repository does not hold. | Re-runs: it is idempotent. A re-run moves only the remoteMounts entries that the declaration has gained since the last run. An entry the index already holds identically is dropped from the declaration. An entry the index holds differently throws, and you reconcile it by hand. | .

987.title: Glossary
987.content: Derived: every term this instance's swimlanes define — the role's title and description, the lane names that bind it, and whether the term has been retired. This is an index, not the documentation. It says what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a process is for, when you would be in it, and what it is not, is authored beside it and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. Filter this table | Artefact | What it declares about itself | . | Activity logglossary-ledger.json | The agent activity log. A MECHANICAL role: it is written to at task start and task end, and emptied by an actor — one entry, all of them, or on a periodic sweep — and it decides nothing. Modelled on work-plan and corpus, the two existing stores; its skill is the contract it is held to. Its entries are held in the layer's unpublished store and never reach a published graph; the activity-log skill names the location, which is deliberately not repeated here because a role description IS published.notation role/logfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Actorbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_LogMessage/lane/Lane_Actorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Adjudicatorglossary-ledger.json | Settles a criterion whose reviewer entries disagree, and records WHY. Inherits reviewer because an adjudicator is a reviewer with one added entitlement — the adjudication permission — and the separation is the point: a reviewer reports, an adjudicator settles, and a process where every reviewer could settle has no way to say who decided. The KNOWLEDGE spreads (several roles carry the adjudication skill, because each has to tell an adjudicable disagreement from a complaint); the ENTITLEMENT does not, and lives on the actor as a permission.notation role/adjudicatorfirst seen 2026-09-22status current | . | Administratorglossary-ledger.json | Administers the role graph itself: who exists, what they may act as, and what they may do. The ONE lane whose activities change the substrate every other diagram's lanes bind to — which is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit. Declared 2026-09-20 on the owner's answer that administration is a swimlane; role-model.md's rule is that a role is never invented to make a diagram drawable, so it waited for that.notation role/administratorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_HumanAgentDiscussion/lane/Lane_Agentfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | Archimateglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/archimatefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Attestation serviceglossary-ledger.json | Signs a QA report's run hashes over an API. A MECHANICAL role, and the one that DISAPPEARS when the actor performing it cannot reach out — which is why the signing process carries a second, human lane rather than a retry.notation role/attestation-servicefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Attestationsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/attestationsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Auditorglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/auditorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Authorglossary-ledger.json | Writes and revises folio content. The position, not the person: an editor and a guideline developer both act as author when they are changing a block.notation role/authorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | The session agent doing the work. The broadest skill set here, and the one whose membership most needs auditing.notation role/authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring Committeeglossary-ledger.json | The people writing a document with its editor, while it is still a working draft: contributors who give feedback through the Contributor Feedback sheet, one change set per row, in their own Blue column. They recommend; an Editor decides, through the sheet's Ready columns. Added 2026-10-31 by the owner, so the drafting sheet names a process role rather than a job title, as the public-comment sheet names the Feedback Review Committee. The lane it binds is in folio-assistant-core/processes/content/contributor-feedback.bpmn and authoring-a-document.bpmn.notation role/authoring-committeefirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Auto docsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/auto-docsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Back-translatorglossary-ledger.json | The checker of a translation round trip: renders a sample of the target-language text back into the source language from the target text alone, with no tools and without seeing the source. It rules on nothing. Its rendering is the intermediate the adjudicator reads (untainted-verification, rule 1: neither party sees what would let it shortcut).notation role/back-translatorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Basic CDN siteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Basic cdn site (node kind)glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bean notesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/bean-notesfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Binary releasesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/binary-releasefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Block kindsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/block-kindsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board positionsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/board-positionsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board rendererglossary-ledger.json | Draws a board and performs what the reader has already decided: reads each kind's declared zoom threshold and the layout layer, swaps a card for its avatar, projects an open window onto the canvas, and carries out a confirmed relocation. A system lane — it runs a fixed program and exercises no judgement, which is exactly why every decision in board-open-close.bpmn and board-relocate.bpmn sits in the reader's lane instead. It is NOT the build pipeline: it runs where the reader is, once per request, and publishes nothing.notation role/board-rendererfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Boardsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/boardsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation harness/bootstrapfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapping Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/bootstrapping-agentfirst seen 2026-09-23status current | . | Build pipelineglossary-ledger.json | Validates, renders and publishes, and watches whether that actually worked. A system lane: it runs a fixed program and exercises no judgement, so anything needing a decision belongs in a different lane. It carries todo-manager for the two CI-watcher dispatch points in content-change-review, which claim and note a bean and never resolve one -- claim is idempotent and note appends, both fixed programs, while deciding that a publish SUCCEEDED is the judgement this lane must not make (bean xom7: docs-site.yml failed 30 times while reporting its own exit code).notation role/build-pipelinefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Building blocksglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/building-blocksfirst seen 2026-11-05status current | . | Business analystglossary-ledger.json | Turns a stated need into a modelled requirement. Owns the CRDM lane and the BPMN/DMN that come out of it.notation role/business-analystfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Business processesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/business-processesfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | C@T Harnessglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation harness/cat-harnessfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Carried noteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/carried-notefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Cat harness declarationglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/cat-harness-declarationfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | CDN siteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Cdn site (node kind)glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Certificate Issuerglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/certificate-issuerfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Certifierglossary-ledger.json | Takes the certification decision on ONE test report: applies the DMN the plan's exitCriteria names (computed from facts, never asserted) and records the decision as a judgement under the declared attestations graph, from which it is signed through qa-report-signing.bpmn. A specialisation of stakeholder — accountable sign-off — but NOT judgementOnly: the exit criteria are a table it applies, and only the decision on top of them is the judgement (owner ruling, 2026-10-01). Never the tester and never the system under test. Bean 3o5b.notation role/certifierfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | CI cachesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/cachefirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Clinical / scientific SMEglossary-ledger.json | Reviewer whose judgement is about the subject matter rather than the artefact. Acts by domain judgement (judgementOnly: no procedure yields the answer, which is why a person is in the lane; bean vljz).notation role/clinical-smefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Cloudflare git (Artifacts)glossary-ledger.json | A git repository hosted on Cloudflare Artifacts, not GitHub. Holds the release history: BagIt tag files, signatures, the cursor, checkpoints and run reports. A mechanical role: written to, deciding nothing.notation role/cloudflare-gitfirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Cloudflare R2 and CDNglossary-ledger.json | Object storage behind the CDN. Every object is named by its SHA-256 and served with an immutable cache policy; an object already present is never written again. Also serves did.json. A mechanical role, held to the contract its skills state.notation role/cloudflare-r2-cdnfirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Codeglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/codefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Code listsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/code-listfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Code reviewerglossary-ledger.json | Judges the knowledge graph's CODE nodes — Tool definitions in the tools graph and schema definition nodes under schemas/. Not ordinary code review: the question is whether the NODE is sound — does it declare what it is, do its references resolve, is the mechanism it advertises the one that runs — which a passing test suite does not answer. Entered by DESCENDING into Process_CodeReview.notation role/code-reviewerfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Compute authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/compute-authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Consent Recorderglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/consent-recorderfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Consent Registryglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/consent-registryfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Content adaptersglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/content-adaptersfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Corpusglossary-ledger.json | The versioned content store and the L1 source knowledge graph. Like the work plan, a MECHANICAL role: written to, deciding nothing, and held to the contract its skills state.notation role/corpusfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Data Provider Administratorglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/data-provider-administratorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Data Recipient Systemglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/data-recipient-systemfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Deep researcherglossary-ledger.json | Answers a question FROM a corpus already held, and is answerable for the answer. 1111.title: auto-docs index
1111.content: Derived documentation over a declared sub-graph. Each entry below is generated from the repository on every build, so it is what the tree actually holds rather than what anybody remembered. These are indexes, not the documentation. They say what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a thing is for, when you would reach for it, and what it is not, is authored beside them and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. | Decisions …every DMN decision table a declared `processes` graph holds, with the decision's own name | Docs …every AUTHORED documentation page an instance publishes, with the title and description its own front matter declares | Processes …every BPMN process, with its own documentation, its lanes, and the skills its activities name | Roles …every role a declared `scenarios` graph defines, with the description it declares | Schemas …every schema module a declared `schemas` directory holds, with the first sentence of its module docblock | Skills …every skill markdown file, with the description it declares in its own front matter | Tasks …every named activity in a declared `processes` graph — task, user, service, manual, script and call activities | Tools …every Tool module a declared `tools` directory holds, with the first sentence of its module docblock | .

1115.doc: The catalogue, as a graph — who-iris
1115.title: The catalogue, as a graph
1115.content: The replica pages show what IRIS looks like. This one shows what this catalogue knows — and, more usefully, what it records that it does not know. The gap is the point, not a backlog. This instance models 211 node(s) against 273,559 items across 1,057,223 files upstream. Cataloguing by reference means recording that something exists without holding it, so a small number here is the design rather than a shortfall.

Scroll horizontally to see all columns → . | locale | catalogues / templatesQ1: availability | entriesQ2: strings | translated | fuzzy | untranslated | officialQ3: signed off | . | ar Arabic | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | es Spanish | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | fr French | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | ru Russian | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | zh Chinese | 2 / 633.3% · view files → | 162 | 162100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . Two questions, not one. catalogues / templates asks whether a .po exists at all for each extractable .pot; the string columns ask how much of the catalogues that DO exist is done. A locale can be near 100% translated across a handful of catalogues while most of its templates have none — which is why the first column is not folded into the rest. “no basis” is not zero. A share over an empty denominator is undefined, and rendering it as 0% would report a measurement this run did not make. One directory per table, each named. translation-sources is a graph KIND, and more than one instance may declare it; the first table measures the directory named in the subtitle, and each instance below it gets its own table for its own declared directory. They are never summed: two instances' catalogues answer two questions. A catalogue sitting in an instance that has not declared the directory is invisible here — which is a gap in that declaration rather than a locale with no work done, and the two must not read the same. Fuzzy is counted apart from translated. A fuzzy entry has a translation and needs review; adding it to translated would flatter exactly the entries a reviewer must look at.

1550.title: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) dak
1550.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . Sources: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099456 — WHO DAK guidance; https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085138 — WHO DAK guidance; https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant/issues/1614 — owner ruling 2026-09-30: ten components .

1551.title: Digital Transformation Handbook (DTH) dth
1551.content: A WHO guidance publication on digitalising one area of a health system — an L1 publication whose body is a planning method rather than recommendations. It sits within the DIIG process and should use the DPI-H Reference Architecture (owner, 2026-10-01). Its domain sections map onto smart-kg L2 (DAK) classes: a DTH states for a health-system area what a DAK states for a guideline. Structure read from the three DTHs ingested in smart-base/library; a section is required only where all three have it. The Reference Architecture for DPI-H calls itself "A Digital Transformation Handbook for DPI-H" and is cited here as the architecture the others should reference. semi-fixed structure · 22 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dth.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Audience and how to use this handbookaudience-and-how-to-use | required | Target users/roles per chapter and the stepwise reading path through the handbook.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng, 2. How to use this handbook > 2.2 Targeted users, p.11 (pdf 23) — this handbook is written for those who will fill the business analyst role on the teamwho-iris/library/9789240101197-eng, Introduction > Who this handbook is for (Table 1), p.8 (pdf 18) — This handbook is for countries, organizations and teams that want to plan and implement digital transformation of the public health supply chain.who-iris/library/9789240116191-eng, Introduction > How to use this handbook, p.8 (pdf 17) — This handbook provides a stepwise approach to implementing standardized NPC and product master data management processes.https://litlfred.github.io/smart-ra/en/cat-harness/library/dpi-h-ra/who-dpi-h-reference-architecture-draft-v1/, 1.1.4 Who can benefit from this guidance, pdf p.23 — Enterprise Architects and Technical Teams: This reference architecture provides TOGAF-based methodology, formal architecture patterns, and systematic requirements frameworks | . | 2 | Position in the DIIG process and SMART Guidelines layersdiig-and-smart-alignment | required | Which phase of the DIIG's "planning and implementing a digital health enterprise" process the handbook supports, and its alignment to the SMART Guidelines layers. The seven phases have ONE source, DIIG §1.1 Fig. 1.1.1 (owner, 2026-10-03, #1984: "use one DIIG seven phase figure as source"); a DTH cites that figure for them, and the copies the handbooks print (PHC Fig. 6, SC Fig 5, PC Fig. 4) are reproductions of it, not further sources. 1552.title: WHO guideline (L1) l1-guideline
1552.content: An L1 publication containing recommendations for clinical practice or public health policy, structured as the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd ed.) §12.1 "Guideline format" requires, with the SMART additions Mehl 2021 names: uniquely identified recommendations and data recommendations. Sections modelled by smart-kg L1 classes are the ones a smart-kg L1 graph of the guideline holds (bean 8pzh). semi-fixed structure · 16 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/l1-guideline.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Executive summaryexecutive-summary | required | A stand-alone summary that states the key recommendations, each with its strength and the certainty of its evidence.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §12.1 Guideline format, PDF p.169; sections/sec-225-121-guideline-format.md — All guidelines should have an executive summary, a main body and appendices. The executive summary should contain the key recommendations of the guideline.who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §12.1 Guideline format, PDF p.169; sections/sec-225-121-guideline-format.md — the strength of the recommendation and the quality of the evidence for each recommendation should be specified in the executive summary | . | 2 | table-of-contents | required | Navigational listing of the main-body sections.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §12.1 Guideline format, PDF p.169; sections/sec-225-121-guideline-format.md — The main text of the guideline should include a table of contents, introduction, methods, recommendations and conclusions. | . | 3 | Target audience and persons affectedtarget-audience | optional | Who will apply the recommendations (end-users), distinguished from the people who receive the interventions.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §2.2.3 Who is the target audience?, PDF p.29; sections/sec-030-223-who-is-the-target-audience.md — Guidelines must have a clearly defined target audience (end-user) which is identified early in the guideline development processwho-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §2.2.3 Who is the target audience?, PDF p.29; sections/sec-030-223-who-is-the-target-audience.md — the end-users are those who will apply the guidelines, not the recipients of the recommended interventions.who-iris/library/9789241548960-eng, §4.5 Table 4.1 Essential components of the planning proposal, PDF pp.53-55; sections/sec-075-44-when-should-the-planning-proposal-be-develope.md — 3. 1556.title: Document kinds
1556.content: . | All instances | smart-base | . A document kind is a named structure of sections that a document authored with a harness follows: fixed (exactly these sections) or semi-fixed (these required, others allowed). Every kind and section names its sources.

1557.title: Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) dak
1557.content: The L2 layer of a WHO SMART Guideline: the ten components that make a guideline's recommendations operational, ahead of the L3 FHIR IG that implements them. Fixed: a DAK has exactly these components, in this order. fixed structure · 10 section(s) · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dak.json · generated by smart-base/scripts/gen-document-kinds.ts . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Health Interventions & Recommendationshealth-interventions-and-recommendations | required | Relevant health interventions and recommendations from the WHO guideline and guidance. To inform DAK scope. | the kind's sources | . | 2 | Generic Personasgeneric-personas | required | Roles, responsibilities, and essential interventions performed by targeted personas. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 3 | User Scenariosuser-scenarios | required | Brief narrative description of how the targeted personas may engage with the digital system. Example for human centered design. | the kind's sources | . | 4 | Business Processes & Workflowsgeneric-business-processes-and-workflows | required | Generic workflows representing clinical and non-clinical processes. To inform when data is collected and used & required features. | the kind's sources | . | 5 | Core Data Elementscore-data-elements | required | Data elements, used for clinical decision-making, indicators, and other data needs. To inform data collection forms and L3 interoperability requirements. | the kind's sources | . | 6 | Decision Support Logicdecision-support-logic | required | Decision tables representing counselling and treatment algorithms, and any other logic used to determine workflow paths or clinical actions. | the kind's sources | . | 7 | Scheduling Logicscheduling-logic | required | Decision tables representing scheduling logic according to care plans. Previously combined with decision support logic. Not yet a field of its own in WHO's DAK logical model. | the kind's sources | . | 8 | Indicators & Monitoringprogramme-indicators | required | Indicators for reporting & monitoring with numerator, denominator of data elements. Linking person centered data to aggregate. | the kind's sources | . | 9 | Functional & Non-functional Requirementsfunctional-and-non-functional-requirements | required | A non-exhaustive list of key functions and non-functional requirements for a digital tracking and decision support system. To inform system features. | the kind's sources | . | 10 | Test Scenariostest-scenarios | required | Test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine components. A test harness to run them. | the kind's sources | . Sources: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240099456 — WHO DAK guidance; https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240085138 — WHO DAK guidance; https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant/issues/1614 — owner ruling 2026-09-30: ten components .

1558.title: Digital Transformation Handbook (DTH) dth
1558.content: A WHO guidance publication on digitalising one area of a health system — an L1 publication whose body is a planning method rather than recommendations. It sits within the DIIG process and should use the DPI-H Reference Architecture (owner, 2026-10-01). Its domain sections map onto smart-kg L2 (DAK) classes: a DTH states for a health-system area what a DAK states for a guideline. Structure read from the three DTHs ingested in smart-base/library; a section is required only where all three have it. The Reference Architecture for DPI-H calls itself "A Digital Transformation Handbook for DPI-H" and is cited here as the architecture the others should reference. semi-fixed structure · 22 section(s) · extends l1 · declared by smart-base in smart-base/document-kinds/dth.json . | # | Section | | What it holds | Source | . | 1 | Audience and how to use this handbookaudience-and-how-to-use | required | Target users/roles per chapter and the stepwise reading path through the handbook.computed from: library | who-iris/library/9789240093362-eng, 2. 1674.title: Términos redactados
1674.content: Bootstrap terms . | término | etiquetas alternativas | definición | . | Nodo | — | Un archivo, o una parte de un archivo direccionable mediante un fragmento de IRI, nombrado por un IRI. | . | Referencia | — | La designación que un Nodo hace de otro Nodo por su IRI. | . | Esquema de nodo | — | Un esquema contra el que se puede validar un Nodo: un JSON Schema, o un esquema externo publicado como el de BPMN. | . | Tipo de nodo | — | Un nombre emparejado con un Esquema de nodo. | . | Subtipo | — | Un Tipo de nodo cuyo Esquema de nodo exige todo lo que exige el de otro Tipo de nodo, de modo que todo Nodo que lo satisface satisface también el otro. | . | Instancia de nodo | — | Un Nodo que nombra su Tipo de nodo, en $schema o en el preámbulo, y satisface el Esquema de nodo de ese tipo. | . | Tipo de grafo | — | Un conjunto con nombre de Tipos de nodo. | . | Declaración | — | Un documento JSON, <name>.json, que da un nombre y enumera entradas de directorio y entradas de archivo. | . | Extensión | — | Un campo de una Declaración, o de una de sus entradas, que no se define aquí. Un lector que no reconoce el campo lo ignora, y el resto de la Declaración conserva su significado. | . | Subgrafo | — | Una entrada de directorio de una Declaración: un id, un directorio y los Tipos de grafo a los que pertenecen los tipos de sus Instancias de nodo. | . | Recurso | — | Una entrada de archivo de una Declaración: un archivo sobre el propio repositorio, cuyo campo role indica para qué sirve. | . | Grafo de conocimiento | — | Los Esquemas de nodo, las Instancias de nodo y los Recursos que enumera una Declaración, en una versión dada del repositorio. 1684.title: Who declares each specification
1684.content: A user declares the specification it depends on; the record names no user. That is data-modelling step 8 — the dependent holds the pointer — and it is why this list cannot drift from the code: a file that stops declaring stops being listed. Four forms are read: a @conformsTo tag, a conformsTo: front-matter list, an xmlns binding, and a graph typology whose typing module declares the spec (bean u63y). Every declaration names a record on this page.

1694.title: Findings
1694.content: Every one of the 50 diagrams has a rendered SVG. Activities carrying no <bootstrap.processes:skill ref> — a census, not a gap list . 22 across 13 diagram(s). This section reported them as defects in its first version, and that was wrong: beans luke and uuhu worked this corpus from 90 down to this remainder and settled what is left. luke: “coverage is deliberately NOT gated — a human sign-off step has no skill”. uuhu added the call-activity exemption and recorded that its own remainder “are not gaps”. 12 are call activities, which delegate to a subprocess — the skill is named there, and naming it twice would be one fact in two places. 1729.title: Findings
1729.content: Every one of the 29 diagrams has a rendered SVG. Activities carrying no <bootstrap.processes:skill ref> — a census, not a gap list . 6 across 3 diagram(s). This section reported them as defects in its first version, and that was wrong: beans luke and uuhu worked this corpus from 90 down to this remainder and settled what is left. luke: “coverage is deliberately NOT gated — a human sign-off step has no skill”. uuhu added the call-activity exemption and recorded that its own remainder “are not gaps”. 3 are call activities, which delegate to a subprocess — the skill is named there, and naming it twice would be one fact in two places. The other 3 are listed by lane, because the lane is what says whether a person, a pipeline or an agent performs the step, and only the last of those has a skill to run. | lane | steps | . | Content Author | 1 | . | Editor / author (person) | 1 | . | Folio-Assistant Agent | 1 | . No verdict is offered on which of these is a gap, and that is the honest state rather than a hedge: distinguishing a person’s judgement step from an agent step somebody forgot needs the lane’s actor KIND, which a free-text lane name does not give — process-model.ts notes sixty lanes spell two dozen positions. The lane’s partitionElementRef is the join that would answer it, and it is present on 3 of these 3 steps — which is the measurement, not an impression. 1758.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1758.title: WireGen: from a written intent to a reviewed, mid-fidelity wireframe
1758.content: Adopted in part, 2026-09-23, by the owner’s direction. In the owner’s words: “make methodology/utilize/integrate into existing processes. need both web and mobile layouts in usability reviews. wireframe is part of design process for adjudication”. Integrated into CRDM, 2026-10-14. crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn calls Process_WireframeDesignReview (Call_Wireframe) whenever a requirement changes a rendered surface, before anything is built; the candidates become assets of the request’s proposal, and the requester or BA chooses one at BA_ReviewReqs. See wireframe-design-review. Placed in cat-harness (owner, 2026-09-23: “put wireframe in cat-harness, not folio-assist(-core)”). The method is domain-neutral, and methodology-adoption §4 puts a domain-neutral method in the harness. It was first drafted in litlfred/ihris, and its first use was that folio’s data-model site. Issue #1023.

1759.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1759.title: What the method says (rendered faithfully)
1759.content: Section numbers below are the paper’s. | Design intent comes first, as language (§3, §5.2). A short natural-language description of what the screen is for and what it holds. | Mid-fidelity is the target (§3.1.1). The wireframe is monochrome and simplified, but it carries real content, semantic icons and interactive elements, not boxes and placeholder text. | HTML is the carrier (§3.1.2, §3.3). The screen is expressed as a UI-specific HTML-like language. Raw output is post-processed against UI guidance: icons chosen by meaning, typography, and layout guidelines (§3.3). | Evaluation is blind and comparative (§4.3). Independent raters with design background see the description and a shuffled grid of candidates, without knowing which generator produced which. They mark candidates significantly better or significantly worse. | Usefulness is asked separately (§5.2): whether a wireframe is effective for inspiration, whether it relates to the description, and whether the candidates are diverse. These are rated on a 5-point scale. | Refinement is iterative (§6). Intent, then wireframe, then a revised intent, then a revised wireframe. | .

1760.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1760.title: What this platform adopts, and what it refuses
1760.content: |   | adopted | refused, with the reason | . | intent statement | yes: every candidate set starts from one, and it is the criterion candidates are judged against | none | . | mid-fidelity with real content | yes: real content from the folio (for iHRIS: real form classes, fields, lists) | none | . | HTML carrier + guideline post-processing | yes: wireframes are HTML, and the mechanical checks are the post-processing gate | none | . | fine-tuning an LLM on Rico / Screen2Words (§3.1, §3.2) | no | That is how the authors generate; it is not a review method. Candidates here may come from a person, an agent or any tool. The method applies to what they produce. | . | blind, shuffled comparison | yes: reviewers are not told a candidate’s author | none | . | better/worse marks and Likert ratings | the structure, not the arithmetic | methodology-adoption refuses scoring and summing. A mean of Likert ratings reads as a measurement of a judgement. Reviewers record per-criterion pass / warn / fail with a reason. | . | mobile only (the paper’s data is Android, §3.1.1) | extended: both web and mobile layouts are required in every usability review (owner, 2026-09-23) | The source’s scope is narrower than our need. We state the extension rather than claim the paper supports it. | . | the reported numbers (77.5%, the user study) | no | They describe the authors’ model and datasets. Nothing here depends on them. | .

1761.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1761.title: How it plugs into existing processes
1761.content: . | Review record: each criterion gets entries from a script (the mechanical checks), an agent and a human, in block-qa/v1 sidecars. This is folio-assistant’s existing multi-reviewer primitive. | Disagreement: when entries for one criterion disagree, the candidate set enters Process_Adjudication (sdlc/processes/adjudication.bpmn). The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and the dispensation carries its reason. | Choice between surviving candidates: a one-off choice, so it uses the decision-analysis methodology. Rejected candidates are kept with the reason they lost. | After build: the rendered result does not go through theme-ui-review.bpmn any more. Theme and UI review moved to ingestion only, by owner ruling (work item 9fdi, 2026-09-24): it runs when the graphical assets arrive, from ingest-theme.bpmn, and still requires both web and mobile layouts (#1023). A post-build visual look for a wiregen output is therefore not provided by that process — recorded so it is not assumed. | . The executable form is processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn. The operating skill is wireframe-design-review. The mechanical checks are the Tool wireframe-check.

1762.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1762.title: Refusals
1762.content: . | Never review a single candidate as if it were a choice. The method is comparative; at least two candidates, or say why only one exists. | Never accept a wireframe reviewed at one viewport. A web-only or mobile-only review is incomplete, not passed. | Never show a reviewer who made a candidate. Blindness is the method’s evidence of fairness. | Never let placeholder text through. Lorem ipsum makes it a low-fidelity wireframe, and the method is about mid-fidelity. | Never average the ratings into a score. | .

1763.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1763.title: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
1763.content: ← All methodologies . wiregen — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Designing a USER INTERFACE, for example a page layout, a navigation scheme or a visualiser, where the choice between candidate designs has to be reviewed and, when reviewers disagree, adjudicated. It is a design-generation and design-evaluation method. It does not choose between non-UI options (use the decision-analysis methodology) or grade evidence. It does not by itself settle a disagreement: that is adjudication. Origin. Sidong Feng, Mingyue Yuan, Jieshan Chen, Zhenchang Xing and Chunyang Chen, “Designing with Language: Wireframing UI Design Intent with Generative Large Language Models”, arXiv:2312.07755v1 [cs.HC], 12 Dec 2023. Ingested in full at cat-harness/library/corpus/ui/arxiv-2312.07755v1/. The source states no licence, and its licence could not be established (see check:source-licence). 1764.content: Adopted 2026-09-23 (issue #1180), on the owner’s choice of permission language: “W3C ODRL 2.2 and W3C PROV-O for logging” — quoted from the docblock of schemas/content/odrl.ts. 1765.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1765.title: Its sources: what is held, what is not
1765.content: | source | held | what this node takes from it | . | ODRL Information Model 2.2 (W3C REC, 2018) | ✅ library/w3c-2018-odrl-model-2-2 | the model, its classes and every MUST quoted below | . | ODRL Vocabulary & Expression 2.2 | ❌ not held | the Common Vocabulary actions (display, modify, …) and their includedIn; the JSON-LD context. The includedIn values in ODRL_ACTIONS are not verified against it here | . | post-REC errata | ❌ not held | none | . A caution on section references. The held sections were split by PDF page, so a section file’s body often begins with the tail of the previous section. References below use the section numbers printed in the text, not the file names.

1766.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1766.title: The load-bearing idea, in the standard’s words
1766.content: “The ODRL Information Model represents Policies that express Permissions, Prohibitions and Duties related to the usage of Asset resources. The Information Model explicitly expresses what is allowed and what is not allowed by the Policy” — §2. Its terms (§1.3): a Policy is “A group of one or more Rules”; an Action “An operation on an Asset”; a Permission “The ability to exercise an Action over an Asset”; a Prohibition “The inability to exercise an Action over an Asset”; a Duty “The obligation to exercise an agreed Action”; a Party “An entity or a collection of entities that undertake Roles in a Rule”; a Constraint “A boolean/logical expression that refines an Action and Party/Asset collection or the conditions applicable to a Rule”. Three mechanisms carry the method, and the platform uses all three: . | Actions inherit through includedIn. “a Permission or Prohibition of an encompassing Action is inherited by all Actions with an includedIn relationship”, and every action other than use and transfer “MUST have one includedIn property value” (§2.4). | Constraints conjoin. “When multiple Constraints apply to the same Rule … they are interpreted as conjunction and all MUST be satisfied” (§2.5). | Conflicts are resolved by a declared strategy: “perm: the Permissions MUST override the Prohibitions; prohibit: the Prohibitions MUST override the Permissions; invalid: the entire Policy MUST be void” (§2.10). | . And one that makes extension legitimate: a policy may “Use an ODRL Profile that declares the supported vocabulary” (§2.1), and new actions are made by creating “an instance of an Action and define its includedIn parent Action” (§3.3).

1767.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1767.title: What this platform adopts — class by class
1767.content: | ODRL | here | where | . | Policy (Set, Offer, Agreement), uid, profile, inheritFrom, conflict | adopted; both live policies are Sets with conflict: odrl:prohibit | OdrlPolicySchema, policies/*.jsonld | . | Permission | adopted: one rule per (actor, action), migrated from the old per-actor lists | policies/folio-defaults.jsonld, policies/http-gateway.jsonld | . | Prohibition | adopted in the schema and the evaluator; no live policy states one — both files’ prohibition is [] or absent | permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts | . | Action + includedIn | adopted: the folio profile’s actions each name a broader action, ending at ODRL’s odrl:display/modify/annotate/derive/translate/execute under odrl:use | skills/permissions/permissions.json, ODRL_ACTIONS, broaderOrSelf() | . | Party — assignee, assigner | adopted as the assignee of each rule, an actor id from scenarios/actors/, plus the profile party cat-harness:anyone for an unauthenticated reader | OdrlRuleSchema, ANYONE | . | Asset — target | adopted as an optional target string | ruleApplies() | . | Constraint | adopted for three profile leftOperands — cat-harness:process, cat-harness:task, cat-harness:role — and four operators eq, neq, isAnyOf, isNoneOf, conjoined | OdrlConstraintSchema, constraintHolds() | . | Profile | profile is required; the action half of the profile is permissions.json | OdrlPolicySchema | . The evaluator is the question every caller asks — the BPMN task gate (src/workflow/authorize.ts, action perform-task), the HTTP routes (src/core/rbac.ts), and the auth_whoami tool (src/tools/auth.ts) — all through decide(), over policies loaded by src/core/access.ts.

1768.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1768.title: What it refuses or departs from, with reasons
1768.content: Each item is a place where the code differs from the held text. They are stated so nobody reads @conformsTo w3c-odrl as full conformance. | Duty, obligation, consequence, remedy — refused. No reader exists, and .strict() rejects the keys “because a rule that silently means less than it says is exactly the failure a permission file must not have” (schemas/content/odrl.ts). A Permission carrying an unfulfilled duty would be read as unconditional, which is worse than refusing it. | Refinements, AssetCollection, PartyCollection, LogicalConstraint, rightOperandReference, dataType, unit, status, implies, partOf, hasPolicy, transfer — refused, for the same reason: no reader. | target is optional; ODRL requires it. §2.6.1: “A Permission MUST have one target property value of type Asset” (Prohibition likewise, §2.6.2). Here an absent target means the layer’s whole graph. Every live rule omits it. | The default conflict strategy is prohibit; ODRL’s is invalid. §2.10: “If the conflict property is not explicitly set, the default of invalid will be used.” The code names this as “OUR rule rather than claimed as ODRL’s”; both live policies set odrl:prohibit explicitly, so the difference does not fire today. Kept by owner ruling, 2026-10-01 (work item jcet): an unstated clash denies rather than voiding the policy — a deliberate profile departure, not an oversight; odrl.test.ts pins it. | Across policies, any deny wins. decide() evaluates each policy and lets a prohibition in one beat a permission in another. ODRL’s merge rule is different — inherited conflict values are replicated and “If a Policy has multiple conflict property values … then the entire Policy MUST be void” (§2.10). Only the child’s conflict is read by permits(). | A circular inheritFrom is tolerated, not refused. §2.9: “Inheritance MUST NOT be circular.” effectiveRules() walks with a visited set, so a cycle terminates silently instead of failing. (Cycles are deliberately allowed in the action graph — the owner’s “doensnt necc need to be rooted acyclic graph”. That sits uneasily with §2.4, which calls includedIn transitive, says “the Actions form ancestor relationships”, and requires every action to reach use or transfer; a cycle among profile actions is a departure, not a reading.) | No-match answers unknown, a third value. This node found no held text that defines the outcome when no rule matches; unknown — never permit, never deny — is the platform’s rule (Decision in schemas/content/odrl.ts), so task-authorization can report it as a finding. | Role eligibility is added on top. permits() denies a permitted request whose cat-harness:role the actor is not eligible for. That is role-model’s separation of what a lane needs from what an actor may do; it is not ODRL. | Cardinalities not enforced: an empty policy validates (§2.1: “MUST have at least one permission, prohibition, or obligation”); an Offer needs no assigner and an Agreement needs no policy-level assignee (§2.1.2, §2.1.3); and the profile IRI is never checked, although §3.2 says a processor that “does not recognise the ODRL Profile identifier(s) … MUST stop processing”. | The profile is not published as RDF. §3.3 asks that new terms “must also be defined as a skos:Concept”; permissions.json is plain JSON with id, title, description, includedIn, and the profile IRI https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/ns/folio-odrl is not shown to resolve. | .

1769.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1769.title: What ODRL is not used for here
1769.content: . | Not for source licences. ODRL’s own subject is content usage, and the natural reading would be a library entry’s licence as an ODRL Offer. That is not what happens: licence.json records a status and an SPDX id, checked by bun run cat check:source-licence (scripts/check-source-licence.ts). | Not for identity. Which login is which actor is GitHub’s answer (src/core/github-auth.ts), never a policy’s — policies/README.md. | Not for logging. That is PROV-O (schemas/content/prov.ts), chosen alongside it. | .

1773.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1773.title: ⚠ The cited source backs ONE sentence of this node, and nothing else
1773.content: evidence points at Dusengumuremyi (2026), ingested 2026-09-23. It earns its place only as a secondary rendering of the four roles — its §2.1, verbatim from sections/page-002.md: . a classic project management instrument delineating four roles: Responsible (doer), Accountable (owner), Consulted (input provider), and Informed (notified). Everything else in that paper is rejected, and the rejection is load-bearing rather than fastidious. Its own Data Availability statement reads “No new datasets were generated or analyzed during this study” while its abstract claims 1,247 decision events and its §4.1 reports t(1245)=47.3, p<.001; its abstract’s headline 92.4 % detection rate appears nowhere in its findings, which say 78.4 %; and its running head claims Journal of International Business Studies “Vol. 1, 2026” while its own reference list cites that journal at vol. 53 in 2022. Work item thb1 holds the full assessment with every item checkable against the ingested pages. So: cite this source for the four letters. Never cite it for a claim about what RACI achieves. No efficacy, latency, error-rate or risk-detection statement anywhere in this repository may rest on it. That split is why evidence here is not the same kind of backing swot has. swot rests on two sources that survive reading whole; this rests on one paragraph of one paper that does not. check:methodology-evidence counts nodes with a resolvable source and will now count this one — the axis measures whether a citation resolves, not whether a reader would accept it, and conflating those is what this box exists to prevent.

1774.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1774.title: The four letters
1774.content: | letter | means | direction | . | Responsible | does the work | may be several | . | Accountable | carries the decision; answers for the outcome | exactly one | . | Consulted | asked for input before | two-way | . | Informed | told after | one-way | . The axis that makes it a method rather than a list is time and direction: C happens before and is a conversation; I happens after and is a broadcast. Collapsing them turns consultation into notification, which is the failure the letters exist to keep apart.

1775.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1775.title: Exactly one Accountable
1775.content: The method’s central constraint, and the one most often broken in practice. A chart with two A’s does not record a shared decision — it records that nobody established who answers for the outcome, and it reads as complete while doing so. Zero is also a breach, once a row claims anything at all. A half-filled row is worse than an empty one for the same reason: the chart looks answered. A row where the same party is both Accountable and Consulted is not a row with two facts in it. Asking yourself is not consultation, and that pairing is how consulted becomes a formality while the chart still reads complete.

1776.doc: RACI — who is involved in an activity, and in which of four ways
1776.title: What RACI is not
1776.content: . | Not a decision method. A is who answers for a decision, not how it is reached. Reaching it is kepner-tregoe or dmn; recording it is madr. | Not an approval gate. Answering for an outcome and signing off on one are different acts, and a method that conflated them would let a chart stand in for a gate. | Not a permission model. What a party may do in general is a different question from who is involved in this activity, and the two cross-cut. | Not a party registry. RACI names roles in rows; it does not establish who exists. Something else has to say that first. | .
