1904.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1904.title: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1904.content: This methodology node completes work item folio-assistant-qh1s (Issue #1164): a literature search over requirements-management practice across the five lifecycle dimensions (organisation, identifiers, traceability, change, and retirement), the explicit adoption or rejection of candidate methodologies through methodology-adoption, and the proposed executable BPMN filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn) put to the owner before automation is built. Whereas sibling methodology requirements-standards-assessment.md (work item folio-assistant-1gf7) assessed open interchange and syntax standards (ReqIF, OSLC RM, EARS, RFC 2119 / RFC 8174, IEEE 29148, Planguage, SysML, Gherkin) to map their constructs onto bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json, this node governs how requirements are organised, identified, traced, amended, superseded, and retired as they are filed into docs/requirements/ once docs/requirements/ grows past a flat hand-maintained list.

1905.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1905.title: 1. Literature search over requirements-management practice
1905.content: Per literature-search, every surveyed source is recorded below with its provenance/access status (ingested library/<bib-slug> node where held on disk, or external standard / open-source specification where copyright or scope keeps the full text outside library/) and with what it offers here across the five dimensions of work item folio-assistant-qh1s: . | Organisation — how a growing corpus of filed requirements is structured and navigated without breaking path stability. | Identifiers — how requirements and sub-clauses receive durable, collision-free, human- and machine-addressable IDs in a distributed Git workflow. | Traceability — how backward lineage (to proposals, user needs, and L1 sources), horizontal dependencies (between requirements), and forward verification (to work items, skills, processes, and test attestations) are recorded and checked. | Change — how in-scope amendments versus scope-altering replacements are distinguished, reviewed, and versioned. | Retirement — how obsolete or superseded requirements leave active force without breaking historical links or audit trails. | . 1.1 Summary matrix across the five filing dimensions . | Source | Provenance / library status | Organisation | Identifiers | Traceability | Change | Retirement | . | ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering, Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, 6.5) | Proprietary ISO/IEEE standard; assessed via public clause structure (no full-text redistributable PDF in library/) | Separates stakeholder requirements (StRS) from system/software requirements (SyRS/SRS); organises by system architecture or functional domain | Unique, persistent requirement identifier (id) independent of document section position | Clause 5.2.7 mandates bidirectional traceability: backward to source/parent need, forward to design elements and verification records | Clause 6.5 requires formal change control, impact analysis over dependent items, and baseline sign-off | Explicit lifecycle status attribute (retired / obsolete / superseded); historical records retained for audit | . | Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson, Mastering the Requirements Process, 4th ed.) | Commercial book / template; assessed via published Volere atomic “Snow Card” specification | Groups requirements by functional area / business event / concern rather than implementation module; pairs functional with non-functional categories | Atomic requirement number + type code + event/use-case reference on each Snow Card | Each card records Source / Originator, Supporting Materials, Dependencies, and a mandatory measurable Fit Criterion | History log on the card tracking creation, amendments, and re-verification | Explicit archived / retired state with reason when business rules change; card number is never reused | . | IREB CPRE Foundation Level (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals, 3rd ed.) | Standard RE body of knowledge; external textbook | Contrasts tree-structured chapter hierarchies against faceted / attribute-driven views over atomic requirement objects | Recommends immutable object identifiers decoupled from chapter headings so restructuring views never renumbers requirements | Defines three explicit trace link directions: pre-RS / backward (to origins), post-RS / forward (to artefacts/tests), and within-RS / horizontal (dependsOn, refines, conflictsWith) | Configuration management and baseline versioning; change impact propagation along trace links | Status state machine (draft → agreed → validated → implemented → deprecated/retired) | . | Doorstop (Browning & Adams, Doorstop: Text-Based Requirements Management Using Version Control, JOSS 2014; github.com/doorstop-dev/doorstop) | Open-source Git-native requirements tool (lgpl-3.0); external software reference | Stores one text file per requirement (YAML or Markdown-with-front-matter) inside version-controlled directories representing document trees | Prefix + identifier per file, addressable in git diffs; supports sub-links and hierarchical parent pointers | Parent/child trace links stored directly in requirement front matter; detects suspect links when a parent requirement changes | Git commits and pull requests are the change-control log; review happens in PR diffs alongside code and tests | active: false / normative: false front-matter flags retire an item in place without git rm, keeping git blame and incoming links intact | . | Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (Nygard 2011; Kopp et al., adr.github.io/madr/, already adopted in methodologies/madr.md) | Adopted harness methodology (methodologies/madr.md) | Flat directory of Markdown files (docs/decisions/ or docs/proposals/), indexed by concern or status in index.md | Filename slug (<slug>.md) serves as the stable human-readable identifier | Cross-references related decisions, issues, and motivating forces in front matter and body | Append-only / immutable intent: minor clarifications edit in place; substantive reversals file a new record that supersedes the old | Explicit status transitions: proposed → accepted → deprecated | superseded by ADR-XXXX; old files are never deleted | . | W3C PROV-O (PROV-O: The PROV Ontology, W3C Recommendation 2013, adopted in methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md) | Ingested in library/w3c-2013-prov-o | Graph of prov:Entity nodes linked by typed provenance relations independent of filesystem nesting | Stable IRIs (req:<slug>, req:<slug>#<key>) identifying each entity | prov:wasDerivedFrom (parent/source lineage), prov:wasGeneratedBy (filing/test activity), prov:wasAttributedTo (actor/sign-off) | prov:wasRevisionOf and prov:specializationOf distinguish revisions from distinct derived entities | prov:wasInvalidatedBy and prov:invalidatedAtTime model retirement/supersession without erasing the entity from the provenance graph | . | RFC 2119 & RFC 8174 (Bradner 1997; Leiba 2017 — BCP 14 key words) | Ingested in library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | Separates normative statements (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) from explanatory prose within a specification | Statement-level addressing (statements[].key → req:<slug>#<key>) so each normative keyword clause is individually citable | Pairs each uppercase keyword statement with its own successCriteria and verification witness | Changing a statement’s modality (SHOULD → MUST) is a normative change requiring re-sign-off | Retiring or relaxing a MUST statement requires explicit normative adjudication | . | Specification-Compiled Agents & Issue-Driven Work Plans (arxiv-2404.04834v4; hmans-2026-beans-readme) | Ingested in library/arxiv-2404.04834v4 and library/hmans-2026-beans-readme | Connects declarative specifications to executable agent work items (beans/) and automated verification gates | Cross-graph IDs: req:<slug> linked to work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) and process IDs (Process_*) | Closed-loop compilation: requirement statement → work-plan work item → implementing skill/process → test attestation | Specification edits trigger deterministic re-check (check:requirements) across all linked sets and attestations | Completed work items archive when closed; filed requirements remain in-force as the persistent invariant until superseded or retired | . | IEEE Std 830-1998 (IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148) | Historical IEEE standard (superseded); external baseline | Monolithic single-document SRS organised by deep numbered outline (3.1.1.1 Functional Requirement 1) | Positional section numbers (§3.2.4.1) tied to document outline location | External traceability matrices (spreadsheets) mapping section numbers to test cases | Document-level revision history table at the top of the monolithic SRS | Striking out or deleting sections in a new SRS edition, causing section renumbering unless placeholder sections are kept | . 1.2 Detailed source notes: what each source offers this harness . 1.2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, and 6.5) . | What it offers here: . | Attribute canon (Clause 6.5): Defines the essential metadata attributes every managed requirement needs beyond its statement text: unique identifier, requirement status, source/origin, rationale, priority/modality, verification method/criteria, and trace links. Our bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json directly embodies this attribute set (id, title, status, proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, statements[], beans, skills, processes, supersededBy). | Bidirectional traceability (Clause 5.2.7): Establishes that forward traceability alone (requirement → test) is half a system; backward traceability (requirement → originating proposal/need/source via proposedIn and derivedFrom) is what prevents gold-plating (orphan requirements with no stakeholder origin) and explains why a constraint exists when an agent later considers changing it. | Change and retirement discipline: Distinguishes an approved baseline from working drafts (RequirementSet.stage: draft → proposed → approved → accepted in bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json) and requires any transition into or out of active force to carry human sign-off. | . | . 1.2.2 Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson) . | What it offers here: . | Atomic “Snow Card” structure with Fit Criteria: Volere’s primary contribution is insisting that a requirement is not filed until its Fit Criterion (our statements[].successCriteria) is written beside the description (statements[].statement). A requirement whose fit criterion cannot be stated is still a proposal or open question. | Organisation by semantic concern / business domain: Rather than organising requirements by the code file they touch or chronological filing date, Volere organises requirements by functional domain / concern area so a reader auditing one domain sees all governing invariants together. In cat-harness, the eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) already partition skills, processes, schemas, and tests; projecting filed requirements under those same eight concern groups in docs/requirements/index.md aligns requirement navigation with the rest of the knowledge graph. | . | . 1.2.3 IREB CPRE (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals) . | What it offers here: . | Decoupling identification and storage from presentation views: IREB highlights the classic failure mode of hierarchical specifications: when chapter structure is used as both the file path and the requirement ID, reorganising chapters breaks every incoming reference. Storing atomic requirements at stable paths with immutable IDs (docs/requirements/<slug>.md → req:<slug>) while providing faceted views (grouped by concern group, by RequirementSet, or by lifecycle status in docs/requirements/index.md) gives both stable URIs and structured human browsing. | Three-axis trace topology: Clarifies the distinction between backward trace (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal trace (dependsOn between peer requirements), and forward trace (beans, skills, processes, and verification attestations). | . | . 1.2.4 Doorstop (Browning & Adams, JOSS 2014) . | What it offers here: . | Git-native file-per-requirement architecture: Doorstop proved that storing requirements as individual text files with YAML front matter and Markdown prose in the same Git repository as the implementation eliminates external ALM database drift. Every requirement filing, amendment, or retirement travels in the same pull request as the code, process diagram, and test attestation that implements or verifies it. | In-place retirement (status: retired / superseded): Doorstop retires requirements by flipping a front-matter status field rather than deleting the file (git rm), ensuring that historical commits, test runs, and child requirements never point to a missing file. | Suspect-link awareness: Doorstop flags downstream items when an upstream requirement changes. In our harness, check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts) provides the deterministic equivalent: it verifies that every derivedFrom, dependsOn, and supersededBy target exists, that no cycle exists in derivedFrom, that no in-force requirement depends on a retired or superseded requirement without updating its own lineage, and that every RequirementSet at approved or accepted has a matching human requirement-signoff attestation and only in-force members. | . | . 1.2.5 Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) . | What it offers here: . | Proposal-to-Requirement continuity (git mv + proposedIn): In cat-harness, a feature starts as a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (where options are weighed using Kepner-Tregoe, SWOT, and MADR). When the feature ships and is signed off, git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md promotes the file in place, preserving its slug, its git log --follow history, and the options analysis that justified it, while proposedIn records the commit SHA and path of the proposal before the move. | Immutable supersession chain: When a shipped requirement’s fundamental contract is replaced by a new design, the old requirement file is not overwritten into a different contract; instead, the new proposal is filed as docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md, and the old requirement’s front matter is updated to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | .

1906.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1906.title: 2. Candidate methodologies: adopted vs rejected with reasons
1906.content: Following skills/process/process-core/methodology-adoption.md, we do not invent an unattributed house method. We adopt four orthogonal practices from the surveyed literature—naming their origins, what is taken, what is left behind, and how each binds into bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and check:requirements—and we explicitly reject five candidate practices with documented reasons. 2.1 Adopted methodologies . M1 — Doorstop + MADR git-native file-per-requirement and two-level semantic identifiers (req:<slug> and req:<slug>#<key>) . | Origin: Doorstop (Browning & Adams 2014) for one-file-per-requirement in Git with YAML front matter + Markdown body; MADR (methodologies/madr.md) for human-readable <slug>.md filenames; RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md) for statement-level normative clauses. | What is adopted: . | Each filed requirement lives in its own Markdown file at docs/requirements/<slug>.md with id: req:<slug> matching its filename stem (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Individual normative clauses inside a requirement are declared in statements[] (key, modality, statement, successCriteria) and addressed as req:<slug>#<key> (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*#[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, every <slug> is globally unique: a slug exists either as an unshipped proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md or as a filed requirement in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, never both (check:requirements refuses a collision). | . | What is left behind and why: . | Doorstop’s auto-incremented numeric filenames (REQ001.yml, REQ002.yml) are left behind because concurrent feature branches in a multi-agent repository collide on sequential integers and opaque numbers hide meaning in prose and test logs. | Doorstop’s content-hash “fingerprint” clearing on whitespace edits is left behind because explicit lifecycle status + human requirement-signoff attestations (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/) provide stronger, semantically intentional governance than raw byte hashes. | . | . M2 — Faceted concern-group organisation (code-lists/concern-group.json) over flat docs/requirements/<slug>.md storage (Volere + IREB faceted view) . | Origin: Volere functional-area grouping (Robertson & Robertson) combined with IREB CPRE’s separation of stable storage identifiers from faceted navigation views (Pohl & Rupp), bound to the harness’s eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json. | What is adopted: . | Physical storage stays flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md: Every filed requirement sits directly in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, preserving 1:1 path parity with docs/proposals/<slug>.md for git mv, keeping req:<slug> → docs/requirements/<slug>.md resolution O(1) without directory searches, and ensuring check:requirements (mdFilesIn) reads 100% of filed requirements. | Logical organisation in docs/requirements/index.md groups by two orthogonal views: . | By Concern Group (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct from code-lists/concern-group.json), so a reader or agent working in a concern domain sees every in-force invariant governing that domain. | By Requirement Set (RequirementSet) and Lifecycle Status (in-force vs superseded / retired), so CRD baselines and historical records are cleanly separated from active invariants. | . | . | What is left behind and why: . | Physical subdirectory nesting (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) is rejected (see R3 below) so that reclassifying a requirement’s concern group or cross-cutting scope never breaks markdown links or requires a second git mv. | . | . M3 — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 + IREB + W3C PROV-O three-axis bidirectional traceability . | Origin: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Clause 5.2.7 (bidirectional traceability), IREB CPRE (backward / horizontal / forward trace links), and W3C PROV-O (library/w3c-2013-prov-o, methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md). | What is adopted: . | Backward traceability (to origin and parent sources): . | proposedIn: required on every requirement promoted from docs/proposals/<slug>.md (commit SHA + path: docs/proposals/<slug>.md), binding prov:wasDerivedFrom to the exact pre-move proposal revision. | derivedFrom: array of parent req:<slug> IDs or library/<bib-slug> L1 sources from which this requirement is derived (checked for existence and acyclicity by check:requirements). | . | Horizontal traceability (between peer requirements): . | dependsOn: array of req:<slug> IDs that this requirement relies on at runtime or design time (checked for existence by check:requirements). | . | Forward traceability (to work items, implementation, and verification): . | beans: work-plan work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) that delivered or amended the requirement. | skills and processes: the Skill and Process (Process_*) nodes that implement the requirement. | Verification & Sign-off: test runs (test/runs/) and attestations (test/attestations/) citing req:<slug> or req:<slug>#<key>, plus RequirementSet membership and human sign-off attestations in test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json. | . | . | . M4 — MADR / ISO 29148 immutable lifecycle for change, supersession, and retirement (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired) . | Origin: MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Clause 6.5 configuration & change control. | What is adopted: . | Four lifecycle states (status in requirement.schema.json): . | proposed: drafted in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or in a RequirementSet at draft / proposed / approved stage) awaiting final delivery and acceptance sign-off. | in-force: shipped, verified, and accepted by human BA/owner sign-off; actively binds the codebase and knowledge graph. | superseded: replaced by a newer requirement; must carry supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (enforced by requirement.schema.json allOf rule and check:requirements). | retired: no longer applicable (the feature or constraint was intentionally removed without replacement); supersededBy is omitted, and the retirement rationale and authorising issue/bean are recorded in the document body. | . | Change decision rule (Amendment in place vs Supersession): . | In-scope amendment (edit in place, keep req:<slug>): When clarifying prose, adding a statements[] sub-clause, tightening a successCriteria check, or updating skills/processes/beans links without reversing the core invariant, edit docs/requirements/<slug>.md in place and record a fresh requirement-signoff attestation if its RequirementSet is approved or accepted. | Scope-reversing replacement (file req:<new-slug>, mark old superseded): When a new proposal reverses or fundamentally replaces an in-force requirement’s contract, file the new proposal at docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md (status: in-force, derivedFrom: [req:<old-slug>]), and update docs/requirements/<old-slug>.md to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | Set membership consistency: Because check:requirements enforces that an approved or accepted RequirementSet may only contain in-force (or proposed at approved stage) members, superseding or retiring a requirement requires updating any RequirementSet that lists it (replacing the old ID with req:<new-slug> or removing the retired ID under a re-signed set amendment). | . | . 2.2 Rejected candidate methodologies (with reasons) . | Candidate methodology | Verdict | Reason for rejection in this harness | . | R1 — IEEE Std 830-1998 monolithic SRS & positional section numbering (§3.2.1.4) | Rejected | Tying a requirement’s identifier to its outline position in a single monolithic file causes cascading renumbering whenever a section is inserted, split, or reordered. Renumbering breaks req: URIs in test runs, attestations, and work items, and a single monolithic SRS file creates constant Git merge conflicts across parallel agent branches. | . | R2 — Centralised sequential integer IDs (REQ-0001, FR-0042) | Rejected | In a distributed multi-agent Git workflow (worktrees, branches, subagents), two branches filing requirements concurrently will allocate the same next integer (REQ-0043) unless gated by an external lock server. Even when unique, opaque integers convey no domain meaning in test logs or prose compared to req:<slug>#<key>. (Note: FR-NNN may still appear as a local table label inside a single CRD proposal during discussion, but the canonical graph identifier is req:<slug>#<key>.) | . | R3 — Physical subdirectory sharding (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) | Rejected (kept as faceted index view in docs/requirements/index.md instead) | 1. check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts, mdFilesIn) scans docs/requirements/ and docs/proposals/ non-recursively and enforces a 1:1 slug namespace between docs/proposals/<slug>.md and docs/requirements/<slug>.md.2. Many proposals span multiple concern groups (e.g., sdlc + process); forcing a single directory path would make paths brittle when concern boundaries evolve.3. Faceted grouping in docs/requirements/index.md delivers the navigational benefit of Volere/concern-group organisation with zero path churn. | . | R4 — ReqIF XML / OSLC RM RDF triples as the primary authored store | Rejected (consistent with requirements-standards-assessment.md) | XML UUID graphs and raw RDF triples are unreadable in GitHub PR reviews and cannot be naturally co-authored as prose + front matter by humans and agents. Our YAML front matter (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) exports cleanly to JSON-LD (bootstrap/ns.jsonld) without burdening authors with XML. | . | R5 — Destructive deletion (git rm) of superseded or retired requirements | Rejected | Deleting docs/requirements/<slug>.md when a requirement is retired or superseded breaks historical provenance: past test/runs/, test/attestations/, beans/, and derivedFrom links would become dangling references. Keeping the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md with status: superseded (supersededBy: req:<new-slug>) or status: retired preserves referential integrity across the graph. | .

1907.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1907.title: 3. Proposed filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn)
1907.content: To fulfil Criterion 3 of work item folio-assistant-qh1s (“a filing PROCESS proposed as BPMN, to be put to the owner before it is built”), the executable BPMN diagram sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (Process_RequirementsFiling) models the end-to-end process for filing, organising,superseding, or retiring a requirement in docs/requirements/. 3.1 Where Process_RequirementsFiling sits in the lifecycle . In the CRDM lifecycle (sdlc/skills/crdm/crdm-requirements-workflow.md): . | Phases 1–4 (crdm-needs.bpmn, crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn, crdm-data-model.bpmn, crdm-signoff.bpmn) produce and sign off a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and optionally a RequirementSet moving from draft → proposed → approved). | Phase 5 (crdm-deliver.bpmn) builds and verifies the MVP in code, skills, and processes. | At Phase 6 (crdm-close.bpmn), when the feature ships and stakeholders/BA confirm acceptance criteria are met, Process_RequirementsFiling (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn) governs the transition of the proposal into docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or the amendment, supersession, or retirement of an existing filed requirement). | . 3.2 Lanes and responsibilities . | Lane | Role (partitionElementRef) | Responsibility in Process_RequirementsFiling | . | BA / Feature Requestor (Lane_BA) | business-analyst | Reviews the filed requirement’s organisation, traceability links, normative statements, and any supersession/retirement transition (BA_ReviewFiling), and issues the human sign-off decision (approve, amend, reject, defer, cancel) required by check:requirements before a RequirementSet can reach accepted. | . | Authoring Agent (Lane_Agent) | authoring-agent | Executes the deterministic filing steps: classifies the requirement’s concern group and filing mode (A_ClassifyFiling), moves or updates the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (A_PromoteOrUpdate), binds the Requirement front matter (A_BindFrontMatter), updates superseded/retired records (A_UpdateLifecycle), indexes the requirement in docs/requirements/index.md (A_UpdateIndex), runs check:requirements (A_RunCheck), and records the human sign-off attestation (A_RecordFilingSignoff). | . 3.3 Step-by-step walkthrough of sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn . | A_ClassifyFiling — Classify filing mode, concern group, and req:<slug> identifier (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Determine which of the three filing modes applies: . | New filing from proposal: promoting docs/proposals/<slug>.md → docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | In-place amendment or supersession: amending an existing docs/requirements/<slug>.md or superseding req:<old-slug> with req:<new-slug>. | Retirement: retiring an obsolete docs/requirements/<slug>.md (status: retired). | . | Assign the primary concern group from code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) for indexing in docs/requirements/index.md. | . | GW_FilingMode — Which filing transition? (cat-harness.processes:judgement): . | Branches on the three modes: promote (from docs/proposals/<slug>.md), amend-or-supersede (on an existing requirement), or retire (marking an active requirement retired). | . | A_PromoteOrUpdate — git mv proposal to docs/requirements/<slug>.md and capture proposedIn (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | On the promote branch, record the pre-move commit SHA (git log -1 --format=%H -- docs/proposals/<slug>.md), execute git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md so Git history stays unbroken, and populate proposedIn: { commit, path: "docs/proposals/<slug>.md" }. | . | A_BindFrontMatter — Bind Requirement front matter, statements, and 3-axis lineage (skill: specification-management): . | Validate or author the YAML front matter against bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>, title, status: in-force (or proposed prior to acceptance sign-off); | statements[] with stable #<key>, RFC 2119 modality (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), normative statement, and measurable successCriteria; | Backward lineage (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal dependencies (dependsOn), and forward implementation links (beans, skills, processes). | . | . | A_UpdateLifecycle — Update superseded or retired requirement records and RequirementSet membership (skill: specification-management): . | When superseding req:<old-slug> or retiring a requirement, set status: superseded + supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (or status: retired with retirement rationale in prose) on the old file without deleting it, and update any RequirementSet in docs/requirements/*.set.json so no approved/accepted set retains a non-in-force member. | . | A_UpdateIndex — Organise entry in docs/requirements/index.md under its concern group and status (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Add or update the requirement’s row in docs/requirements/index.md under its code-lists/concern-group.json section (for in-force requirements) or the Superseded and Retired Requirements archive table, and regenerate directory READMEs (subgraph-readmes.ts). | . | A_RunCheck — Run check:requirements gate (skill: specification-management): . | Execute bun run cat check:requirements to verify schema validity, slug uniqueness across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, derivedFrom acyclicity, resolution of all derivedFrom / dependsOn / supersededBy / skills / processes references, and RequirementSet invariants. | . | GW_CheckPassed — Does check:requirements pass?: . | If fail, loop back to A_BindFrontMatter to fix schema, collision, or broken-link findings before asking a human reviewer. | If pass, proceed to BA_ReviewFiling. | . | BA_ReviewFiling — BA / Owner reviews filed requirement, organisation, and sign-off (calledElement: Process_Adjudication, skill: adjudication, fulfilment: person): . | The Business Analyst / Owner reviews the filed requirement, its concern-group placement in docs/requirements/index.md, its traceability links, and its verification evidence, deciding approve, amend, reject, defer, or cancel (adjudication-requirement-set). | . | A_RecordFilingSignoff — Record requirement-signoff attestation and set stage (skill: adjudication): . | Append the human decision to test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json and update the RequirementSet stage (accepted on approval). | . | GW_FilingAccepted — Filing accepted?: . | approve / amend → End_RequirementFiled (“Requirement filed and indexed in docs/requirements/”). | reject / defer / cancel → End_FilingHeld (“Filing held or deferred — recorded with reason”). | . | . 3.4 Open design choices put to the owner before automation is built . Before any new CLI subcommand or schema extension is built on top of check:requirements, the following three design choices from this proposal are put to the owner: . | Concern-group tagging — index-only vs schema field: . | Option A (current zero-schema-change baseline): Keep bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json unchanged (additionalProperties: false) and organise requirements by concern group in docs/requirements/index.md. | Option B (optional schema field): Add an optional "concernGroup" (or "concerns": string[] referencing code-lists/concern-group.json) to bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json so docs/requirements/index.md can be generated deterministically from front matter. | . | Enforcing in-force dependency health in check:requirements: . | Today check:requirements verifies that every dependsOn and derivedFrom target exists. Should check:requirements also fail (or warn) when an in-force requirement dependsOn a requirement whose status is retired or superseded? | . | Standalone requirement sign-off vs RequirementSet sign-off: . | Today test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json attaches to a RequirementSet (*.set.json), and a standalone docs/requirements/<slug>.md promoted via git mv only needs proposedIn. Should every filed requirement belong to a concern-group RequirementSet (docs/requirements/<group>.set.json), or remain standalone unless grouped by a CRD? | . | .

1909.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1909.title: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — generate the rule, then execute it
1909.content: Adopted 2026-09-23. The source was uploaded, ingested whole through the pdf-structure rung (12 outline entries, structure read rather than inferred) and read before this node was written.

1910.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1910.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
1910.content: Have the model emit a RULE that deterministic machinery then validates and executes — not the RESULT. The paper’s schema-mapping half is the clean case (§III-B): rather than asking the model to transform a document, it asks for a JSONata expression, checks that expression parses, and then runs it deterministically over the data. The model never touches the data at scale. Its output is a program, and a program can be checked before it is trusted in a way a transformed dataset cannot. That inversion is what makes the rest of the method work, and it is the part worth carrying anywhere. A generated result must be verified by inspecting every item; a generated rule is verified once and then applies at any volume.

1911.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1911.title: The five safeguards, as the source enumerates them
1911.content: §III-A, numbered there and renumbered nowhere here: . | # | safeguard | what it refuses | . | 1 | Prompt construction and context management — the tool builds the prompt, sets the model’s role, and states the expected output format | an ad-hoc prompt nobody can reproduce | . | 2 | Integrated validation and visualization — output is validated and shown immediately | an unvalidated artefact entering the system | . | 3 | Scalability through targeted context — send the user-selected sub-schema, never the whole thing | degradation the model will not report | . | 4 | Automated response post-processing — strip code fences and language hints | a wrapper artefact read as content | . | 5 | Human-in-the-loop editing — on incomplete or incorrect output the raw response is shown, and the person corrects, accepts or discards | a silent accept | . Safeguard 5 shows the raw response, and that detail is the method rather than an implementation nicety. A tool that hides the failed output leaves the person deciding whether to trust something they cannot see.

1912.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1912.title: Why the safeguards exist — three cited failure modes
1912.content: The source does not assert that models need guarding; it cites three measurements (§II-B), and they are reproduced here because a reader is entitled to check them rather than take the premise: . | LLMs can be distracted by irrelevant context — Shi et al., ICML 2023. | Accuracy drops on low-probability inputs even for deterministic tasks — McCoy et al., arXiv:2309.13638. | Reasoning degrades as input length increases, before the context window is reached — Levy et al., arXiv:2402.14848. | . The third is why safeguard 3 is about targeted context rather than merely sufficient context: staying under the window is not the same as staying in the range where the model reasons well. These three are second-hand here — cited by the ingested source, not themselves ingested, and marked as such per literature-search §”Never fill the gap with recall”. The source also reports, from Buss et al. on LLM schema mapping, that “due to the difficult nature of data integration, human-in-the-loop approaches are required” — which is safeguard 5 arrived at independently.

1913.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1913.title: Bounded truncation — the one technique worth naming separately
1913.content: §III-B. Where the input is too large, the source does not summarise it and does not silently clip it. It recursively truncates arrays to length n and object properties to 8n, halving n from 64 until the document is under 64 KB or n = 2 — properties trimmed more conservatively than array items, because array items tend to share a schema while properties usually differ. The part that makes it a method rather than a hack: the schema inferred from the COMPLETE document is included in the prompt, so what truncation removed is still described even though it is no longer present. The source states the consequence rather than hiding it — there is an upper bound on document complexity that this supports.

1914.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1914.title: What it refuses
1914.content: . | Never let the model’s output be the thing that is acted on, where a rule could be generated instead. That is the whole method; everything else is support. | Never send the whole context because it fits. Fitting the window is not the criterion — safeguard 3 and the Levy et al. finding are about the range in which reasoning holds, which is smaller. | Never accept silently on failure. Safeguard 5 requires the raw response to be visible to the person who is being asked to accept it. | Never treat syntactic validation as semantic validation. The source is explicit that its JSONata check is “for syntactical correctness (not semantics)”. A method that blurred those would present an expression that parses as an expression that is right. | .

1915.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1915.title: Where this rendering stops
1915.content: methodology-adoption step 2: both halves stated. Adopted — the rule/result inversion, the five safeguards, the three cited failure modes, bounded truncation with schema preservation, and the syntactic/semantic distinction. Not adopted, and deliberately — every tool choice in the paper. MetaConfigurator, JSONata, gpt-4o-mini, jsonhero/schema-infer and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint are one instantiation. The owner’s instruction on ingesting this source, 2026-09-23: “do not need to match tools in paper, start with process, determine most appropriate tools (known or which can be added).” A node that named those tools would be adopting an implementation and calling it a method. Not assessed — the paper’s chemistry application example (§IV) is a demonstration, not an evaluation. It reports no accuracy measurement, no baseline and no comparison, so nothing here rests on a claim about how well the approach performs. The source does not make such a claim, and this node must not manufacture one.

1916.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1916.title: How this platform applies it
1916.content: This repository was already navigating the deterministic-to-agentic spectrum before this node existed, through four mechanisms that do not refer to each other. That application — and the open research questions this source bears on — is in the skill: skills/process/workflow/deterministic-and-agentic.md. The method lives here once; the skill names it and does not restate it.

1917.doc: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1917.title: Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it
1917.content: ← All methodologies . hybrid-llm-deterministic — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. An agent must produce an artefact that something downstream will act on. Use it when a language model is in the loop and a wrong output would be acted on rather than merely read — a schema, a mapping, a classification, a branch, a judgement. It answers how to get the output safely, never which option to choose: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, who is involved is raci, and situation analysis is swot. Those pick an answer; this one constrains how an answer is produced. Not applicable where no model is involved, and unnecessary where the output is only ever read by a person who will notice it is wrong. Origin. Felix Neubauer, Jürgen Pleiss and Benjamin Uekermann, “AI-assisted JSON Schema Creation and Mapping” (arXiv:2508.05192v2), University of Stuttgart. The authors’ own word for it is a “hybrid approach that combines large language models (LLMs) with deterministic techniques”. Open access, read whole and ingested here — unlike most nodes in this graph, the primary IS held. It is a tool paper reporting one implementation (MetaConfigurator), so what is adopted below is the METHOD it generalises, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. 1919.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1919.title: 1. The PHII and PATH CRDM method
1919.content: PHII developed CRDM as a process-centric methodology grounded in business process management that brings multi-disciplinary subject matter experts (SMEs) together to document how work is performed, redesign how it should be performed, and derive what an information system must do to support that work (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 1–3; path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, pp. 4–7). 1.1 The three concentration areas . PHII organises CRDM around three sequential concentration areas (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 2–9): . | Concentration area | Guiding prompt | Core artefacts | What happens | . | 1. Business Process Analysis (BPA) | Think: How do we do our work now? | Business Process Matrix (process goal, inputs, activities, outputs, actors/roles, business rules, issues/opportunities) and Task Flow Diagrams (swimlane diagrams showing the sequence of tasks across pools and actors) | SMEs map current-state operations end to end, making implicit workflows, hand-offs, and decision points explicit (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 3–6). | . | 2. Business Process Redesign (BPR) | Rethink: How should we do our work? | Redesigned Business Process Matrix and updated Task Flow Diagrams | Before automating anything, participants examine the current-state model to eliminate bottlenecks, redundancies, policy barriers, and information gaps (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 7–8). | . | 3. Requirements Definition | Describe: How can an information system support our work? | Functional User Requirements (anchored to numbered task-flow activities) and Non-Functional / General System Requirements | Every activity in the redesigned task flow is examined to state the information system capabilities needed to support it, followed by structured SME validation (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 8–9; phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, pp. 1–5). | . 1.2 PATH (2012): domain-scale health information system artefacts . PATH & PHII (2012) demonstrate how CRDM scales across a clinical and public health domain (path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm): . | Process Framework (Table 1, PDF p. 8): Inventories all domain business processes across functional columns (Patient Administration, Patient Care, Patient Fees and Accounting, Planning, Management & Surveillance) and selects priority processes for deep modeling (sec-009-outputs-of-the-crdm-process.md). | Task Flow Diagrams with Activity Narratives (Appendix 1, PDF pp. 11–20): Draws each priority process using a ten-element notation (Pools, Swim Lanes, Start Event, End Event, Sequence Flow, Activity, Subprocess, Decision, Multi-Page Connector, Annotation) paired with numbered activity details and narratives (sec-013-appendix-1-business-process-flows.md). | Activity-Linked Functional User Requirements vs. General System Requirements (Appendices 2–3, PDF pp. 21–36): Groups functional requirements by process and numbered activity ID, and separates cross-cutting system requirements (security, audit logging, reporting, interoperability, offline operation) into a dedicated general system requirements catalogue (sec-014-appendix-2-requirements.md, which also holds the general and nonfunctional requirements). | . 1.3 Quality criteria and validation techniques . PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, pp. 3–5) checks every requirement against nine quality criteria — Correct, Unambiguous, Complete, Consistent, Ranked for importance and/or stability, Verifiable, Modifiable, Traceable, and Comprehensible — using three validation methods: . | Desk checking: Individual review of the specification against the business process models and quality criteria. | Walkthrough: Facilitated step-by-step group traversal of task flows and requirements with the SMEs who perform the work. | Peer review: Independent structured inspection by peers to catch ambiguities, omissions, and conflicts before sign-off. | .

1920.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1920.title: 2. How the harness adapts PHII and PATH CRDM
1920.content: The relation between crdm-requirements-workflow and PHII/PATH CRDM is adapts: Phases 1–3 and the SME validation walkthrough follow PHII/PATH CRDM directly, while the facilitation channel, Phase 4/4b codebase impact and dependency analysis, Phase 5 work-item and filing decomposition, and Phase 6 pull-request sign-off are the platform’s own extensions. | Workflow phase / mechanism | Relation to PHII & PATH CRDM | What follows PHII/PATH CRDM vs. what is the platform’s own | . | Facilitated elicitation channel (crdm-requirements-workflow § Core Principle) | Platform adaptation of CRDM workshop facilitation | PHII/PATH run multi-stakeholder SME workshops facilitated by a human business analyst. The harness adapts this into an LLM agent acting in the Business Analyst role (Role_BusinessAnalyst) conversing with the human SME (Role_SME) over an issue/PR thread before any code is modified. | . | Phase 1: Needs Assessment & Problem Framing | Follows PHII CRDM (Business Process Analysis — context & scope) | Establishes the business problem, actors/personas (Role_*), scope boundaries (in-scope vs. out-of-scope), and information inputs/outputs, matching PHII’s Business Process Matrix header and PATH’s process framework scoping. | . | Phase 2: Business Process Analysis & Redesign | Follows PHII & PATH CRDM (Concentration Areas 1 & 2: BPA + BPR) | Models current-state (“as-is”) and redesigned (“to-be”) workflows using swimlane task-flow diagrams (BPMN 2.0 / Mermaid) across pools and actor lanes, paired with a gap analysis table (bottlenecks, redundancies, missing rules). | . | Phase 3: Requirements Definition (Functional, Non-Functional & Data Model) | Follows PHII & PATH CRDM (Concentration Area 3) + BCP 14 keywords | Derives atomic Functional Requirements (FR-001, …) linked to redesigned process steps, Non-Functional / General System Requirements (NFR-001, …), business rules/decision tables, and domain data entities with cardinalities and validation criteria. | . | Phase 4: Impact Analysis & Effort Estimation | Platform’s own extension | Inspects the repository’s existing schemas, skills, BPMN/DMN models, UI components, pipelines, tests, and downstream consumers across 7 impact dimensions to identify breaking changes and t-shirt effort estimates. PHII/PATH CRDM is technology- and codebase-agnostic and has no code impact phase. | . | Phase 4b: Capability Area Grouping, Dependency Ordering & Formalize-First Rule | Platform’s own extension | Groups requirements into capability areas (CA-1, CA-2, …), orders them by a dependency DAG, and enforces the platform’s formalize-first rule (formalizing existing implicit behavior before adding net-new capabilities). | . | Phase 5: Work Breakdown, Work Items & Specification Filing | Platform’s own extension (+ PHII Walkthrough / Peer review) | Writes the specification to docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and upon filing to docs/requirements/<slug>.md per requirements-filing-and-organisation), decomposes work into agent work items (beans/) and human todos (todos/), and conducts the SME walkthrough on the proposal PR. | . | Phase 6: Implementation & Merge Sign-Off | Platform’s own extension | Implements approved requirements on a feature branch, publishes a branches/<branch-slug>/ preview, verifies every acceptance criterion against automated gates, and requires explicit human owner sign-off before merging. | .

1921.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1921.title: 3. Priority scale and normative conformance keywords
1921.content: In CRDM and in the harness’s requirement template (crdm-requirements-template), implementation priority and normative conformance level are two distinct fields with different semantics and different standards origins: . 3.1 Priority weighting (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) . PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 2) and PATH (2012) (path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, p. 1 / Appendix 2) rank requirements by relative implementation importance using a three-tier priority scale. The harness aligns its three priority labels one-to-one with PHII’s scale: . | PHII / PATH priority rank | Harness template label | Meaning when sequencing or trading off scope | . | High | Must-have (High / Must-have) | Essential to the core business process; the system cannot satisfy the process goal without this capability. | . | Medium | Should-have (Medium / Should-have) | Important for operational efficiency or completeness; expected in standard operation, though a temporary workaround may exist. | . | Low | Nice-to-have (Low / Nice-to-have) | Desirable enhancement that improves convenience or secondary workflows when resources permit. | . 3.2 Normative conformance keywords (SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT) . While PHII’s informal prose grammar phrases requirement statements as “The system must or should…” (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 1), the harness’s separate Conformance field (SHALL / MUST, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT / MUST NOT) uses uppercase normative keywords governed by IETF BCP 14: . | RFC 2119 (Bradner 1997, library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels): Defines MUST / SHALL (absolute requirement of the specification), MUST NOT / SHALL NOT (absolute prohibition), SHOULD (recommended; valid reasons may exist in particular circumstances to ignore, but full implications must be understood and weighed), SHOULD NOT (not recommended), and MAY (truly optional). | RFC 8174 (Leiba 2017, library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words): Clarifies that only UPPERCASE words carry the RFC 2119 normative meanings; lowercase “must”, “should”, and “may” in surrounding prose carry only their normal English meaning. | . Keeping Priority (High / Must-have, Medium / Should-have, Low / Nice-to-have) separate from Conformance (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT) avoids conflating when a capability is scheduled for delivery (priority) with how strictly an implementation must behave once it claims conformance to that requirement (BCP 14 modality).

1922.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1922.title: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1922.content: ← All methodologies . crdm — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Eliciting, structuring, prioritising, and validating functional and non-functional requirements from current-state and redesigned business processes before implementation begins. Use it when a capability, specification, or workflow spans actors and tasks that must be analysed and redesigned first so every requirement traces to a concrete business activity. Not a replacement for filing and lifecycle governance (requirements-filing-and-organisation), interchange standards mapping (requirements-standards-assessment), one-off option trade-offs (kepner-tregoe), recurring decision logic (dmn), or architecture decision records (madr). Origin. Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII, a program of The Task Force for Global Health), “Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems” (2021, updated 2023-08-29, https://phii.org/crdm/) and companion EHR Toolkit guide “5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide” (2016/2021, https://phii.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Defining-and-Validating-Requirements-Guide_0.pdf); applied to health information systems in PATH & PHII, “Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology” (December 2012, https://media.path.org/documents/MCHN_mhis_crdm.pdf); combined in the harness’s requirement statement template with IETF BCP 14 / RFC 2119 (Bradner 1997) and RFC 8174 (Leiba 2017) for normative conformance keywords. 1923.doc: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality
1923.title: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling
1923.content: Adopted 2026-09-29, from the source the owner supplied for the decision-methodology cluster. It is the one part of that thesis that is a METHOD rather than a result, and it is the part that bears on how this repository writes anything formal.

1924.doc: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality
1924.title: The rule
1924.content: A model is evaluated against its declared epistemic purpose, never against “how accurately it reflects reality”. Parker, quoted in the chapter: for a model to be adequate-for-purpose “it must stand in a suitable relationship not just with a representational target but with a target, user, methodology, and background circumstances jointly.” . Ravichandran’s framing of why this matters: “I never claim that a model will be correct in an absolute sense; the processes of abstraction and idealization inherent to modeling necessarily excise the complexity, and often messiness, of the real world.” The familiar “all models are wrong, but some are useful” is taken as the starting point rather than the conclusion — the question becomes in which way is this one useful.

1925.doc: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality
1925.title: Three purposes, ordered, and a model must serve at least one
1925.content: | purpose | what the model must do | how it is judged | . | reproduce | there exist initial conditions under which the model’s outcome matches the observed one | consistency with the observation; it establishes SUFFICIENT conditions, not necessary ones | . | explain | posit a mechanism for why, modularised so the mechanism can be intervened on | the mechanism should be falsifiable, and must answer both why the outcome occurs and what would change if the setting changed | . | suggest intervention | name a place in the model where a change would move the outcome | utility under resource- and information-poor conditions, not accuracy | . The order is a ladder — each purpose subsumes the one before — and the chapter’s claim is that “typically, a model should achieve at least one”. Reproduction alone is worth something on its own terms: it “proposes a sufficient set of conditions under which the phenomenon of interest occurs, which is valuable even without establishing necessity”.

1926.doc: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality
1926.title: Two distinctions that decide what a model may claim
1926.content: How-possibly against how-actually. A how-actually explanation says this is how the phenomenon does arise; a how-possibly explanation says only that the outcome is not impossible, giving a mechanism without claiming it is the operative one. The chapter defends how-possibly explanations as legitimate in specific circumstances rather than treating them as failed how-actually ones. A model that supports only the weaker claim must say so, and that is the single most transferable rule here. Confirmatory against applied prediction (Elliott-Graves). Confirmatory prediction tests a theory and is judged on accuracy and variance; applied prediction is made in order to intervene and is judged on usefulness where data and resources are short. They are different products, and a model built for one is not thereby good at the other.

1927.doc: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality
1927.title: What the chapter says models CANNOT do
1927.content: . | Nothing is evaluable without a declared purpose. Stated as the first caveat: a model can only be judged relative to what it was for, at the level of both the overall goal and the specific phenomenon. | An unrealistic assumption is not automatically a defect. The chapter’s own example is the oracle — ERM oracles are assumed routinely although ERM is hard — because an absurd assumption can “evince structure in a problem that gets to the heart of what is difficult”. So “the assumptions are unrealistic” is not a finding on its own; what it costs depends on the purpose. | The freedom is the point: “by accepting the limitations of the model, we can use it to its fullest in its legitimate setting.” | .

1928.doc: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality
1928.title: What this repository takes, and what it refuses
1928.content: Taken. The declare-the-purpose-first rule, the three-purpose ladder, and the how-possibly / how-actually distinction as something a model must state about itself. Refused: the thesis’s own models are not adopted. The improving-bandit results, the pessimism-trap subsidy scheme and the grit model are this author’s research, not a method for anyone else’s, and nothing here depends on them. Their figures are described in library/corpus/image-verdicts.json as readings of charts, never as findings imported into this corpus. Refused: this is not a licence to put empirical claims into formal work. The chapter is about models of social and algorithmic processes, where an empirical target exists. A formal mathematical result in a folio has no such target, and the owner’s standing rule — “I do not want empirical predictions to enter formal math proofs” — is untouched by it. If anything this node sharpens that rule: a how-possibly mechanism is exactly the kind of claim that must not be laundered into a theorem.

1929.doc: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality
1929.title: See also
1929.content: . | methodology-adoption — the protocol that routes a question to a methodology in the first place. | consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation — the same instinct one level down: judge against a declared standard, and never let one aggregate stand for the thing being judged. | .

1930.doc: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality
1930.title: Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality
1930.content: ← All methodologies . adequacy-for-purpose-modelling — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A formal model is being built, and somebody will later ask whether it is right. Use it when the artefact is a mathematical model of a process — agents, action and reward spaces, update rules — and the question is what the model is allowed to claim. It answers what would count as this model succeeding, and nothing else. Reach for it BEFORE the model is written, because its whole force is that the purpose is declared first and the evaluation follows from it. Reaching for it afterwards turns it into a defence of whatever the model happens to do. Do NOT reach for it to choose between options (kepner-tregoe), to grade evidence, to settle a recurring rule (dmn), or to pick an algorithm (probabilistic-decision-analysis, mcdm-aggregation). It is not a decision method at all: it is a rule for judging a model, and it is filed here because methodology-adoption routes “how do we evaluate X” to a methodology node. Origin. Kavya Ravichandran, “Algorithmic Approaches to Sequential Decision-Making and Social Epistemology”, PhD thesis, Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago, August 2026; arXiv:2607.20636v1 [cs.DS], 22 July 2026. Chapter 5, “Why Algorithmic Approaches” — an essay inside the thesis rather than a result of it. Open access, ingested whole. The view it builds on is Wendy Parker’s (2020) “adequacy-for-purpose”, quoted directly in that chapter; the how-possibly / how-actually distinction is from the philosophy-of-explanation literature the chapter cites, and the confirmatory / applied prediction split is Elliott-Graves’. Ravichandran’s contribution adopted here is the ORDERED three-purpose taxonomy and the evaluation rule that follows from it. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2607.20636v1 | . Node file: adequacy-for-purpose-modelling.md .

1933.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
1933.title: The load-bearing idea, in the specification’s words
1933.content: “The System Package Data Exchange (SPDX®) specification defines an open standard for communicating bill of materials (BOM) information for different topic areas. SPDX defines an underlying data model as well as multiple serialization formats to encode that data model.” — §1 Scope (sec-007) . Its scope lists, among others, “software composition”, “software build information”, “provenance and integrity”, “licenses and copyrights, including a curated list of licenses and exceptions”, and “security vulnerabilities, defects, and other quality data” (§1). It is profiled. “The Core Profile is mandatory. All others are optional” (§5.2, sec-015): Core, Software, Security, Licensing, Dataset, AI, Build, Lite and Extension. A producer conforms at a profile, not to the whole. The Lite Profile “captures the minimum set of information required for license compliance in the software supply chain” (§5.10, sec-023). Everything is an Element with creation info. CreationInfo requires specVersion, created and createdBy (Figure A.1). The specification qualifies created in a way that matters here: “The dateTime created is often the date of last change (e.g., a git commit date), not the date when the SPDX data was created, as doing so supports reproducible builds” (CreationInfo, sec-044, where the page split carries it; also sec-072). A generator that uses the source commit’s date writes the same document twice for the same commit. Serialisation is JSON-LD with ONE global context. “The SPDX global JSON-LD context file must be used universally for all SPDX documents in JSON-LD format that adhere to a specific SPDX version … "@context": "https://spdx.org/rdf/3.0.1/spdx-context.jsonld"” (sec-032). There is also a “canonical serialization”: “a single, consistent, normalized, deterministic, and reproducible form” (sec-029). That is the form to hash and sign. “Known unknown” is not the same as absent. For licences: “a missing hasDeclaredLicense is not the same as a relationship to NoAssertionLicense since the latter is a ‘known unknown’ whereas no assumptions can be made from a missing hasDeclaredLicense relationship”, and “A written explanation of a relationship to a NoAssertionLicense MAY be provided in the comment field for the relationship” (Licensing, sec-210).

1934.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
1934.title: How it would sit beside what this platform already holds
1934.content: These are the mappings the proposal rests on. Each is ours, read against the held text, and none is adopted. | house fact | SPDX 3 term | fit | . | licence.json status: stated + id | simplelicensing_LicenseExpression via hasDeclaredLicense | exact, once ids are validated against a pinned License List | . | status: unknown + searched[] | hasDeclaredLicense → NoAssertionLicense, the search log in the relationship’s comment | exact. The three states survive: SPDX’s absent relationship is our absent record | . | bun.lock, python-deps.ts | software_Package + purl (packageUrl) + dependsOn | exact for npm. Python is blocked: requirements*.txt pin no versions | . | kg-to-portal’s manifest of digests | software_File with verifiedUsing: Hash inside a software_Sbom | exact | . | a published layer’s needs[] / FHIR dependsOn | dependsOn between software_Packages | exact, but only GENERATED from one authoritative record (#592) | . | folio-tool-run/v1, attribution.ts toolchain / inputDigest | build_Build (buildType, configSourceDigest, parameter, environment) | close, and it competes with prov-o-provenance for “what ran” | . | a QA or test report about a released package | ExternalRef with externalRefType: qualityAssessmentReport, “A reference to a quality assessment for a package” (sec-123) | exact as a POINTER. The report stays ours | . | bun audit advisories | security_Vulnerability + security_Vex*VulnAssessmentRelationship | exact, and a VEX not_affected needs a person’s decision | .

1935.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
1935.title: What it refuses, with reasons
1935.content: . | A QA verdict store. SPDX 3.0 has no verdict class. A result is an Annotation (“An assertion made in relation to one or more elements”, free-text statement; sec-039) or a relationship (hasEvidence, hasTest, testedOn). A house sidecar holds {criterion, result, reviewer, field_hash} per criterion, many reviewers over time, with four-state freshness. Serialising that into SPDX turns validated fields into a string. 3.1 changes the first half of this, and the change is recorded rather than smoothed over: the RC1 schema has functionalsafety_EvaluationResult (evaluation ∈ {pass, fail, inconclusive}, a required evaluationBasedOn → RequirementVerification with verificationMethod ∈ {analysis, assessment, audit, demonstration, inspection, review, test, other}, and a required rationale), plus a Core Requirement class. That is a verdict class. It makes an SPDX export of a certification report plausible, once 3.1 is final. It does not make SPDX the store, for the remaining reasons: the records are mutable, they would churn, the class sits in a functional safety profile whose semantics a non-safety QA run would be borrowing, and “stale” and “absent” have no SPDX term (inconclusive covers only could-not-determine). | A second execution log. “What ran, as whom, under which plan” is prov-o-provenance’s, by owner decision. A release document that must say how it was built references the PROV record, or generates build_Build from it. It never authors one beside it. | The AI profile for agent authorship. ai_AIPackage describes a model distributed as a package (training, energy consumption, limitations). The platform ships no model. Who wrote a block is provenance. | Authoring SPDX by hand, or committing it where its facts already live. A document generated from bun.lock that is also committed is a second answer to “what are we running”, the failure upstream-pins.json names. | .

Every 3.1 statement above comes from an RC1 schema that was not compared with its published copy, or from a conference deck. | That the OMG edition and the Linux Foundation 3.0.1 web edition are identical. Not compared. | Which buildType IRIs to use. The Build profile requires one (buildType: anyURI[1], Figure A.7) and leaves it to the producer. | How to sign. SPDX carries verifiedUsing integrity methods. Signing the document is outside it, and is qa-report-signing.bpmn’s question. | .

1937.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
1937.title: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
1937.content: ← All methodologies . spdx-3 — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Describing an artefact that LEAVES this repository so that a party who does not run our tooling can check what is in it, what it depends on, under which licences, and that it arrived intact — a release, a signed package, a published layer’s dependency set, the licences of what we redistribute. It answers what is this, what is it made of, who supplied it, under what licence, with what known vulnerabilities. It does NOT answer what happened inside the repository or who answers for it (prov-o-provenance), what an actor may do (odrl-policies), how a node is serialised internally (json-ld-serialisation), or whether a block passed its QA criteria (the house QA schemas; see §”What it refuses”). Origin. The Linux Foundation and its Contributors, with SPDX Model contributions from OMG, “System Package Data Exchange (SPDX) Specification Version 3.0”, OMG formal/24-11-01, March 2025 (https://www.omg.org/spec/SPDX); its model is the SPDX 3.0.1 model (Annex A points at https://spdx.org/rdf/3.0.1/spdx-model.ttl). Licensed Community-Spec-1.0, with pre-existing portions CC-BY-3.0. SPDX® is a registered trademark of The Linux Foundation. SPDX 3.1, a release candidate since 2026-01-26, is held only as a secondary source (a 2025 conference deck, CC-BY-SA-3.0) and as its RC1 machine-readable schema queued in uploads/, NOT as a specification. 1938.title: DMN — the computable case
1938.content: Present in this repository since before this adoption, and never written down as a methodology. Five .dmn tables exist under processes/decisions/, the BPMN engine evaluates them, and dmn-authoring sits on the business-analyst role. What was missing is the statement of when a decision should be a table at all — which is what made it possible to reach for DMN by habit, or to miss it.

1939.title: The test, in one line
1939.content: Would the same inputs have to produce the same branch next month? . Yes → a table. No → a judgement, and a table would lie about its own repeatability.

1940.title: What this platform already enforces
1940.content: A hand-supplied outcome is refused. A DMN-backed gateway computes its branch from the table; an agent cannot assert which way it went. That is a stronger guarantee than the methodology itself asks for, and it is the reason a table is worth the ceremony: the decision cannot be quietly overridden at the call site. See bpmn-processes for the gateway contract and dmn-authoring for authoring the table.

1941.title: Hit policy is a modelling decision, not a detail
1941.content: UNIQUE says the rules cannot overlap and the engine may check it. FIRST says they may overlap and order decides. COLLECT returns every match. Prefer UNIQUE, because it is the only policy under which an overlapping pair of rules is an error rather than a silent precedence. FIRST makes rule order load-bearing, and a reader of the table cannot see that the order was deliberate.

1942.title: What the research adds
1942.content: The specification says what a table means. Four sources say how to use one well: . | Overlap and gaps can be checked mechanically. Calvanese et al. 2016 (arxiv-1603.07466v1) give algorithms that find overlapping rules and input combinations no rule covers, on tables up to 1,506 rules. This is formal analysis, not a user study. dmn-qa checks the same two properties (dmn-rule-shadowed, dmn-table-complete), by enumeration. | Tables read better than trees, and compact tables best. Djurica et al. 2024 (djurica-2024-decision-model-comprehension-emisa, 139 participants, 32 questions): tables beat trees on accuracy, and contracted (“frugal”) versions beat expanded ones. Colour helped trees but lowered accuracy on tables (92.8% to 86.5% for frugal tables). So: keep tables contracted, and do not colour their cells. | Take decision logic out of the process. Hasić et al. 2018 (hasic-2018-5pdm-decision-intelligence), principle P2: no cascades of exclusive gateways in BPMN; put the logic in a decision table. This is the computed gateway above. Their validation is one case study, not an experiment. | Hit policy and input count drive perceived complexity. Hasić et al. 2019 (hasic-2019-complexity-metrics-dmn): of 26 metrics, hit-policy usage and the number of input variables tracked perceived complexity best. The paper sets no cut-off, so this methodology sets none either. | .

1943.title: Where DMN and the other methodologies meet
1943.content: . | A kepner-tregoe analysis whose criteria turn out to recur becomes a table. That promotion is the good case, and the MADR record of the original decision is what explains why the table has the columns it has. | A table can encode which methodology applies — a decision about decisions. The repo already does this shape in folio-intent.dmn. | GRADE is not a DMN table. Certainty of evidence is a judgement over a body of evidence; tabling it would assert a repeatability the method explicitly denies. | .

1944.title: Refusals
1944.content: . | Never table a one-off to make it look rigorous. A table asserts the decision recurs; if it does not, the assertion is false and the next author will trust it. | Never hand-supply a gateway outcome. Already enforced; stated here so the reason travels with the methodology. | A table with one rule is not a decision model. It is a constant, and should be written as one. | .

1945.content: ← All methodologies . dmn — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. The criteria RECUR and the inputs are data. A gateway that must branch the same way on the same facts every time. Not for a one-off judgement — that is kepner-tregoe, recorded per madr. Origin. Object Management Group, Decision Model and Notation (DMN) Version 1.5, OMG document formal/24-01-01, January 2024 (omg.org/spec/DMN). RECORDED, not held: its licence forbids posting copies on a network, so the library entry identifies the exact PDF (sha256) and its outline and holds no text.
