2010.title: Tools
2010.content: A skill states a capability generically: what an actor needs to know to perform a task. A Tool is one concrete way to exercise it, with an installation, an invocation and typed inputs and outputs. One skill may be satisfied by several tools, and one tool may satisfy several skills. They are separate graphs and this is the tools one. The relation between them is satisfies, and it runs from a tool to a skill — this tool is one way to do that, never this skill is a tool. 224Tool nodes 98skills satisfied 202invoked as a shell command 23reachable over MCP

2011.title: Glossary: Schema fields, S
2011.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2477 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 147 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 265 terms and is 154 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 265 shown . S

2014.title: Glossary: Schema fields, A–C
2014.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2477 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 147 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 520 terms and is 362 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 520 entries say otherwise. Filter terms . 520 shown . A B C

2019.title: Glossary: Schema fields, D–E
2019.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2477 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 147 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 215 terms and is 152 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 215 entries say otherwise. Filter terms . 215 shown . D E

2023.title: Glossary: Schema fields, T–Z
2023.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2477 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 147 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 506 terms and is 344 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 506 entries say otherwise. Filter terms . 506 shown . T U V W

2029.title: Glossary: Schema fields, P–R
2029.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2477 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 147 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 565 terms and is 386 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 565 entries say otherwise. 2034.title: Glossary: Schema fields, F–L
2034.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2477 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 147 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 606 terms and is 416 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 606 entries say otherwise. Filter terms . 606 shown . F G H I J K L

2043.title: Glossary: Schema fields, M–O
2043.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2477 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 147 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 232 terms and is 163 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2864 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 232 entries say otherwise. 2048.title: Glossary: Schema fields
2048.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2477 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 147 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 207 (SKOS) · smart-base 33 (SKOS). Split by first letter. 2909 terms are too many for one page within its budget of 1.0 MB, so they are on 7 pages by the first letter of the label. The ranges are fixed, so a term’s address does not move as terms are added. A label that does not start with a letter is on the first page. | A–C: 520 terms | D–E: 215 terms | F–L: 606 terms | M–O: 232 terms | P–R: 565 terms | S: 265 terms | T–Z: 506 terms | .

2454.content: Documentation, using open standards, of reusable enterprise architecture patterns for health systems, describing the diverse digital interconnections of systems and capabilities (including trust networks, services, registries, access controls). 2609.content: Gender refers to the characteristics of women, men, girls and boys that are socially constructed. 2649.title: Facility Type candidate
2649.content: Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. Also called: Facility type . 2724.title: Public Health Workforce candidate
2724.content: The public health workforce comprises all individuals who contribute to the delivery of at least one of the essential public health functions as part of integrated services and systems. This workforce comprises diverse and multidisciplinary occupations, from the health as well as other non-health sectors. This workforce can be conceptualized as three broad groupings: core group of public health personnel who have undergone professional training and/or registration with professional bodies in public health and could be from either health or another background; health and care workers who contribute to one or more public health functions as part of their clinical and/or social care roles; and personnel from a wide group of other allied occupations who contribute to addressing the determinants of health – for instance, personnel engaged in water and sanitation, food supply chains and road safety. Also called: Public health workforce . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 2764.doc: Health Workforce Education and Training Institution
2764.title: Health Workforce Education and Training Institution candidate
2764.content: An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. Also called: Health workforce education and training institution . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 2814.title: Remuneration candidate
2814.content: Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 2972.title: quality of the evidence
2972.content: In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. Also called: certainty of the evidence, confidence in the estimates of effect . The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout.

The handbook cites its reference 108 for this entry. | Health Workforce Education and Training Institution (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 2982.title: F
2982.content: Facility Type candidate Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 2988.content: National Capacity to Monitor Key Metrics for Health Workforce Planning and Global Monitoring Frameworks 4-05 candidate Capacity of national human resources for health information systems to monitor key metrics relevant for national health workforce planning and policy-making and for global monitoring frameworks . NHWA indicator 4 – 05. The definition is the sheet's "Indicator name"; the label is its "Abbreviated name". Candidate definitions (7) . | International Health Regulations (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))An international legal instrument that is binding on 196 countries across the globe, including all Member States of WHO. Its aim is to help the international community prevent and respond to acute public health risks that have the potential to cross borders and threaten people worldwide. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 91; PDF page 105). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 109 for this entry. | Subnational Level (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))To be defined according to the specific conditions, governing structures, and constitutional provisions existing in a given country. Disaggregation based on administrative boundaries down to the first or second subnational level is recommended (depending on the structure of administrative boundaries and the size of subnational territories), without overlaps between the administrative units. Examples for subnational administrative units are states, regions, provinces, counties, and districts. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 93; PDF page 107). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 47 for this entry. | Active Health Worker (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))One who provides services to patients and communities (practising health worker) or whose medical education is a prerequisite for the execution of the job (e.g. education, research, public administration) even if the health worker is not directly providing services (professionally active health worker). If data are not available for practising or professionally active health workers, data with the closest definition can be used, such as “health worker licensed to practice”. Categories of level are based on the definitions of OECD/Eurostat/WHO-Europe Joint questionnaire on non-monetary health care statistics. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 88; PDF page 102). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. A job is defined as “a set of tasks and duties performed, or meant to be performed, by one person, including for an employer or in self-employment”. The National Health Workforce Accounts covers health and health-related occupations grouped according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations 2008. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 46 for this entry. | Remuneration (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. 2991.title: Q
2991.content: quality of the evidence In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout. 3390.title: A
3390.content: activate-accepted-guidance candidate, extracted The point-of-care system carries out the health worker's decisions on decision-support guidance: each accepted action's request becomes active (intent plan or order) and joins the client's CarePlan; a declined action is not written. Input is the guidance and the decisions; output is the transaction Bundle saved. Skills of smart-base · source smart-base/skills/content/authoring-who-smart-guidelines/activate-accepted-guidance.md . Mapping: fhir cannot be told from the committed result: no row for scheme kg-skills of smart-base on fhir · skos cannot be told from the committed result: no row for scheme kg-skills of smart-base on skos . adopt-methodology-from-source candidate, extracted The general process for turning a shared paper, book or standard into an adopted methodology: establish origin and licence, ingest the source, find and summarize related work items and issues and ask whether to coordinate, render the method with its adopted and refused parts, place it by ownership, integrate it by calling existing processes, give every tool it uses a Tool node, and put it to the owner. Process: library/processes/methodology-from-source.bpmn. Skills of cat-harness · source cat-harness/library/skills/library-core/adopt-methodology-from-source.md . Mapping: fhir unmapped · skos unmapped . agent-memory candidate, extracted Durable memory for a subagent — the three entry labels and what each promises, why entries are authored as graph nodes rather than in the generated file, the injection budget that silently truncates, and archiving as the third state between "reaches everybody" and "deleted". Skills of cat-harness · source cat-harness/skills/conduct/conduct-core/agent-memory.md . Mapping: fhir unmapped · skos unmapped . agent-permissions candidate, extracted Securing what a coding agent may do without asking, from the person who can grant it: the secure-agent-permissions sub-process, run at session start and on demand when an action is denied. Vendor-neutral: the coding agent is a Tool (Claude Code is one; Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot and Codex are others), and each Tool's own config format belongs to its adapter, not here. Covers the permissions the harness's processes need, least privilege, how each one is explained before it is granted, how a grant is recorded, and the rules that no grant relaxes: never self-granted, generated projections are CI's, and merging to main is never a standing permission. Not between Task_AssessImpact and Task_ReviewImpact: those are in different processes with no sequence flow between them; the assessment reaches the committee through Task_CompareBeforeAfter. Routing them through it would run the subprocess on every iteration of the inner loop, which is the ceremony this design refuses: a gate invoked on every pass stops being read. 3437.title: Q
3437.content: QA gate: check dispositions against the people and the pull request candidate, extracted Before Ready for merge. Reads: the change set's Disposition (change set), each comment's Blue Disposition on Review Public Comments, the PR's diff at its head commit, and the staging QA report. Checks that every comment number has one disposition; that each agrees with the people's Blue Disposition; that each Accepted or Partially accepted comment has its change in the diff, and a Not accepted, Noted, Deferred, Duplicate or Out of scope one has none; that the diff changes nothing no disposition accounts for; and that the QA report for the staged commit has no failing gate. Writes: QA gate (change set), first line "Passed <head sha>: …" or "Failed <head sha>: <why>", and QA report (change set), the report's link. The sheet shows both under Staging review; a pass for an older commit reads as stale. Nothing is written to ENQUEUE a block: the queue is derived (every prose block in every declared library, minus those whose summaries.json record is a current draft or confirmation), so a promoted entry is in it the moment its blocks are. A re-ingested document whose text changed re-enters it on its own, because the record's source_hash no longer matches. What an agent doing ingestion work does here is DRAIN a few: bun run cat summaries:next -- --n K hands it the next K blocks with their text, it writes a short summary of each in its own words, and bun run cat summaries:record writes them into library/<bib-slug>/summaries.json as drafts naming the agent and its model. 3439.title: Glossary: BPMN activities, R–Z
3439.content: Candidate terms extracted from every BPMN task and call activity: name as the label, its own <documentation> as the definition, the element id as the code. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap 38 (SKOS) · bootstrap-tools 7 (SKOS) · cat-harness 352 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 50 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 224 (SKOS) · smart-base 161 (SKOS) · who-iris 34 (SKOS). One of 3 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 316 terms and is 286 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 965 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 965 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 316 entries say otherwise. This step rewrites bytes that a materialization record describes, so leaving the old digest behind would make a CORRECT run of this process fail check:materialized-fixity as a mismatch — the gate reading "somebody edited held content without saying so" about the one process whose job is to replace it. This is the publication exception, stated as a rule rather than as a carve-out, because a list of permitted writers goes stale when a writer is added. The exception is NOT "these actors may skip the rule"; it is "say what you did". A writer that updates the digest alongside the bytes passes, and the record then describes what is actually there. Sign the package and/or each asset candidate, extracted THE TRUST ANCHOR IS GDHCN, SPECIFIED BY THE WHO SMART TRUST IG. READ OFF THAT IG rather than from general knowledge: a GDHCN trustlist distributes KEY MATERIAL as W3C DID documents, and says nothing about what you wrap your bytes in — the health-certificate envelope is a separate specification in the same IG, and a document package is not a health certificate. So what is settled is where a verifier GETS THE KEY, not what it verifies. A portal that can fetch the bytes but not reach the trustlist cannot verify, which is unknown and not a failure — air-gapped is a declared deployment value, so that case is answered rather than assumed away. Still OPEN and unread: the rotation and revocation model, and whether a document-package signature can be expressed for a GDHCN-aware verifier at all. Two schemes with different properties remain to choose between, and the trustlist does not choose between them. A PACKAGE signature over the manifest verifies the SET — nothing added, removed or altered — and must be reissued whenever any file changes. A PER-ASSET signature verifies one file independently, which is what an edge cache serving one asset can actually check, and it cannot detect a removal because there is nothing left to verify. They compose; composing them is the safer and more expensive default, and it is the deployment's choice rather than the pipeline's. 3447.title: Glossary: BPMN activities, A–D
3447.content: Candidate terms extracted from every BPMN task and call activity: name as the label, its own <documentation> as the definition, the element id as the code. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap 38 (SKOS) · bootstrap-tools 7 (SKOS) · cat-harness 352 (SKOS) · fhir-harness 50 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 224 (SKOS) · smart-base 161 (SKOS) · who-iris 34 (SKOS). One of 3 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 282 terms and is 266 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 965 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 965 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is in no single state on fhir, so each entry states its own, and in no single state on skos, so each entry states its own, unless its entry says otherwise. 282 entries say otherwise. Filter terms . 282 shown . 0–9 A B C D

3474.title: Already somebody else’s concept?
3474.content: Extracted candidates are minted from this repository’s own assets and are not, by themselves, checked against any vocabulary. check:term-mapping asks whether each already exists as a concept somebody is authoritative for — SKOS for what a term MEANS, FHIR for a clinical code’s operational semantics — and the two are separate questions with separate answers. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 1 | 4491 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 4492 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin.

3479.doc: [Pilot study of antiretroviral therapy in Djibouti]
3479.title: [Pilot study of antiretroviral therapy in Djibouti]
3479.content: Ahmed, A.A.; Latoundji, S. (2007). [Pilot study of antiretroviral therapy in Djibouti]. Title[Pilot study of antiretroviral therapy in Djibouti] AuthorsAhmed, A.A.; Latoundji, S. Issued2007-12-31 Typedocument Languagefr AbstractA cross-sectional survey was conducted among 112 HIV positive patients who had received antiretroviral therapy for > 3 months to assess the efficacy of treatment [viral load < 400 copies/mL]. The median age at enrolment was 36 years, 90% of patients were at the AIDS stage and median CD4 rate was 118/mm[3]. Patients received a combined treatment of 2 NRTI +1 NNRTI [51%], 3 NRTI [45%] and 2 NRTI+1 PI [4%]. Virological efficacy was seen in 74% of the patients, irrespective of the prescribed protocol and the initial clinical and immunological profile. Mean improvements measured were 20% on the Karnofsky index [KI], 2.1 kg/m[2] in body mass index and 82 cells/mm[3] in CD4. The prevalence of side effects was 84%. The predictors for treatment success were quality of care and KI > 70% Sources . | iris.who.int/handle/10665/117378 (canonical) | repository record (repository) | . 3495.content: World Health Organization (2022). Guidelines for diagnosing, preventing and managing cryptococcal disease among adults, adolescents and children living with HIV. World Health Organization. TitleGuidelines for diagnosing, preventing and managing cryptococcal disease among adults, adolescents and children living with HIV AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2022-6-23 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240052178 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis guideline provides updated, evidence-informed recommendations for diagnosing, preventing and managing cryptococcal disease among adults, adolescents and children living with HIV. Developed in accordance with WHO Guideline Review Committee procedures, it replaces the 2018 guidance and incorporates important new evidence published in 2021 on the preferred antifungal induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis. The recommendations are based on systematic reviews using the GRADE approach and are supported by considerations of acceptability, values and preferences, feasibility and cost–effectiveness. The document addresses cryptococcal disease as a major opportunistic infection contributing substantially to HIV-related illness, disability and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, and identifies priority knowledge gaps to inform future research. The guideline recommends updated approaches to the diagnosis, prevention and treatment of cryptococcal disease, including revised guidance on induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis, while maintaining earlier recommendations where evidence remains unchanged. It also outlines principles for implementation within a public health approach and is intended to support HIV programme managers, policy-makers, health-care professionals and people living with HIV in improving the prevention, early diagnosis and clinical management of cryptococcal disease. 3501.doc: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
3501.title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
3501.content: World Health Organization (2016). WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2016-11-7 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241549912 Languageen AbstractThis guideline presents the World Health Organization’s evidence-based recommendations on routine antenatal care to support a positive pregnancy experience for pregnant women and adolescent girls. It aims to provide a comprehensive, consolidated framework for antenatal care that complements existing WHO guidance on the management of specific pregnancy-related complications. The recommendations promote a person-centred, rights-based approach that extends beyond the prevention of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality to enhance women’s physical, psychological and sociocultural well-being, support healthy pregnancies, and improve the quality and utilization of antenatal care. Intended for policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals, the guideline informs the development of national policies, clinical protocols and service delivery models. Developed according to the WHO guideline development process, the document draws on systematic reviews and applies the GRADE and GRADE-CERQual approaches together with the DECIDE evidence-to-decision framework. It contains 49 recommendations covering nutritional interventions, maternal and fetal assessment, preventive measures, management of common physiological symptoms, and health system interventions to improve antenatal care utilization and quality. The guideline also introduces the 2016 WHO antenatal care model, recommending a minimum of eight contacts during pregnancy, and emphasizes implementation, dissemination and periodic updating as new evidence becomes available. 3503.doc: WHO recommendations on home-based records for maternal, newborn and child health
3503.title: WHO recommendations on home-based records for maternal, newborn and child health
3503.content: World Health Organization (2018). WHO recommendations on home-based records for maternal, newborn and child health. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations on home-based records for maternal, newborn and child health AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2018-8-27 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241550352 Languageen AbstractThis WHO guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of home-based records for maternal, newborn and child health (MNCH). Home-based records, whether paper or electronic, are household-held documents that complement facility-based records by documenting health services received and supporting continuity of care. Developed through the WHO guideline development process using systematic reviews, GRADE and GRADE-CERQual approaches, the guideline evaluates the effects of home-based records on MNCH outcomes, health service delivery, acceptability, feasibility and equity, addressing an important evidence gap despite their widespread use in at least 163 countries. The guideline recommends the use of home-based records alongside facility-based records for pregnant women, mothers, newborns and children to improve care-seeking behaviours, household support and male involvement, maternal and child home care practices, infant and child feeding, and communication between health providers and women or caregivers. It concludes that current evidence is insufficient to identify a superior record type, format or design, and advises policy-makers to engage stakeholders when determining record content and implementation. The publication also discusses implementation considerations, highlights privacy and sustainability issues, identifies research gaps, and outlines priorities for future evidence generation and guideline updates. 3517.doc: Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture
3517.title: Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture
3517.content: World Health Organization (2024). Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture. World Health Organization. TitleDigital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2024-11-11 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240101197 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis handbook provides practical guidance for countries seeking to digitally transform public health supply chains through the development of coherent strategies, interoperable architectures and sustainable implementation approaches. Developed within the WHO SMART Guidelines framework, it addresses the growing need for integrated digital ecosystems that support forecasting, procurement, warehousing, distribution, dispensing and traceability of health products. The publication outlines the role of digital technologies in improving efficiency, data availability, interoperability and decision-making across supply chain processes, while helping ensure timely access to quality-assured medicines and health products. The publication presents a stepwise approach for defining a digital health supply chain (DHSC) strategy, assessing existing health supply chain information systems, designing a target architecture, planning implementation and supporting product traceability. It emphasizes stakeholder engagement, alignment with national health, digital health and supply chain strategies, use of open standards, and long-term scalability and sustainability. Drawing on country experiences and established digital health frameworks, the handbook offers practical tools, templates and examples to support governance, planning and coordination of digital transformation initiatives, with the aim of strengthening supply chain performance, improving visibility across the supply chain and enhancing patient safety. TitleWHO recommendations on maternal health: guidelines approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2017-10-17 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis publication compiles WHO recommendations on maternal health that have been approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee into a single, accessible reference for WHO staff, policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals. It brings together current WHO guidance covering the continuum of maternal care during pregnancy, childbirth and the postnatal period, with the dual purpose of facilitating access to recommendations and helping identify areas where further guideline updates are needed. The document indicates newly issued and updated recommendations since 2013 and provides, for each recommendation, its strength, the quality of supporting evidence and the corresponding source guideline. The compilation addresses interventions to promote, prevent and protect maternal and perinatal health, including antenatal care, prevention and management of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, peripartum infections, labour and childbirth, postpartum haemorrhage, postnatal care and health promotion, as well as the management of maternal conditions such as HIV infection, malaria and tuberculosis. Developed according to WHO’s guideline development process using the GRADE approach and structured evidence-to-decision frameworks, it presents evidence-informed recommendations intended to support consistent policy development, clinical practice and programme implementation across diverse health-care settings. TitleWHO implementation tool for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV infection: module 13: integrating STI services AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2022-9-5 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240057425 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis module of the WHO Implementation Tool for Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV Infection provides operational guidance on integrating sexually transmitted infection (STI) services into HIV PrEP programmes. Developed for programme managers, decision-makers, facility managers and health-care workers, it compiles existing WHO recommendations and evidence to support the planning, implementation and scale-up of integrated, people-centred sexual health services. The document outlines the epidemiology and burden of STIs, particularly among populations who may benefit from or use PrEP, and highlights the public health rationale for strengthening STI prevention, testing, treatment and follow-up within PrEP delivery platforms. The module describes practical approaches to integrating STI services across different service delivery models, including considerations related to workforce capacity, task sharing, monitoring, financing and demand generation. It presents guidance on counselling, health promotion, screening, diagnostic testing, partner services, clinical management, referral pathways and prevention measures such as condom provision and vaccination. Emphasizing differentiated service delivery and human rights principles, the publication aims to improve access to comprehensive sexual health care, enhance service quality and support efforts to reduce the burden of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections through coordinated and efficient health-system responses. TitleConsolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring: recommendations for a public health approach AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-7-16 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240031593 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThese consolidated guidelines provide comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations for HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and programme monitoring across the continuum of HIV care. Updating the 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines, this edition integrates guidance issued between 2016 and 2021 and reflects major advances in clinical practice, diagnostics and service delivery. Developed using the GRADE approach and informed by expert consultation and country experience, the guidelines aim to support countries in implementing high-quality, person-centred HIV services while advancing universal health coverage and progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. The publication addresses HIV testing strategies, prevention interventions, antiretroviral therapy, management of advanced HIV disease, care for common coinfections and comorbidities, differentiated service delivery, procurement, laboratory services and programme monitoring. It incorporates updated recommendations on HIV self-testing, pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis, dolutegravir-based treatment, rapid antiretroviral therapy initiation, viral load monitoring and community-based models of care. Intended primarily for national HIV programme managers, policy-makers and health-care providers, the guidelines also serve as a resource for technical partners, community organizations and people living with HIV to support the implementation of effective, equitable and people-centred HIV programmes. TitleDigital adaptation kit for immunizations: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2024-12-31 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240099456 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis publication presents the World Health Organization’s digital adaptation kit (DAK) for immunizations, developed within the SMART Guidelines framework to support the implementation of WHO immunization recommendations in digital systems. The document provides operational and software-neutral specifications intended to facilitate the translation of immunization guidance into interoperable digital health applications, particularly person-centred point-of-service systems and electronic immunization registries. It outlines the role of digital adaptation kits in strengthening digital health systems by improving the consistency, transparency and standardization of health content, workflows, data structures and decision-support logic used in immunization programmes. The publication also situates the DAK within broader digital health strategies and interoperability standards. The document describes eight core components of the immunization DAK, including health interventions and recommendations, generic personas, user scenarios, workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and functional requirements. It incorporates WHO guidance related to routine immunization, electronic immunization registries and digital health interventions, while emphasizing adaptability to country-specific policies and implementation contexts. Additional sections address interoperability, data standards, workflow optimization and the use of digital systems to support longitudinal tracking, reporting, decision support and communication within immunization services. The publication is intended for immunization programme managers, digital health teams, software developers and implementers involved in designing and deploying digital immunization systems. TitleWHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 1: prevention: tuberculosis preventive treatment AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2020-2-25 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240001503 Languageen AbstractThis guideline provides updated WHO recommendations for the programmatic management of tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) as part of the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis. It focuses on the prevention of active tuberculosis among people at increased risk of disease progression, particularly people living with HIV, household contacts of patients with tuberculosis and other vulnerable population groups. The document incorporates new evidence on shorter rifamycin-containing preventive treatment regimens and updates previous WHO guidance to improve the clarity, consistency and global applicability of recommendations. Developed in accordance with WHO Guideline Review Committee requirements, the publication presents 18 evidence-based recommendations covering the identification of populations eligible for preventive treatment, exclusion of active tuberculosis, testing for latent tuberculosis infection, recommended preventive treatment regimens, monitoring and evaluation, and implementation considerations. Recommendations were formulated using the GRADE approach, taking into account the certainty of evidence, effectiveness, safety, values and preferences, equity, resource implications, acceptability and feasibility. The guideline is intended to support national policy-makers, programme managers and health-care providers in strengthening tuberculosis prevention and advancing implementation of the WHO End TB Strategy. TitleDigital transformation handbook for health product catalogue AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2025-10-30 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis handbook provides guidance for the implementation of standardized product master data management through national product catalogues (NPCs) to support digital transformation in health supply chains. Developed within the framework of the WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide and aligned with the SMART Guidelines initiative, the publication outlines regulatory, governance, technological and operational approaches for establishing interoperable product registries and harmonized product information systems. It explains the importance of standardized product master data for ensuring accurate identification, tracking and management of health products across manufacturers, regulatory authorities, procurement entities, warehouses, health facilities and other supply chain stakeholders. The handbook describes policies and procedures for data governance, coding structures, interoperability standards, change management and capacity-building to support sustainable implementation. It also presents guidance on integrating standardized product master data with digital health, regulatory and supply chain systems to improve forecasting, procurement, inventory management, pharmacovigilance, product recalls and traceability. In addition, the publication highlights mechanisms for sharing product master data as a global good and leveraging WHO-hosted tools and open standards to strengthen coordination, data quality and supply chain efficiency across countries and organizations. TitleConsolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis and STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care for key populations AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2022-7-22 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240052390 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis guideline provides consolidated, evidence-based recommendations for the prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care of HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among key populations. It responds to the disproportionate burden of these infections in groups such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, people in prisons and other closed settings, and trans and gender diverse individuals, and to the structural barriers that limit their access to health services. The document aims to support countries in strengthening integrated, people-centred responses to these interconnected epidemics. Developed using WHO guideline standards and the GRADE methodology, the publication brings together existing and new recommendations and organizes them into comprehensive packages of interventions. It addresses enabling factors such as legal and policy environments, stigma, discrimination, violence and community empowerment, alongside essential health interventions including prevention, testing, treatment and harm reduction. The guideline also outlines service delivery approaches, such as community-led services, integration and decentralization, and provides guidance for programme planning, implementation and monitoring. Intended for policy-makers, programme managers and health-care providers, it supports the prioritization of effective, context-appropriate strategies to improve access, coverage and health outcomes for key populations. TitleNational health workforce accounts: health workforce levels and trends 2026 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2026-6-22 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240122925 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis report presents the 2026 edition of the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) series, providing an overview of the status of NHWA implementation and an analysis of global and regional health workforce levels and trends based on official data reported by countries to the World Health Organization. Developed to support evidence-informed health workforce policy-making and planning, the report examines progress in strengthening national health workforce information systems, data availability and reporting across countries, and the use of standardized indicators to monitor human resources for health in support of universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals and other health objectives. Drawing on the 2025 NHWA data release, the report analyses the distribution, density and composition of the health and care workforce across regions and income groups, highlighting persistent disparities in workforce availability. It also examines trends in workforce growth since 2006 and presents a thematic analysis of population ageing and health workforce ageing, assessing their implications for future workforce needs. The findings demonstrate substantial improvements in the availability and quality of health workforce data through NHWA implementation while underscoring continuing challenges related to workforce shortages, inequities in distribution and the need for sustained investment in health workforce planning and monitoring. TitleGuidelines for the prevention and control of infection with LAV/HTLV III AuthorsWorld Health Organization. Control Programme on AIDS Issued1986-12-31 Typedocument PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThese guidelines provide recommendations for preventing and controlling infection with LAV/HTLV-III, the retrovirus recognized at the time as the etiological agent of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Developed as part of the WHO AIDS Control Programme, they are intended primarily for public health authorities and health professionals, who are responsible for adapting the guidance to different populations and settings. The document summarizes available knowledge on transmission, clinical manifestations, laboratory detection, surveillance, notification and confidentiality, and case definitions for AIDS. The guidelines emphasize routine precautions to prevent exposure to blood and other potentially infectious body fluids, particularly among health care workers, laboratory personnel and providers of home and emergency care. They address prevention and management of needlestick, parenteral and mucous-membrane exposures, safe handling of specimens and contaminated equipment, and precautions for non-health-care workers. Guidance is also provided on disinfection, sterilization, and the safe processing of reusable needles, syringes and other instruments. 3585.title: Consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, 2019
3585.content: World Health Organization (2020). Consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, 2019. World Health Organization. TitleConsolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, 2019 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2020-11-3 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241550581 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis guideline provides comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations to support countries in delivering high-quality, person-centred HIV testing services (HTS) across diverse populations and settings. Updating and consolidating previous WHO guidance issued in 2015 and 2016, it incorporates new evidence on HIV self-testing, social network-based HIV testing approaches, western blotting, and strategic service delivery to strengthen progress towards global HIV targets. Developed using the GRADE methodology and informed by systematic reviews, modelling studies and expert consultation, the guideline aims to improve the effectiveness, efficiency and quality of HIV testing while promoting timely linkage to prevention, treatment and care. The publication addresses the full continuum of HIV testing services, including demand creation, pre- and post-test services, facility- and community-based testing, implementation considerations for priority populations, strategic planning, diagnostic testing strategies, quality assurance and programme monitoring. It provides updated recommendations on HIV self-testing, provider-assisted referral, social network-based approaches and the use of dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests, while emphasizing the WHO 5Cs of HIV testing services: consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct results and connection. Intended for policy-makers, national programme managers, health-care providers and implementing partners, the guideline supports the expansion of equitable, evidence-informed HIV testing services to improve diagnosis and strengthen national HIV responses. 3591.content: World Health Organization (2021). Guidelines: updated recommendations on HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, antiretroviral initiation and monitoring. World Health Organization. TitleGuidelines: updated recommendations on HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, antiretroviral initiation and monitoring AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-3-17 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240022232 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis guideline presents updated WHO recommendations on selected priority areas across the HIV prevention, diagnosis and treatment continuum, developed in response to emerging evidence, implementation experience and evolving clinical practice. Prepared according to WHO Guideline Review Committee procedures and informed by systematic reviews using the GRADE approach, it updates and complements the 2016 consolidated HIV guidelines. The publication addresses key public health challenges affecting the global HIV response, particularly in resource-limited settings, and supports progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 through a public health approach to service delivery. The guideline introduces or updates recommendations on the use of the dapivirine vaginal ring as an additional HIV prevention option for women at substantial risk of infection, point-of-care technologies for infant HIV diagnosis and viral load monitoring, revised treatment monitoring algorithms, and earlier initiation of antiretroviral therapy for people living with HIV and tuberculosis. It also provides updated clinical considerations for rapid antiretroviral therapy initiation and outlines implementation principles to support national adaptation. Intended for policy-makers, programme managers, clinicians and implementing partners, the guideline aims to strengthen evidence-based HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment monitoring and care across diverse settings. TitleGlobal guidance on criteria and processes for validation: elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B virus AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-11-25 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240039360 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis guidance document provides updated World Health Organization criteria and processes for validating the elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B virus (HBV) as public health priorities. Building on previous editions focused on HIV and syphilis, this third version incorporates validation guidance for HBV within the framework of the Triple Elimination Initiative. The document outlines standardized indicators, targets and assessment procedures for evaluating progress towards EMTCT across diverse epidemiological and programmatic settings. It addresses impact and process indicators, surveillance and laboratory quality standards, programme assessment, and requirements related to human rights, gender equality and community engagement. The document emphasizes integrated maternal and child health approaches, universal access to quality antenatal and prevention services, and the importance of strong health systems and surveillance mechanisms. It also provides guidance for countries with high disease burdens through the Path to Elimination framework, as well as for countries with small numbers of affected pregnant women and special populations. Intended for national, regional and global validation bodies, the document supports harmonized validation processes while allowing countries to pursue single, dual or triple EMTCT validation according to national readiness and regional priorities. TitleWHO guideline for screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions for cervical cancer prevention AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-7-6 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240030824 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis second edition of the WHO guideline provides updated evidence-based recommendations for screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions to prevent cervical cancer in both the general population of women and women living with HIV. Developed in support of the WHO global strategy to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem, the guideline responds to advances in screening technologies and implementation approaches by updating previous recommendations and introducing new guidance to simplify clinical algorithms while improving feasibility, acceptability and programme performance across diverse health system settings. The recommendations were developed in accordance with WHO guideline development procedures using systematic reviews, mathematical modelling where necessary, GRADE assessments of the certainty of evidence, evidence-to-decision frameworks, and consideration of feasibility, costs, acceptability and users’ values and preferences. The guideline presents recommendations and good practice statements on primary screening tests, screening intervals, age at initiation and cessation of screening, triage strategies, follow-up after positive screening results, treatment approaches, and programme implementation for both population groups. It addresses service delivery, integration with HIV care, implementation considerations, research gaps and dissemination, while emphasizing the transition to HPV DNA testing, the use of evidence-based screening and treatment algorithms, and country adaptation according to available resources and local context to improve coverage, quality of care and cervical cancer prevention.
