3611.content: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe (2008). 8th National Tuberculosis Programme Managers Meeting and 13th Wolfheze Workshop: Wolfheze 2008: tuberculosis management, surveillance and evaluation in Europe with high rates or threat of multidrug resistant tuberculosis: The Hague, the Netherlands, 1–2 June 2008. World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe. Title8th National Tuberculosis Programme Managers Meeting and 13th Wolfheze Workshop: Wolfheze 2008: tuberculosis management, surveillance and evaluation in Europe with high rates or threat of multidrug resistant tuberculosis: The Hague, the Netherlands, 1–2 June 2008 AuthorsWorld Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe Issued2008-12-31 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe Languageen AbstractThe WHO European Region has the highest rates in the world of drug-resistant tuberculosis and increasing rates of HIV/tuberculosis coinfection. Eighteen high-priority countries have been identified to urgently scale up tuberculosis control interventions: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Bulgaria, Estonia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia, Lithuania, the Republic of Moldova, Romania, the Russian Federation, Tajikistan, Turkey, Turkmenistan, Ukraine and Uzbekistan. Five of these countries are members of the European Union. Migration and pockets of poverty increase vulnerability to tuberculosis in many western European countries. Related areas, such as the rapid detection of drug-resistant tuberculosis, contact tracing, infection control, health system strengthening and the review of national tuberculosis programmes, are of equal concern among eastern, central and western countries of the WHO European Region. While general awareness and political commitment were raised during the Ministerial Forum held in Berlin in October 2007, how to ensure the follow-up of the Berlin Declaration on TB and monitor its implementation is currently under discussion. The 8th National Tuberculosis Programme Managers Meeting and the 13th Wolfheze Workshop, jointly organized in June 2008 in The Hague, provided a forum for discussion on each of the aforementioned topics and facilitated the sharing of experiences between countries in the Region – which are very different from an epidemiological, organizational, cultural and wealth perspective. 3613.content: World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe (2014). The case for investing in public health: the strengthening public health services and capacity. A key pillar of the European regional health policy framework Health 2020. World Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe. TitleThe case for investing in public health: the strengthening public health services and capacity. A key pillar of the European regional health policy framework Health 2020 AuthorsWorld Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe Issued2014-12-31 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization. Regional Office for Europe Languageen AbstractThe economic crisis has led to increased demand and reduced resources for health sectors. The trend for increasing healthcare costs to individuals, the health sector and wider society is significant. Public health can be part of the solution to this challenge. The evidence shows that prevention can be cost-effective, provide value for money andgive returns on investment in both the short and longer terms. This public health summary outlines quick returns on investment for health and other sectors for interventions that promote physical activity and healthy employment; address housing and mental health; and reduce road traffic injuries and violence. Vaccinations and screening programmes are largely cost-effective. Population-level approaches are estimated to cost on average five times less than individual interventions. This report gives examples of interventions with early returns on investment and approaches with longer-term gains. Investing in cost-effective interventions to reduce costs to the health sector and other sectors can help create sustainable health systems and economies for the future. 3621.doc: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis: module 5: management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents
3621.title: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis: module 5: management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents
3621.content: World Health Organization (2022). WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis: module 5: management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents. World Health Organization. TitleWHO operational handbook on tuberculosis: module 5: management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2022-3-18 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240046832 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis operational handbook provides practical guidance for implementing World Health Organization recommendations on the prevention, screening, diagnosis and management of tuberculosis (TB) in children and adolescents under programmatic conditions and across different levels of the health system. Developed alongside the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, the publication addresses the specific epidemiological, clinical and psychosocial vulnerabilities of children and adolescents affected by TB, including challenges related to diagnosis, treatment adherence, prevention and continuity of care. The handbook aims to support the development and revision of national policies, operational guidance and service delivery approaches tailored to the needs of these populations. The handbook covers the full continuum of TB care, including contact investigation, systematic screening, preventive treatment, diagnostic approaches for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB, and treatment of drug-susceptible and drug-resistant disease. It also addresses decentralized and family-centred models of care, management of TB in children and adolescents living with HIV, TB during pregnancy, malnutrition, pneumonia, adolescent health needs and palliative care. Practical tools, implementation guidance and standard operating procedures are included to support programme managers and health-care providers in strengthening child and adolescent TB services. 3623.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 2: screening: systematic screening for tuberculosis disease
3623.title: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 2: screening: systematic screening for tuberculosis disease
3623.content: World Health Organization (2021). WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 2: screening: systematic screening for tuberculosis disease. World Health Organization. TitleWHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 2: screening: systematic screening for tuberculosis disease AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-3-22 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240022676 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractTuberculosis remains one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent despite being largely preventable and curable. This updated WHO guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on systematic screening for tuberculosis disease to support earlier diagnosis, timely initiation of treatment and reduced transmission. It revises the 2013 guidance in light of new evidence on the effectiveness of screening interventions and the performance of screening tools, using the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence and the strength of recommendations. The document is intended to assist countries in planning and implementing screening strategies adapted to their epidemiological and health system contexts. The guideline presents recommendations for systematic screening in the general population and in groups at increased risk of tuberculosis, including people living with HIV, household contacts, prisoners, miners, migrants and other vulnerable populations. It also reviews the use of symptom screening, chest radiography, computer-aided detection software, C-reactive protein and molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests as screening tools, together with guidance on monitoring, evaluation and implementation considerations. The publication identifies research gaps and is accompanied by an operational handbook providing practical guidance for applying the recommendations in national tuberculosis programmes. 3631.doc: Consolidated guidelines on person-centred HIV strategic information: strengthening routine data for impact
3631.title: Consolidated guidelines on person-centred HIV strategic information: strengthening routine data for impact
3631.content: World Health Organization (2022). Consolidated guidelines on person-centred HIV strategic information: strengthening routine data for impact. World Health Organization. TitleConsolidated guidelines on person-centred HIV strategic information: strengthening routine data for impact AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2022-7-28 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240055315 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThese consolidated guidelines provide normative guidance for strengthening HIV strategic information through person-centred routine data systems that support both clinical care and programme management. Developed in response to persistent gaps in HIV prevention, testing, treatment and retention despite substantial progress in the global HIV response, the guidelines promote the collection and use of individual-level longitudinal data to improve continuity of care, strengthen linkage across services and enhance monitoring of programme performance. They consolidate and update previous WHO guidance while introducing recommendations on person-centred monitoring, digital health information systems, interoperability, data quality, surveillance and the integration of HIV services with tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections and other related conditions. The publication outlines recommendations and operational guidance on HIV prevention monitoring, patient monitoring, surveillance, digital health data, routine data use, priority indicators and implementation considerations. It emphasizes the transition from aggregate reporting to person-centred, digital information systems that support clinical decision-making, programme improvement and public health action while ensuring data privacy, confidentiality and security. The guidelines also describe minimum datasets, standardized monitoring tools and approaches to improving data quality and using routine information to strengthen service delivery and measure progress towards global HIV targets. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations: optimizing health worker roles to improve access to key maternal and newborn health interventions through task shifting AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2012-12-19 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241504843 Languageen AbstractThis WHO guidance provides evidence-based recommendations on optimizing health worker roles through task shifting to improve universal access to key maternal and newborn health interventions. Developed in response to health workforce shortages and inequities in access to care, it assesses whether specific interventions can be delivered safely and effectively by different health worker cadres, including lay health workers, auxiliary nurses and nurse midwives, nurses, midwives, associate clinicians, advanced level associate clinicians and non-specialist doctors. The guidance presents 119 recommendations, ranging from practices recommended for implementation to those requiring targeted monitoring and evaluation, rigorous research, or not recommended. It emphasizes that task shifting should complement efforts to increase skilled care and should aim to expand access while maintaining safety. Implementation should consider health-system capacity and local sociocultural, political and financial conditions, with recommendations adapted through national dialogue and considered as packages of interventions rather than in isolation. 3647.doc: The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance
3647.title: The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance
3647.content: World Health Organization (2016). The use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance. World Health Organization. TitleThe use of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis: policy guidance AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2016-8-8 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241511186 Languageen AbstractTuberculosis remains a major global public health challenge, and the WHO End TB Strategy emphasizes the need for early diagnosis and universal drug-susceptibility testing. This policy guidance presents evidence-based recommendations on the use of the commercial loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay (TB-LAMP) for the diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis. Developed following a systematic review of studies conducted since 2012 and assessment using the GRADE approach, the document evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of TB-LAMP as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy, as an add-on test after negative smear microscopy, and in comparison with the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, while also assessing the frequency of indeterminate or invalid results. Based on the available evidence, WHO recommends that TB-LAMP may be used as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy in adults with signs and symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis and as a follow-on test when further investigation of smear-negative specimens is required. The guidance emphasizes that these conditional recommendations are based on very low-quality evidence, apply to sputum specimens from patients with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, and should not replace rapid molecular tests capable of detecting rifampicin resistance. It also highlights the limited evidence for use in people living with HIV, notes the extrapolation of recommendations to children, and provides implementation considerations and priorities for future research. 3651.title: Global hepatitis report 2026
3651.content: World Health Organization (2026). Global hepatitis report 2026. World Health Organization. TitleGlobal hepatitis report 2026 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2026-4-24 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240122383 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis report provides a comprehensive assessment of the global burden of viral hepatitis and progress towards the goal of eliminating hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. Drawing on data reported by Member States and modelled estimates, it analyses trends in incidence, prevalence and mortality associated with hepatitis B and C, covering the period from 2015 to 2024 based on the latest available data. It also situates these trends within the context of global commitments, strategies and targets. The publication reviews the coverage and impact of key interventions for prevention, diagnosis and treatment, including vaccination, infection prevention and control, harm reduction and access to antiviral therapies. It identifies persistent gaps in testing and treatment, marked regional disparities, and the need for accelerated scale-up of services, particularly in high-burden settings. The report concludes that progress towards the 2030 elimination targets remains off track despite the availability of effective interventions. Intended for policymakers, programme managers and public health stakeholders, it serves as an analytical and strategic resource to guide national and global responses to viral hepatitis. 3663.doc: WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention
3663.title: WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention
3663.content: World Health Organization (2013). WHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention. World Health Organization. TitleWHO guidelines for screening and treatment of precancerous lesions for cervical cancer prevention AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2013-11-19 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241548694 Languageen AbstractThese guidelines provide recommendations for screen-and-treat strategies to prevent cervical cancer by detecting and treating precancerous cervical lesions. The screen-and-treat approach bases treatment decisions on screening results, allowing treatment soon or ideally immediately after a positive test, rather than requiring histological confirmation. The guidelines compare strategies using human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), and cytology, linked to treatment with cryotherapy or loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP). They are intended primarily to support policy-makers, programme managers and other health professionals in selecting appropriate cervical cancer prevention strategies according to available resources and existing programmes. Nine recommendations are provided. HPV-based screening is generally preferred where feasible, while VIA is suggested where HPV testing is not feasible; cold knife conization is not recommended as part of a screen-and-treat strategy. Recommendations apply to all women, with specific guidance for women living with HIV. Decision-making and implementation flowcharts support adaptation of the recommended strategies to country and regional contexts. 3667.doc: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis
3667.title: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis
3667.content: World Health Organization (2025). WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis. World Health Organization. TitleWHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 3: diagnosis: web annex B: evidence synthesis and analysis AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2025-4-10 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization DOIhttps://doi.org/10.2471/B09341 Languageen AbstractThis web annex to the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 3: Diagnosis, compiles the evidence synthesis and analyses used to inform WHO recommendations on diagnostic technologies for tuberculosis and drug-resistant tuberculosis. The publication presents systematic reviews, meta-analyses, qualitative evidence syntheses and economic evaluations examining the diagnostic accuracy, safety, cost–effectiveness and implementation considerations of multiple diagnostic approaches, including low- and moderate-complexity nucleic acid amplification tests, targeted next-generation sequencing technologies and Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests. The annex describes the methods applied to identify, assess and synthesize evidence across diverse populations and settings, including adults, adolescents, children and people living with HIV. It addresses the detection of pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis, rifampicin resistance and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis using respiratory and non-respiratory specimens. The document also examines stakeholder and user perspectives, operational feasibility and factors influencing implementation. Developed in accordance with WHO guideline development standards, the annex provides the technical evidence base underpinning updates to WHO policy guidance on tuberculosis diagnosis and drug-resistance testing. 3675.title: WHO guideline: recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening

TitleWHO guideline: recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2019-4-16 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241550505 Languageen AbstractThis WHO guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of digital interventions to strengthen health systems and support progress towards universal health coverage (UHC). Developed in response to the growing adoption of digital technologies and the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on digital health, it addresses the need for rigorous evaluation of digital health interventions to ensure that investments are informed by evidence of their benefits, harms, acceptability, feasibility, resource implications and equity considerations. The guideline emphasizes that digital technologies should complement, rather than replace, the fundamental components of well-functioning health systems. The recommendations focus on a prioritized set of digital health interventions accessible at a minimum through mobile devices, including birth and death notification, stock notification and commodity management, client-to-provider and provider-to-provider telemedicine, targeted client communication, digital tracking of clients’ health status and services, health worker decision support, and digital learning for health workers. The guideline also outlines implementation considerations, identifies research gaps, and supports ministries of health, public health practitioners, development partners and other stakeholders in making evidence-based decisions on the adoption, scale-up and institutionalization of effective digital health interventions. 3693.title: Toolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data: integrated health services analysis: district and facil…
3693.content: World Health Organization (2023). Toolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data: integrated health services analysis: district and facility level. World Health Organization. TitleToolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data: integrated health services analysis: district and facility level AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-6-16 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240060609 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis guidance document, part of the WHO Toolkit for analysis and use of routine health facility data, provides practical guidance on the integrated analysis and use of routine health information system (RHIS) data at district and health facility levels. It is intended to support managers, analysts and other health system stakeholders in monitoring health service delivery and using routine data for operational decision-making. The document promotes an integrated, standards-based approach that uses a limited set of tracer indicators representing multiple programmes and service components, thereby supporting primary health care, universal health coverage and the health-related Sustainable Development Goals. The publication presents principles for RHIS data analysis, including integration across programmes, focused use of key indicators, standardization of analyses and visualizations, routine assessment of data quality, and purpose-oriented use of information for management and planning. It organizes indicators into three groups: health status and epidemiological profile, health service performance, and health service resources. For each group, the publication provides indicator definitions, metadata, recommended disaggregations, analytical approaches, and examples of dashboards and visualizations. It emphasizes the interpretation of routine data within local contexts and illustrates how standardized dashboards can support supervision, performance review, resource allocation and continuous improvement of health services at subnational levels. 3709.content: World Health Organization (2018). National health workforce accounts: implementation guide. World Health Organization. TitleNational health workforce accounts: implementation guide AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2018-10-19 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241514446 Languageen AbstractThe National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) Implementation Guide provides practical guidance for countries on establishing and sustaining systems to collect, analyse, use and report standardized health workforce data. Developed as a companion document to the NHWA Handbook and in support of the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030, the guide outlines a structured approach to strengthening health workforce information systems and improving the availability, quality and use of human resources for health data. It is intended for policy-makers, programme managers, technical experts and stakeholders involved in health workforce planning, monitoring and governance, and emphasizes collaboration across sectors such as health, education, labour, finance and statistics. The guide presents an implementation framework organized into three phases—conceptualization, operationalization, and scaling up and sustainability—comprising eight steps that address political commitment, governance arrangements, planning, legal considerations, data compilation and analysis, validation, dissemination, and process review. It describes the roles of national institutions and multistakeholder coordination mechanisms, provides guidance on data quality, reporting and communication processes, and promotes the integration of existing information systems. By supporting the systematic monitoring of health workforce indicators, the guide aims to strengthen evidence-informed decision-making and contribute to health workforce development, universal health coverage and broader national and global health objectives. TitleDigital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing: WHO recommendations in digital systems: web annex D: function and non-functional requirements AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-12-14 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis web annex provides the high-level functional and non-functional requirements supporting the WHO Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. It translates WHO HIV recommendations and service delivery workflows into standardized system requirements to guide the design, development, procurement and implementation of interoperable digital health solutions. The annex defines functional requirements for key business processes across HIV prevention, testing, treatment, care, diagnostics, referral, follow-up and reporting, together with non-functional requirements addressing system performance, security, confidentiality, privacy, interoperability, usability, reliability and offline functionality. Structured as a software-neutral implementation resource, it enables consistent interpretation of operational requirements while allowing adaptation to national policies and digital health architectures. Intended for digital health architects, software developers, implementers, procurers and programme managers, this resource supports the development of standards-based HIV information systems that accurately implement WHO recommendations while ensuring robust, secure and sustainable digital health solutions. Poliovirus containment: guidance to minimize risk for facilities collecting, handling or storing materials potentially infectious for polioviruses: web annex A: country and area specific poliovirus data, April 2023 update. World Health Organization. TitlePoliovirus containment: guidance to minimize risk for facilities collecting, handling or storing materials potentially infectious for polioviruses: web annex A: country and area specific poliovirus data, April 2023 update AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-7-24 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis web annex provides updated country- and area-specific poliovirus circulation data to support the assessment of potentially infectious materials in facilities collecting, handling or storing samples that may contain polioviruses. It accompanies the second edition of Poliovirus containment: guidance to minimize risks for facilities collecting, handling or storing materials potentially infectious for polioviruses and is intended to assist facilities in identifying samples requiring appropriate risk mitigation or containment measures. The annex presents Table A2.1, which compiles poliovirus circulation dates by country and area, including wild poliovirus (WPV), vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) and oral polio vaccine type 2/novel oral polio vaccine type 2/Sabin2 potentially infectious material periods. The data were derived from national poliovirus reports, systematic literature searches and consultations with WHO regional offices, and are regularly revised and updated. The information supports the identification and management of potentially infectious materials according to the containment requirements outlined in the accompanying guidance. 3731.doc: Use of tuberculosis interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) in low- and middle-income countries : policy statement
3731.title: Use of tuberculosis interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) in low- and middle-income countries : policy statement
3731.content: World Health Organization (2011). Use of tuberculosis interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) in low- and middle-income countries : policy statement. World Health Organization. TitleUse of tuberculosis interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) in low- and middle-income countries : policy statement AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2011-12-31 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241502672 Languageen AbstractThis policy statement provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of commercial interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) for tuberculosis (TB) in low- and middle-income countries, particularly settings with a high TB and/or HIV burden. Based on systematic reviews and GRADE assessment, it evaluates IGRAs for diagnosis of active TB, detection of latent TB infection (LTBI) in children and people living with HIV, screening of health care workers and contacts, outbreak investigations, and prediction of progression to active disease. The evidence was generally of low or very low quality and did not demonstrate superior performance of IGRAs over the tuberculin skin test (TST). WHO recommends that IGRAs and the TST not be used to diagnose active TB or identify individuals at risk of developing active disease, and that IGRAs not replace the TST for LTBI diagnosis in children, people living with HIV, or contacts. Given comparable performance, greater cost and technical complexity, replacing the TST with IGRAs as a public health intervention in resource-constrained settings is not recommended. 3733.content: World Health Organization (2023). Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health. World Health Organization. TitleClassification of digital interventions, services and applications in health: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-10-24 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240081949 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis second edition of the Classification of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health provides a standardized taxonomy for describing how digital technologies are used to address individual and health system needs. Developed by WHO, the classification establishes a shared language to support communication among policy-makers, health programme managers, researchers, implementers, technology developers and other stakeholders involved in digital health. It organizes digital health interventions around discrete technological capabilities designed to address health system challenges and links these interventions to the digital services and application types through which they are delivered. The publication updates and expands the first edition published in 2018 to reflect advances in digital health technologies, evolving implementation practices and lessons learned from global use. The framework is structured around three interconnected axes: health system challenges, digital health interventions and digital services and application types. It includes interventions for persons, health-care providers, health system managers and data services, alongside categories of digital applications and information systems. The classification is intended to support planning, implementation, investment analysis, research, interoperability considerations, policy development and the governance of digital health initiatives, thereby facilitating more consistent and effective use of digital technologies in health systems. 3745.doc: Contingency fund for emergencies: 2020 annual report
3745.title: Contingency fund for emergencies: 2020 annual report
3745.content: World Health Organization (2021). Contingency fund for emergencies: 2020 annual report. World Health Organization. TitleContingency fund for emergencies: 2020 annual report AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-7-2 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis annual report presents an overview of the activities, financing and operational impact of the World Health Organization’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE) in 2020. The publication describes how the CFE enabled WHO to respond rapidly to 14 emergencies in 13 countries and to support the global response to COVID-19 through the release of nearly US$ 44 million. It outlines the Fund’s role in supporting outbreak control, emergency health operations, supply chain management, surveillance, vaccination activities, procurement of essential medical supplies and continuity of health services during infectious disease outbreaks, humanitarian crises, natural disasters and technological emergencies. The report highlights WHO-supported responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Beirut port explosion, Tropical Cyclone Harold in Vanuatu and the humanitarian crisis in north-eastern Syria. It also examines funding allocations, reimbursement mechanisms, donor contributions and accountability arrangements governing the CFE. Through operational examples and financial analysis, the publication demonstrates the importance of rapid, flexible and predictable financing for strengthening emergency preparedness and enabling timely public health action in complex and evolving emergencies. TitlePandemic influenza preparedness framework: annual progress report, 1 January – 31 December 2022 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-8-4 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240076907 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThe Pandemic Influenza Preparedness (PIP) Framework: annual progress report, 1 January–31 December 2022 presents technical and financial progress in implementing the PIP Framework, which aims to strengthen the sharing of influenza viruses with human pandemic potential and improve developing countries’ access to pandemic vaccines and other response supplies. The report assesses progress under the High-Level Implementation Plan II (2018–2023), including activities financed through the industry-funded Partnership Contribution mechanism. The report documents achievements and challenges in influenza laboratory capacity and surveillance, virus sharing, disease burden estimation, regulatory preparedness, risk communication and community engagement, deployment planning, and national pandemic preparedness. In 2022, 91% of Partnership Contribution recipient countries reported influenza data to FluNet, 48 countries had implemented regulatory approaches for pandemic influenza products, and 37 countries had developed or updated pandemic preparedness plans. It also presents progress in securing pandemic response products through benefit-sharing agreements, alongside financial allocations, expenditures and implementation milestones. 3769.content: World Health Organization (2020). WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis: module 1: prevention: tuberculosis preventive treatment. World Health Organization. TitleWHO operational handbook on tuberculosis: module 1: prevention: tuberculosis preventive treatment AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2020-3-23 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240002906 Languageen AbstractThis operational handbook provides practical guidance for the programmatic management and scale-up of tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) in line with WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis. The publication addresses the global burden of tuberculosis infection and the need to expand preventive interventions among populations at high risk of developing TB disease, particularly people living with HIV, household contacts of TB patients and other vulnerable groups. It supports implementation of commitments made at the United Nations High-Level Meeting on Tuberculosis and outlines strategies to strengthen national responses through integrated, people-centred approaches. The handbook describes the cascade of care for TPT, including identification of target populations, exclusion of active TB disease, testing for TB infection, treatment options, management of adverse events, adherence support, monitoring and evaluation, and ethical considerations. It also provides operational guidance for contact investigation, integration of preventive services with active TB case finding and HIV services, health system strengthening, and resource mobilization. Practical implementation tools, policy considerations and monitoring indicators are included to assist national TB programmes, policy-makers and health-care providers in adapting and scaling up TPT services in diverse epidemiological and health system settings. 3771.doc: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006
3771.title: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006
3771.content: World Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia (2006). Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006. WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia. TitleEnumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes : report of a workshop, Bangkok, Thailand, 6-10 June 2006 AuthorsWorld Health Organization. Regional Office for South-East Asia Issued2006-12-31 Typedocument PublisherWHO Regional Office for South-East Asia Languageen AbstractDescription: Enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes is essential for initiation of antiretroviral therapy for a person with HIV as well as for monitoring the response to treatment. The techniques for enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes are evolving. The flow cytometry continues to be the gold standard of CD4 T lymphocytes enumeration in spite of the fact that the technology is expensive both in terms of initial investment in sophisticated equipment and running cost. The newer techniques may be economical to procure and maintain. The latter are particularly intended for countries with limited resources. WHO conducted a workshop to orient the nationals about these technologies and integration of a quality system into routine testing, at Siriraj Hospital Bangkok. The report describes the status of CD4 testing in these countries. While Indonesia, India and Thailand have developed a good infrastructure for enumeration of CD4 T lymphocytes, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Sri Lanka have made a beginning in this direction. The workshop focussed on principles of various techniques and imparted a hands-on training for performing the same. The issues regarding selection of technology, procurement of equipment and their maintenance; ensuring continuous supply and economical use of reagents and biosafety in laboratory were discussed and have been presented in this Report. TitleDigital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-12-21 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240085138 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis second edition of the digital adaptation kit for HIV provides operational, software-neutral requirements to support the incorporation of WHO clinical, public health and data use recommendations into digital systems. Developed within the SMART Guidelines approach, it focuses on the content requirements for person-centred digital tracking and decision support systems used by health workers for HIV services in primary health care settings. The kit is intended to facilitate transparent, consistent and adaptable translation of narrative guidance into digital implementations while supporting interoperability and local customization. The publication organizes HIV-related requirements into eight components: health interventions and associated recommendations; generic personas; illustrative user scenarios; business processes and workflows; core data elements; decision support and scheduling logic; indicators and performance metrics; and high-level functional and non-functional requirements. It covers processes including HIV testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis, care and treatment, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, infant diagnosis, diagnostics, client follow-up, referral, and aggregate reporting and data use, with complementary operational resources provided in web annexes. 3777.content: World Health Organization (2022). WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 5: management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents. World Health Organization. TitleWHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: module 5: management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2022-3-18 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240046764 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractTuberculosis (TB) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality among children and adolescents, with substantial gaps in case detection, diagnosis and access to preventive treatment worldwide. This guideline consolidates new and existing WHO recommendations for the management of TB in these populations, replacing the 2014 guidance and reflecting the latest evidence on prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment and models of care. It aims to support countries in strengthening the continuum of TB care and improving health outcomes through evidence-based policies and practices tailored to the specific needs of children, adolescents and their families. The publication provides recommendations on TB screening and contact investigation, TB preventive treatment, diagnostic approaches, treatment of drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB, management of TB meningitis, and decentralized, family-centred models of care. It incorporates updated evidence on the use of Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, integrated treatment decision algorithms, shortened treatment regimens for non-severe TB, and therapeutic options for multidrug- or rifampicin-resistant disease in children. Developed according to WHO guideline development standards, the document is intended for national TB programmes, policy-makers, health professionals and implementing partners, and contributes to global efforts to reduce TB-related morbidity and mortality in line with the End TB Strategy and Sustainable Development Goals. 3781.title: Consolidated HIV guidelines: service delivery
3781.content: World Health Organization (2026). Consolidated HIV guidelines: service delivery. World Health Organization. TitleConsolidated HIV guidelines: service delivery AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2026-7-22 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240124233 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractHIV remains a major public health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, despite the availability of effective treatment and prevention tools. Many evidence-based interventions are not implemented consistently or delivered in a timely manner, contributing to ongoing HIV transmission, advanced disease and preventable mortality. These consolidated WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to strengthen HIV service delivery through people-centred, integrated and equitable approaches that improve access to care, continuity of treatment and accelerate progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat. The publication consolidates all WHO recommendations on HIV service delivery issued between 2013 and 2025. It is intended to support the development of national and subnational policies, clinical guidelines and implementation guidance. It addresses key components of HIV service delivery, including linkage to care and antiretroviral therapy initiation, clinical follow-up and medication refills, adherence support and re-engagement in care, services for adolescents and young people, task sharing, decentralized service delivery, and integration with maternal and child health, tuberculosis, sexual and reproductive health, diabetes, hypertension and mental health services. Recommendations are classified as new, updated or revalidated according to WHO guideline development procedures. 3783.title: Understanding national health workforce accounts
3783.content: World Health Organization (2017). Understanding national health workforce accounts. World Health Organization. TitleUnderstanding national health workforce accounts AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2017-12-31 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractUnderstanding National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) is an introductory guidance document developed by the World Health Organization to explain the purpose, policy relevance and structure of the National Health Workforce Accounts framework. The publication outlines how NHWA supports the standardization of health workforce information systems, improves the quality and comparability of data, and strengthens the evidence base for health workforce policy, planning and monitoring. Positioned within the context of universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals, the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030, and related international commitments, the document highlights the importance of reliable workforce information for addressing current and future health system challenges. The publication describes the benefits of NHWA at national, regional and global levels and presents key policy questions that can be informed through systematic workforce data collection and analysis. It introduces the health labour market framework used by NHWA, emphasizing workforce production, labour market flows, distribution, productivity and regulation. The document also summarizes the development process of the NHWA indicators and explains the modular structure of the framework, which comprises ten modules covering workforce stock, education, labour market dynamics, employment conditions, financing, governance, planning and information systems. Together, these elements provide a foundation for evidence-informed decision-making and strengthened health workforce monitoring. 3809.content: Khadijeh Ezoji; Mohsen Yaghoubi; Marzieh Nojomi; et al. (2019). Cost-effectiveness of introducing the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine for children under 5 years in the Islamic Republic of Iran. World Health Organization. Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean. TitleCost-effectiveness of introducing the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine for children under 5 years in the Islamic Republic of Iran AuthorsKhadijeh Ezoji; Mohsen Yaghoubi; Marzieh Nojomi; Sussan Mahmoody; Seyed Mohsen Zahraie; Maziar Moradi-Lakeh; Sedigheh R. Tabatabaei; Abdollah Karimi Issued2019-10-29 Typedocument PublisherWorld Health Organization. Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean DOIhttps://doi.org/10.26719/emhj.19.039 Languageen AbstractBackground: Pneumococcal disease caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae results in considerable mortality and morbidity. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV), such as PCV-13, can prevent invasive pneumococcal disease and avoid disability and death. The cost of introducing PCV-13 in childhood immunization schedules should be assessed against the cost of pneumococcal diseases for each community. Aims: This study aimed to evaluate the cost–effectiveness of introducing PCV-13 in the national immunization programme for children under 5 years in the Islamic Republic of Iran. Methods: The TRIVAC decision support model was used to estimate total costs of introducing PCV-13 and the disability-adjusted life years (DALYs)averted. The main pneumococcal diseases were considered—pneumonia, meningitis, acute otitis media, and non-pneumonia, non-meningitis infections—in terms of hospital admissions, outpatient visits and deaths. Local data were used to estimate costs. Results: Pneumococcal disease is estimated to affect 18 713 211 children under 5 years (519 412 pneumonia, 18 148 116 acute otitis media, 6884 meningitis, and 38 799 non-pneumonia, non-meningitis)in 10 years (2014–2023)without use of the vaccine. Introduction of PCV-13 would prevent 4 900 084 cases of pneumococcal disease (190 849 pneumonia, 4 692 450 acute otitis media, 2529 meningitis, and 14 256 non-pneumonia, non-meningitis). Pneumococcal infection would cause 287 950 hospital admissions and 29 399 deaths; vaccination could avert 105 802 hospital admissions and 9997 deaths. The incremental cost–effectiveness was estimated to be US$ 1890 and US$ 1538 per averted DALY for the government and society respectively. Conclusion: According to WHO-recommended thresholds for interpreting cost–effectiveness, introduction of PCV-13 for children under 5 years in the Islamic Republic of Iran would be cost-effective Sources . | iris.who.int/handle/10665/385346 (canonical) | doi:https://doi.org/10.26719/emhj.19.039 (doi) | repository record (repository) | . 3815.doc: Digital transformation handbook for reporting substandard and falsified medical products
3815.title: Digital transformation handbook for reporting substandard and falsified medical products
3815.content: World Health Organization (2026). Digital transformation handbook for reporting substandard and falsified medical products. World Health Organization. TitleDigital transformation handbook for reporting substandard and falsified medical products AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2026-6-9 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240120747 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis handbook provides practical guidance to support countries in planning, designing and implementing digital solutions for reporting substandard and falsified medical products. These products pose a significant threat to public health, contributing to therapeutic failure, adverse effects, loss of trust in health systems and broader socioeconomic impacts. Effective detection and reporting are essential to enable regulatory authorities to investigate suspected cases, remove harmful products from circulation and contribute to global surveillance efforts through mechanisms such as WHO’s Global Surveillance and Monitoring System. The document outlines a structured approach to digital transformation, covering assessment of the current environment, stakeholder engagement, governance and policy alignment, definition of system requirements, implementation planning, and monitoring and evaluation. It emphasizes the transition from fragmented or paper-based reporting systems to interoperable digital platforms that improve data quality, standardization and timeliness. Drawing on global experience and existing WHO frameworks, the handbook promotes the use of user-centred design, open standards and integration with pharmacovigilance systems. It is intended for ministries of health, national regulatory authorities and partners seeking to strengthen reporting systems and enhance the capacity to detect and respond to substandard and falsified medical products. 3821.title: Consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection: recommendations…
3821.content: World Health Organization (2016). Consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection: recommendations for a public health approach. World Health Organization. TitleConsolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection: recommendations for a public health approach AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2016-6-6 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241549684 Languageen AbstractThis evidence-based guideline consolidates World Health Organization recommendations on the use of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, providing a comprehensive public health framework for HIV diagnosis, prevention, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring and evaluation across all age groups and populations. Developed in response to advances in scientific evidence and evolving programmatic needs, the second edition updates the 2013 consolidated guidelines and incorporates new recommendations, including universal eligibility for antiretroviral therapy (ART) regardless of CD4 cell count, expanded use of pre-exposure prophylaxis, and optimized approaches to HIV testing, treatment monitoring and management of coinfections and comorbidities. The guideline also outlines the methods used for guideline development and the principles underpinning a public health approach. The publication provides evidence-based recommendations on HIV testing services, antiretroviral therapy, prevention interventions, differentiated service delivery models, linkage to care, adherence, decentralization, task sharing, laboratory services and programme monitoring. It emphasizes integrated, people-centred and community-based approaches to improve access to high-quality HIV services, strengthen health systems and support implementation in diverse epidemiological settings. Intended primarily for national HIV programme managers, clinicians, policy-makers and implementing partners, the guideline aims to accelerate progress towards universal access to HIV services and the global goal of ending the HIV epidemic as a major public health threat by 2030. TitleGlobal strategy on digital health 2020-2025 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-8-18 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240020924 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThe Global strategy on digital health 2020–2025 provides a framework to support Member States in strengthening health systems through the appropriate adoption and use of digital technologies. Developed in response to World Health Assembly mandates and aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals and WHO’s Triple Billion targets, the strategy outlines a shared vision for improving health and well-being through accessible, affordable, secure and sustainable digital health solutions. It emphasizes the importance of strong governance, interoperability, ethical use of data, privacy protection, workforce capacity-building and investment in digital infrastructure to support national health priorities and universal health coverage. The document establishes four strategic objectives: promoting global collaboration and knowledge exchange; advancing the implementation of national digital health strategies; strengthening governance for digital health at global, regional and national levels; and advocating people-centred health systems enabled by digital technologies. It also presents guiding principles, an implementation framework and monitoring mechanisms to support countries in developing interoperable digital health ecosystems. Particular attention is given to addressing barriers faced by low- and middle-income countries and ensuring that digital transformation contributes to equitable, effective and resilient health systems. TitleDigital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing: WHO recommendations in digital systems: web annex B: decision-support logic AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-12-14 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis web annex provides the standardized decision-support logic supporting the WHO Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. It translates WHO HIV recommendations into structured, software-neutral decision tables that can be incorporated into digital tracking and decision-support systems to support consistent clinical and public health decision-making. The annex includes decision logic for HIV testing, prevention, treatment, advanced HIV disease, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, diagnostics, follow-up and related service delivery workflows, using standardized input expressions, decision rules, outputs, scheduling logic and triggering events. It also provides implementation guidance on rule syntax, comparison operators, hit policies and coding conventions to promote transparency, interoperability and consistent interpretation across digital platforms. Intended for software developers, digital health architects, implementers and programme managers, this resource supports the development and adaptation of standards-based decision-support functionality that accurately reflects WHO recommendations while allowing contextualization for national policies and health system requirements. 3843.doc: National health workforce accounts: a handbook
3843.title: National health workforce accounts: a handbook
3843.content: World Health Organization (2017). National health workforce accounts: a handbook. World Health Organization. TitleNational health workforce accounts: a handbook AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2017-10-26 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241513111 Languageen AbstractThis handbook introduces the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA), a standardized framework developed by the World Health Organization to strengthen health workforce information systems and support evidence-based workforce planning and policy-making. The publication is intended to assist countries in monitoring and analysing health workforce capacity, distribution, education, labour market dynamics, financing, governance and information systems in the context of universal health coverage and the health-related Sustainable Development Goals. It outlines the rationale for improved health workforce data and highlights the role of harmonized metrics in addressing challenges related to workforce availability, accessibility, performance and retention. The handbook presents a modular framework comprising 78 core indicators organized across 10 modules covering active workforce stock, education and training, regulation and accreditation, education financing, labour market flows, employment conditions, workforce spending and remuneration, skill mix, governance, and health workforce information systems. For each indicator, it provides definitions, methodological guidance, reporting requirements, data sources and disaggregation options. The publication also describes implementation principles, reporting standards and potential applications of the NHWA, supporting countries in strengthening health workforce monitoring, facilitating international comparability and informing policies aimed at improving health system performance and population access to quality health services. 3859.doc: Guidelines on long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV prevention
3859.title: Guidelines on long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV prevention
3859.content: World Health Organization (2022). Guidelines on long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV prevention. World Health Organization. TitleGuidelines on long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV prevention AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2022-7-27 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240054097 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis guideline provides evidence-informed recommendations on the use of long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention in people at substantial risk of HIV infection. Developed according to WHO guideline development procedures, it is based on systematic reviews, GRADE assessments and additional evidence on effectiveness, safety, acceptability, feasibility, equity and cost–effectiveness. The document reviews the global HIV prevention context, the rationale for expanding HIV prevention choices, and the evidence supporting CAB-LA as an additional PrEP option. It also outlines the principles guiding implementation within a public health and human rights framework and identifies the intended audiences for the recommendations. The guideline recommends that long-acting injectable cabotegravir may be offered as an additional HIV prevention choice as part of combination prevention approaches for people at substantial risk of HIV infection. It discusses key implementation considerations, including HIV testing, service delivery models, comprehensive prevention services, community engagement, provider training and adherence support. The publication also identifies priority research gaps related to safety, drug resistance, delivery strategies and population-level impact, and describes the guideline development process, dissemination strategy and supporting evidence underpinning the recommendation. TitleClassification of digital health interventions v1.0: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2018-3-14 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis publication presents version 1.0 of the World Health Organization’s Classification of Digital Health Interventions (DHIs), a taxonomy developed to provide a shared and standardized language for describing how digital and mobile technologies are used to address health system needs. Intended primarily for public health audiences, the framework supports communication among policymakers, programme planners, implementers, researchers, donors and technology specialists by defining digital health interventions as discrete digital functionalities linked to specific health objectives. The classification was developed to facilitate evidence synthesis, landscape analyses, planning processes and the articulation of digital solutions to identified health system challenges. The framework organizes digital health interventions into four primary groups according to the main user: clients, health-care providers, health system managers and data services. It links digital interventions to broader health system challenges and to system categories such as electronic medical records, logistics management information systems and telemedicine platforms. Developed through technical consultations, literature review and public feedback, the classification builds on existing mHealth and eHealth frameworks while providing a simplified and practical reference for health programmes. The document is intended to support the design, implementation, evaluation and interoperability of digital health initiatives and will be periodically updated to reflect emerging technologies and evolving practices in digital health. TitleNational health workforce accounts: a handbook AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-11-23 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240081291 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThe National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) Handbook, second edition, provides the conceptual framework, standards, methods and indicators that support the systematic collection, analysis and use of health workforce data for evidence-informed policy-making and planning. Developed by the World Health Organization, the handbook supports implementation of the National Health Workforce Accounts as a country-led system to strengthen human resources for health information systems, improve data quality and availability, and monitor progress towards universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals and other global health objectives. It describes the rationale, principles and applications of NHWA at national, regional and global levels and outlines a modular approach to health workforce monitoring. The handbook presents guidance on implementation and reporting methods and defines a set of standardized indicators organized into four modules covering workforce stock and flows, education, finance and expenditures, and working conditions, governance and leadership. It explains indicator metadata, calculation methods, disaggregation requirements and reporting standards, and illustrates how NHWA data can be used to support workforce planning, policy development, retention strategies, equity analyses and monitoring of health workforce trends. The revised edition incorporates updated indicators, occupational classifications, tools and guidance to address evolving health workforce priorities and emerging global health challenges. 3867.content: World Health Organization (2024). Digital transformation handbook for primary health care: optimizing person-centred point of service systems. World Health Organization. TitleDigital transformation handbook for primary health care: optimizing person-centred point of service systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2024-11-4 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240093362 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis handbook provides practical guidance for countries seeking to digitally transform primary health care through the development and implementation of person-centred point of service systems (PCPOSS). It addresses the transition from paper-based and fragmented digital systems towards integrated, interoperable digital solutions that support service delivery, continuity of care, data use and health system strengthening. Grounded in WHO recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening and aligned with the SMART Guidelines framework, the publication outlines approaches for translating clinical and public health guidance into digital systems while maintaining fidelity to normative standards. The publication presents a stepwise methodology covering assessment of digital readiness, identification of user requirements, workflow and business process mapping, system design and adaptation, software selection, testing, deployment and scale-up. It emphasizes person-centred care, interoperability, longitudinal health records, decision support and the use of standards-based digital architectures. Through practical tools, worksheets and implementation guidance, the publication supports policy-makers, programme managers, digital health practitioners and software developers in designing and optimizing digital systems that improve service quality, strengthen accountability and enable more effective, integrated and responsive primary health care services. 3871.title: Лечение и уход в связи с ВИЧ/СПИДом в Беларуси: отчет оценочной миссии: январь 2014 г.
3871.content: Lundgren, Jens D; Raben, Dorthe; Ерамова, Ирина; et al. (2014). Лечение и уход в связи с ВИЧ/СПИДом в Беларуси: отчет оценочной миссии: январь 2014 г.. Всемирная организация здравоохранения. Европейское региональное бюро. TitleЛечение и уход в связи с ВИЧ/СПИДом в Беларуси: отчет оценочной миссии: январь 2014 г. AuthorsLundgren, Jens D; Raben, Dorthe; Ерамова, Ирина; Ильенкова, Вера Issued2014-12-31 Typereport PublisherВсемирная организация здравоохранения. Европейское региональное бюро Languageru AbstractОценка лечения и ухода в связи с ВИЧ/СПИДом выполнена с учетом стратегии или концепции ВОЗ/ЮНЭЙДС «Лечение 2.0», где указаны пять приоритетных областей: оптимизация лекарственных схем, обеспечение доступа к диагностике в местах оказания помощи, снижение стоимости, адаптация систем оказания услуг и мобилизация сообществ или гражданского общества. Для оценки использованы результаты анализа существующих документов и отчетов и страновой миссии, которая состоялась 11-14 ноября 2013 года в гор. Минске и Солигорске, Беларусь. Особое внимание было уделено практике тестирования на ВИЧ, поскольку именно здесь начинается лечение и уход в связи с ВИЧ, а также уязвимым группам и обеспечению доступа к лечению и уходу. Кроме того, была проанализирована устойчивость программ в свете используемых в настоящее время и будущих международных и национальных схем финансирования. 4092.title: indicator-extraction
4092.content: Skill indicator-extraction: Extract the indicators an L1 source prints (indicator reference or metadata sheets: name, numerator, denominator, disaggregation, definition, data sources) as L1 indicator nodes with every printed field, then draft one L2 program indicator per indicator, derived from its L1 node. Read before adding a WHO handbook’s or guideline’s indicators to a DAK or a DTH, and whenever an L2 indicator has to trace to its source. Part of L1 → L2 extraction for every DAK and DTH, beside recommendation-extraction. Named by: DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . Skill id: indicator-extraction · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Follows dak-l1-library, which ingests the source. Sibling of recommendation-extraction: that one takes a source’s recommendations, this one its indicators. It is a step of L1 → L2 extraction for a DAK or DTH, bound to Task_Indicators in l2-dak-authoring and Call_Data in dth-authoring.

4093.title: Two layers, kept apart
4093.content: | layer | what | kind / model | written by | . | L1 | the indicator as the source prints it, verbatim | indicator block (folio type smart-base:Indicator; KG L1 indicator, kg/src/l1.ts) | scripts/l1-indicator-sheets.py → candidates.json → gen-library-jsonld | . | L2 | the DAK’s or DTH’s own operational measure, a draft that points back | program-indicator (sgkg-l2), logical model ProgramIndicator | scripts/l2-program-indicators.py | . sgkg-l2 keeps them apart: merging them would merge a WHO definition with a country’s implementation of it. The L2 record is a draft with derivedFrom its L1 node, and the L2 author adopts, edits or drops it.

4094.title: Rules
4094.content: . | Ids come from the source. number / indicatorId is the printed indicator number (“1-01”, “4-01.3”). A sheet whose header prints none is reported and skipped, never numbered by an agent. The L2 id is <prefix>.<number> (“NHWA.1-01”); the prefix only namespaces it. | Verbatim. Every field is the printed text: lines joined, letter-spacing artefacts closed up, nothing reworded. A printed list (glossary terms, data sources) is one string joined with “; “. | Every printed field, not only name, numerator and denominator. The L1 node’s meta holds indicatorId, module, abbreviatedName, name, numerator, denominator, disaggregation, definition, glossary, reportingFrequency, reportingFrameworks, dataSources, furtherInformation and dimension where printed; a sub-indicator adds parentIndicator and guidingQuestions. These are the keys the structured-block cards read. | No gap is filled. ProgramIndicator makes definition, numerator, denominator and disaggregation 1..1. Where the source prints none (a composite or self-assessed indicator), the L2 draft lists it in gaps and the L2 author decides. Nothing is copied from another source to fill it. | A composite indicator keeps its sub-indicators as their own L1 nodes; in L2 they are the parent’s components, not program indicators of their own. | Read the page layout, not the section text, when the source prints sheets as a label column and a value column: Stage A’s text reads side bars and columns out of order. | .

4095.title: Steps
4095.content: . | The source is in the library (dak-l1-library), with its PDF in uploads/<doc-id>/. | L1 candidates. From the library repository root: . python3 smart-base/scripts/l1-indicator-sheets.py --entry library/<doc-id> \ --pdf uploads/<doc-id>/<doc-id>.pdf --pages <first>-<last> --json # look first python3 smart-base/scripts/l1-indicator-sheets.py --entry library/<doc-id> \ --pdf uploads/<doc-id>/<doc-id>.pdf --pages <first>-<last> --write . --write merges into candidates.json as the indicators aspect, replacing an indicator candidate with the same number (re-runs are idempotent). Check the count against the source’s own list of indicators (NHWA: the synthesis table, 29 indicators). | L1 nodes. bun cat-harness-tools/pipeline/gen-library-jsonld.ts --entry library/<doc-id> writes blocks/indicator-<section>-NN.{jsonld,md}, each derivedFrom its section, provenance: ingested, with the fields in meta. Existing indicator IRIs do not change when the first candidate of a section stays the same indicator. | L2 drafts. python3 smart-base/scripts/l2-program-indicators.py --entry library/<doc-id> \ --prefix <PREFIX> --out <where the L2 author will review them> . | Into the DAK or DTH. The L2 author takes the drafts into the guide’s indicators component (DAK component 8; a DTH’s data elements, indicators and requirements), through the guide’s own review (l2-component-edit-review) and, for a DTH, a change set. | .

4096.content: . | NHWA handbook, 2nd edition (who-iris 9789240081291-eng): 29 indicators, 33 sub-indicators, PDF pages 51-91. | . Not yet run on a guideline whose indicator sheets use a different layout (HIV SI 2022’s reference sheets: “What it measures”, “Rationale”, “Method of measurement”). Those labels are in the script’s label list, but the header number pattern may need a per-source ID_PATTERN.

4098.title: Inform the client
4098.content: Skill inform-client: A health worker tells the client (or caregiver) what was decided and what happens next, in words and, where the DAK gives one, on a slip or card: a referral, a return date, a result. Input is what to tell and the client’s language; output is that the client was told, and what they were handed. Generic for any DAK step that ends with the client being informed. Named by: Act on decision-support guidance, Capture data with an SDC questionnaire . Skill id: inform-client · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Performed by a person in a health-worker lane. WHO’s immunization DAK has it as IMMZ.D7 “Counsel client” and IMMZ.D9 “Inform client when to return”.

4099.title: Input and output
4099.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: the about (a referral, a return visit, a result, a decision), the facts to convey, the language the client understands, and any handout the DAK gives (a referral slip, a vaccination card). | Out: informed (true once said and understood), the handedOver items, and the questions the client raised that need follow-up. | .

4100.title: What the health worker does
4100.content: . | Say what was decided and what happens next, in the client’s language, without jargon; check it was understood. | Hand over the slip or card when the DAK gives one. | Note any question that needs a follow-up. Nothing else is recorded: this step adds no form. | .

4101.title: Success criteria
4101.content: . | The client can say where to go, when, and why. | Every handout the DAK names was given. | .

4116.title: Steps
4116.content: Every one of the 5 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Extract the text layerTask_ExtractText | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | The document has a text layer: extract it with pdf-extract (pdfminer.six, then a zero-dependency content-stream reader). Exit 2 means no text layer — a scan — and routes to OCR; it is not an empty document. | . | OCR to ocr/page-*.txtTask_Ocr | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | A document ingested this way keeps its text in ocr/ and only a stub in sections/, which the documented sections/ grep cannot see. That asymmetry is why the corpus-grep checklist has a fourth tier. The run also records WHICH SOFTWARE made the pages, in ocr/run-context.json: a folio-run-context/v1 (cat-harness schemas/run-context.ts, the record test runs and QA reports use for the same question), naming the OCR engine, the rasteriser and each language model with its version and the sha256 of the bytes that ran. Two OCRs of one scan can read differently (“Manual” and “Manval”), and without it neither could be told from the other or reproduced. | . | Split into sections/*.md with doc_brief front-matterTask_Sections | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Contextual retrieval: a chunk in isolation loses what makes it mean anything, so each section carries the document brief. | . | Write structure.jsonTask_Structure | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Write structure.json (pdf-structure/v1): doc id, TOC from the PDF outline or inferred from headings, page ranges, metadata, and source{} with the sha256 and a mimetype sniffed from the bytes, never the extension. A structure that could not be determined says so in structure_note rather than being rendered as one. For OCR’d text, source.runContext cites the OCR step’s run context by sha256. A title already known for the document (the catalogue’s dc.title, or one given with –title) is passed through as the raw title, so the sections’ doc_title does not carry a scan’s misreading. | . | Extract claim candidatesTask_Candidates | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | candidates.json holds extracted theorems and definitions. Proposals only – never adjudicated verdicts. | .

4121.title: Lanes — who acts
