4577.title: Semantic Ontologist (Ambiguity Detection & Glossary)
4577.content: Skill ontologist: Semantic Ontologist — scans narrative text for ambiguous terms, generates a formal glossary/registry, and produces a mapping linking narrative strings to formal identifiers. Acts as the “Gatekeeper” ensuring every term has a unique type/identity assignment before formalization proceeds. Named by: Classify and code content .

4578.title: Overview
4578.content: The Gatekeeper for definitions: before any narrative-to-formal translation proceeds, every term has a unique identity (and, where the project has a formal layer, a unique type assignment). The Ontologist detects ambiguities, maintains the formal glossary, and produces the machine-readable mapping.

4579.title: Formal-layer tooling (when available)
4579.content: When the project has a formal-proof layer with language-server / MCP tooling, prefer those tools for type checking over re-building: . | Goal | Prefer | Why better | . | Find type mismatches | structured diagnostics tool | per-file error messages | . | Resolve a symbol’s type | hover-info tool | see the resolved type in place | . | Find an existing definition | local search tool | search project + stdlib | . | Check whether a type exists in the stdlib | symbol/type search tool | locate the exact declaration | . | Find where a type is declared | declaration-file tool | jump to source | . | Guess an import path | completion tool | auto-complete import paths | . Consistency loop . When the formal build or the diagnostics tool reports a type mismatch: . | Identify the glossary entries involved and flag them as ambiguous. | Hover the mismatched symbol → see expected vs actual type. | Search for the intended type → find the correct import. | Read the actual definition to understand the mismatch. | Update the glossary with the corrected assignment. | Regenerate the formal glossary, re-run the scan with the error context, and re-check diagnostics. | .

4580.title: When to Use This Skill
4580.content: . | New terms or definitions are added to chapter files. | The formal build fails due to type mismatches (consistency loop). | The formalizer reports an unresolved term. | Reviewing changes that introduce new notation. | Before running the formalizer on any chapter. | .

4581.title: Workflow
4581.content: 1. Scan narrative text for terms . Run the project’s ontologist scanner over the source chapters. It parses for definitions, symbols, and terms and outputs candidates to the glossary. 2. Detect ambiguities . The scanner flags terms that lack a unique assignment. Trigger phrases (require disambiguation) are bare nouns used without their distinguishing structure — “the mapping” without domain/codomain, “the space” without which kind of space, “the group” without which kind of group, and bare single-letter symbols without an annotation. Action: interrupt the pipeline and request a Type/Identity Assignment. 3. Generate the formal glossary . Run the generator. It produces a formal-glossary file with each term as a declaration, docstrings containing the original narrative definition, and any required annotations. 4. Generate the mapping . Run the mapping generator. It produces a file linking narrative strings to formal identifiers.

4582.title: Glossary entry structure
4582.content: Each glossary entry follows this pattern: a docstring with the human-readable definition, the source location of the narrative definition, and (when relevant) the stdlib reference the term maps to, followed by the declaration itself. Bibliographic reference requirement . Every unproved gap (sorry-style stub) in the formal glossary must be preceded by a reference comment linking to the foundational source, whose key matches a citation key in the project’s reference registry exactly. (Auto-generated bibliography files are derived from the registry — never edit them directly.) .

4583.title: Ambiguity Resolution Format
4583.content: Standing disambiguation rulings . The project’s notation / terminology register holds a table of author-resolved terms; agents MUST apply them when scanning. A ruling fixes the canonical term, any banned synonyms or notations, and when a qualifier is required. Banned notations and “always qualify” entries are hard rules. When an ambiguity is detected, the Ontologist outputs a record naming the narrative term, a message describing the ambiguity, the candidate resolutions, and a resolved_to field that is null until the author fills it. The pipeline halts until resolved_to is filled.

4584.title: Output Files
4584.content: | File | Purpose | . | glossary (machine-readable) | glossary with ambiguity flags | . | formal glossary | formal file with definitions | . | mapping | narrative-to-formal identifier mapping | .

4585.title: Blueprint Integration
4585.content: Every glossary entry that has a label in a chapter file must also appear in the project’s blueprint with the matching formal-declaration macro. The Ontologist ensures: . | Label consistency between chapters and blueprint. | Declaration consistency between blueprint macros and the formal glossary. | Dependency edges in the blueprint reference only labels that exist and whose glossary entries are resolved. | Bibliography references: every reference comment in the formal glossary matches a citation key in the reference registry; new terms get a foundational reference added to the registry. | .

4586.title: Content Object Integration
4586.content: Glossary terms should link to content-object labels. Each definition block has a .ts manifest with a label and a .md narrative. | Definitions in .md blocks reference glossary entries by their formal name and cross-ref by label. | New glossary entries record the content-object label they originate from for bidirectional traceability. | The formal-reference URI in a definition’s .ts manifest matches the corresponding formal-glossary declaration name. | Before creating a glossary entry for a term detected in a .md file, check whether a content object already exists, to avoid duplication. | .

4587.title: Glossary Block Policy
4587.content: A dedicated glossary chapter can contain glossary blocks — remark blocks tagged "glossary" — that map project terminology to canonical stdlib declarations. These are the content-object counterpart of glossary entries. When to use a glossary block vs. a definition block . | Criterion | Glossary block (remark) | Definition block | . | Novelty | none — the term is a synonym/light wrapper for a stdlib type | the project introduces genuinely new material | . | Formal file | not required | required | . | Label prefix | rem:glossary-<term> | def:<term> | . | Chapter | glossary chapter | relevant content chapter | . Decision tree for new terms . | Does the term exist in the stdlib under a different name? → glossary block mapping project name to stdlib name. | Is it a lightweight restriction/specialization of a stdlib type? → glossary block with a note about the restriction. | Does the project add new axioms, fields, or structure? → definition block in the relevant chapter. | Ambiguous? → ask the author. | . Glossary block structure . Each glossary block is a .ts + .md pair: the .ts declares a remark with the glossary tag and a rem:glossary-<term> label; the .md gives a 1–3 sentence definition as used in the project plus the stdlib reference (fully-qualified name, kind, and import path). Snippet validation (mandatory after creating .md) . After creating any glossary .md, validate its embedded math/markup snippets with the project’s snippet validator before committing, and fix any errors. Maintaining consistency . | When a new stdlib-equivalent term appears in any chapter .md, check the glossary chapter for an existing entry before creating a definition. | When the glossary is regenerated, cross-check against the glossary chapter’s entries. | The chapter-analysis skill’s glossary-gap analysis should include the glossary-chapter blocks in its coverage check. | . Wrap-every-occurrence . Every term registered in a block’s defines: [...] must appear wrapped at every mention — the canonical-definition directive once at the canonical site, the reference directive everywhere else. The ontologist owns the choice of canonical site: pick the block whose .md carries the most authoritative definition (stdlib synonym → glossary block; new material → the relevant def: block), add the slug to its defines, and rewrite the canonical mention. Backfilling reference mentions across the project is the codemod’s job.

4588.title: Checklist
4588.content: . | Every definition in the source chapters has a glossary entry | No unresolved ambiguities in the glossary | The formal glossary compiles (gap warnings OK) | The mapping covers all formal-declaration macros | Type/identity assignments have correct annotations | Docstrings in the formal glossary match narrative definitions | Every gap in the formal glossary has a reference comment | All reference keys exist in the reference registry | The blueprint has entries for all glossary definitions | Dependency edges in the blueprint are bidirectionally valid | .

4595.title: pcf-consent
4595.content: | Skill pcf-consent: Model IHE Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF 1.1.0, Trial Implementation) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use) resources referenced by canonical URL only, translate PCF Basic and Additional PurposeOfUse Consents plus the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets into W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policies (consentToOdrl()), and evaluate three-valued access-control decisions (permit | deny | unknown) across decide() / permits(), odrl:obtainConsent duties, IHE ITI-108 Consent Registry reads, and PROV-O decision records citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. | . Named by: Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review, L2 DAK to L3 FHIR IG . Skill id: pcf-consent · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Layer: fhir-harness · Modules: schemas/pcf-consent.ts (consentToOdrl, decide, evaluatePcfPolicy, PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS), schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts (findAccessConsents, Iti108ConsentClient), schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts. Model patient privacy consent directives in FHIR Implementation Guides, translate them into W3C ODRL 2.2 policies, and evaluate three-valued access-control decisions (permit | deny | unknown). Standards and scope: . | Specifications: IHE IT Infrastructure Technical Framework Supplement — Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) 1.1.0 (Trial Implementation, 2023-08-04) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use, FMG maturity level 2). | Profiles: IHE PCF Basic (IHE.PCF.consentBasic) and Additional PurposeOfUse (IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate: extended HL7 PurposeOfUse codes and nested provision exceptions). The translator also handles IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced security-label sensitivity tags when declared. | Referenced by canonical URL only: never copy or re-author IHE PCF StructureDefinitions or ValueSets in an IG; pin the upstream packages in sushi-config.yaml and reference IHE profiles and value sets by their canonical URLs. | No IUA claim: do not claim conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA), and do not profile ITI-71 / ITI-103 OAuth token exchange; HTTP Authorization headers on ITI-108 reads are passed through opaque to the transport. | Trust-anchor neutral: any consent-bearing workflow or verifiable link depends on an abstract trust anchor (a national PKI, a regional federation, did:web, the Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN), …); none is hardcoded. | .

4596.title: 1. Model — Authoring IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent in a FHIR IG
4596.content: 1.1 Package dependencies in sushi-config.yaml . An IG that profiles, instantiates, or references IHE PCF consent directives or Verifiable Health Links pins the upstream IHE packages in sushi-config.yaml and references their artefacts by canonical URL only: . dependencies: ihe.iti.pcf: id: ihe_iti_pcf uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.pcf version: 1.1.0 ihe.iti.vhl: id: ihe_iti_vhl uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.vhl version: 1.0.0-comment . FHIR R4 Consent in an R5 IG (could-not-determine): ihe.iti.pcf@1.1.0 is an R4 (4.0.1) package. When an R5 (fhirVersion: 5.0.0) IG compiles against it and SUSHI or the IG Publisher rejects cross-version R4-in-R5 profile resolution, report that cross-version outcome explicitly as could-not-determine with the exact tool diagnostic rather than silently dropping the dependency or hand-copying the profile. 1.2 Canonical URLs (never re-declared locally) . Reference the IHE PCF profiles, value sets, and HL7 code systems by their canonical URLs exported in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts: . | Artefact | Canonical URL | Constant in schemas/pcf-consent.ts | . | PCF Implementation Guide | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF | PCF_IG_CANONICAL | . | PCF Basic Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic | PCF_CONSENT_BASIC_PROFILE | . | PCF Intermediate Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate | PCF_CONSENT_INTERMEDIATE_PROFILE | . | PCF Advanced Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced | PCF_CONSENT_ADVANCED_PROFILE | . | PCF Basic Purpose ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/BasicPurposeVS | PCF_BASIC_PURPOSE_VS | . | PCF Advanced Security Tag ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/AdvancedSecurityTagVS | PCF_ADVANCED_SECURITY_TAG_VS | . | HL7 v3 ActReason (PurposeOfUse) | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason | HL7_ACT_REASON_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 Confidentiality | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-Confidentiality | HL7_CONFIDENTIALITY_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ActCode | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActCode | HL7_ACT_CODE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ParticipationType | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ParticipationType | HL7_PARTICIPATION_TYPE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 ConsentScope | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope | HL7_CONSENT_SCOPE_SYSTEM | . | LOINC Privacy policy / Consent | http://loinc.org (59284-0) | LOINC_SYSTEM / LOINC_CONSENT_CODE | . 1.3 Required structure of a PCF Consent instance . Every conformant IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent resource carries: . | meta.profile: one of IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, or IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced (detectPcfProfile(consent) inspects meta.profile and falls back to structural inspection). | status: "active" for an enforceable consent directive ("draft", "proposed", "rejected", "inactive", and "entered-in-error" carry no active permissions or prohibitions). | scope: http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope#patient-privacy. | category: includes http://loinc.org#59284-0 (Consent). | patient: reference to the Patient subject (Patient/<id>). | dateTime and performer (the consenting patient or authorized representative, which becomes the ODRL assigner) and organization (the custodian organization). | sourceReference or sourceAttachment: the signed paper/electronic consent artifact or questionnaire response. | policy: policy[].uri naming the overarching privacy policy (such as one of the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit policy URIs). | provision: root provision (type: "permit" or "deny"), purpose codings from http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason (TREAT, HPAYMT, HOPERAT in BasicPurposeVS, or extended PurposeOfUse codes such as HRESCH, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, PUBHLTH, ETREAT, BTG, PATRQT), optional period, actor, action, dataPeriod, data, securityLabel, and optional nested provision.provision exceptions. | . No draft purpose vocabularies: W3C DPV is a Community Group report and is refused (dpv:* or /dpv returns false in isKnownHl7PurposeOfUse). Always use HL7 v3 ActReason PurposeOfUse codes.

4597.title: 2. Translate — consentToOdrl() and the Four Implicit Policies
4597.content: consentToOdrl(consent, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts translates a FHIR R4 Consent into a W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policy (PcfOdrlSet). 2.1 Field-by-field mapping (Consent → ODRL Set) . | FHIR R4 Consent element | ODRL 2.2 Set element | Translation rule | . | id + meta.versionId | uid | consentPolicyUid(consent) → urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId> (or urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id> when unversioned). | . | performer[0] (fallback patient) | assigner | The party granting or withholding consent. | . | status !== "active" | permission: [], prohibition: [] | Non-active consents emit an empty Set, which evaluates to "unknown" (or defers to implicitPolicy). | . | provision.type ("permit" / "deny") | permission / prohibition | Root provision defaults to "permit" when provision.type is omitted, per FHIR R4 Consent.provision.type. | . | provision.purpose[] (v3-ActReason) | constraint (odrl:purpose) | Each HL7 PurposeOfUse code becomes { leftOperand: "odrl:purpose", operator: "odrl:isA", rightOperand: code }, so ontological parent codes (TREAT, HRESCH, ETREAT, …) permit their sub-concepts (CLINTRL, BTG, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, …) via broaderOrSelf over HL7_PURPOSE_OF_USE (IHE PCF Vol 3 §3:5.8.2). Non-HL7 local project codes become odrl:eq. Multiple purpose codings expand into one rule per purpose (logical OR). | . | provision.period (start, end) | constraint (odrl:dateTime) | period.start → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:gteq", rightOperand: start }; period.end → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:lteq", rightOperand: end }. Date-only bounds (YYYY-MM-DD) expand to 00:00:00.000Z (start) and 23:59:59.999Z (end). | . | provision.actor[].reference | assignee | One rule per actor reference; defaults to ANYONE ("*") when actor is omitted. | . | provision.action[] | action | "read" → "odrl:display", "correct" → "odrl:modify", "access" / "collect" / "use" / "disclose" (and default) → "odrl:use". | . | provision.data[] (meaning: "instance") | target | Direct resource references (DocumentReference/ex-doc, Observation/ex-obs) become rule targets. | . | provision.data[] ("authoredby" / "related") | constraint (pcf:author / pcf:encounter) | meaning: "authoredby" → leftOperand: "pcf:author"; meaning: "related" → leftOperand: "pcf:encounter". | . | provision.dataPeriod | constraint (pcf:dataPeriod) | Clinical data creation/effective period (odrl:gteq / odrl:lteq on pcf:dataPeriod). | . | provision.securityLabel[] | constraint (pcf:securityLabel) | Confidentiality / sensitivity tags (R, V, ETH, PSY, SDV, HIV, …) become odrl:eq or odrl:isAnyOf on pcf:securityLabel. | . | Nested provision.provision[] | permission / prohibition + conflict | Child provisions inherit parent period (intersected via mergePeriods). A root permit with nested deny exceptions sets conflict: "odrl:prohibit". A root deny with nested permit exceptions (e.g. dissent except for Break-Glass BTG) sets conflict: "odrl:perm". | . 2.2 The four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets . When a patient has no explicit active Consent on file (or when their explicit Consent has expired), IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 and §1:53.4.2.4 define four overarching jurisdictional baseline policies, exported in PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS and resolved by getImplicitPolicySet(uriOrAlias): . | Canonical URI (PCF_POLICY_*_URI) | Alias(es) | Constant | Semantics | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-basic-normal | "basic-normal" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BASIC_NORMAL_SET | Permit Clinical Treatment: permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA TREAT (including ETREAT, BTG, CLINTRL, POPHLTH); non-treatment purposes return deny. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-all-normal | "all-normal", "opt-out" | PCF_IMPLICIT_ALL_NORMAL_SET | Permit All Authorized (opt-out baseline): permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA PurposeOfUse. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-break-glass-only | "break-glass-only" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BREAK_GLASS_ONLY_SET | Break-Glass Only: prohibits all uses except when odrl:purpose isA BTG (medical patient-safety override). | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-deny | "deny", "opt-in" | PCF_IMPLICIT_DENY_SET | Deny All (opt-in baseline): prohibits all odrl:use until an explicit active Consent permits access. | .

4598.title: 3. Decide — Three-Valued Evaluation, ITI-108 Reads, obtainConsent, and PROV Citations
4598.content: 3.1 decide() and evaluatePcfPolicy() (permit | deny | unknown) . decide(consentOrPolicy, req, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts evaluates a PcfDecisionRequest (actor, actorRoles, actorGroups, action, and scope / top-level purpose, dateTime, target, securityLabel, dataPeriod, author, encounter): . | Active explicit Consent governs: if one or more active, non-expired Consent resources (or translated PcfOdrlSets) are supplied, any deny across them returns "deny" (odrl:prohibit), any "permit" (with no "deny") returns "permit", and unresolved scope operands return "unknown". | Missing Scope Operand is "unknown", never "permit": if a rule constrains odrl:purpose, odrl:dateTime, pcf:securityLabel, target, or assignee and the request omits that dimension, evaluation yields "unknown". Under conflict: "odrl:perm" (such as a root deny with a Break-Glass permit exception), if the exception’s constraint is unresolved, evaluatePcfPolicy() returns "unknown" rather than prematurely denying before purpose is supplied. | Expired or absent Consent: . | If options.implicitPolicy is provided, decide() falls back to the configured implicit-policy Set (IHE PCF Vol 1 §1:53.2.2 & §1:53.4.2.5). | If no implicitPolicy is configured: an expired active Consent returns "deny", and an absent or non-active Consent returns "unknown" — never a silent "permit". | . | . 3.2 Reading consents via IHE ITI-108 (findAccessConsents) . findAccessConsents(query) and Iti108ConsentClient in fhir-harness/schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts implement the IHE ITI-108 (Find Access Consent, [ITI-108]) RESTful search transaction (GET <baseUrl>/Consent) as a Consent Consumer: . | Search parameters (buildIti108SearchUrl): patient / patient.identifier, status (defaults to "active"), actor, purpose, security-label, period, date, data, _profile, and _count. | Client-side validity filtering (evaluateConsentValidity / filterIti108Bundle): every Bundle.entry.resource of type Consent is verified against FhirConsentSchema. Entries whose status !== "active", whose patient does not match the queried patient, or whose provision.period is expired (end < now) or future-dated (start > now) are excluded from consents and recorded in ignored[] with a structured Iti108IgnoredReason ("not-active", "expired", "not-yet-valid", "patient-mismatch", "invalid-period", "invalid-consent"). | Third-state failure handling (status: "unknown"): network failures, DNS errors, request timeouts, non-2xx HTTP responses, malformed JSON, non-searchset payloads, or OperationOutcome errors return { status: "unknown", reason, detail } — never an empty consents: [] that a caller could mistake for “no consent on file”. When passing an ITI-108 result into decide(), check result.status === "unknown" first and propagate "unknown". | . 3.3 Fulfilling odrl:obtainConsent duties on DSAs via injected createPcfConsentEvaluator . cat-harness/schemas/content/odrl.ts holds no FHIR resource types or pcf:* keys. A Data Sharing Agreement (@type: "Agreement") carrying an { action: "odrl:obtainConsent" } duty evaluates consent through an injected consentEvaluator: createPcfConsentEvaluator(consents, options) callback from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts, which returns { verdict, consent: { id, versionId, uid } } to permits() / permitsWithConsent() / decideWithConsent(): . | DSA + no Consent (or unreachable ITI-108 registry) → "unknown": when odrl:obtainConsent is due and no active matching PCF Consent (or consent-verification record) is provided, permits() returns "unknown". | DSA + matching deny Consent (or expired Consent) → "deny": when the patient’s PCF Consent denies the requested actor, action, purpose, or target, the decision is "deny". | DSA + matching active permit Consent → "permit": when an active, in-period PCF Consent permits the request’s actor, action, purpose, and target (and any other DSA constraints and duties hold), permits() returns "permit". | . 3.3a Consent rules for agreements . Four rules govern consent-based agreements. Rules 2 and 4 are enforced here; rules 1 and 3 are authored in the agreement itself (the dsa document kind and its lifecycle process in folio-assistant-core). | Legal basis. An agreement carries odrl:obtainConsent only when consent is its legal basis. Agreements resting on treatment, public-health law or a research waiver carry no such duty, and this evaluator is never asked. | Version pinning. A Consent names the agreement’s fixed-version URL in R4 Consent.policy.uri. createPcfConsentEvaluator counts a Consent only when that URI equals the agreement’s version (the agreement policy’s uid, or agreementPolicyUri); consentsCitingAgreement() is the filter. An amendment that widens use is a new version URL, so the old Consent no longer counts. An amendment that narrows use needs no new consent: pass the agreement’s DCAT 3 version chain as agreementVersions (each version’s ODRL policy and its dcat:previousVersion), and an older Consent still counts while every step back to its version is a narrowing amendment. isNarrowingAmendment() decides that from the ODRL rules alone: every newer permission sits inside an older one (same or narrower action, same target and assignee, each older constraint matched by one at least as tight, each older duty kept), and every older prohibition and obligation remains. A widening step, a missing version or anything it cannot compare (such as inheritFrom) stops the walk, and new consent is needed. | Plain language. Every agreement that needs consent publishes a plain-language summary, hashed with the agreement. That summary is what the person consents to. | Scale. The jurisdiction picks one of PCF’s implicit default policies (opt-in or opt-out) and passes it as implicitPolicy. Registry reads may be cached: new Iti108ConsentClient(base, defaults, { ttlMs }). An entry ends at its TTL, at the earliest provision.period.end of its Consents, or when consentWithdrawn(id) is called for one of its Consents. | . 3.4 Citing Consent.id + Consent.meta.versionId in PROV-O decision records . Every consent-based access decision recorded in the hash-chained W3C PROV-O decision log (cat-harness/schemas/content/prov.ts, cat-harness-tools/src/workflow/prov-record.ts) must cite the exact Consent resource version used: . | Use extractConsentCitation(consent) / consentPolicyUid(consent) from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts to obtain { id, versionId, uid, status, patient, performer, policyUris }. | Include the translated consent policy uid (urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId>) in "cat-harness:underPolicy" on the prov:Activity decision record alongside the governing DSA Agreement uid, and record the Consent’s id and meta.versionId citation so any auditor can verify which version of the patient’s consent directive was in force when the decision hash (cat-harness:recordHash chained via cat-harness:previousHash) was computed. | . 3.5 One-way renderer: ODRL 2.2 Agreement to FHIR R5 Permission (output only) . HL7 FHIR R5 Permission (Trial Use) is output only: W3C ODRL 2.2 is the source of truth and nothing reads Permission back. schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts provides odrlAgreementToFhirR5Permission(agreement, options) and fhirR5PermissionToFsh(permission, options): . | FhirR5PermissionSchema and its required value-set code lists are built from hl7.fhir.r5.core#5.0.0’s StructureDefinition-Permission.json and CodeSystem-*.json (permission-status, permission-rule-combining, consent-provision-type, consent-data-meaning), so no field outside FHIR R5 Permission is ever invented. | Maps conflict (prohibit / perm) to combining (deny-overrides / permit-overrides); assigner to asserter; shared dateTime constraints to validity; the agreement’s fixed-version uid and dcterms:source to justification.evidence / justification.basis; permission / prohibition to rule.type (permit / deny); target to rule.data.resource; assignee, action (consentaction), and purpose (HL7 v3-ActReason PurposeOfUse) to rule.activity; and delete duty roughly to rule.limit (v3-ActCode#DELAU). | Every ODRL 2.2, DCAT 3, or SPDX term with no exact home in FHIR R5 Permission (including @type, profile, inheritFrom, spdx:checksum, isA, exclusive lt/gt bounds, elapsedTime, refinement, and duties or duty constraints) is returned explicitly in dropped: DroppedOdrlTerm[] rather than dropped silently. | .

4599.title: pcf-consent (skill)
4599.content: The skill pcf-consent as its source file fhir-harness/skills/content/fhir-ig-authoring/pcf-consent.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

4600.title: Placement — decide where it goes before you write it
4600.content: Skill placement: Establish where a new node belongs BEFORE you create it — which layer, which declared graph, which kind of node, and which of the two “stub” conventions applies. Read before adding a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision table, schema, tool or content object, and before writing any literal that names one folio. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Code node review, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . One question, answered before the first file exists: . Which layer owns this, which of its declared graphs does it go in, and what kind of node is it? . An agent that starts writing and works the answer out afterwards produces a node in the wrong repository, under a hardcoded path, named by a composed string. All three are silent: the tests pass, and the damage lands on the next consumer. This is a decision procedure. Four steps and a stop. Run it in order; the later steps are meaningless if an earlier one is a guess.

4601.title: Step 1 — which layer?
4601.content: folio-assistant is the platform, not the content. It holds skills, schemas, the pipeline and the MCP server an agent uses to author a folio — a paper, a WHO SMART Guideline, an IG — and the folio lives in a separate repository. Ask of the thing you are about to write: . Does this name, assume, or default to one folio? . A paper directory, a document title, a badge URL, an owner/repo, a Lake library prefix, a workflow filename, a simulator path, a licence block, a vocabulary, a constant with a subject-matter value. If the answer is yes, it does not belong in platform code. There are three destinations, not two, and collapsing the third is the common mistake: . | destination | what goes there | test | . | the platform | the mechanism, parameterised | the same code is correct for every folio | . | the folio’s tree | the subject matter itself | a reader of that folio would look for it | . | the folio’s config | the value the mechanism reads | it varies per folio but platform code needs it | . A value that varies per folio and is consumed by platform code is a config field — <name>.config.json, <name>.json, lakefile.toml — never a literal in a script and never a file the platform has to go and find. A Lake prefix, for example, is read from lakefile.toml, and left unprefixed when no lakefile names one, because a wrong namespace is worse than none. Do not infer the layer from the directory you are standing in. Read the declaration at the repository root, carrying name, stub and directories. basename($PWD) is not an identity — a repo cloned into a differently-named directory resolves to nothing, and reports no config rather than an error.

4602.title: Step 2 — which declared graph, and where does that layer put it?
4602.content: A node’s location is not a path you memorise. Every layer declares the directories it scans in <name>.json, and each entry names the kind of graph it holds — cat-harness (skills, roles, workflows, decisions, requirements, permissions), schemas, tools, qa, beans, folio and the rest. The vocabulary is open. | Ask for a skill, do not open a file. skill_list for what exists here, skill_fetch to load one, work_plan_prime for the work plan. With no MCP, resolve the graph from the declaration (readDeclaration in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) and read the directory it names. | In this repository the skills graph’s path is skills/. That is a fact about this layer, not a convention you may carry to another one. Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. | Overrides match on the entry’s id, never on its path. A layer that sites its knowledge graph elsewhere redeclares the same id with a different path. Matching on path makes two knowledge graphs out of one relocation, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | Declare only what exists. A declared-but-absent directory is worse than an undeclared one: every consumer scans nothing and reports a clean run over it. | . Full rules, inheritance order and the three read states: directory-conventions.md. The docs graph, and the filing question it answers . docs is an authorable destination like the others, and the one an agent most often forgets to consider when it derives a destination list: deriving the list is not enough if the derivation drops a declared graph. What goes there: a design-memory asset — something produced while BUILDING, rather than the thing built. kg-contribution-offer carries the one question that identifies the class and why fsh-guts is the tempting wrong answer (its content may be thrown away; a design record’s value is that it survives). WHOSE docs/ comes first, and it is Step 1’s question again. Detailed information, design and planning for a harness, feature or tool go into that harness’s docs/: docs is a declared graph, and the layer that owns the feature owns the record of why it is shaped that way. A feature’s reasoning filed in the wrong layer’s docs/ reads fine and is unreachable from the place that needs it. Then where inside it, which is this skill’s question and not kg-contribution-offer’s: . | the asset is | it files under | . | why a subsystem is shaped as it is — requirements, options, rulings | <instance>/docs/architecture/, with parent: Architecture in the front matter | . | options for a decision not yet taken, with what each costs | <instance>/docs/proposals/, kind: proposal, and a row in its index.md | . | what was FOUND — prior art, a survey, a measurement, a comparison — that informs a decision without proposing one | <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/, kind: research, and a row in its index.md | . | how a person does a task with it | <instance>/docs/guides/ | . | how to REACH a data source the content describes — endpoints, shapes, quirks | <instance>/docs/, beside the subject it serves | . | what a declared thing IS, generated from source | <instance>/docs/reference/ — never hand-edited | . Three rules that catch the usual mistakes: . | A design record is dated and says what it was true OF. It is history, so it carries the commit, PR or issue it describes. A record written in the present tense becomes a claim about today, and goes stale invisibly. | It states what it could NOT establish. A requirement referenced but never defined, a measurement not taken: named as such. A design record that reads complete when it is not is worse than a short one. | It is prose for a person, not instructions for an agent. If you find yourself writing “the agent SHALL”, it is a skill and it is in the wrong graph. | . The line between the two, stated as a test: . A skill carries what a competent practitioner needs IN ORDER TO DO the task. Anything beyond that is documentation. Background, derivations, options not taken, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls: real, worth keeping, and none of it needed to act. Both directions fail silently — a skill that swallows them makes every agent read a chapter to find a rule, and a rule filed in docs/ because it arrived with context is a rule skill_fetch will never serve. Inheritance . A layer inherits its dependencies’ directories and skills, deepest dependency first and root last so the root wins: declarationChain + resolveDirectories for directories, and resolveSkillDirs in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts for the cross-layer skill overlay. So a skill placed in the platform reaches a downstream folio through its declaration; never copy a skill into the folio, which mints a second copy free to drift.

4603.title: Step 3 — which KIND of node?
4603.content: The axes below are distinct. Ask the separating question; do not pattern-match on what the thing resembles. | you are about to write | ask | the two answers | . | a new content type | does it need different code, or only different rules? | different code → an adapter; only rules → a profile plus a subclass | . | something a participant is or does | must the performer know it, or may the participant do it? | know → a skill, on the lane’s role; do → a permission, on the actor | . | a participant | does it persist across processes, or is it a position inside one? | persists → an actor; a position → a role, which is the BPMN swimlane | . | a sequence of steps | does it have actors, activities and a control flow? | yes → BPMN under the workflows directory, not a Mermaid fence and not prose | . | a branch at a gateway | is the answer computed from facts, or chosen by a person? | computed → a DMN table plus a <cat-harness.processes:decision/> ref; chosen → an ordinary gateway | . | a durable fact for one agent | does it govern, or summarise what governs? | governs → a skill; summarises → a memory entry under the memory nodes | . | subject matter | would a reader of one folio look for it? | yes → the folio, as data — never the platform | . Adapter vs profile is the expensive one. Adapters (paper, dak) partition block kinds into disjoint namespaces, and adapterForKind — what QA-criterion scoping reads — must stay total and unambiguous. Profiles (document, paper) nest: every document kind is also a paper kind. Making document a third adapter would make adapterForKind ambiguous on every shared kind. Actor / role / skill / permission. One sentence carries the model — an actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Permissions stay on the actor: moving them onto Role, which looks right, conflicts wherever a permission is held by some but not all actors sharing a role. Resolution rules, how to bind a lane, and how to add a role: role-model.md. Do not re-derive them here. A .md under the cat-harness path that declares its own $schema is not a skill. The audit walks that directory recursively; declaration beats location, the same contract part-of: carries. Adding a graph typology is a registry change, not a new top-level directory. If nothing in the open vocabulary fits, that is a decision to hand over (Step 5), not one to settle by creating a folder.

4604.title: Step 4 — which stub? There are two, and they are unrelated
4604.content: This is the step most often skipped, because “stub” reads as one word. The agent-file stub — a pointer, never a home . AGENTS.md is the agent-generic source of truth. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are thin stubs whose entire content is a pointer to it; scripts/init-folio.ts writes all three for a new folio. | Never put guidance in a stub. It reaches one tool’s agents and nobody else, and the other two stubs are then quietly wrong. | And prefer not to put it in AGENTS.md either. That file’s own banner says it: it is a bootstrap pointer, and the discipline lives in the skills graph. A rule that exists only in AGENTS.md is not in the generated reference, not in the published skill docs, and not found by an agent that went looking for the skill first. | . So: new guidance is a skill. Add a pointer from AGENTS.md if it needs one, and register the skill in its package manifest. The artefact stub — resolve it, never compose it . The declaration carries stub, the filename stem of every artefact this layer publishes. artefactStub() is the one function that answers it (stub when declared, otherwise name), and renderingPath() / siteDir() derive the published paths from it: . <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld <base>/<name>/<stub>.json <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json <base>/<stub>/ docs/<stub>/ . The graph document is under the layer’s own directory, the host’s included: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document (instance-publication §”Which base an @id is minted against”). Compose nothing; resolve everything. A hand-written path such as /kg/ 404s, because the real path comes out of renderingPath. A naive guess is not merely fragile, it is wrong on real layers. WHO’s SMART Base IG publishes under a stub shorter than its repository name, so “the stub is the repo name” fails on the reference implementation the convention was modelled on. The declaration file itself is NOT stub-named: it is <name>.json, found by findDeclarationFile() matching a file’s stem to its own name. Everything it describes is named after the stub, because by the time you fetch those you have read the declaration that names them.

4605.title: Step 5 — when you cannot tell, stop and ask
4605.content: Placement has three states, like everything else here: determined, determined-empty (this layer genuinely has no such directory — a real answer), and could-not-determine. The third is never to be rendered as the first. Do not guess and do not pick the repository you happen to be standing in. A misplaced node is not a typo: it is a second copy of something, free to drift, that a later agent will find and believe. Hand the decision over the way interaction-modality.md §4.1 requires — context → options with what each costs → your recommendation, marked → what happens if they say nothing → the question. The test is one pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . Every identifier expanded on first use. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. I need to place <thing>, which <one sentence on what it does>. Two candidates: A. <instance/graph> — costs <what this makes harder, concretely> B. <instance/graph> — costs <…> Recommend B, because <the property that decides it>. If you say nothing I will do B and note it in the PR body. A or B? .

4606.title: The worked failure this skill exists to prevent
4606.content: A platform script that writes a whole README holding one folio’s title, badges and licence destroys the README of every other folio it runs in, because prose about a folio belongs to that folio. Every step above catches it: Step 1, the content names one folio; Step 2, a helper path is composed rather than resolved; Step 4, published paths are built by convention and checked against nothing. The pattern that replaces it: the folio owns the file; the platform owns the markers, and writes a section only where the README carries its marker pair (readme-sections).

4607.title: Checklist
4607.content: Before you create a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision, schema, tool or content object: . | Layer — platform, folio, or the folio’s config? Does anything in it name one folio? | Graph — which declared entry, resolved from <name>.json by id? Not a path you remember. | Kind — which side of the separating question in Step 3, and can you say why in one sentence? | Stub — if it is guidance, is it a skill rather than a stub or AGENTS.md? If it publishes, does every path come from artefactStub() / renderingPath()? | Registered — bun run cat skill:register (skill-registration), and bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts run, so the published mirror is not stale. | Could not determine? Stop. Ask in the Step 5 frame. Do not default to the repo you are in. | .

4609.title: Process state — the task you are in, inside the process you are running
4609.content: Skill process-state: Track where you are inside a running process — which task, in which swimlane, under which role — and recover deliberately when you find yourself outside it. Read before completing a workflow step, and whenever something unexpected interrupts one. Covers what to do about notes and stickies you re-anchored while off-process, which leave no trace in the artefact. Named by: Hand back to the discussion . An agent working a BPMN process holds nested state: a task, inside a process instance, under a role that owns a swimlane. Losing track of the outer level while still acting on the inner one looks like ordinary work and produces changes nobody authorised.

4610.title: The three levels, and what each one answers
4610.content: | level | answers | where it lives | . | process instance | which run of which process is this? | beans/workflows/ (workflow-state graph in work-plan-store) | . | swimlane / role | am I the actor who may do this? | the lane on the activity; checked by the executor (task-authorization) | . | task | which step am I on, and is it enabled? | workflow_next | . workflow_next reports what is enabled now, which lane owns it, and which skill implements it. workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. Those two are the ground truth; your memory of where you were is not. Name yourself when you complete a step. Pass actor as a declared actor id, not a free-text name: workflow_complete checks that actor against the lane’s role and the ODRL policies before recording anything, refuses a role mismatch or a deny, and writes the verdict into the history. An actor you type is recorded as asserted, not authenticated. Say so rather than presenting it as identity. workflow_gate takes the same actor and target, so ask it before doing the work (task-authorization). The history is checked again afterwards. bun run cat prov:qaqc turns every instance’s history into a W3C PROV-O log and re-runs the same check on each step; claude or a login in actor, rather than a declared actor id, shows up there as undeclared-actor. It is advisory: the findings are listed on the /prov-qaqc/ page, and CI fails only when that page is stale (task-authorization §”The after-check”).

4611.title: Say which process you are in — every turn
4611.content: Claiming a work item says what you are working on. This says where in the process you are working, which is the question a reader cannot answer from an id. Name the process, the lane and the task, and say when you switch: . Process: crdm-requirements, Agent lane · Phase 6 — implement. Completed A_Implement; next is A_Summary. The engine’s “what is enabled now” call (workflow_next) reports the enabled step, the lane that owns it, and the skill that implements it. Say which permission you are acting under. Entering a task in a lane means performing it as that lane’s role, and that needs an ODRL rule that permits it there (permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts: the actor, the action, and the process, task and role as scope). If the answer is unknown or deny, you are out of process for that task: route it to a lane whose actor holds the permission, or stop and ask. The engine enforces this before the task at the deterministic end of the spectrum; at the agentic end nothing stops you, and the QA/QC report over the PROV-O record finds it afterwards (agentic-harness.html#bpmn-execution). Switching processes is the case that matters. Moving between processes changes who is accountable for the next step and which gates apply, and a reader who does not know you switched will assume the old lane’s rules still hold. Naming it is not the same as recording it (advisory) . A turn that is in a process has an INSTANCE under the declared workflow-state graph. Naming the process in prose is the report; the recorded instance in the work-plan store is the evidence. Without recorded instances, a reviewer sweeping a window of merged work cannot classify a single session by lane. workflow_start creates it, workflow_next and workflow_complete advance it, and the state lives in the work-plan store precisely so a sibling session reads the same position — workflow-state.md §”Where running instances live”. Opening or claiming a work item for a process step means starting or resuming its workflow instance: . | Claiming or starting work in a process (code-change-review, merge-train, crdm-requirements, etc.): start an instance with workflow_start passing bean: "<id>" (CLI: bun run cat workflow:start --process <process> --subject <subject> --bean <id>), or resume the running instance that already names that work item. workflow_start writes the process:<Process_Id> tag and Workflow: backlink onto the work item so the visualiser can place the work item on its current BPMN step. | Advancing through tasks: call workflow_complete (bun run cat workflow:complete --id <instance> --task <node> --actor <actor>) as each step finishes so the token moves with the work. | Closing the work item: complete the final step so the workflow instance reaches status: "completed". If a work item is closed (completed or scrapped) while its workflow instance still sits running, run bun run cat workflow:instances --sweep to close stale instances while preserving their history and PROV-O trail (cat-harness#988). | . The session-start sweep reads the work-plan store and reports “no instance recorded” as a FINDING, not as silence, when the directory holds none. A finding is not a failure — plenty of turns are legitimately outside any process — it is the prompt to say which. This rule is ADVISORY: nothing gates on it. Record the instance when the turn is in a process, but no check refuses a merge without one, and none should be added without a new ruling from the owner. It is labelled advisory because a rule called STRICT that nothing enforces teaches readers that the word is decoration, including where it is enforced. The gap is computed, never quoted, because a count written down goes stale with nothing to say so. bun run cat workflow:instances prints today’s count: instances recorded, instances started since the rule, first-parent merges in the same window, running instances whose work item is closed or missing from the store (staleInstances), in-progress work items carrying a process:<id> tag with no running instance (untrackedProcessBeans), and the CI workflows that read the graph. Merges are an upper bound on the instances owed, since a steward’s train, a docs-only fix or a revert may have none. The command reports the gap and exits 0 by default (--strict exits 1 on stale or untracked process work items; --sweep closes running instances whose work item is completed, scrapped, or missing); only a count it cannot make (store unmounted, shallow clone, an undatable instance) exits 2. Arriving without the sweep — a mid-session clone, a project thread . A session that clones a harness repository after it started has no route to this skill: . | the sweep above runs from .claude/hooks/session-start.sh, and a hook runs only when the repository is there at session start; | the workflow_* and skill_fetch tools come from the folio-assistant MCP server (.mcp.json), which starts with the session, so a mid-session clone has neither; | the repository’s CLAUDE.md reaches the agent only once the clone is registered. | . So, when you clone a harness repository after the session started: . | Register it if the platform offers that (Claude Code on the web: register_repo_root), so its CLAUDE.md and skills load. | Run the sweep by hand, from the checkout root: bash .claude/hooks/session-start.sh. It lays the mounts down and prints ## Running processes, the prompt this section depends on. | Name the process before the first edit. A code fix in a layer is sdlc/code-change-review; a repin is sdlc/upstream-version-adoption; a preview is sdlc/feature-staging. A delivery is delivery-summary plus the deep-link rule in feedback-deep-links. | With no workflow_* tools, say so. “Process X, not recorded: this session has no workflow engine” is the true third state. Never write it as recorded, and never leave it out. | . A coordinator that briefs a thread (a project’s coordinator session, a swarm lead, anything that spawns an agent) puts the process, or “none”, the governing skill and the repository in the brief. A spawned thread starts with nothing else that would tell it, and the coordinator’s own memory holds no process rules by design. When the brief is written during a live discussion with a person, it also names the discussion: who is talking with the person, how to reach them, the standing card rules, and any feedback channel in play (a review sheet’s id and tab, an issue). That is definitions.discussion of the hand-back-to-discussion input schema, and it is what lets the thread hand its cards, questions and results back instead of leaving them in its own channel.

4612.title: How to tell you are out of process
4612.content: You are outside the process if any of these is true, and each is cheap to check: . | workflow_complete refused a step you believed was next. The refusal is not an obstacle to route around — it is the detector working. | You are about to change a corpus file and cannot name the instance that authorised it. scripts/check-corpus-gate.ts refuses exactly this at the commit boundary; discovering it there is late. | workflow_next returns a step in a lane whose role you are not playing. | You cannot say which process instance you are in without looking it up — and looking it up returns nothing, or more than one candidate. | The work you are doing was not in the brief you opened the turn with. An unplanned detour is the most common way this happens, and the least likely to be noticed from inside it. | .

4613.title: Recovering
4613.content: When one of the five fires, stop making changes and recover in this order: . | Re-read the instance. work_plan_prime reports every instance’s position next to its work item. State is committed, so a sibling session’s progress is visible too. | Reconstruct from context what you were doing and which task it belongs to. You usually can: the branch name, the claimed work item, and the opening brief together pin it. | Say what you concluded, and confirm it with the user before resuming: . I completed the QA sweep but never completed Task_ReviewFindings, so the instance is still sitting before the editor decision. I believe I am in content-lifecycle instance cl-2f9, in the editor lane, at Gateway_EditorDecision. Confirm before I proceed? . This confirmation is not optional and not a formality. An agent that silently re-enters a process it inferred its way back into is asserting authorisation nobody gave it. The whole point of the swimlane guardrail is that the actor is assigned, not self-declared. The person owed the confirmation may give it in advance for a stated scope — see confirmation-waiver.md. | If you cannot reconstruct it, say so and stop. A wrong instance is worse than none: completing a step in the wrong run records an authorisation that did not happen. | .

4614.title: What you MOVED while you were out of process
4614.content: Steps 1–3 reconstruct where you were. They do not reconstruct what you changed position of, and for notes and stickies that is a separate problem with a sharper edge: . A move is not self-documenting. moveNote (schemas/ui/note-anchor.ts) returns the note with its new anchor and nothing about the old one. A note that has been moved cannot say where it was. So a sticky re-anchored during an off-process detour leaves no trace in the artefact. There is no field to read back, no diff that distinguishes “moved deliberately” from “moved by an agent that had lost the thread”, and — because a move keeps the id — nothing that even looks unusual. The only possible record is what was written to a work item at the time. Work items carry no anchor: a work item is not a thing pinned to a block, it is the record that a pinning changed. workflow/bean-link.ts has the note op that writes it. So, as part of recovery, before step 3’s confirmation: . | Name every note or sticky you re-anchored during the detour, with its anchor before and after. Read them off the work item’s note trail — not off the notes, which no longer know. | If the trail is silent and you moved things, say that. A gap is a finding. “I moved stickies and did not record where from” is recoverable by a person who remembers; “everything is fine” is not. | Do not move anything back on your own judgement. Re-anchoring to undo is another unlogged move, and it is a durable change made to cover one — see deletion-requires-confirmation.md, which is the same rule about a different verb. | . A note carries no movedFrom history. History kept in the artefact being moved is lost when the note is deleted, or moved by a tool that does not maintain the field. The work item is a separate record, which is what an audit trail has to be. Reading a bean back as the trail . A work item is a usable trail when a wrong claim is left in place, with the correction appended beside it rather than replacing it. Read back, the work item shows the premise, the disproof, and the re-scoped work in order, so an agent resuming can see that the original framing was abandoned and why, which is what it needs to avoid re-deriving the same mistake. A work item tidied to show only the correct conclusion reads as though the work had always been aimed there. That is why bean-coordination.md has unwanted work scrapped with its reasons rather than deleted: a record that shows only outcomes cannot distinguish a dead end somebody ruled out from one nobody tried.

4615.title: What not to do
4615.content: . | Do not start a fresh instance to escape a confusing one. Two instances for one piece of work is two answers to “was this authorised”, free to disagree. | Do not complete a step to “unstick” the process. Task_ReviewFindings, Gateway_EditorDecision, Task_Commit, Task_AuthorizeRelease and Task_PublishRelease are marked relaxable="false" precisely because they are the steps where skipping is most tempting and most costly. | Do not treat a refusal as a bug. workflow_complete refusing a step is the system telling you your model of where you are is wrong. | .

4616.title: Relationship to the opening brief
4616.content: The brief you open a turn with (turn-reporting.md) is what makes detector 5 usable: without a stated plan there is nothing for the current work to have diverged from. The two skills are one loop — brief the route, notice the divergence, confirm the recovery.

The edit is made on a feature branch, which may carry the edits for several comments, and recorded on each comment it answers, so a comment shows where its change is being made while it is made. | . | Change set — feature branch and staging | build-pipeline | Where the author’s edit is reviewed and lands: the feature branch’s staging preview gives before/after deep links to each comment’s anchor, the change set is reviewed as any content change, and each comment it answers is marked incorporated when it merges. | . | QA reviewer (independent) | qc-reviewer | Whoever runs the QA gate: an agent session that did not author the change set, or a person; never the author’s own session. Writes only QA gate (change set) and QA report (change set) on Agent - Change Sets. | .

4621.doc: Make a decided public comment change
4621.title: Steps
4621.content: Every one of the 4 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Edit the document as decided, on a feature branchTask_AuthorEdits | Author (human or agentic) | public-comment | public-comment edit –branch: the author (human, or an agent in the author role) edits the folio’s blocks as the decision says, on a feature branch for one change-set. Its PR says Closes #N for the change-set issue, and opening it moves that issue’s accepted comments to editing. Before its preview is staged, the author writes the change set’s Disposition (change set) on the Agent tab: one line per comment (No. 136: Accepted. …), starting from each comment’s Blue Disposition on Review Public Comments, after an optional Overall statement. Quality check: every comment number in the change set has a disposition; the sheet flags gaps and words that differ from the people’s. | . | Review the change set on its staging previewCallActivity_ChangeSet | Change set — feature branch and staging | calls Content Change and Reviewstaging-review | The content-change review of the author’s branch: its PR lists the PC refs it answers, and its staging preview is the after side of every deep link. A change the reviewers send back returns to the author inside that process. | . | QA gate: check dispositions against the people and the pull requestTask_QaGate | QA reviewer (independent) | public-comment | Before Ready for merge. Reads: the change set’s Disposition (change set), each comment’s Blue Disposition on Review Public Comments, the PR’s diff at its head commit, and the staging QA report. Checks that every comment number has one disposition; that each agrees with the people’s Blue Disposition; that each Accepted or Partially accepted comment has its change in the diff, and a Not accepted, Noted, Deferred, Duplicate or Out of scope one has none; that the diff changes nothing no disposition accounts for; and that the QA report for the staged commit has no failing gate. Writes: QA gate (change set), first line “Passed <head sha>: …” or “Failed <head sha>: <why>”, and QA report (change set), the report’s link. The sheet shows both under Staging review; a pass for an older commit reads as stale. | . | Mark incorporated when the change set mergesTask_Incorporate | Change set — feature branch and staging | public-comment | public-comment incorporate, naming the branch, PR and staging URL; done by the folio’s workflow when the PR that closes a change-set issue merges. A PR closed unmerged moves nothing. Ready for merge is set only once the QA gate has passed for the PR’s head commit; set earlier, the agent does not merge until it passes. The change set’s Dispositions blurb, as it stands when Ready for merge is set to Yes, is the summary that closes its issue. | .

4624.title: Public comment channels and intake
4624.content: Skill public-comment-channels: Set up the channels a public-comment release goes out on (an offline Excel sheet, a Google Form, a GitHub issue form, and the review sheet), each limited to the release’s fixed references, with the editor’s instructions and the announcement, and bring every channel back in through one intake path that ends in agent triage into thematic change-sets. Use when a draft is released for public comment, when a channel is added to a running review, or when returned comments arrive from any channel. Named by: Release a draft for public comment . Process: folio-assistant-core/processes/content/public-comment-release.bpmn (Process_PublicCommentRelease): Task_SetUpChannels and Task_WriteAnnouncement. Intake lands in public-comment.bpmn (Process_PublicComment): StartEvent_CommentsReturned, then Task_Ingest, Task_Triage and Task_ProposeChangeSets. Tool: folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment-channels.ts. The comment store, the importer and change-sets are the public-comment skill’s. The review sheet’s script is review-sheet-script. A public-comment release is a frozen, line-numbered draft with an id, for example “Draft for Public Comment Release v0.9” (dpi-h-pc-v0.9). Every comment cites that draft, and nothing else, so every channel offers only the release’s own references: its numbered sections, its printed pages, and its captioned tables and figures. A channel that lets a reviewer type any section number brings back comments that cannot be placed.

4625.title: 1. The release’s fixed references
4625.content: Once the release is built (Task_BuildPcRelease), make the one list every channel is generated from: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment-channels.ts refs folio/<document>/review-anchors.json \ --release <release id> --title "<release title>" --draft-url <the release's draft link> \ --out review/public-comment/release-references.json . release-references.json holds the release id and title, the sha256 of the frozen PDF and .docx, and three lists: sections as a reader cites them (“3.4.5 Governance”, “Appendix C: Glossary”), printed pages in reading order, and table and figure captions. Commit it beside the comment store. It does not change while the release is open. A new release gets a new file and new channels.

4626.title: 2. The editor sets up the channels, before anything is announced
4626.content: The editor chooses which channels the review uses, and sets every one of them up before the announcement goes out, so the instructions can link to each one. Each is generated from release-references.json. Nobody edits a list by hand. | channel | make it | what the reviewer sees | limited to the release by | . | Offline Excel sheet | … xlsx release-references.json --out <release id>-comments.xlsx | Instructions, a Comments tab (their details at the top, one row per comment), a locked References tab | drop-down lists on Section, Page and Comment type that refuse anything else; the Release row | . | Google Form | … google-form release-references.json --out CreatePublicCommentForm.gs, paste into Apps Script, run createPublicCommentForm | “About you”, then one comment per response, with Submit another response | list questions for Section and Page; the release in the title | . | GitHub issue form | … issue-form release-references.json --out .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/public-comment.yml in the folio’s repository | one issue per comment, titled [<release id>] …, labelled public-comment | drop-downs for Section, Page and Comment type; the title prefix | . | Review sheet (committee, not the public) | the review-sheet-script skill, from the release’s template | Review Public Comments and Review Change Sets | the script’s Sections, Pages and Lines links, built from the same review anchors | . Line numbers stay free text in every channel: a line range or “Table 3.1” is one field, and a list of every line would be useless. The importer resolves them against the frozen draft and reports a miss. The editor’s set-up checklist. Done in this order, and every link is recorded for the announcement: . | The release is published: the line-numbered PDF and the comment-period site (its address says it is the public comment release, not branches/, and it is kept, not deleted on merge to main). Record both links. | release-references.json is made and committed. | Each chosen channel is made from it, as above. Record each channel’s link: the Excel sheet’s download link, the Form’s published link, the issue form’s …/issues/new?template=public-comment.yml link. | The review sheet is copied from its template, its Config set for this release, and an agent is asked to watch it (skill review-sheet-script). | Each channel is tried once by someone other than the editor: one comment in, then the check below run on what came back. Delete the trial comment. | The submitter records are ready (§4). The announcement is written last. | .

4627.title: 3. The announcement (Task_WriteAnnouncement)
4627.content: A short communication for the public. It names the release, says what is asked and by when, and links to everything. Keep the process description to a few sentences and link to the published process for the rest. Subject: Public comment: <document title>, <release title> <Organisation> invites comments on <document title>, <release title>, from <open date> to <close date>. Read the draft (line-numbered PDF): <PDF link> Read it online: <comment-period site link> Comment in whichever way suits you: - Online form: <Google Form link> - Offline: download <Excel sheet link>, fill in the Comments tab, and email it to <address> - On GitHub: <issue form link> (comments there are public) Please cite the section, page and line numbers of this draft. Your email is used only to contact you about your comments. Your name is published in the acknowledgements only if you say yes. What happens next: each comment is placed on the text it is about, grouped with related comments into proposed changes, and reviewed by <committee>. The editor decides each one, with a reason. How the review works: <link to the published public-comment process>. Only the channels the editor set up are listed. The links are the ones recorded in §2. Nothing goes out until every link has been opened once.

4628.title: 4. Who submitted: the Public Comment Source tab
4628.content: Submitters are recorded in the review sheet’s Public Comment Source tab, one row per public comment. The columns are No., date received, channel, reviewer name, organisation, country / region, stakeholder type, email, and “Acknowledge by name (Yes/No)”. Every column is Grey: the tab is the external source, copied in mechanically. The tab is locked, and it is the only place a submitter’s name and email are kept (the public-comment skill, §”The live review sheet”). | Each channel asks for the details once per submission: at the top of the Excel sheet’s Comments tab, on the Form’s “About you” page, and from the GitHub login on an issue. At intake, the submission’s details are copied onto every one of its comments’ rows in Public Comment Source, with the comment’s No. and its channel. | A returning submitter is recognised by the importer’s pseudonymous id r-<hash>, which comes from the email or else the name (reviewerId in schemas/public-comment.ts). Someone who comments through two channels with the same email is therefore one reviewer. | The repository gets only that id, the organisation and the country. It gets the name only when the submitter answered Yes to “Acknowledge by name”, and never the email. The importer follows this rule (the public-comment skill, §”Privacy”). | Submitter details are not configuration, so they never go in the Config tab. That tab holds the script’s settings and is written by the agent. | .

4629.title: 5. Intake: each channel has one path back
4629.content: All four channels end in the same importer (public-comment.ts import), because each returns a table whose headers are the importer’s own. Before importing, check that every reference is in the release: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment-channels.ts check <returned file> --refs review/public-comment/release-references.json . check lists each row that cites a section or page outside the release, or whose Release row names another release, and exits non-zero. It changes nothing. A flagged row is still imported (it arrives unplaced and triage places it); the list tells the triager where to look. | channel | what comes back | command (from the folio’s repository) | . | Excel sheet | the reviewer’s .xlsx, by email | public-comment.ts import <file> --channel comment-matrix --batch <release id>-<reviewer org> | . | Google Form | the response sheet, downloaded as CSV | public-comment.ts import <responses.csv> --channel online-form --series <release id>-form | . | GitHub issues | issues titled [<release id>] | gh api 'repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues?labels=public-comment&state=all&per_page=100' --paginate > issues.json, then public-comment-channels.ts issues-csv issues.json --release <release id> --out gh.csv, then import gh.csv --series <release id>-github | . | Review sheet | committee feedback, not public comments | the sheet sync (skill public-comment, §”The live review sheet”) | . | A letter or email that used no channel | prose | public-comment.ts import-narrative <file> --reviewer … | . Re-importing is safe: a file already imported is recognised by its sha256, and a form or issue export re-downloaded later adds only the rows (No.) it has not seen, because each carries a --series. Keep the returned files in the review owner’s private store, never in the repository: they hold emails.

4630.title: 6. Triage into thematic change-sets
4630.content: After each intake batch, the intake agent proposes change-sets (Task_ProposeChangeSets, the public-comment skill, §”The agent proposes; nobody is notified”): . | public-comment-changesets.ts seed lists the comments in no change-set, bucketed by section. A bucket is a starting point, not a change-set. | The agent groups comments by theme: comments that ask for the same change, or for changes that must land together, wherever they are in the document. A cross-cutting theme (a term, consent, normative keywords) is one change-set across sections. | Each change-set gets a title, requirements (what the text must do, not the new text), and its linked public comments (refs). Record them with propose --file proposals.json. They are proposed: no issue is opened and nobody is notified. | A comment that fits no theme stays out, on the dashboard’s open, in no change-set tile, for a person to place. | . The review sheet then shows the new change-sets on its next sync, and the committee reviews them there or on GitHub.

4631.title: 7. Closing
4631.content: At the agreed close: run closePublicCommentForm in the Form’s script, and remove the issue form (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/public-comment.yml) from main, so nobody is offered a closed release. The kept release site and PDF are not touched. Do a last intake from every channel. A comment that arrives after the close is imported like any other, and the editor decides whether it is considered.

4632.title: What not to do
4632.content: . | Do not type a list of sections into a form by hand, or edit the generated questions or headers: they are the importer’s column headers, and a renamed question is a column the importer cannot read. Regenerate instead. | Do not reuse one release’s channels for the next release. Its references are different. | Do not announce a channel before it has been tried once and check passed. | Do not put an email, or a name without consent, in the repository, an issue body the agent writes, or the Config tab. | .

4639.title: public-comment
4639.content: Named by: Draft, review and publish, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, DTH authoring . Skill id: public-comment · Package: folio-document-adapter · Process: folio-assistant-core/processes/content/public-comment.bpmn (Process_PublicComment), which calls its change phase public-comment-change.bpmn (Process_PublicCommentChange) · Tool: folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment.ts · Schema: folio-assistant-core/schemas/public-comment.ts. Run a public review of a document folio. A frozen, line-numbered draft goes out. Comments come back as spreadsheets, form exports, letters and GitHub comments.
