4966.title: Adding a skill
4966.content: Skill skill-registration: Adding a skill is never a one-file change. What a new skill file owes, the one command that performs the derived half, the one declaration it deliberately leaves to you, why running it once is not enough, and the two orphan directions it reports rather than fixes. Read this before adding, renaming or removing a skill. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . One command, before you commit: . bun run cat skill:register . It generates everything derived from the skill and verifies each artefact landed. bun run cat skill:register:check is the same question without writing, and it is a gate — a skill that arrives undeclared fails CI. skill:register, singular. If you find skills:register in older text, it means this.

4967.title: What a skill file owes, and why you cannot see it
4967.content: Three things nothing derives for you, and none of them is in the file you just wrote: . | artefact | where | produced by | . | a skills entry | the package’s package-manifest.json | you — see below | . | a published reference page | the site’s reference/skill-instructions/<name> | skills:docs | . | a kg-qa sidecar | test/results/kg-qa/skills/<pkg>/<name>.kg-qa.json — the working copy | kg:audit | . The kg-qa sidecar is a derived QA result, and its record is not the committed file. The CI job qa-publish stores every run’s test/results/ on the orphan qa-reports branch under main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/. The file is also committed on main and kg:audit:check reads it, so skill:register writes it — but a judgement about your skill (an agent’s voice review, a pair attestation) does not go in it: that is test/attestations/kg-qa/…, on main, because no writer can regenerate it. Then a cascade: the schema reference, the glossary and its SKOS export, the auto-docs index and the detangle measurements all read something that just changed. The reason this needs a skill at all is that the feedback arrives somewhere else. CI judges the merge of each pull request’s head into the base, so an undeclared skill on main fails the gate set on every open pull request — and the author who sees the failure is whoever opens the next one.

4968.title: The manifest entry is yours, on purpose
4968.content: skill:register will not add it. Which package a file belongs to is your assertion, not a derivable fact, and a command that guessed it would register files somebody was still drafting. The command names the file and the remedy; you add the slug, sorted. Everything else it either performs (the derived artefacts, and stripping a retired key — see below) or reports and leaves alone. One exception to “commit what it writes”: skill:commands, one of its steps, writes .claude/commands/ in a composed checkout. That directory is a projection CI writes (harness-projections), so leave its changes unstaged and let the workflow commit them.

4969.title: A new folder is a named subgraph of its harness — declare it
4969.content: If what you are adding needs a new folder, decide first which of three kinds of folder it is. Each has exactly one way to be declared, and the place the folder sits decides which: . | A folder directly under the harness root (a new code area, a new graph): an entry in the harness’s own declaration (<harness>.json, e.g. cat-harness.json), under directories, with an id, the path, its graphTypologies and a one-line description. | A folder inside a folder the harness already declares: declared from within, in that directory’s own <dir>.json (as skills/skills.json declares voices). This is not a matter of taste: check:layout-norms fails a new top-level entry whose path lies inside another declared directory (the pairs it only lists are a baseline). Add subgraph: true when the new folder is a subgraph of the LAYER rather than a part of its parent’s graph (voices is the first kind, beans.json’s defs the second). | A folder that holds ONE node — one Tool, one voice: it is not declared. It sits inside the declared graph that owns the node and is found through that graph’s reader, as each voice folder is found by its voice.json. Never declare one Tool’s folder as a tools directory: discovery refuses a harness that declares two tools directories. The Tool’s folder is found by the loader (toolsFromFolders, in the tools layer), as each voice is by its voice.json. | . Both declared forms say what a folder holds the same way, by its graphTypologies: a from-within entry names its own kind (voices.json declares vendors as voice-vendors), it does not inherit its parent’s. One folder per Tool, always. A Tool is declared in tools/<id>/<id>.json ("$schema": "tool-definition/v1") inside the harness’s declared tools directory: the folder, the file stem and the Tool’s id are one string, and the folder also holds whatever is that Tool’s alone (its script, fixtures, tests). toolsFromFolders refuses a folder that breaks the convention. The tools/ directory is data only; the loader and shared helpers live in the tools layer. The JSON-LD of each Tool (<doc dir>/tools/<id>.jsonld, its own IRI) and the JSON Schema of each I/O type are written when the site is published, never committed. Why declaring is part of the process, not tidying: . | A folder nothing declares is a folder nothing reasons about. No check catches it for you: check:undeclared-files sweeps the repository root only, so a new undeclared folder inside a harness passes it. | Declared directories are what can be mounted and exported. A remote mount lays down declared directories only, so an undeclared code folder is missing downstream. A harness’s package exports are derived from its declared, shipped code directories (check:package-exports), so an undeclared one cannot be imported by package name either. A from-within id can be mounted on its own (remote-mount resolves it through instanceDirectories). | bun run cat harness:dirs then materialises every declared directory, so the folder exists in every checkout rather than only in yours. | .

4970.title: Why one pass is not enough
4970.content: skill:register runs each writer and then re-runs every :check on its own to assert the artefact landed. That second pass is the point: a writer can exit 0 over an artefact it failed to update, and only the :check form catches it. Do not re-derive the chain through bun run cat gates. bun test runs the detangle and kg-audit writers, so by the time those checks execute the artefacts are already repaired. A chain measured through gates comes out two steps short, and both omissions look correct. Do not recall the list from memory: recall goes wrong in both directions, naming steps that adding a skill does not stale and omitting ones it does. Each step in the command was measured red-then-green in isolation. Add one only with the same experiment, and put the measurement in the docblock. One pairing is worth knowing because it reads like a typo and is not: glossary:page is verified by check:glossary, which is that same script with --check. glossary:check is a different program over the SKOS projection. Do not “fix” the pairing to make every check end in :check.

4971.title: Do not re-add roles:
4971.content: roles: is retired front matter: nothing reads it, and the actor ids it named do not exist. Copying an adjacent skill’s front matter brings it back, so skill:register strips it and tells you it did — safe to perform automatically, since a retired key carries no author intent to guess at. A field saying who performs a skill must be declared in the schema before it is written.

4972.title: Removing or renaming a skill: two orphans, and they are yours
4972.content: skill:register reports these and does not fix them. That is deliberate, not an omission. | A manifest entry with no file. kg:audit calls this manifest-skill-exists at severity critical. Pruning it automatically would decide, on your behalf, that nothing referenced the name — and KNOWN_DANGLING in skill-manifest-coverage.test.ts is empty on purpose “so a future entry is added here consciously, with the reason, instead of the check being loosened”. | A derived artefact whose subject is gone. kg:audit reports SUBJECT GONE and refuses to delete it. That is deletion-requires-confirmation: an agent never removes a durable artefact on its own initiative. No amount of regenerating settles it, which is why the command reports the check as still red rather than looping. | .

4973.title: What this does not decide
4973.content: Whether a skill should exist, what it should say, or which package it belongs in. This is about the declarations a skill owes once you have decided to add it. For where a new thing goes at all, start at where-does-this-go.

4975.title: Skill voice review
4975.content: Skill skill-voice-review: Reviews a skill against a voice that judges skills — the base agent-skill-authoring voice or a vendor override such as Claude’s, Gemini CLI’s or OpenAI’s — rule by rule, with each rule’s citation open, and records the verdicts with voice:review. Use when skill-voice-review-current reports a skill never reviewed or reviewed before the skill or the voice changed, or when asked whether a skill follows a vendor’s authoring guidance. The agent half of that axis; the mechanical half, in scripts/skill-voice-review.ts, only says whether a current review exists. Named by: Code node review .

4976.title: What this axis is, and what it deliberately is not
4976.content: A voice whose rules declare appliesTo: ["skill"] judges skill files. In agent-skills that is the shared base agent-skill-authoring and one override per vendor under skills/voices/vendors/ (vendors/vendors.json lists them), each extending the base. A voice counts only once the harness config activates it (voice.active in its index.config.json entry) — the same switch every other voice uses. The boundary: an agentic review, with no formal gate on rule content. “Best practice” drifts, and a vendor describing its own product is an assertion, not evidence. So: . | the criterion skill-voice-review-current (minor, gated by nothing) asks only whether a review exists for the skill and voice as they are now; | a rule you judge fail is recorded in the skill’s attestation file and printed — it is not a finding, and it must not be turned into one here. | .

4977.title: Reviewing one skill against one voice
4977.content: . | Print the rules you are judging, resolved through extends: . bun run cat voice:review -- --rules agent-skill-authoring-claude . A vendor voice lists its own rules and the base’s, because an inherited rule keeps the scope it was declared under. | Open each rule’s citation before judging it. Every rule carries the library entry, page and quote it was read from. Uphold a verdict from the source, never from the one-line title: the title is a summary, and the rule is what the quote says. | Judge the skill as the platform would load it — the front matter the router sees, the body, and the files the body points to. One verdict per rule: . | verdict | when | note | . | pass | the skill does what the rule asks | optional | . | fail | it does not | required — what is missing, where | . | n/a | the rule cannot apply to this skill (a scripts rule, and the skill has no scripts) | required — why not | . n/a is not a softer fail. If the rule could apply and the skill does not meet it, that is a fail with a note. | Record it — the writer refuses a set that misses a rule, judges one twice, or leaves a fail/n/a unexplained: . bun run cat voice:review -- --sidecar <instance>/test/results/kg-qa/<skill path>.json \ --voice agent-skill-authoring-claude --by agent --verdicts verdicts.json . verdicts.json is [{ "rule": "<id>", "result": "pass"|"fail"|"n/a", "note": "…" }]. The review pins the skill’s content hash and the hash of the voice’s skill rules, and replaces any earlier review of that skill against that voice. --sidecar names the subject, not where the review is written. A voice review is a judgement, so it is kept as voice_reviews in the skill’s attestation file, <instance>/test/attestations/kg-qa/<skill path>.attestations.json (qa-attestations/v1), on main — not in the derived kg-qa sidecar, whose record is on the qa-reports branch. Commit the attestation file. A store that cannot be read is UNKNOWN and the writer refuses rather than overwriting it. | Run bun run cat kg:audit so the sidecar’s criterion reads the new review from the store. | .

4978.title: When the criterion reports stale
4978.content: A review goes stale when the skill changes or the voice’s skill rules change. The earlier review is kept, not deleted — it is evidence of what was checked — and the finding stays until a new review replaces it. Re-review the whole voice rather than patching the one rule you suspect moved: a changed skill can break a rule nobody was looking at.

4979.title: Fixing what you found
4979.content: A fail verdict is information for whoever owns the skill. Editing the skill is a separate change with its own review. Do not edit a skill to make your own verdict pass in the same step: record the verdict first, change the skill, then review again — so the sidecar shows both states.

4981.title: Skills and Tools — the skill says what, the Tool says how
4981.content: Skill skills-and-tools: A skill states a capability generically; a Tool node carries the concrete mechanism. Read before writing or editing any skill, and whenever a skill is about to name a vendor, a CLI, a binary or an API endpoint. Named by: Code node review . A skill is a capability stated generically. A Tool content node is one concrete way to exercise it. One skill may be satisfied by several Tools; a Tool names the skills it satisfies through its satisfies field. This is the standard operating procedure for every skill in the harness, not a guideline for new ones. A skill that names GitHub, names the beans binary, or embeds a shell invocation has swallowed a Tool, and the swallowing is what makes a layer un-portable. Schema for the Tool node: schemas/tools/tool.ts in the tools layer; carrier convention (Zod authoritative, JSON-LD and JSON Schema generated) in directory-conventions §”What lives in the schemas graph”.

4982.title: The test, in one line
4982.content: Would this sentence still be true on a different forge, a different binary, a different machine? If yes it is skill. If no it is Tool. Applied: . | sentence | verdict | . | “Open a change proposal as soon as there is one commit to hang it on.” | skill — true anywhere | . | “gh pr create”, or the REST call it wraps | Tool — one forge, one transport | . | “Claim the item before you work, so a sibling session does not pick it up.” | skill | . | “beans update <id> --status in-progress” | Tool | . | “If the CLI is unavailable, the store is still writable by hand.” | skill — the fact is portable | . | “Edit the status: line in the front matter of beans/defs/<id>--*.md.” | Tool | . That last pair is the one people get wrong. Having a fallback is a property of the capability; performing the fallback is a mechanism. The skill must say a fallback exists and when to reach for it, because an agent that does not know one exists will stop. What it must not do is spell out the edit. When the mechanism is itself a procedure, it is the Tool’s subprocess (§”A Tool may describe its own subprocess”). The Tool node names the BPMN in subprocesses (process ids, checked by check:tools), conventionally under processes/tools/; the skill keeps the portable sentence. See bpmn-processes.

4983.title: Every bean skill has (at least) two Tools
4983.content: The work-plan skills are the worked example: . | Tool | when | . | beans CLI | normal case — installed via scripts/install-beans.sh | . | hand edit / scripts/beans-fallback.ts | CLI absent or cannot be installed here | . Both satisfy the same skills. Neither is the skill. A fresh container has no beans on PATH, so an agent that only knows the CLI reads the plan and touches nothing. The fallback is a second Tool with equal standing, and the skill must present it that way. An external project is a candidate Tool before it is anything else. When somebody asks whether another project could do a skill’s job — Beads for the work plan, say — that survey is research, not a proposal and not a skill edit: it files under <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/ per placement, dated, with each project’s health measured rather than recalled (for example research-and-analysis/prior-art.md). Only if a candidate is adopted does it become a Tool node, with the selection its derived alternatives call for, below.

4984.title: Substitutable Tools are derived, and each says how to choose
4984.content: A pair like that is substitutable: same job, different mechanism, pick one. Nobody declares it. Two Tools are alternatives when they satisfy a common skill AND have the same I/O signature — the same input names, types and required flags, the same outputs, the same renders and maintains (deriveAlternatives in schemas/tools/tool.ts). A shared skill alone is not enough: most skills with several Tools have complementary ones, steps rather than choices, and their I/O is what tells them apart. So the discipline moves to the ports. Type and name a port for what it really takes and gives. A CSV reader and a workbook reader typed Text would derive as alternatives; DelimitedTextPath and WorkbookPath keep them apart. Two generators whose output is a bare pages would too; naming each output for what it writes does not. Each Tool with a derived alternative then carries selection — three fields, all required together (check-tools fails one without it): . | field | answers | . | when | the case this Tool is the right answer to | . | limits | where it stops, and which sibling picks up | . | cost | what having it available costs | . Do not skip limits: without it an agent reaches for the tool and discovers the boundary by failing. State it even when it is “none”, for the same reason install.none exists — so “no limits” is distinguishable from an unfinished record. cost is not install. install says how to obtain the tool; cost says what having it costs — CI minutes, a wheel needing a C toolchain, a network round trip. Two Tools can be equally easy to install and very differently expensive to keep. Not in description. It is projected verbatim as the MCP tool description and into the exported graph, and answers “what does this do”; comparative prose about cost does not belong there, because it would degrade the surface an agent reads when choosing among tools. Sharing a skill does NOT make two Tools alternatives . Most skills with several Tools have complementary ones: workflow-list, -start, -next, -gate and -complete are five steps of process-state, not five ways to perform it. Only Tools that also share an I/O signature are alternatives, and scripts/check-tools.ts checks that the relation is mutual, because a one-sided one means an agent arriving at the silent end never learns a choice exists. Keying substitutability on a shared skill alone would demand comparative prose where there is nothing to compare, and an author obliged to write it writes noise. The worked pair: stdlib vs extensions . ingest-stdlib and ingest-extended both satisfy library-ingestion, and the split falls where the dependency boundary actually is rather than on principle: . |   | ingest-stdlib | ingest-extended | . | install | nothing (install.none) | PyMuPDF, pypdf + Pillow, tesseract | . | covers | archives, CSV/spreadsheets, technical metadata, content routing | PDF outline, page text, OCR, images | . | runs in CI here | yes | no — CI installs ruff and nothing else | . Reading a zip’s central directory, sniffing magic bytes and parsing an xlsx’s XML are all in the Python standard library; rendering a PDF’s text layer is not and never will be. An agent picks by what the machine has, not by what the document is — and the stdlib arm refuses a PDF outright rather than half-ingesting one, so the choice is never made silently. This is also the shape to reach for whenever a capability has a heavyweight backend: two Tools, one skill, the dependency posture legible on each node, instead of a repository-wide yes/no that no reader of a skill can see.

4985.title: The harness assumes no MCP — and knows how to emit one
4985.content: agentic-harness must work with no MCP server running. Everything it needs is files in directories the layer declares: skills in the kg graph, Tool nodes beside them, the work plan in the beans graph. An agent with nothing but a filesystem and <name>.json can read all of it. MCP is acknowledged as a future transport, not assumed as the present one. Where a downstream layer runs a server, skill_list / skill_fetch / work_plan_prime are a convenience over the same files — and ToolDefinition accordingly declares invoke.mcp as one optional arm beside shell and container. A Tool whose only invocation is an MCP call is not usable by the harness that defines it. Editing a skill goes through skill_update, not a raw file write. Where the server runs, it is the write side of skill_fetch. It refuses unless every gate passes: . | the skill resolves as skill_fetch serves it; | the file is tracked in this repository, so not another layer’s skill and not a mounted copy; | the file is not generated; | a policy grants skill-update to the actor (no default policy does); | the file is unchanged since it was read; | the front matter parses and keeps the skill’s name; | every link the edit adds resolves. | . A gate that cannot decide refuses. The Tool writes the working tree, and the caller commits the change. That is a statement about dependency, not about ignorance. MCP is an output of this harness: mcp-projection is how an agent takes a Tool node describing a CLI and produces a working MCP service from it, mcp-assembly covers composing several into one namespace, and mcp-contract checks the result still matches its sources. The harness is the thing that knows the mapping; it just does not need the result in order to run. It is what makes the harness bootstrappable: the layer that defines what a Tool is cannot require a tool server to read its own definitions without arguing in a circle. It is also why sovereign-compute and air-gapped operation are reachable later without a second design — a layer with no server loses a transport, not a capability. So when this skill says “reach a Tool through the graph”, the floor is: read <name>.json, find the kg entry, open the directory. Anything richer is an optimisation a layer may offer.

4986.title: GitHub is a Tool node, not a layer
4986.content: The PR-choreography skills — prepare-merge-auto, pickup, watch, coordinate — assume a forge, but most of their text is portable: “pull request”, “PR”, “GitHub” as a noun. Only a few lines are concrete invocations. So forge-specificity is isolated at the Tool layer: the skills stay in the harness, stated generically, and Tool nodes carry the invocations — one per forge operation (table below). Adding another forge is more Tool nodes satisfying the same skills, not a repository or a fork. The forge operations, one Tool node each . One Tool node per forge operation, using the fields Tools already have. A skill names the operation in neutral words, and this table is where an operation meets its nodes. An agent picks the node for the forge the checkout’s remote is on; each pair is a derived alternative carrying selection (check:tools holds it). These Tool nodes sit in the opt-in integrations sub-graph (integrations/tools/): a layer that uses them lists cat-harness.integrations in its enableSubgraphs. | operation (as a skill names it) | GitHub | GitLab | . | list change proposals | github-pr-list | gitlab-mr-list | . | read change proposal (body, comments, reviews) | github-pr-view | gitlab-mr-view | . | read change proposal (check runs) | github-pr-checks | — | . | list changed files | github-pr-files | gitlab-mr-files | . | comment on change proposal | github-pr-comment | gitlab-mr-comment | . | request review | github-pr-request-review | gitlab-mr-request-review | . | resolve review thread | github-pr-resolve-thread | gitlab-mr-resolve-thread | . | list branches | github-branches | gitlab-branches | . A dash is a known gap. Two GitLab nodes run a script rather than glab directly: glab mr diff has no --name-only, so gitlab-mr-files reads the paths out of the raw diff; and glab mr update --reviewer NAME replaces the reviewers, so gitlab-mr-request-review passes +NAME, which adds one. Its names are GitLabUsernames, since GitLab usernames do not fit Login. Branches alone are also listable with git ls-remote --heads origin, which needs no forge. Subscribing to a change proposal’s activity is not a forge operation. It is the session platform’s (in a Claude Code remote session, its PR-activity subscription), so no forge Tool node offers it, and a skill says so rather than naming a forge for it. A Tool may describe its own subprocess . When one mechanism takes several steps, they belong to the Tool, not to the general skill: the Tool lists subprocesses (process ids, each the stem of a .bpmn the checkout declares), and a general diagram’s call activity is bound by it. General skills name the Tool, never its steps. Example: render-kg-to-cdn is the general step (render a Knowledge Graph for a CDN at a publication root URL; output a status and a message), and gh-pages is one Tool for it whose subprocess is bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn — declared below the harness, so the reference points down. Vocabulary — name the concept, not the vendor’s word for it . GitHub calls it a pull request; GitLab calls it a merge request; Gerrit calls it a change. A skill that says “pull request” has picked one vendor’s noun, which is a milder form of the same defect. Prefer the neutral term on first use and the local term thereafter, rather than scrubbing every occurrence — a skill written entirely in invented vocabulary is unreadable, and unreadable is worse than mildly GitHub-flavoured. The rule is that an agent must never have to resolve a vendor noun to act: it is fine for a skill to say “pull request (PR)” once and use PR after it; it is not fine for the only statement of what to do to be gh pr create.

4987.title: Writing or editing a skill — the checklist
4987.content: . | Grep your own draft for vendor names, binaries, endpoints, file paths under a tool’s control, and flag characters. Each hit is a Tool that has not been declared. | State the capability first, in a sentence that survives the mechanism being replaced. 2b. If an input reaches a command line, give it a type that cannot be a payload — and put free prose on stdin. See untrusted-input; check:tools fails CI on a violation. | Say a mechanism exists and where to find it — never inline it. A Tool is reached the same way a skill is: resolve the kg graph from the layer’s declaration and read from the directory it names. Not a remembered path, and — see below — not necessarily a tool call. | Say when each Tool applies if there is more than one, because choosing between them is judgement and judgement is skill. | Name what happens when no Tool is available. Three states, as everywhere here: the Tool worked, the Tool is absent and here is the fallback, and we could not tell — which is never rendered as success. | .

4988.title: The Tool schema, and the remaining debt
4988.content: schemas/tools/tool.ts (in the tools layer) defines a Tool, tools/ holds the nodes, and bun run cat check:tools fails when a satisfies names a skill that does not exist. ToolInput.repeated marks a list input (rather than a list type per scalar type, which would multiply the shared $defs and break the identity property the shared vocabulary exists for). invoke.inProcess names a TypeScript function for a Tool with no shell equivalent; it is runnable by the harness directly, and is the projection source rather than something to proxy, so the refusal of an mcp-only Tool does not reach it. Many skills still carry their invocations inline. Most of the remainder is fine — a great many skills are pure judgement (interaction-modality, one-voice-style-guide) and have no mechanism to name. check:tools reports the coverage count rather than failing on it, for exactly that reason. What it cannot tell you, and what needs a human eye, is which of the uncovered skills describe an action — those are the ones whose mechanism is still swallowed. A satisfies edge is checkable against the skill’s own contract . satisfies is the one part of a Tool node a schema cannot check, and it was being written on judgement alone. bun run cat check:tools compares a Tool’s io against the input contract of every skill it claims — the contract the skill names in its own front matter (input:), never one found by directory name. Two rules: every required property of the contract must appear as an input on the Tool, and where a Tool input and a contract property share a name, their JSON types must agree (an integer port may serve a number property). If either fails, the Tool cannot exercise the skill and the edge is false. What is compared, and what is not. A skill’s contract is free-form JSON Schema; a Tool’s io is named ports referencing shared $defs IRIs, so they meet only at names and at the JSON type each port’s vocabulary type projects to. The type rule is weak — nearly every contract property here is a bare {"type": "string"} — but not vacuous: it catches an array contract served by a string port, which the name rule passes. A mismatch that is “only” a naming difference — path against targetPath — is a finding, not a false positive to suppress. Two names for one input, across a skill and the Tool claiming to implement it, means an agent reading the contract cannot call the Tool. Three states, as everywhere. No contract (the common case, not a defect) is undefined; a contract requiring nothing is [] and passes; a contract that is declared but missing or unparseable is reported and fails, never counted as agreement. An external https:// contract is not fetched by this offline check. For example, a Tool that validates a .po against its .pot does not satisfy content-validate, whose contract requires targetPath: validating translations is not validating a folio’s content. Which uncovered skills actually need one — bun run cat tools:coverage . The count alone does not say which. A grep for shell blocks over-reports, because a skill may legitimately QUOTE a command while stating its capability generically. The corpus carries a better signal — BPMN task type. A process step is a serviceTask (runs without a person) or a userTask (performed by one), and the diagrams already say which. Triaged on that, plus an I/O contract under schemas/skills/, the tiers are A (automation evidence), B (userTask-only), C (ambiguous) and D (nothing), and only C needs a human read. Run it for the numbers; do not quote them from prose: a count in prose is a claim that nothing re-checks, and it drifts unnoticed. Many skills are both: two activities name interaction-modality, a serviceTask that reads the preferences file — a mechanism — and a userTask about how to frame a question — judgement. The question is not “is this skill a Tool?” but “which PART of it is.” . A skill with both halves is not mis-modelled. Migrating it is a split: the mechanical half becomes a Tool, the judgement half stays as prose. Expecting a clean move makes the migration look bigger than it is. So when you write or edit a skill: follow the checklist above and reference a Tool. When you read one that inlines gh pr create or beans update, that is the debt, not the pattern — do not propagate it. Authoring a Tool node: tools/<id>/<id>.json, one folder per Tool, a "$schema": "tool-definition/v1" document validated against the Tool schema; the loader lives in the tools layer. io ports reference the shared vocabulary in schemas/tools/tool-types.ts by its type name ("$type") — never a free-form string, because a reference nothing checks is eventually wrong. For the end-to-end guide on authoring, implementing, packaging, and registering concrete tools across separated repositories, see tool-authoring. For runtime conventions, test preloading, and TypeScript configuration, see bun-use.

4989.title: Covered is not reachable — see its own skill
4989.content: A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism itself is reachable from nothing, and check:tools reports it as covered and is right to. That discipline, the two questions it keeps apart, what to do when you meet one, and the two reasons not to write maintains: covered-is-not-reachable.

4991.doc: Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file
4991.title: Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file
4991.content: Process_SliceSqlitePublish · strict · 7 step(s) . Build one named slice of a knowledge graph as a SQLite file a browser mounts without parsing, and publish it beside its manifest and its payloads. The contract is kg-export §”Per-slice SQLite”; the builder is the slice-sqlite Tool (cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-slice-sqlite.ts), one table-driven builder with one definition per slice; the search is one page, slices/search.html?slice=<name>. THE SIZE IS MEASURED BEFORE THE SLICE IS WIRED. A slice that is wired first and measured afterwards ships whatever it weighs, because by then a manifest, a gate, two deploy steps and a page depend on it. The budget gateway sits between measuring and wiring so that an oversized slice stops with its measurement reported, rather than arriving on a reader’s connection. NO BINARY IS COMMITTED. The file is built at deploy from the tree being published, so the gate cannot compare against a committed copy; it proves determinism (two builds, one sha256) and a row-content digest read back from the file against one computed from the source. i i i i i i i

4994.title: Steps
4994.content: Every one of the 7 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Write the slice definitionA_Define | Platform authoring agent | kg-export | Add one SliceDef to the builder’s slice table: the DDL (one table per node type, edge tables, one CONTENTLESS full-detail FTS5), the order each table’s rows go in, the load that turns the source into rows, where the payloads live (written at deploy, or already published), and the search block the generic page reads. Never copy the builder. | . | Build it locally and measure the fileA_Measure | Platform authoring agent | kg-export | Run bun run cat slice:sqlite -- --slice <name> --out <scratch> and read the manifest: bytes, the row counts, the payload count and bytes, overBudget, duplicateIds and findings. Record the measurement in the work context with its provenance (the command and the date), beside the size of the source it replaces. | . | Report the measurement; ship nothingA_Report | Platform authoring agent | kg-export | Write the measurement and what was tried into the work context, and ask the owner whether the slice should ship at that size, be cut further, or not exist. Nothing is wired: no manifest is published, no gate added, no deploy line written. | . | Wire it: gate, deploy line, search, testsA_Wire | Platform authoring agent | kg-export | Give the slice everything a slice owes: its manifest (written by the builder from the definition), its --check (covered by slice:sqlite:check), one deploy line in docs-site.yml and in feature-staging.yml, its search (the generic page needs no code, only the definition’s search block), a unit test over a fixture and over the real source, and a search in slice-sqlite.e2e.ts. | . | Gate every slice: slice:sqlite:checkA_Check | CI/CD Pipeline | kg-export | For every slice: build twice and require one sha256; read the row digest back from the file and require it to equal the digest computed from the source without SQLite; run an FTS5 phrase query for a known row; and audit the payloads with auditPayloadTree (deploy payloads as written, the kg slice’s pointers against the committed payload tree). A slice whose rows do not match its source fails; it never passes as whole. | . | Build each slice into _site at deployA_Deploy | CI/CD Pipeline | kg-export | gen-slice-sqlite.ts --out ./_site/assets/slices --payload-out ./_site/payload/sha256 --slice <name>, once per slice, from the tree being published: the file, its manifest, the slice index, and the deploy payloads beside the committed KG payloads. Never into the committed docs/payload/, whose orphan audit admits KG nodes only. | . | Search the published slice in a browserA_Verify | Platform authoring agent | rendered-verification | Open slices/search.html?slice=<name> on the deployed site, run a phrase search for a known row, open it so its payload is fetched, and look at the result; send the screenshot rather than a description of it. Report the mode the page says it used (OPFS or in memory), never an assumed one. | .

The no-body variant (nodes, edges and an FTS over names, titles and summaries, bodies as payload pointers) is the first thing to try before reporting. | yes — under → Wire it: gate, deploy line, search, testsno — over → Report the measurement; ship nothing | . | Every slice green?GW_Green | Answered by the exit code of slice:sqlite:check, one line per slice. 4997.title: smart-base Toolchain
4997.content: Named by: SMART Guideline end to end . Skill id: smart-base-tools · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines . Run WHO’s DAK toolchain from a smart-base checkout. Load it; never vendor it. smart-base/tools/ holds Tool nodes: declarations of what each upstream capability consumes, produces and satisfies, so a BPMN activity can bind it. A Tool node duplicates no code. The Python stays in WorldHealthOrganization/smart-base, which the DAK repositories’ GitHub Actions run in place; a copy here would be a second, drifting toolchain. Declare here, execute upstream, until the execution moves as one migration with a cutover (toolchain-ownership). strip_library_binaries.py and strip_library_content.py are not declared here: they are not DAK-shaped and belong to fhir-harness (smart-stack-layering).

4998.title: Before you start
4998.content: export SMART_BASE_HOME=/path/to/smart-base # default: /opt/smart-base python3 smart-base/scripts/smart-base-transform.py --check . --check exits non-zero and names what is missing. Without a checkout the skill degrades to skip — it does not report a clean run over a toolchain it never had.

4999.title: Transforms
4999.content: Both render an authored source artefact into a published representation (the extractors go the other way). # BPMN → FHIR Shorthand python3 smart-base/scripts/smart-base-transform.py bpmn2fsh <file.bpmn|dir> -o OUTDIR # DMN → HTML python3 smart-base/scripts/smart-base-transform.py dmn2html <file.dmn|dir> -o OUTDIR . Omit -o for a dry run that reports counts and writes nothing.

5000.title: Two things to expect
5000.content: bpmn2fhirfsh.xsl emits many files per input. Its output is an envelope, <files><file name="…">…</file>…</files>, and each entry is a separate artefact at the path the transform names. Measured on smart-dak-immz: 8 business processes → 313 files, one process alone accounting for 157. Paths collide across inputs. Those 313 land at only 201 distinct paths, because shared actors and near-duplicate processes name the same outputs. The runner counts and names every collision on stderr instead of overwriting silently. Decide for each whether it is a duplicate input to remove or two processes that legitimately contribute the same actor.

5001.title: What else is in there
5001.content: smart-base carries ~54 Python scripts: extractors (dd_extractor, dt_extractor, req_extractor, extractpr), generators (generate_jsonld_vocabularies, generate_*_schemas, dmn_questionnaire_generator), a translation subsystem, and IG build/CI orchestration. The two transforms above are wrapped, and extract_dak.py (which runs dd_extractor, req_extractor and dt_extractor) is declared as the Tool extract-dak. The IG build and CI scripts want no skill: GitHub Actions is their caller.

5002.title: Adapting a DAK: use the toolchain the upstream used
5002.content: An adaptation changes the upstream’s components, so it produces them the way the upstream produced them. Before writing any converter, generator, checker or test runner, find that way, in this order, and record it in the stage-3 or stage-5 dependency row of smart-guideline-end-to-end (toolchain): . | The tools graph. bun run cat check:tools from the layer root lists every Tool the mounted layers declare (smart-base, fhir-harness, folio-assistant-core, cat-harness), with the skills each satisfies. | The upstream repository’s own toolchain. Read the dependency’s repository, not only its published IG. For the WHO immunizations DAK (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-immunizations), what it uses: . | component | upstream source | how it is produced | . | decision-support logic | input/decision-logic/IMMZ DAK_decision-support logic.xlsx, DAK template | the repository’s own tools/node/processDTInput.js, processDTOutput.js, processDTCheck.js (node-xlsx → CQL, FSH); extract-dak (dt_extractor, → DMN) reads the same layout | . | scheduling logic | the schedule tabs of that spreadsheet | tools/node/processDTSchedule.js <xlsx> <sheet> … | . | core data elements, indicators | input/L2/IMMZ DAK_core data dictionary.xlsx, IMMZ DAK_indicators.xlsx | tools/node/processDAK.js -f <xlsx>, processIND.js; extract-dak (dd_extractor) where the layout is input/dictionary/ | . | requirements | DAK requirements template (input/system-requirements/, empty in this repository) | extract-dak (req_extractor) | . | CQL libraries (compile and refresh) | input/cql/*.cql | cqf tooling-cli -RefreshIG (_refresh.sh); the IG Publisher compiles CQL in the build | . | test cases | input/tests/plandefinition/<Library>/*.yaml | tools/node/makeExample.js into FHIR test bundles | . | L1 recommendations transcribed verbatim | *.l1.yaml (measles) | litlfred/test tools/build_l1.py | . | L1 authored from pictures (posters, slides) | *.l1.yaml with image: / from: | the smart-base Tool l1-transcription-verbatim | . | WHO’s method. The WHO IG Starter Kit (smart.who.int/ig-starter-kit: l2_dak_authoring, l3_decisiontables, l3_cql, l3_testing) and its DAK templates (decision-support, scheduling, requirements, data dictionary, indicators). Jurisdiction training material where there is some, e.g. litlfred/uganda-sg-training for Uganda. | . Only when all three come back empty is something new written, and then as a Tool node under tool-authoring, with the search recorded in the dependency row (toolchain: none, and where it looked). Never write a script into the adaptation repository without a Tool node. Step 2 is not optional: upstream converters, CQL refresh scripts and test formats are usually not declared Tools, so the graph search alone misses them. There is no PDF renderer in smart-base. Its only PDF dependency is pdfplumber, used to read PDFs when extracting personas.

5003.title: What the generic authoring skills need to know here
5003.content: The platform’s bpmn-authoring, dmn-authoring and translation-manager are generic and name no DAK. What a DAK adds to each: . | BPMN is a source artefact. bpmn2fsh turns an authored business process into FHIR Shorthand, so names and ids chosen in the diagram appear in the generated FSH. Author it knowing it will be transformed. A changed diagram also changes its picture and its translation templates: re-render it (bun run cat render:bpmn) and run bun run cat regen (prepare-merge), which re-extracts the .pot files translate-bpmn:check gates on. | DMN is a source artefact. dmn2html renders decision tables for human review, and dmn_questionnaire_generator derives questionnaires from them; the caveats are §”Two things to expect” above. | Translation. smart-base defines the formal actor SGAuthoring.Persona.Translator, with the skill requirements SGAuthoring.Skills.TranslateContent and SGAuthoring.Skills.ReviewTranslations. The translation subsystem is invoked from a smart-base checkout, never copied. | .

5005.title: SMART Guideline end to end
5005.content: Process_SgEndToEnd · advisory · 18 step(s) . From a use case to a consuming application: identify the L1 guidelines, ingest them into an L1 knowledge graph, choose the L2 DAKs to build on, create or adapt the L2 assets, choose the L3 IGs to build on, produce the L3 assets, then build the L4 consuming application the requester describes. Adjudication follows every stage as QA, not as a gate, but the order is strict: no L3 asset before the L1 extraction and L2 assets it derives from exist with their review requested (Gateway_L3Ready). Each stage forks into the next stage and its adjudication, and each adjudication has its own end event, so the instance completes only when all are recorded. Each stage runs the skill named on its activity, with its own input and output contract (l2-dak-authoring.bpmn for stage 4, dak-l3-ig.bpmn for stage 6), and its output is the next stage’s input. The smart-guideline-end-to-end skill orchestrates the stages and says who adjudicates each. i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i

5011.title: Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history

5017.title: Sub-KG lifecycle — staged here, separated later
5017.content: Skill sub-kg-lifecycle: A sub-KG is a knowledge graph staged as a directory inside a harnessed repository, declared as its own layer, that may later leave for a repository of its own. The lifecycle: declare it in place, grow it, stage it for separation (one import seam, the separation guard, a self-contained rehearsal), and then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, create the repository, copy the staged contents in with history, re-point the declaration, verify on a fresh clone and delete the in-repo copy. The light sibling of kg-separation: use this for a DATA layer that leaves whole, and kg-separation when a graph must split into a content repository and a tools repository. A sub-KG created inside a folio or harnessed repository can move to its own repository later: once it is staged for separation, a new repository is created and the staged contents are copied into it.

5018.title: Which skill, this one or kg-separation?
5018.content: | the graph | use | . | holds data — an artefact index, generated pages, a library, a folio — and leaves whole | this skill | . | holds data and the code that writes it, and the two must become a content repository and a tools repository | kg-separation — its fourteen stages, the pair, FR-7 | . | is not yet a graph at all — tangled into its host | graph-detanglement first | . The two share their gates on purpose. Ready to seed? here is the same decision table, seed-readiness-gate.dmn, evaluated by the same command, and the owner’s confirmations here are the same rule, deletion-requires-confirmation. What this skill adds is the part kg-separation does not cover: a sub-KG born in the host, with no tools pair, that leaves in one piece.

5019.title: How a sub-KG is born — the intent question
5019.content: A content type’s own creation skill asks whether the new thing goes in a new repository or inside this one, and routes here for the second answer. For a folio in general that is getting-started’s add-folio branch. A harness above this one may own a creation skill for its own kind of graph; ask skill_list for it rather than improvising. In-repository is the cheaper default whenever the session is already in a harnessed repository. Every stage up to 6 is reversible with git revert, and nothing outside the repository changes until stage 7. A new repository is the first irreversible, outward-facing act, and this lifecycle puts it behind a confirmation rather than at the start.

5020.title: The stages
5020.content: Each stage names its lane (a role in scenarios/roles.json) and what decides that it is done. A stage is done when its check is green, never when the work looks finished. | # | stage | lane | done when | . | 0 | Brief, claim the work item (opening-brief) | authoring-agent | work item claimed with bun run cat beans:claim | . | 1 | Declare it in place | authoring-agent | the declaration parses; instance-repositories.test.ts green | . | 2 | Grow it in place | authoring-agent | the content type’s own gates | . | 3 | Push generic down | platform-authoring-agent | check:import-direction, check:reference-direction, check:process-bindings add nothing | . | 4 | One import seam | platform-authoring-agent | every climb out of the directory goes through <name>/platform.ts | . | 5 | Rehearse self-contained | build-pipeline | bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse | . | 6 | Report what would move | authoring-agent | the report is in the work item (as kg-separation stage 9) | . | 7 | Owner confirms: create the repository | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 8 | Create the repository | administrator | it exists, empty, and was read before writing | . | — | Ready to seed? | build-pipeline | seed-readiness-gate.dmn answers settled | . | 9 | Copy the staged contents in, with history | authoring-agent | a reviewed PR on a branch of the new repository | . | 10 | Re-point the declaration | platform-authoring-agent | the host is green consuming the new repository | . | 11 | Verify on a fresh clone | build-pipeline | the new repository’s gates green from git clone in an empty directory | . | 12 | Owner confirms: delete the in-repo copy | administrator | an answer, recorded in the work item | . | 13 | Cutover commit | administrator | one commit, revertable (as kg-separation stage 13) | . 1 · Declare it in place . A directory <name>/ at the host’s root, with <name>/<name>.json: . { "name": "<name>", "repository": "<owner>/<name>", // the PLANNED home; IRIs key on it "livesAt": { "repository": "<owner>/<host>", "path": "<name>" }, // where it sits TODAY "version": "0.1.0", "needs": ["<the harness it instantiates>"], "directories": [ /* only directories that exist, each with its graphTypologies */ ] } . | repository differs from livesAt.repository — that difference is what makes the directory a staged layer, and it is what the separation guard and seed:ready read. Nothing lists the staged layers by hand. | The directory may sit anywhere — a root sibling is the convention, but the tools read livesAt.path, so folio/<name>/ works the same. | Scaffold it with init-folio --staged <path>: . bun run cat init-folio --staged <path> --title "<title>" \ --repository <owner>/<name> --needs <harness> # --host-repository when origin cannot say . It writes exactly two files, <path>/<name>.json and an empty <path>/platform.ts, and nothing at the host’s root; init-folio-staged.test.ts snapshots the whole host tree to hold that. Never --instance inside a host: it writes a repository’s worth of scaffolding (AGENTS.md, .mcp.json, a work items store, a session hook; 15 files, measured with --dry-run). --instance is for stage 8’s repository. | Declare a directory with its files, in one commit: a declared-but-absent directory is scanned as empty and reported clean. | . 3 · Push generic down — before the seam, not after . Move everything generic into the harness below, consolidate what the sub-KG needs into its own harness, and only then seed. The other order copies generic code into a repository that has to give it back. Wrong-direction edges hide in declarations and data, not only in imports: a skill definition naming a package one layer up, a dependsOn, a publication target enumerated in an input schema, prose links, a needs edge to an empty layer. So run all three direction checks, not one. 4 · One import seam: <name>/platform.ts . Every symbol the sub-KG uses from the platform is re-exported from one file, and nothing else in the directory climbs out of it. On the day it leaves, re-pointing the platform is a one-file edit instead of a sweep. cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/instance-separation-imports.test.ts is the guard. It covers every layer whose repository differs from its livesAt.repository, not only those that opted in, because an opt-in guard is silent for exactly the layer that has no seam. Layers other layers build on are an explicit, checked exemption, and a layer that still climbs has a ceiling that may only fall. Create the seam at stage 1, not here. It costs one file on day one, and every later climb is a reroute. A merge from main is where new climbs arrive, so a red guard after one is the expected signal to reroute, not a regression. 5 · Rehearse self-contained — run the gates, do not scan . bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse --text # exit 0 settled, 1 not yet, 2 unknown . It copies the layer and what it needs into a scratch workspace of sibling directories and runs the tests there. It is a run rather than a reading because: . | a static import scan misses files the gates load at run time — a JSON code list read by URL, for one; | renaming the directory can change every generated page, when a URL prefix or a chrome lookup keys on the directory name. Take the identity from the declaration’s name, never from the path, and check for that before seeding into a different directory name. | . 7 and 12 · The two confirmations . Both are userTasks in the administrator lane, marked relaxable="false", and both follow deletion-requires-confirmation: the agent reports what would happen, how large it is and how it is undone, then waits. Silence is not a yes. The questions are numbered, four options at most, the recommended one first, with a stated default: . Before stage 8: . <name> is staged and rehearses green: N files, M MB, history of K commits. Creating <owner>/<name> is visible outside this repository and is not undone by a revert. May it be created? . | Yes — you create it, and tell me when it exists (recommended) | Yes — I create it (only if this session has that permission) | Not yet — keep it staged here | . Default if you do not answer: 3. Nothing is created. Before stage 13: . <owner>/<name> is green from a fresh clone and the host consumes it. The in-repo copy is N files. Deleting it is one commit, revertable. | Delete the in-repo copy now (recommended) | Keep it until the new repository’s first release | Show me the file list first | . Default if you do not answer: 2. Nothing is deleted. When the repository must be created by someone with credentials this session lacks, the hand-over is agent-handoff: one work item, one sentence for the person to relay. 9 · Copy the staged contents in, with history . The staged directory becomes the new repository’s content with its history: git subtree split --prefix=<name> in the host, then git subtree add (or a merge of the split branch) in the new repository. It goes in on a branch, as a draft PR, never straight to main. The new repository’s own root files — its declaration at the root, its config, its README — are a second commit in the same PR, so the copy itself stays byte-identical and reviewable. Ready to seed? comes first, at seed time, because the tree has moved since the rehearsal: every open PR touching the layer when the copy is taken is orphaned. Its criteria and thresholds are in kg-separation §”Ready to seed?”, and not restated here. 10 · Re-point the declaration . | what changes | how | . | livesAt | removed in the new repository — absent means “sits at the root of repository” | . | the seam | platform.ts points at wherever the platform now is: a remote-mounted path, or a sibling checkout | . | the host | remote mount if the host imports code from the sub-KG — a source.remote layer in the host’s root index.config.json (remote-mount; never a submodule); subscription (kg:subscribe) if it only reads its content | . | pins | the host pins a commit while staging, a version once released (upstream-version-adoption) | . | its site | the new repository publishes and previews itself (feature-staging, Which site): "site": { "agentRun": true } in its index.config.json when an agent publishes it, plus whatever workflow its publisher layer’s own creation skill requires (an IG’s AST-cache refresh, for one) | . | its checks | .github/workflows/harness-pr-checks.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-pr-checks.yml, so its gates run on every pull request | . | its QA record | when it declares a qa directory with storage (test/results/, cat/cat-harness/qa-reports, keyed by commit): .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml calling the tools layer’s layer-qa-publish.yml, so every push to main and every pull request publishes its results to its own qa-reports branch, and test/results/ in .gitignore. A host reads them at the commit it pins. Without the job, the declaration names a store nothing writes | . | .gitignore | the mount block, written by the mount tool between its own markers. Never typed: a hand-written marker makes remote-mount.ts refuse (markers unpaired) | . Copy these from a sibling repository of the same kind; never type them. A repository scaffolded by hand misses them, and its site cannot be built until each is copied in. The host keeps its own copy through this stage. The re-point is additive. 11 · Verify on a fresh clone . bun run cat sub-kg:verify-clone --repo <owner>/<name> --ref <seeding branch> --text # exit 0 green, 1 red, 2 unknown . The Tool sub-kg-verify-clone clones the new repository into an empty scratch directory with its submodules (and each --sibling beside it), installs, and runs its own gates script, else its test script. An empty tree, a failed clone or a repository with no gate is unknown, never green. Nothing in a seed runs standalone until the seam is re-pointed, so a test that climbs out (Cannot find module '../../../<harness>/…') fails here. A rehearsal in the host’s scratch space is not this check; it shares the host’s node_modules and network. The new repository’s own site is part of this check: bun run cat stage:local --repo . --dry-run from the fresh clone must build. A refusal names what stage 10 left out.

5021.title: Stage 13: the frozen copy
5021.content: After cutover the host keeps a frozen copy in fsh-guts, not a refreshed mirror and not a deletion. Step 12 asks (1) move to fsh-guts now, (2) keep in place until the first release, (3) show the file list first, default (2). Step 13 deposits the directory into the PARENT’s fsh-guts as a verified archive (not plain trees, which CI would audit as live content), then removes it from main. The deposit is the one state:seed --cutover makes for a state graph: an archive that must extract to the exact tree being removed, plus a provenance note (movedFrom, movedOn, sourceCommit, tree), and the removal commit is made only once it has landed. A separation targets the parent’s fsh-guts rather than the departing layer’s, which --cutover does not yet do. The live copy is the remote mount (index.config.json source.remote), npm package retrieval (kg-retrieve-npm), or subscription (kg:subscribe) from stage 10; the frozen one is never refreshed and never rendered. How checks treat a frozen subtree . This is the one place the rule is stated; scanners point here. A frozen subtree is one retired item, and its sibling note is the node that answers for it. Every reader of fsh-guts — the fsh-guts.jsonld export, the fsh-guts page, the render-pipeline and bean-reference tests, check:materialized-fixity — reports the note and does not enter the directory. The page shows it as one row in the via sidecar state. | Recognised by declaration, never by path. A directory is frozen because <name>.md beside it declares $schema: folio-fsh-guts/v1 and kind: separated-instance (isFrozenSubtree in schemas/kg/fsh-guts.ts). A copy dropped in with no note, or under a note of another kind, is walked like any directory, so its files fail self-declaration loudly rather than vanishing from every check. | The note must carry all four stage-13 fields — movedFrom, movedOn, repository, matchesCommit — because it is now the only thing any check reads about thousands of files. Those beyond the common set are exported under the node’s data. | Materialization records inside are not judged. They claim bytes in the repository the graph now lives in, which the copy deliberately does not carry. | The note’s bean: resolves against main’s work plan, with no pending escape. So the deposit lands on the fsh-guts branch in the same step that merges the PR carrying that work item, never before it; a deposit pushed ahead of its PR turns every PR’s CI red. | .

5022.title: Anti-patterns
5022.content: . | Creating the repository first. It is the one irreversible step; everything that can be done in place is done before it. | A seed with no history. A one-commit seed severs blame for every line, and the history is cheap to keep. | Re-pointing by sweep. If more than one file changes when the platform moves, the seam was skipped. | Reading the rehearsal as the fresh-clone check. They catch different things: the rehearsal catches climbs, the fresh clone catches everything the host’s environment was quietly supplying. | Deleting the in-repo copy because the new repository is green. Green is the precondition for asking, not the answer. | Committing mounted directories to the host repository. Remote mounts populate layer directories locally. If .gitignore does not ignore the mounted paths, external files pollute downstream git status. index.config.json must generate gitignore entries for all remoteMounts. | Breaking dependents when dependencies fold. If a dependency layer folds into another (e.g. cat-openapi into cat-harness), downstreams that still reference the folded layer fail unless FOLDED_INSTANCE_ALIASES maps them. | Separating before resolving withheld asset clearance. If library items are withheld or unpermitted in the separated repository (as with the IRIS replica), materialization results in broken links. Clearance must be verified at seed time. | .

5024.title: A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository
5024.content: Process_SubKgLifecycle · strict · 11 step(s) . The light sibling of kg-separation, which splits a graph into a content and a tools repository; this moves a data layer whole, and shares kg-separation’s seeding gateway and decision table. DRAWN IN PHASES (owner, 2026-11-08, Q-B1-3 A): it keeps its own grow-in-place and staging steps, and calls the authorise, move and cut-over phases it shares with kg-separation. i i i i i i i i i i i

5026.title: Lanes — who acts
5026.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Authoring agent | authoring-agent | Declares the sub-KG in place and grows it, reports what would move before each irreversible step, drains the open pull requests that keep the source from settling, and copies the staged contents into the new repository with their history. | . | Platform authoring agent | platform-authoring-agent | The platform-side stages: pushing generic code and declarations down into the harness below, routing every climb out of the sub-KG through its one import seam, and re-pointing the declaration, the seam and the host’s consumption once the new repository exists. | . | Build pipeline | build-pipeline | Runs the checks that decide the gateways: the separation guard and the three direction checks, the self-contained rehearsal, the seed-readiness table at seed time, and the gates of the new repository from a fresh clone. 5027.doc: A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository
5027.title: Steps
5027.content: Every one of the 11 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Brief the workTask_Brief | Authoring agent | shared step GT_Briefopening-brief | What the work is and why, what is already measured with its provenance, how it will be done, and what would falsify the approach. 5030.doc: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph
5030.title: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph
5030.content: Process_SubscribeKg · strict · 11 step(s) . Subscribe a folio or harness to an external knowledge graph pinned to a full commit SHA, then take each chosen part from referenced to materialized through materialize-remote and instantiate each chosen harness once its needs are held, so the harness appears in the subscriber’s navbar. A SUBSCRIPTION IS NOT A NEW MECHANISM, and this diagram is where that claim is kept honest. Every byte that arrives does so through Process_MaterializeRemote, called once per chosen subgraph or asset; every held copy is refreshed through Process_RefreshMaterialized. Neither is re-described here. What this process adds is only the walk: pin, validate, choose, and then carry each chosen part from referenced to materialised one at a time. A SUBSTRATE is a repository whose root declaration meets bootstrap’s schema requirements and declares at least one harness. Both are answerable from the declaration file alone, so validating one never needs the whole repository. WHERE IT LIVES: library/processes/, beside Process_MaterializeRemote and Process_RefreshMaterialized, which it calls, naming the kg-subscription and materialize-remote skills in library/skills/large-datasets/; every ref stays inside the harness. STRICT. The pin and the five gates are the reason: an unpinned subscription is how two subscribers see two graphs under one name, and a gate that only warned is a gate nobody fails. i i i i i i i i i i i

5032.title: Lanes — who acts
5032.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Subscriber (the folio’s owner) | user | Every CHOICE in the walk is made here and nowhere else: which substrate and at which commit, which of its subgraphs, asset classes and harnesses to hold. The engine never chooses a part on the subscriber’s behalf — a subgraph not chosen stays referenced, which is a state, not an omission — and the pre-check on harness needs sends the choice back here rather than resolving it silently. | . | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | ingestion-agent | Validates the substrate at the pin, then walks the chosen parts one at a time: each subgraph or asset through the shared materialisation subprocess, each held copy through the shared refresh, each harness by writing its config. Every loop here re-enters its decision after each part, so a refusal on one part is recorded and the walk continues to the next rather than aborting the subscription. | .

The schema refuses anything else (SubscriptionSchema.ref), and this step exists so the refusal is met while choosing rather than at commit time. Two questions: does it parse as bootstrap’s KnowledgeGraphDeclarationSchema, and does it declare at least one harness? could not fetch is a third answer and is never read as conforms. | . | Record why it is not a substrate; write no entryTask_Refuse | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | kg-subscription | No subscription entry is written for a repository that is not a substrate. What is recorded is the reason (non-conforming, no harness, or unreachable) and the pin it was asked at, so a later attempt at a different commit starts from what failed. | . | Write the entry and cache the declarationTask_Record | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | kg-subscription | The subscriptions entry in the subscriber’s layer declaration — id, repository, ref, and nothing chosen yet — plus a cached copy of the substrate’s declaration at the pin. 5036.title: Surprise to corpus — notice it, filter it, then ask
5036.content: Skill surprise-to-corpus: What was unexpected in that task, and does it belong in the corpus? Logical surprise is the detectable kind, recurrence is the filter that stops this generating noise every turn, and the agent PROMPTS — it never writes corpus guidance unasked. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . Skill id: surprise-to-corpus · Package: folio-core . When something unexpected happens during a defined process that runs often, it may be worth a new skill, guidance or tool refinement: prompt the person to add it to the corpus. Three clauses: notice, filter by recurrence, prompt. The first alone is a diary; the first two are an agent rewriting the corpus on its own authority; the third without the second is a prompt every turn until people stop reading them.

5037.title: 1. What counts as a surprise
5037.content: Ask it as an after-action review asks it: . What did you expect to happen, what actually happened, and why the difference? . This makes the surprise articulable BEFORE you know whether it matters. “Something felt off” is not reviewable; “I expected the tracer to read the mask as ink and it read the ground” is. The filter in §2 then operates on a statement rather than on a feeling, so it can be applied consistently. Only LOGICAL surprise is detectable. Statistical surprise implies a base rate, and the corpus carries none — nothing records how often a gate fires, a merge conflicts, or a selector breaks. Do not claim a statistical surprise: it would assert a distribution nobody measured. Logical surprise needs no baseline. It is any of: . | A premise turned out false. You believed something about the system, acted on it, and the system disagreed. | A gate fired for a reason nobody predicted — including a gate that passed when you expected red. | A command failed and the failure was invisible, because whatever ran next produced plausible output anyway. | Two things that looked like one thing, or one thing that turned out to be two. | . Examples of the general shapes . | the surprise | the general shape | . | potracer treats ZERO as foreground — the inverse of what the name suggests | a library whose convention is the opposite of its name | . | Image.crop past the edge pads with BLACK, which a tracer reads as ink | a default that is invisible until another tool interprets it | . | a CSS class used as an IDENTITY is reused by a second button as a box class, breaking every selector at once | a name doing two jobs, discovered when the second arrives | . | an id sliced one character short fails silently behind a tail -1 | a truncated identifier that still LOOKS like an identifier | .

5038.title: 2. The recurrence filter — the part that stops the noise
5038.content: A surprise inside a one-off is an anecdote. The same surprise inside a process that runs often is a defect in the process. Without this filter the rule fires every turn, because every non-trivial turn contains something somebody did not expect. With it, the question is narrow and answerable: . Did this happen inside a defined process that runs often — and would the next agent running that process hit it too? . Both halves. A rare process can still be worth guarding if its failure is expensive, but then say that rather than claiming a recurrence you have not seen. “The next agent would hit it too” separates a fact about the system from a fact about your own mistake. Three ways a candidate fails the filter, all of which end in silence rather than a prompt: it happened once, in a process nobody runs twice; it was your own slip and the system behaved as documented; or the corpus already says it and you had not read that part. The third is the common one, and checking costs one grep. Read the slip blamelessly . A finding is about the SYSTEM rather than about the person. “My own slip” fails the filter only when the system behaved as documented AND nothing about the system made the slip easy. Where the system DID make it easy, would the next agent hit it too is true, and the candidate passes. A mis-copied id is not just a slip: a truncated id is still a well-formed id, and a | tail -1 hides a non-zero exit — both properties the next agent meets unchanged.

5039.title: 3. PROMPT, never write
5039.content: The agent proposes; a person decides. This is deletion-requires-confirmation pointed the other way: that skill governs removing a durable artefact on your own initiative, this one governs ADDING durable guidance on your own initiative. The corpus is read by every future session, so the person who has to live with a line in it should be the one who agreed to it. What a good prompt contains — the same parts interaction-modality §4.1 binds every handed-over decision to, and the test is identical: can the reader answer without opening anything? . | What happened, concretely, with the measurement or the error text. | Which process it happened in, named. | Why it will recur — the filter above, argued rather than asserted. | What you propose: a new skill, a line in an existing one, or a tool change. Say which, and where it would live — where-does-this-go is how you answer that. | Your recommendation, marked as such. | What happens if they say nothing: nothing gets written, and the candidate is filed as a work item so it is not lost. | . A work item is the third state — recorded, unactioned, findable — so silence is not expensive and an unanswered prompt is something the next session can pick up rather than rediscover.

5040.title: 4. When to run this
5040.content: At the end of a task, not continuously: one pass over what actually happened. Most turns produce nothing and should say nothing — a loop that reports “no surprises” every turn is a loop people stop reading. It pairs with turn-reporting, which governs the shape of the report you were already writing.

5041.title: What this skill deliberately does not do
5041.content: . | No severity scale. Ranking surprises would invite filing the low ones, which is the noise the recurrence filter exists to prevent. A candidate either passes the filter or is worth a work item at most. | No automated corpus change. A mechanism that could write guidance would be used to write guidance. | No timeline reconstruction. The agent was present for the whole turn, and the transcript is the timeline. | No routing method. Where a surprise goes is where-does-this-go, which needs an index rather than a taxonomy at its size. | .
