5201.title: uses[] Editorial Review
5201.content: Skill uses-editorial-review: Adjudicate uses-editorial-completeness — read a block as a reader would and judge whether its uses[] is complete and genuinely expository. The human/agent half of the uses QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-uses.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review, Committee review of a content change .

5202.title: The relation you are auditing
5202.content: uses[] is the editorial dependency relation: what must a reader have read to follow this block? It is authored content — a deliberate judgement about narrative order — and it is maintained by agents and humans, not generated. The same relation exists at term scale: a glossary term’s requires, and a schema term’s uses in bootstrap’s graph.schema.json, say what a reader must know before the definition. Same discipline — AUTHORED, never inferred, with a text matcher kept only as a guard that list and prose agree (see the glossary ordering discipline, §”Ordered glossaries”). It is not any machine-derived dependency graph. A content type with a formal layer also derives a formal relation, from what its proofs actually invoke, and the two relations answer different questions and diverge in both directions, correctly. The layer that ships such a content type holds that comparison and names this skill from its side (for a paper folio, the science layer).

5203.title: interprets is the same relation under a second field name
5203.content: uses[] is the curated list. interprets states the same reader-facing fact for a remark or example about one specific block, and the content graph counts both. Each editorial edge carries editorialField so a tool proposing an edit can still tell which field an author wrote: they are interchangeable to a reader and not to a writer, and collapsing them would make an automated edit rewrite the wrong field. Two caveats, both of which change what a number means: . | detangler-no-forward-ref builds its own uses-only adjacency and does not consume the shared graph, so forward-pointing interprets edges are outside what it counts. | The editorial graph is not acyclic. Counting both fields reveals genuine editorial cycles. Do not “fix” one without reading whether it is real. | . Do not quote a count from prose — run the check against the corpus in front of you. A number in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. For impact questions — what breaks if this changes? — use the union, via the content graph’s accessors, which default to it.

5204.title: The prime directive
5204.content: Never populate uses[] from a machine-derived dependency graph. Copying derived dependencies in destroys the editorial signal and inflates every ordering metric computed from it (graph energy, forward refs, cone size, PageRank). Never “sync” the two. When reviewing, do not open a block’s formal or generated sibling to decide what belongs in uses[]. The question is about the reader.

5205.title: Workflow
5205.content: . | Read the .md as a reader. Cold. Do not read the .ts first — you want your own sense of what the block presumes before you see what the author declared. | List what the narrative actually leans on. Note every point where the prose: . | uses notation it does not introduce, | names an object (“the canonical $X$”) defined elsewhere, | argues against or refines a prior result, | presumes a construction the reader would otherwise have to reconstruct. | . | Now read uses[] in the .ts manifest and compare both ways. | Judge completeness. Anything from step 2 missing from uses[] that a reader would genuinely stumble over ⇒ fail (major). A reader who could carry on unbothered ⇒ at most warn. | Judge editorial fitness. For each listed entry, ask: would a reader be worse off having not read this first? . | Yes ⇒ fine. | No, and it looks like a derived artefact (an entry the prose never mentions, copied from a generated dependency list) ⇒ fail (major). This is the pollution case. | No, but it is defensible context ⇒ warn. | . | Write the sidecar entry under uses-editorial-completeness with reviewer.kind: "agent" (or "human"), citing file:line and a verbatim quote for every finding — the block-QA evidence contract. | .

5206.title: Verdict rubric
5206.content: | Verdict | When | . | pass | List reads as a deliberate editorial judgement; nothing a reader needs is missing; nothing present is dead weight. | . | warn | A marginal entry, or a missing dependency a reader could shrug off. | . | fail | A missing dependency a reader would stumble over, or an entry that is plainly a copied-in derived dependency. | .

5207.title: Forward references and foreshadows[]
5207.content: A uses[] entry pointing at a block that appears later in the chapter is a detangler-no-forward-ref finding. Sometimes that is right — the exposition really does defer — and foreshadows[] records it. foreshadows[] is independent of uses[], so a chapter overview can name results it previews without asserting a dependency that is not real. It covers two cases you must keep apart: . | case | in uses[]? | who records it | cost | . | Pure forward pointer — the prose names something coming later and does not depend on it | no | derived from the .md, not authored | zero by construction: it never enters the dependency graph | . | Deferred prerequisite — a real dependency the paper states later on purpose | yes | declared by the author, and only the author | exempt from ordering cost; still counted for cycles, cones and depth | . Do not hand-author the first case. deriveForeshadows reads the block’s own markdown links and backticked labels, keeps those that resolve to a real block sitting later in reading order and are not already in uses[], and loadChapterGraph re-derives on every load. Writing them into the manifest duplicates the prose into metadata, where it goes stale. The derivation never reads deferral language; it matches links and labels only (phrasing detection misreads e.g. “Below $n^*$”, a numeric comparison).

5208.title: Declaring the second case
5208.content: Only a deferred prerequisite needs your judgement: it exempts a real uses[] edge from the ordering metrics, hiding a genuine defect behind an authored claim that the disorder was intended, and nothing downstream re-opens it. The contract in BlockBase.foreshadows is strict — the prose must frame the reference as deferred (“we will need X, proved in chapter 9”). The bar is a first-person authorial hand-off that says the treatment happens elsewhere: “we establish this in X”, “we work this out separately”, “the derivation is recorded in X”. | Looks like a deferral | Actually | . | Bare cross-reference — “See [X] in Chapter 7” | ordering. Says nothing about direction. | . | Organizational pointer — “these tables are projections of this master table” | ordering. About structure, not sequence. | . | Block asserts the target’s conclusion as background, then reasons onward from it | ordering. Consuming a result is the opposite of deferring it. | . | Target listed under “## Rigorous results” / “## Consumers / downstream” | ordering — and check the direction; these often run target→source. | . | A forward-looking word (“below”, “later”, “we must show”) | ordering unless the sentence is about this target’s placement. “Below $n^*$” is a numeric comparison; “we must show” is usually about research, not chapter order. | . Two failure modes survive a verbatim quote, so check both before declaring: . | False locator. “the functor of the next subsection” where the target is 21 sections and ~300 blocks away. The prose defers; it does not defer this far, and the edge is a real defect. | Mis-aimed deferral. The quoted sentence hands off to a different block than the edge under review. A deferral pointed elsewhere cannot exempt this one. | . Both are about the declared case only. A derived pointer is aimed by the link itself, so it cannot be mis-aimed, and it carries no exemption to abuse. Two rules police the field: foreshadows-resolve (every target must exist) and foreshadows-not-self. The foreshadows-point-forward criterion catches a target the reader has already passed, which is either a prerequisite filed in the wrong field or an inert back-reference.

5209.title: A block’s uses[] may be carrying the whole family
5209.content: Never judge an entry from the block’s own .md alone. A block is the head of a family — X-proof, X-interpretation, X-tableN-data — and the dependency you are looking for is often in a child while the declaration sits on the parent. | Table children. Pointer-style blocks (“See Table 3”) keep their substance in tbl:…-data. A name-and-notation search of the parent’s .md reports an absence that is not real. | Proof children. A proof cites what the statement assumes. The parent’s prose may never name a target its proof child cites by label; if the proof declares no uses[] of its own, the parent’s entry is the sole record of the dependency, and deleting it as “unsupported by the prose” erases the edge entirely. | . So before removing an entry, check whether any child leans on the target, and whether that child declares anything itself. An entry that looks like dead weight on the parent may be the family’s only declaration. Searching for the target’s words also misses a lean on the target’s object — a source writing “the canonical $\tilde w_\lambda$” depends on whatever defines the undeformed $w_\lambda$, whether or not it ever says so.

5210.title: Sibling parity is evidence only until a bulk edit touched the family
5210.content: “All the siblings declare nothing, so declaring it here would be the anomaly” is evidence only if no bulk operation has run over the family: a bulk edit (for example a transitive-prune pass) produces parity by construction, so parity cannot distinguish a shared convention from shared damage. Before resting on it, check the family’s history, not just the block’s: . git log --oneline -- <chapter>/<sibling>.ts # for two or three siblings . A convention shows up as blocks that were authored empty. Damage shows up as one commit emptying all of them on the same day. If the emptiness has a single commit behind it, parity tells you nothing about intent. The same caution applies to any evidence drawn from what “the corpus does”: a corpus that has been swept is a record of the sweep as much as of the authors.

5211.title: One reading is not the standard
5211.content: A single careful pass is not enough: on re-review, destructive uses[] verdicts and foreshadow declarations are overturned often, and keyword search over the .md alone misses real dependencies. Use two readers who cannot see each other’s verdicts for anything that edits the graph, and treat agreement as the signal. Where they disagree, or where either is unsure, leave the edge alone: a wrongly deleted editorial edge silently corrupts every ordering metric computed from the graph. A retarget carries both burdens. It asserts this edge is wrong and that one is right, so it needs evidence for each half separately. When only the second half holds, it is an addition, not a swap.

5212.title: Reading the mechanical findings first
5212.content: Run the script half before adjudicating — it is cheap and it changes what you should look at: . bun run pipeline/qa-checkers-uses.ts # via qa-sweep --axis uses . | Mechanical finding | What it means for your review | . | uses-editorial-hygiene fail — unresolvable label | A dangling reference. Fix the label or add the missing block before judging completeness; the graph is wrong until you do. | . | uses-editorial-hygiene warn — transitive redundancy | Tidiness only. The graph is correct, just not minimal. Do not let it distract from the completeness question. | . A content type with a formal layer adds its own advisory finding here; the layer that ships it says how to read it.

5215.title: Vocabulary authority — one fact, one home, N renderings
5215.content: Skill vocabulary-authority: One vocabulary is authoritative for one kind of fact, and every other is a derived rendering reached by a declared mapping. Which vocabulary owns what here, the pros and cons behind each ruling, how DC and SKOS overlap and what stops them drifting, and the normalisation-first rule for any modelling or mapping exercise. Named by: Classify and code content, DTH authoring, L2 DAK authoring . Skill id: vocabulary-authority · Package: folio-core .

5216.title: The rule
5216.content: A fact has ONE authoritative vocabulary. Every other vocabulary that carries it is a RENDERING, reached by a declared mapping with stated equivalence — never a second copy of the fact. | the fact | authoritative | why not the others | . | what a term MEANS | SKOS | the only candidate here whose subject IS a meaning | . | a resource’s metadata | Dublin Core | a document has a title; a concept has a preferred label. Different subjects | . | a clinical code’s operational semantics | FHIR CodeSystem / ValueSet / ConceptMap | versioning, designations with a use, expansion-as-release. SKOS has none of these | . | a release of any of the above | DCAT (held, not built) | it is not a term model at all; it describes a published dataset | . ┌──────────────────────────────┐ AUTHORITATIVE ──▶ │ skos:Concept = the MEANING │ └───────────────┬──────────────┘ skos:exactMatch / closeMatch / broadMatch / relatedMatch │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ FHIR Code- Dublin Core schema.org TBX DCAT System (resource DefinedTerm termbase (release of (clinical metadata, (SEO / (CAT-tool any of these operations) bib records) discovery) exchange) as a dataset) . SKOS is the hub because its mapping properties exist for exactly this, and because it is the only one of the five whose subject is a meaning rather than an artefact, a record, or a distribution.

5217.title: Pros and cons, as ruled
5217.content: The reasons are measured against this corpus, not read off the specs. SKOS — adopted, authoritative for meaning . |   |   | . | Pro | Native JSON-LD. Multilingual labels first-class. notation is the code — TermGloss’s prefixed names. Mapping properties with stated equivalence. Carries the vocabulary terms and swimlane roles here | . | Con | No versioning model at all. No designation use. No post-coordination. Mapping properties carry no provenance | . The con is why convergence STOPS at SKOS. The failure this exists to prevent: reading “one glossary mechanism” as “one terminology mechanism” and binding an ICD-11 code to a skos:Concept with a notation and no version. That graph validates, publishes, and is wrong the next release. Dublin Core — kept, authoritative for resources . |   |   | . | Pro | ISO 15836. Qualified, repeatable and language-tagged as IRIS actually uses it — the content core’s schemas/dublin-core.ts is shaped by one measured record that does all three | . | Con | Two predicates overlap SKOS (below) | . schema.org — kept at 3 predicates; never a source of truth . |   |   | . | Pro | Search engines consume it. Native JSON-LD | . | Con | A publishing vocabulary, not a terminology one. DefinedTerm has name + description and stops: no versioning, no designation concept at all, no mapping semantics, no deprecation-with-successor | . It has no definitions to speak of. Used for 3 predicates (softwareVersion, codeRepository, text). Measuring usage: a naive grep for schema.org mostly matches json-schema.org (JSON Schema’s $schema keyword) and the schema:viz npm script. Never cite that count. TBX — not closed, and still not adopted . ISO 30042:2019 is published both as an ISO standard and as a free open industry standard; dialects and schemas are public. So “closed” is false and the ruling does not rest on it. |   |   | . | Pro | Genuinely open. Purpose-built for multilingual term entries | . | Con | Its niche is CAT-tool termbase interchange. This repo translates through gettext .po, not a termbase. XML-only | . Legitimate as an export if translators ever ask for a termbase. Rejected outright . SKOS-XL — it reifies labels to fix part of the designation gap and nothing else; the gap it does not fix is the one that matters. OWL — overkill: prose definitions, no reasoner in the pipeline. DCAT — held, for the render of whatever is landed on.

5218.title: DC ↔ SKOS: the overlap, and what stops the drift
5218.content: | pair | relation | . | dcterms:title ↔ skos:prefLabel | real overlap | . | dcterms:description ↔ skos:definition | real overlap | . | dcterms:subject → skos:Concept | not overlap — the designed JOIN. DC points at a concept | . | dcterms:hasPart, dcterms:source | no SKOS equivalent | . DC describes a RESOURCE. SKOS describes a CONCEPT. One object, one type, one naming predicate. They collide only where a node is genuinely both — such as the glossary document, which is a file and a skos:ConceptScheme, carrying both skos:prefLabel and dcterms:title. Two predicates for one fact, with nothing declaring which is authoritative, drift apart. The node is a concept scheme, so skos:prefLabel is the source and dcterms:title is the derived copy for resource-metadata consumers.

5219.title: Guidance for schema and data modelling
5219.content: . | Model in an open standard. Not a proprietary or house schema that happens to be convenient. | Proprietary input is mapped, not adopted. A mapping is a declared artefact with stated equivalence — not a rename in a loader. | Normalise FIRST. The first step of any mapping exercise is data normalisation. Mapping un-normalised data encodes the source’s accidents into the target and they are invisible afterwards. | The exercise runs as a defined process, not as a one-off script. | .

5220.content: cat-harness/external-schemas/ — one record per specification, pinning the edition and carrying the operative terms derived from the corpus, never hand-listed. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/external-schemas.ts --check. A vocabulary can be used in more than one syntax (a BPMN file, a JSON-LD @context); a usage check that reads only one reports the other as absent.

5223.title: Voice overlay review
5223.content: Process_VoiceReview · advisory · 6 step(s) . The voice axis: load whichever editorial voices are active, run each rule’s mechanical half, and decide — for each finding — whether the prose is wrong, the rule does not apply to this content, or this block is a stated exception. You are in this process after the base voice has been adjudicated, and only if a voice is active at all: the first gateway ends the process honestly when none is, rather than reporting a clean review of nothing. Three outcomes, all legitimate, and the third is the one that needs recording: an exception without a reviewer entry is indistinguishable from a rule nobody ran. There is also a fourth path the diagram draws deliberately — if the rule’s own citation does not support it, the RULE is the defect, and that becomes a bean rather than a finding against the prose. i i i i i i

5226.title: Steps

Opening it is what lets a reviewer say WHY the rule applies — and it is the only way to catch a rule that misread its own source. | . | The RULE is the defect — bean itTask_RuleIsWrong | Narrative reviewer | voice-overlay-review | A rule its own quote does not support is a finding against the voice, not against the block. | . | Adjudicate: prose, scope, or exceptionTask_Adjudicate | Narrative reviewer | calls Process_CriterionAdjudicationvoice-overlay-reviewadjudication | The same three outcomes as the base voice axis. The register is wrong for this block (fix the prose); the rule does not apply to this content (scope it on the voice, one edit rather than ten overrules); or the rule applies and this block is an exception (a reviewer entry saying why). | . | Record on the block’s QA sidecarTask_RecordOnSidecar | Narrative reviewer | voice-overlay-review | Through qa-merge-findings, so the icon and the published witness agree with the decision. 5232.title: Two uses
5232.content: | use | candidates | review | . | Design: a new or changed UI | at least two, compared blind | per-criterion, then adjudication, then options analysis | . | As-is: an existing visualiser, drawn as it renders on main | exactly one, marked as-is | the same criteria. A finding becomes a work item against the visualiser, not a redesign | .

5233.title: 1. Intent
5233.content: A few sentences: who the screen is for, what they need to do, and what it must show. For an as-is wireframe, the intent is read off the visualiser’s own declaration and generator, not invented.

5234.title: 2. Candidates
5234.content: . | Mid-fidelity HTML: monochrome, real content from the graph it shows, semantic icons, and no placeholder text. | Web and mobile in every candidate, through responsive CSS or two layouts. A candidate with one layout does not enter review. | .

5235.title: 3. Mechanical checks (wireframe-viewport-check)
5235.content: bun run cat wireframe:check --use as-is --topic <topic> --surface <visualiser ref> bun run cat wireframe:check --use design --topic <slug> --surface <surface> . The three flags are this skill’s input. --topic picks the directory in the table above and every candidate in it (name candidates to check fewer; one outside it is refused), and the report goes to its checks/. --use design needs at least two candidates; --use as-is needs each marked as-is in its file name, and a --surface that is the topic or a ref index.json says it covers. The use, topic and surface are recorded in report.json. This renders each candidate at web (1280×800) and mobile (390×844) sizes. It records script entries for renders, no-overflow and no-placeholder, each pass or fail with a note, and writes a screenshot per viewport. Any fail sends the candidate back to step 2.

5236.title: 4. Blind review, per criterion
5236.content: Reviewers include at least one agent that did not author the candidate and one human. For Design use called from CRDM, the human is the requester or the BA who owns the request: the person who will accept the delivered feature chooses its design. They see the intent, the screenshots and the HTML, without the authors. For each criterion they record pass, warn or fail, with a reason: . | criterion | question | . | intent-fit | Does it do what the intent says, for the person it names? | . | web usability | Can the task be done at desktop width? | . | mobile usability | Can the task be done at phone width, by touch? | . | accessibility | Contrast, a non-colour channel, accessible names, keyboard, reading order | . | alternatives | Do the candidates differ in the ways that matter? (Design use only) | . There are no scores and no averages (methodology-adoption, Refusals).

5237.title: 5. Adjudication and choice
5237.content: . | When entries for one criterion disagree, call Process_Adjudication. The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and a dispensation needs its reason. | The choice between surviving candidates is Process_OptionsAnalysis. Rejected candidates stay, each with the reason it lost. | .

5238.title: Staging links
5238.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

5239.title: Showing it to the requester
5239.content: Design use from CRDM ends in a person’s choice, so the candidates must be in front of that person before implementation starts: . | Commit the candidates, intent.md, checks/ (screenshots) and reviews/ under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, so feature-staging publishes them with the rest of the branch. | Show them where the requester will look, chosen from context: the conversation, the issue the request came from, the pull request, or more than one of these. Where it goes is a judgement (feedback-deep-links, point 5); every place chosen carries the same content: a short narrative of what each candidate does differently; branches/ deep links to each candidate’s HTML (not the site root); and its web and mobile screenshots shown as images, not only linked. Say which could not be linked or rendered, and why. | Ask the requester or BA to choose, with the comparison (one row per candidate, from A_CompareOptions) and a recommendation, per interaction-modality where it applies. | Record their choice in the proposal and in the output’s chosen. An agent never chooses on their behalf. Implementation (CRDM Phase 6) builds against the chosen candidate, and the delivery summary links it beside the after-screenshot. | .

5248.title: State in a running process
5248.content: Skill workflow-state: Where a running process keeps what it knows, and which store answers which question. The three records a step may touch, the one it may not, what <cat-harness.processes:bean op> actually performs, and why an instance and a work item must be one answer rather than two. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Classify and code content, L2 component edit and review, SMART Guideline end to end . A process instance is not self-contained. It walks a diagram that lives somewhere else, records its position somewhere else again, and reads facts it must not change. Five stores; confusing any two of them is how a work plan comes to disagree with itself.

5249.title: Which store answers which question
5249.content: | question | store | graph typology | layer | . | what does this process DO? | processes/**/*.bpmn | cat-harness | content | . | where did this instance GET TO? | the workflow-state node of the work item graph | workflow-state | state | . | what is being worked on? | the bean-defs node of the work item graph | bean-defs | state | . | what does a PERSON still owe? | todos/ | todo-items | state | . | what do I already know? | agent memory | memory | context | . The layer column says what a step may do. A step may write to a state graph; that is what state is for. A step that writes to context is a defect, not an update: memory changes when a human directs an authoring act, outside any instance. content-context-and-state-graphs carries the axis; processMayWrite() is the predicate.

5250.title: The diagram is content and the instance is state, and that is the whole model
5250.content: A .bpmn is authored, reviewed, versioned and read by anyone — it stands on its own. An instance is a token position in that diagram plus a history: it means nothing detached from the file it walks. That is why the two live in different graphs and why an instance names its process rather than embedding it. Two consequences: . An instance is never edited by hand. It carries "$schema": "folio-workflow-instance/v1" and the interpreter owns it. Hand- editing a token is asserting a step happened, which is precisely what the gate exists to refuse. A diagram change does not rewrite history. An instance records where it got to under the diagram as it stood. If a step is renamed, the honest answer is that the old instance names a node that no longer exists — not that it retroactively took a different path.

5251.title: Beans and instances are ONE answer, not two
5251.content: bean-defs says what is being worked on; workflow-state says where it got to. Those must be one answer or they diverge, and a work plan that disagrees with itself is worse than one that is merely coarse. The loop is closed by <cat-harness.processes:bean op="…"> on an activity. A bean-marked step is not a step about the work plan — it IS the work-plan operation, so completing the step performs it: . | op | on completing the step | . | claim | status → in-progress, idempotent | . | note | append the caller’s note to the body | . | resolve | status → completed, only if the instance itself finished (or only archive steps are left) | . | archive | move a completed or scrapped work item into the archive, only once the instance finished | . claim is drawn only in Process_BeanOpen, and resolve and archive only in Process_BeanClose; every process that works on a work item calls both (check:bean-calls). note is drawn where the work happens. resolve is the careful one. A work item is never closed on somebody else’s judgement, so it does not fire on the caller’s say-so: the work item completes only when the instance tracking it has completed, which is a fact derived from the process rather than asserted by the agent calling it. A still-running instance gets a note. An op the build does not implement fails at process load. A step that says it resolves a work item and quietly does nothing is exactly the divergence the extension exists to close.

5252.title: What state does NOT buy you
5252.content: Ordering is not quality. A completed instance means the gates ran in order and a person saw the findings. Whether the content is correct is what the QA axes, the build and the validators are for. A green process must never be read as a reviewed artefact, and any dashboard built on this has to say so. A position is not a claim. An instance at Task_Commit says the token arrived, not that the commit is good.

5253.title: Where running instances live — the state graph on the branch store
5253.content: Running instances are part of the work-plan store (workflow-state graph typology; positions in work-plan-store). Where the deployment uses the git state-branch Tool, the store is mounted and pushed as described in work-plan-store-git-branch. The container is ephemeral and a work plan only one agent can see is not a work plan. Instance state lives in the shared work-plan store for the same reason work item definitions do: a sibling session, or the same session resumed in a fresh container, reads the store to find the position that exists rather than starting a second one beside it. When an instance advances, its state is written through the store’s Tool (bun run cat state:push when backed by the git state branch). This keeps instance state globally visible without cluttering code PR diffs on main. Instance ids are derived from the subject rather than random, so re-entering a step finds the instance that is already there: beans create is not idempotent and dedupes on nothing, so an id you can recompute is what prevents duplicates.

5254.title: Reading the state you did not write
5254.content: Before acting on an instance you did not start, ask what it is waiting on. A work item’s status defaults to non-blocking; a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff — because a block with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work. bean-blocking carries that, and bean-coordination carries the rule that a claim announces rather than reserves until your PR exists.
